...unmistakable evidence of musical criticism. Certain men are generally acknowledged to be "good singers," and certain songs are said to be "good songs." This implies that the songs and the singers satisfy some standard of evaluation. The Indian may not be able to formulate this standard, but its existence is evidence of an aesthetic impulse.

We may note at this time a few observations on this subject, opening it for further investigation. First, in the matter of composition, it is observed that the oldest songs—which are considered the best—were "composed in dreams." This means that they came in a supposedly supernatural manner to the mind of a man who was hoping for such experiences and who had established the mental and physical conditions under which they were believed to occur. In this, we have the native concept of what we call "inspiration." The Indian isolated himself by going away from the camp, while the white musician or poet locks his door, but both realize the necessity of freedom from distraction. A majority of the songs said to have been received this way by the Indians have a rhythmic and melodic unity which is not always present in songs said to have been "made up." Thus, the writer once heard a song which was said to have been recently composed, and on inquiry learned that several men had "composed it together." This was evidenced by a lack of unity in the melody, which contained too many peculiarities. The form of the melody suggested the possibility that each man had incorporated in it a favorite interval or some other musical whim of his own. The result was a composite rather than a unit.

The comparative analyses in <note>Bureau of American Ethnology</note> Bulletin 53 (pp. 51–58) suggest a relation between a mental concept and the form of its musical expression. The significant prominence of the ascending and descending interval of a fourth in songs concerning motion was noted in Bulletin 53 (pp. 99–101) and is found also in songs of the present series. A comparison of the structure of the old songs with that of songs said to be somewhat modern shows that the more recent songs contain a smaller vocal range, a larger number of progressions, and a more regular rhythm. The latter tendency was shown by the following incident: In recording a Chippewa song from an old Indian, the writer found the rhythm peculiar, with frequent changes of measure lengths; later, the same song was recorded by a young man, said to be an excellent singer. On comparing the phonograph records, it was found that the younger singer had slightly changed the rhythm so as to avoid the irregularity in the measure lengths. The song had lost its native character and also its musical interest.

The various occasions for music which exist among civilized races are found also among the Indians. It is a custom that songs connected with ceremonial acts shall be sung only by those who have

<header>BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61</header>

The singers received these songs in dreams, or they inherited or purchased the right to sing them. Such songs form one category of Indian music. Another category includes songs for games and dances, songs of war and hunting, and songs that celebrate the deeds of a chief or a successful warrior. Although the lyrics of all these songs often show a high degree of poetic feeling, they appear to be less subjective in character than the lyrics of similar English songs. It is difficult to determine which Indian songs correspond to the folk songs of the white race, but such a group should probably include songs connected with folk tales. These are numerous and are usually represented as being sung by animals. An example of this is the story and song of the crawfish <note>Bulletin 53, page 305</note>. Songs of this class are found to vary more than any others when performed by different people; this is perhaps because they were more generally known and sung than others, with less concern for the correctness of the performance.

Among musicians of modern societies, the standards of excellence for a singer include (1) intonation, (2) tone quality, (3) vocal range, (4) memory, and (5) interpretation (both intellectual and emotional).

(1) *Intonation.*—In observing Indian singers according to these standards, the author has noticed that "good singers" keep their pitch approximately to the tones of the diatonic scale, and that in songs recorded by such men and women, the pitch of "accidentals" is practically the same in every rendition of the song. This is not the case in songs recorded on the phonograph by men whose musical standing among their own people is not as high. One instance of this is as follows: during the transcription of a song recorded by an old man, it was found that the melody showed no sense of a keynote. Inquiry among the Indians revealed that the man was not considered a good singer by his people. Consequently, the same song was obtained from a man of recognized musical proficiency. Upon comparing the performances, it was found that through slight alterations in pitch, the song had become diatonic in character, with intervals closely resembling those of the scale and ending on a keynote. Experience in listening to the melodies of the Chippewa and Sioux makes it possible to distinguish between a melody that has unusual native peculiarities and one that is simply distorted by a poor singer.

The accuracy of an Indian in repeating a song should also be considered. For this purpose, several consecutive repetitions of each song were recorded. As evidence of accuracy in repeating ceremonial songs, the following incident may be cited: In 1912, the author recorded four songs of the Mandan Creek Women's society from Mrs. Holding Eagle, one of its members. In 1915, Mrs. Holding Eagle recorded the songs a second time, and upon comparison, it was found that the pitch and metronome speed of all the songs were the same.

In two of the songs, there was no difference whatsoever; in one, what appeared to be a glissando progression in the first recording was sung in definite intervals in the second; and in the fourth song, there was a slight difference in the opening measures but none in the part containing the words. Several consecutive performances of the songs were recorded on both occasions. Another similar instance occurred among the Chippewa. Ŏdjib'we <note>See Bulletin 53</note> recorded certain songs in August 1909 and March 1910; the two recordings showed the same pitch for the song as a whole, as well as a slight deviation from diatonic pitch on the same tones—a deviation that was perceptible but not significant enough to be indicated by an accidental.

See also the analysis of song No. 209 in this volume.

(2) *Quality of tone.*—The Indian's manner of tone production is different from that of white people. The former cultivates and greatly admires a pronounced vibrato; a falsetto tone is also considered a sign of musical proficiency. An instance of this is mentioned in Bulletin 53 <note>p. 252</note>: A singer at Red Lake, Minnesota, “sang in a falsetto voice with a peculiar throaty vibrato. He said that he discovered his ability to do this when he was a boy and had cultivated it ever since.” This vibrato is not always found in a good singer, but, as with the white race, it is frequently present. A peculiar nasal tone is always used in the love songs, so that anyone accustomed to the music of these tribes can recognize these songs by the tone quality, as well as by a melodic freedom greater than that found in other songs. Another quality of tone is that used in songs of hopeless illness, or in the “wailing songs” following a death. To these may be added the crooning tone of lullabies. Other tone qualities are undoubtedly and perhaps intentionally used, though these are the most easily recognized.

(3) *Compass of voice.*—An expanded vocal range is admired among the Chippewa and Sioux, as well as among white musicians. Songs No. 55, 195, and 202 each have a range of 17 tones; two of these were recorded by Kills-at-Night, who has a wide reputation as a singer. Other songs have a range of 13 or 14 tones each.

(4) *Memory.*—The test of memory (the “repertoire”) is found among these Indians just as it is among civilized musicians. The author has never attempted to exhaust the number of songs a good singer could record. The largest number of songs recorded by one individual are those of Ŏdjib'we in Bulletin 53. Since he was recording songs known to no one else, he was asked to record more than 80. These songs were practically all of the same class; he undoubtedly remembered many others of different kinds. Recording 50 or 60 songs by one individual is not unusual in the present work, with selections being made from this number after transcription—

description, and many records being used for comparison with records of the same song by other singers.

(5) *Interpretation (intellectual and emotional).*—Among these Indians, as among white musicians, there must be a convincing quality in a singer's performance of a song. It has frequently been said to the writer, "So-and-so knows the old songs, but he is not a good singer; he can give you the melody, but it will not be well sung." Into this "convincing quality" enters another element—the personality of the singer. It is required that a good singer among Indians, as well as among white people, shall carry full confidence in himself and perform his work with authority.

From the data provided, it appears that in general character, the musical standards of the Chippewa and Sioux Indians bear a resemblance to those of the white race.

# CEREMONIES

## THE WHITE BUFFALO CALF PIPE (PTEHIN'ĆALA ĆANON'PA)

It is appropriate that a narrative of the gift of the White Buffalo Calf pipe to the Sioux should introduce this account of the ceremonies and customs of the tribe. Throughout this memoir, reference will be made to ceremonial acts performed according to the instructions of the White Buffalo Maiden, a supernatural being through whose intervention the ceremonial pipe was given to the Sioux.<note>1 Regarding this chapter, see Fletcher, Alice C., *The White Buffalo Festival of the Uncpapas*, Peabody Museum Reports, III, Nos. 3 and 4, pp. 260-75, Cambridge, 1884.</note>

The narrative in its present form was provided by Íšna'la-wića' (Lone Man; see pl. 23), and is recorded in the words of the interpreter, Mr. Robert P. Higheagle. Before this narration by Lone Man, the subject had been studied with other informants for more than two years. A summary of this study was read to Lone Man and discussed with him, after which he was requested to give the narrative in a connected form, including the material he wished to add.<note>2 Additional material obtained from Lone Man can be found in the chapters on the Sun dance (p. 92), the heyo'ka (pp. 159-170), and the sacred stones (pp. 214-217).</note>

The ancient and sacred tradition of the Sioux was given by Lone Man as follows:

In the old times, it was a general custom for the Sioux tribe (especially the Teton band of Sioux) to assemble as a group at least once during the year. This gathering usually took place around midsummer, when everything looked beautiful and everyone rejoiced to see nature at its best—that was the season when the Sun-dance ceremony took place and vows were made and fulfilled. Sometimes the tribal gathering took place in the fall, when wild game was in the best condition, when all kinds of wild fruits were ripe, and when the leaves on the trees and plants were at their brightest.

One reason why the people gathered as they did was so that the tribe as a whole might celebrate victories, successes on the warpath, and other good fortunes that had occurred during the year while the bands were scattered and each band was acting somewhat independently. Another reason was that certain rules or laws were made by the head chiefs and other leaders of the tribe, by which each band of the tribe was governed. For instance, if a certain band got into trouble with another tribe, such as the Crows, the Sioux tribe as a whole should be notified. Or, if an enemy or enemies entered their hunting grounds, the tribe should be notified at once. In this way, the Teton band of Sioux was protected regarding its territory and its hunting grounds.

After these gatherings, the various bands would scatter. On one such occasion, the Sans Arc band started toward the west. They were moving from place to place, expecting to find buffalo and other game to store for their winter supply, but they failed to find anything. A council was called, and two young men were selected to go in search of buffalo and other game. They started on foot. When they were out of sight, they each went in a different direction but met again at a place they had agreed upon. While they were planning and planning

what to do, there appeared from the West a solitary object advancing toward them. It did not look like a buffalo; it looked more like a human being than anything else. They could not determine what it was, but it was coming rapidly. Both considered themselves brave, so they decided that they would face whatever it might be. They stood still and watched it very eagerly. At last, they saw that it was a beautiful young Maiden. She wore a beautiful fringed buckskin dress, leggings, and moccasins. Her hair hung loose except on the left side, where a tuft of shed buffalo hair was tied. <note>See pp. 126, 458.</note> In her right hand, she carried a fan made of flat sage. Her face was painted with red vertical stripes. Not knowing what to do or say, they hesitated and said nothing to her.

She spoke first, saying: “I am sent by the Buffalo tribe to visit the people you represent. You have been chosen to perform a difficult task. It is right that you should try to carry out the wishes of your people, and you must try to accomplish your purpose. Go home and tell the chief and headmen to put up a special lodge in the middle of the camp circle, with the door of the lodge and the entrance into the camp facing the direction where the sun rolls off the earth. Let them spread sage at the place of honor, and behind the fireplace, let a small square place<gloss>1</gloss> be prepared. Behind this and the sage, let a certain frame, or rack, be made. Right in front of the rack, a buffalo skull should be placed. I have something of importance to present to the tribe, which will have a great deal to do with their future welfare. I shall be in the camp about sunrise.”

While she was speaking to the young men, one of them had impure thoughts. A cloud came down and enveloped this young man. When the cloud left the earth, the young man was left there—only a skeleton. The Maiden commanded the other young man to turn his back toward her and face the direction of the camp, then to start for home. He was ordered not to look back.

When the young man came in sight of the camp, he ran in a zigzag course; this was a signal required of such parties when returning home from a searching or scouting expedition. The people in the camp were on the alert for the signal, and preparations began at once to escort the party home. Just outside the council lodge, in front of the door, an old man qualified to perform the ceremony was waiting anxiously for the party. He knelt in the direction of the party’s approach to receive the report of the expedition. <note>See p. 441.</note> A row of old men were kneeling behind him. The young man arrived at the lodge. The people showed great curiosity because of the missing member of the party. The report was made, and the people received it with enthusiasm.

The special lodge was made, and the other requirements were carried out. The crier announced to the whole camp what was to take place the following morning. Great preparations were made for the occasion. Early the next morning, at daybreak, men, women, and children assembled around the special lodge. Young men who were known to have unblemished characters were chosen to escort the Maiden into the camp. <note>See pp. 72, 103, 111.</note> Promptly at sunrise, she was in sight. Everybody was anxious. All eyes were fixed on the Maiden. Slowly, she walked into the camp. She was dressed as when she first appeared to the two young men, except that instead of the sage fan, she carried a pipe—the stem was carried with her right hand and the bowl with her left.

The chief, who was qualified and authorized to receive the guest on behalf of the Sioux tribe, sat outside, right in front of the door of the lodge, facing the direction from which the Maiden was coming. When she reached the door, the chief stepped aside and made room for her to enter. She entered the lodge, went to the left of the door, and was seated at the place of honor.

The chief made a speech welcoming the Maiden, as follows:
“My dear relatives: Today Wakan'taŋka has again looked down and smiled upon us by sending us this young Maiden, whom we shall recognize and consider as a sister. She has come to our rescue just when we are in great need. Wakan'taŋka wants us to live. Today we lift up our eyes to the sun, the giver of light, who opens our eyes and gives us this beautiful day to see our visiting sister. Sister, we are glad that you have come to us, and we trust that we may be able to abide by whatever message you have brought. We are poor, but we have great respect for visitors, especially relatives. It is our custom to serve our guests special food. We are currently in need, and all we have to offer you is water that falls from the clouds. Take it, drink it, and remember that we are very poor.”

Then braided sweetgrass was dipped into a buffalo horn containing rainwater and was offered to the Maiden. The chief said, “Sister, we are now ready to hear the good message you have brought.” The pipe, which was in the hands of the Maiden, was lowered and placed on the rack. Then the Maiden sipped the water from the sweetgrass.

Then, taking up the pipe again, she arose and said:
“My relatives, brothers and sisters: Wakan'taŋka has looked down and smiles upon us today because we have met as members of one family. The best thing in a family is good feeling toward every member. I am proud to become a member of your family—a sister to you all. The sun is your grandfather, and he is the same to me. Your tribe has the distinction of always being very faithful to promises and of possessing great respect and reverence for sacred things. It is also known that only good feeling prevails in the tribe, and that whenever any member has been found guilty of committing any wrong, that member has been cast out and not allowed to mingle with the other members of the tribe. Because of all these good qualities in the tribe, you have been chosen as worthy and deserving of all good gifts. I represent the Buffalo tribe, who have sent you this pipe. You are to receive this pipe in the name of all the common people <note>Indians</note>. Take it, and use it according to my directions. The bowl of the pipe is red stone—a stone that is not very common and is found only at a certain place. This pipe shall be used as a peacemaker.<sup>1</sup> The time will come when you shall stop hostilities against other nations. Whenever peace is agreed upon between two tribes or parties, this pipe shall be a binding instrument. By this pipe, the medicine men shall be called to provide help to the sick.”

Turning to the women, she said:
“My dear sisters, the women: You have a hard life to live in this world, yet without you, this life would not be what it is. Wakan'taŋka intends for you to bear much sorrow—and to comfort others in their time of sorrow. By your hands, the family moves. You have been given the knowledge of making clothing and of feeding the family. Wakan'taŋka is with you in your sorrows and joins you in your griefs. He has given you the great gift of kindness toward every living creature on earth. He has chosen you to feel for the dead who are gone. He knows that you remember the dead longer than the men do. He knows that you love your children dearly.”

Then turning to the children:
“My little brothers and sisters: Your parents were once little children like you, but in time they became men and women. All living creatures were once small, but if no one took care of them, they would never grow up. Your parents love you and have made many sacrifices for your sake so that Wakan'taŋka may listen to them, and so that only good may come to you as you grow up. I have brought this pipe for them, and you shall benefit from it. Learn to

Turning to the men:
> "Now, my dear brothers: In giving you this pipe, you are expected to use it for nothing but good purposes. The tribe as a whole shall depend upon it for their necessary needs. You realize that all your necessities of life come from the earth below, the sky above, and the four winds. Whenever you do anything wrong against these elements, they will always take revenge upon you. You should revere them. Offer sacrifices through this pipe. Then she took the buffalo chip which lay on the ground, lit the pipe, and pointing to the sky with the stem of the pipe, she said, "I offer this to Wakaŋ'taŋka for all the good that comes from above." (Pointing to the earth:) "I offer this to the earth, from which all good gifts come." (Pointing to the cardinal points:) "I offer this to the four winds, from which all good things come." Then she took a puff from the pipe, passed it to the chief, and said, "Now, my dear brothers and sisters, I have done the work for which I was sent here, and now I will go; but I do not wish for an escort. I only ask that the way be cleared before me."

Then, rising, she started to leave, leaving the pipe with the chief, who ordered that the people be quiet until their sister was out of sight. She came out of the tent on the left side, walking very slowly; as soon as she was outside the entrance, she turned into a white buffalo calf.<sup>1</sup>

It is said that the chief who received the pipe from the White Buffalo Maiden was Buffalo Stands Upward (*Tataŋ'ka-woslal'-nažiŋ*). The pipe has been handed down from one generation to another, and is said to be now in the possession of Elk Head (*Heha'ka-pa*), who lives at Thunder Butte, on the Cheyenne River Reservation. He is said to be of "about the third generation" to have kept the pipe, and is 98 years of age.<sup>2</sup> Each preceding keeper of the pipe lived to be more than a hundred years old.

The Indians named the pipe the White Buffalo Calf pipe. Duplicates of it were made, and soon every male member of the tribe carried a similar pipe. The stem was made to resemble the wind-pipe of a calf. Whenever this pipe is used in a smoking circle, or even when two men are smoking together, the rule is that the pipe

*Analysis.*³—This song is minor in tonality and melodic in structure. Thirty-four progressions are found in the melody, 22 (65 percent) of which are minor thirds. This is an unusually large proportion of any one interval in a song. Ten of the remaining intervals (29 percent) are major seconds, while the others are an ascending fifth and a descending fourth. The tempo of the song is slow, and the short tones at the end of the first and similar measures were performed in correct time. As in all the songs, vocables are italicized here. In this song, they were sung with marked emphasis.
The final measure of this song is transcribed as a complete measure, even though the song begins on an unaccented tone. This precedent will be followed throughout this work; instances where the repetition of a song begins without a break in the time are indicated by the usual symbol for repeat.

## THE ALO'WANPI CEREMONY

This ceremony has been used by the Pawnee, Omaha, Osage, Ponca, Iowa, Oto, and Dakota tribes. The ceremony among the Omaha and Pawnee has been studied by Miss Alice C. Fletcher, whose research includes the ceremonial songs of these tribes.⁴ Since the ceremony has not been used among the Dakota for many years, it was impossible to study it exhaustively, but enough information was available for a general comparison with the customs of the tribes mentioned above. From this comparison, it is evident that the

The ceremony, in its transmission to other tribes and localities, has undergone modifications and changes in detail.

Among the Teton Sioux, the ceremony is known as *Alo'waŋpi*, meaning "to sing for someone," and also as the *Hunka*, this being the name applied to the child who fills an important role in the ceremony.

Among the Sioux, this ceremony was closely associated with the White Buffalo Maiden and her mysterious visit to the tribe. The following account concerns the usage of the Teton Sioux. The subject was studied by the author during two visits to the reservation, and Mr. Higheagle continued the work for several months, consulting the older Indians as he had opportunity. The material includes the original narrative by Weasel Bear and also many points contributed by Chased-by-Bears, Eagle Shield, White-paw Bear, Jaw, and others

who were qualified to express opinions on the subject. The account in its final form was translated for, and pronounced correct by, Weasel Bear and others who were equally well-informed.

In a picture-calendar of the Teton Sioux, there is a native drawing of this ceremony (fig. 20). The year represented by the drawing is called "*Awi'ća alo'waŋpi wani'yetu*," meaning literally "truthfully singing winter," understood as "ceremonial singing winter." This is the first year recorded on this calendar, and the author's informant said it represented the first year in which the *Alo'waŋpi* ceremony was held by the Standing Rock Sioux. The date corresponds to the year 1801. The calendar, which is owned by Black Thunder of Eagle River, closes with a representation of the Black Hills council which took place in 1912. The dates of other historical events are correctly indicated.

BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61]

In describing the purpose of the ceremony, Looking Elk (Heha'ka-wa'kita), a Teton Sioux, said:

The great result of this ceremony is that the man who performed it was regarded as a father by the child for whom he performed it. He made a solemn vow, taking that child under his protection until one or the other died. He became like a brother to the man whose children he sang over and painted with the <term>hunka</term> stripes. Among all the great ceremonies of the Sioux, there is not one that binds two men together as strongly as this.

The keynote, or central idea, of this ceremony (as held by the Teton Sioux) is the affection of a father for his child and his desire that only good should come to them. The following statement is given in the words of Mr. Higheagle:

The Sioux strictly believe and understand that a child is the greatest gift from <term>Wakan'tanka</term>, given in response to many devout prayers, sacrifices, and promises. Therefore, the child is considered "sent by <term>Wakan'tanka</term>" through an element—specifically, the human being. So that the child may grow up in health with all the expected virtues, and especially so that no serious misfortune happens to the child, the father makes promises or vows to <term>Wakan'tanka</term> as manifested by the different elements of the earth and sky. During the period of youthful blessedness, the father spared no pains to let the people know of his great love for his child or children. His fellow men measured this love according to the sacrifices or gifts he gave, or the number of ceremonies he performed. In order to have a standard by which this love could be shown, the first thing considered and adopted was the White Buffalo Maiden, sent to the Sioux tribe by the Buffalo tribe. The impression left upon the people by the Maiden and her extraordinary good qualities were things much admired by every parent as a model for their children. This Maiden was pure white, without a blemish—that was the father's principal desire for the character of his child. The Maiden addressed men, women, and children.

The Maiden had told them that good things would come to the people by means of the pipe, so it seemed necessary to have a ceremony connected with both the Maiden and the pipe. For this reason, the essential article in the <term>Alo'wanpi</term> ceremony is the "Hunka Ċanon'pa," a decorated wand that represents the pipe given to the Indians by the Maiden, as the original pipe was not available when needed for this ceremony. <note>1</note> This wand, or pipestem, was carried and employed by the <term>itan'ċan</term>, or "leader," <note>2</note> during the ceremony; when it was finished, the wand was given to the child for whom the ceremony had been performed. In many families, such a pipestem was handed down for many generations. The method of decorating the pipestem has also been passed down, and neither the shape nor the decoration can be changed. A new pipestem might be made by someone who had undergone the ceremony, but an old one was generally used. The wand, or pipestem, was usually about 20 inches long. On it were fastened tufts of the feathers of the <term>kank̇e'ċa</term>, or pileated woodpecker, and above each tuft of feathers was the head of

A woodpecker (*Phloeootomus pileatus*) was used in the decorations. <note>The decorations of the calumet more frequently consisted of the feathers or heads of the duck, owl, eagle, or other birds. See J. N. B. Hewitt, article *Calumet* in the Handbook of American Indians, part 1.</note> The tail feathers of an eagle, arranged in the shape of a fan, and strands of horsehair were also hung from the wand. [See plate 3.] <note>The pileated woodpecker is commonly called a woodcock, and, due to a misunderstanding, the bird heads shown in plate 3 are those of the common woodcock.</note>

In explaining the use of the woodpecker in decorating the <term>Huŋka Ćanoŋ'pa</term>, it was said that this is "a simple, humble bird that stays near its nest and is seldom seen." <note>Compare the following instances in which the characteristics of a bird or an animal were desired by the Indians who, in some cases, wore a part of the bird or animal on their persons: the deer (in a decoration), because this animal can endure thirst for a long time (page 125); the hawk as "the surest bird of prey" (page 139); the elk, in gallantry (page 176); the frog, in watchfulness (page 160); the owl, in "night-wisdom and gentle ways" (page 181); the bear, which "though fierce, has given many medicinal herbs for the good of man" (page 195); the kit-fox, which is "active and wily" (page 314); the crow, which is especially direct as well as swift in flight (page 319), and the wolf, in hardihood (page 388).</note> This bird seems to have been considered especially appropriate because children who underwent this ceremony were more closely guarded and protected than others. They usually belonged to well-to-do families, in which the girls were seldom seen in public until they were grown up. The ceremony could be held for several children at a time and often took place to fulfill a vow. <note>Compare the piercing of a child's ears at the Sun Dance in fulfillment of a similar vow (page 137).</note>

The parents' wish for this ceremony to be performed for their child or children was first declared. An invitation was then sent to the man whom the father desired to perform the ceremony; thereafter, that man would be bound to the father by a tie even stronger than natural brotherhood because he had assumed a responsibility not placed on him by nature. An invitation was usually delivered by means of a pipe, but for this ceremony, a different form of invitation was used. The father of the child made a case from the dried bladder of a buffalo, into which he put many small packages of tobacco, with one or two pipefuls wrapped in membrane, similar to the packets fastened to sticks as offerings at the <term>Sun Dance</term> (page 102). The case, after being tied or sealed, was wrapped in a cloth. This was taken to the man selected to perform the ceremony. If he accepted the invitation, he opened the case; otherwise, he returned it unopened.

Upon acceptance of the invitation, great preparations began. Two large lodges were erected in the middle of the camp circle and joined together to make one lodge of double the usual size, opening toward the west. This and the other details of the ceremony were in accordance with the instructions given by the <term>White Buffalo Maiden</term> during her first appearance to the Indians. The lodge was like the one they built to receive her. There was no fire within, but opposite the door and slightly behind the middle of the lodge, a square of exposed and "mellowed" earth was prepared. (See page 64, footnote.) In the two corners of this square farthest from the door

Two buffalo chips were placed there to be used in lighting the ceremonial pipes. Sweet grass was also prepared for lighting the pipes. Fresh sage was spread on the ground at the back of the square, and a buffalo skull was laid on it. This skull was painted with red lines, and its openings were filled with sage (see pages 64 and 185). The nose of the skull was near the side of the square but did not touch it. Strips of red flannel were tied to the horns. Behind the buffalo skull stood a pipe rack made of two upright sticks, each with a crotch at the top, with a crossbar laid between them; the entire rack was painted blue. This pipe rack was similar to the one used in the Sun Dance, but the position of the pipe (or wand) was reversed: in the Sun Dance, the pipe bowl rested against the forehead of the buffalo skull (as shown in plate 20), while the Hunka pipe was placed with its stem toward the skull. If more than one child was to be "sung over," there was a pipe for each one. Beneath each pipe was placed a white eagle plume to be tied to the child's head during the ceremony. The rattle to be used by the <term>itanʹćan</term> leaned against one of the posts of the pipe rack. Against the rack was also placed an ear of corn on a stick, decorated in blue as shown in plate 3. It was essential that this ear of corn be particularly regular in shape, with an even number of kernels arranged in straight lines.<sup>1</sup> Thus, the ceremonial items included the ear of corn, the decorated pipe (or wand), the pipe rack, the tuft of white down, and a clump of shed buffalo hair used in the ritual. These were provided by the man who performed the ceremony, who kept them wrapped in a red cloth. The preparation of the lodge was completed by erecting a barricade of hides around it, positioned to keep spectators at a proper distance.

<note><sup>1</sup> Articles for ceremonial use had to be as perfect as possible. Compare the choice of the buffalo skull and the tree for the sacred pole in the Sun Dance (pages 102, 111), as well as the axe used to cut the tree (page 112). The sacred stones were regular in shape and not shaped by any tool (page 205). Leaders in all ceremonies were required to live pure lives. See also the statement on page 173, in the footnote, that genuine items should be preferred over artificial ones.</note>

The Teton Sioux were not originally an agricultural people, and the use of corn in this ceremony prompted much inquiry. In response to these questions, the author was told the following legend of the arrival of corn, which is presented here in the words of the interpreter, Mr. Higheagle:

There was an old couple living on a riverbank. They had been married for a long time but had no children, even though they had often asked <term>Wakaŋʹtaŋka</term> to send them a child. This special request was always made when they were in the sweat-bath booth. On one of these occasions, while they were praying, they heard someone outside saying that their prayer had been heard and would be granted the next morning. They were very happy and felt quite anxious.

The next morning the old man went out, and there, right in front of the door, a greenish sprout of some seed peeped out of the ground. The old man was very excited. Not knowing what to do, they both went into the sweat-bath booth and asked for guidance. As before, they heard a voice—

saying: “Do not be afraid. This plant that you see is going to grow into the most beautiful child you have ever seen. Watch for its development. Take good care of it. In the past, this ceremony lasted for several days, and many ceremonial songs were sung. In later practices by the Teton Sioux, it is said that the entire ceremony was completed in a single day. Only two of the songs were recorded by the writer.

*Analysis.*—It is interesting to note how the rhythmic unit relates to the use of the song. As previously mentioned, this is a song of search; the singer moved around the camp pretending to look for a specific tent. He hurried to a tent, paused, and then moved on, repeating this process until he reached the tent that was his destination. Consequently, in the rhythmic unit, we find a hurried triplet of eighth notes, followed in the next measure by a note held for the length of four quarter notes. The song is simple in structure and has a range of eight notes, descending from the octave to the tonic. The notes belong to the second five-toned scale, and the tonic chord is prominent in the melody. One-third of the intervals are

minor thirds. Five performances were recorded with no break in timing; these are uniform in every respect.

When the man (or men) arrived at the door of the children’s home, they did not enter at once. Instead, they began to recount their past deeds as evidence of their right to perform the *Alo'waŋpi* ceremony. Without this narration, they would not be allowed to enter and collect the children, as no one could perform this sacred rite over children except those who had possessed the necessary qualifications in the past and still held them.

If the children were small, they were carried to the double lodge in blankets on the backs of the *itaŋ'ćan*. On their way to the lodge, the men stopped four times (see pages 78, 83, 113, 116, 167, and 328) and gave the "wolf howl," which was used to signal their approach. When they reached the double lodge, the *itaŋ'ćan* sat in the place of honor behind the pipe rack. There might be one man for each child who was to be "sung over," and each of these men had his own pipe, or wand, which was placed against the pipe rack.

Describing the performance of the ceremony for his two daughters, Weasel Bear said:

> Everyone could see the old man as he painted the girls' faces. He painted a blue line from the parting of the hair down to the end of the nose, then across the upper part of the forehead and down to the cheek, ending at a point opposite the end of the nose. Red stripes could be added after the blue paint had been applied to the face. These red stripes were narrow, extending downward from the line across the forehead and being the same length as the vertical blue lines. Additional red stripes could be added at any time by a person qualified to do so, with a horse being given for the right to wear two or three more stripes.

On many important occasions, this face decoration was used by those who had the right to use it. A white eagle plume was fastened in the hair of a girl whose face was to be painted. Plate 8 shows a spirit post decorated with the plume worn by Weasel Bear’s daughter in the *Alo'waŋpi* ceremony he described; the tip of the quill was covered with duck feathers similar to those used on a Sun-dance pipe. A strand of red-colored horsehair was fastened to the eagle plume, and the whole ornament was suspended by a narrow strip of hide so that it hung lightly.

Continuing his narrative, Weasel Bear said:

> After the girls' faces were painted, the *itaŋ'ćan* stood with his rattle in his right hand and the decorated wand in his left, waving the wand over them as he sang the following song. Each girl held a decorated ear of corn in her hand while the song was sung. <note>This scene is shown in a native drawing on cloth made by Jaw (plate 4).</note>

*Analysis.*—This song contains only the tones of the minor triad and fourth. Similar tone material is found in so many of these songs that it deserves special attention. A look at Table 6 shows that it makes up the tone material of 12 percent of the songs; this is the largest proportion except for that of the second five-tone scale (13 percent) and the fourth five-tone scale (18 percent). There are two ways in which this tone material may be viewed—as a minor triad with the fourth as a passing tone, or as a combination of tones leading toward the second five-tone scale. If the first is the correct perspective, we might expect a large proportion of songs containing either the minor triad alone or with some other tone used as a passing tone, but such songs are not found. We note only 1 percent containing the minor triad alone, and less than 1 percent with another tone as a passing tone. Looking at the matter from the second perspective, we note that the percentage of songs on the second five-tone scale is less than that of those on the fourth five-tone scale. It is observed, however, that the proportion of songs containing the major triad and sixth is 12 percent. This has the same relationship to the complete fourth five-tone scale that the minor triad and fourth have to the complete second five-tone scale. In this connection, see Bulletin 53, pages 4–5. Tests and comparisons similar to these are presented merely as suggestions for the practical use of the current method of analyzing Indian music.

Like the preceding song, this has a range of 12 tones, beginning on the octave and ending on the tonic. It is, however, harmonic in structure, while the preceding song is melodic. The proportion of minor thirds is larger than in the preceding song, making up about 39 percent of the intervals. As in the preceding song, the vocables were slightly emphasized, and the words of the many performances were clearly sung. Neither this nor the preceding song contains a change of meter. Only 23 percent of the 340 Chippewa songs are without a change of meter, and this consistency appears in only 16 percent of this series.

After the ceremony (which, as already stated, was not studied in detail by the writer), the decorated pipe (or wand) and the corn became the property of the child for whom the ceremony had been performed. As they left with the children, the *<term>Itaŋ'ćan</term>*, pausing four times, gave the long "wolf call" that had signaled their approach to the ceremonial lodge. Liberal rewards were given to those who performed this ceremony; Weasel Bear stated that he gave three horses and a pipe to the old man who painted and "sang over" his daughters.

The celebration of this ceremony placed a child in a highly respected position in the tribe. Such a child was seen as possessing that which would "make it nothing but good in every way," and was "recognized by all as ranking above an ordinary child."

A young girl for whom the <term>Alo'waŋpi</term> ceremony had been performed might wear a calfskin robe similar to the one shown in Plate 5. The decoration on this robe indicates that the wearer had participated in the <term>Huŋka</term> ceremony and that her relatives had been successful in war. Red, blue, and yellow are the colors used in the decorations. It was said that "red represents blood, blue is a 'blue cloud' indicating success, and yellow is the color of the sky at morning." <note>Other symbols mentioned in this work include: the white buffalo robe used in the <term>Huŋka</term> ceremony (p. 80); the colors red, blue, yellow, white, and black (p. 124); the rising smoke of sweetgrass (p. 127, footnote); a hoop (pp. 139, 295); water, fire, and steam (p. 167); the shape and structure of sacred stones described by Chased-by-Bears (p. 205) and by Brave Buffalo (p. 208); and a hand (p. 330). The symbolism of the "earth space" is explained on page 122 in a footnote.</note> The stripes on the head of the calfskin are red and represent the <term>Huŋka</term> stripes painted on the face of the child for whom the ceremony was held. The two lines bordering the entire decoration are blue, and the space between them is yellow. Near the left margin are red lines, said to represent a spider's web. The crescents along the right margin represent the phases of the moon, with blue used to represent a quarter moon and red representing a full moon. These are the phases during which the child's relative engaged in the war expeditions recorded in the robe's decoration. Next to this border are parallel lines; the dots on these lines represent the number of camps made during a specific expedition. The panel in the center of the robe represents the "warrior's path." A war party with eight camps is shown here, with each round dot representing a camp. Such a robe could be made only by a woman whose relative had been successful in war. The robe illustrated was made by the wife of Dog Eagle. (See p. 349.)

## THE CEREMONY OF SPIRIT-KEEPING <note>Regarding this subject, see Fletcher, Alice C., "The Shadow or Ghost Lodge: A Ceremony of the Ogallala Sioux," in *Peabody Museum Reports*, volume III, numbers 3 and 4, pages 296–307; see also Dorsey, James Owen, "A Study of Siouan Cults," in the *Eleventh Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*, pages 487–489, 1894.</note> (<term>WAKI'ĆAGAPI</term>)

In the past, a Sioux person filled with grief at the death of a near relative might prolong their period of mourning by "keeping the spirit" for several months or a year, and then "letting it go" through a specific ceremony. This was a demanding custom that, once begun, had to be carried out consistently, either by the person who undertook it or, in the event of their death, by their nearest relative. A man considered this carefully before announcing his intention of "keeping the spirit" of a relative. He weighed the fact that for many months he could not hunt, go to war, or participate in the social activities of the tribe; he also calculated the cost of the gifts he would have to distribute at the feast for releasing the spirit. If he felt he could meet these requirements, he made his decision known. Those who wished to join him were free to do so, with each person providing a "spirit bundle" (<term>wana'ġi wapa'hta</term>).

to represent the spirit of a relative, and also his share of food and gifts for the final feast.

The Ceremony of Spirit-keeping, like the <term>Alo'waŋpi</term>, was inspired by the Coming of the White Buffalo Maiden, and everything was done in accordance with her instructions. The method of studying this subject was similar to that used in connection with the two preceding chapters. The spirit of a child was "kept" more frequently than that of an adult, and the author's first work on this ceremony consisted of taking down a narrative by Weasel Bear (interpreted by Mrs. McLaughlin), in which he told of keeping the spirit of a little daughter. A year later, this narrative was discussed by Bear Face<note>1 Bear Face died in December 1914.</note> and other old men (with Mr. Higheagle interpreting), and many points were added. In its final form, the first part is based on a narrative by Bear Face, while the latter part incorporates information supplied by Weasel Bear, together with details supplied by other reliable informants.

Concerning this ceremony, Bear Face (<term>Mato'-ite'</term>) said:

> It is one of the great undertakings of the tribe, not simply for the honor which surrounds it, but because of the work and obligation it involves, so that a man who can carry this through successfully is recognized by the tribe as a man who is qualified to fulfill large responsibilities.

Bear Face said that his first spirit-keeping was for a son who died at the age of 15. The body of the boy was placed on a scaffold, and his best horse was killed beneath it. Before this was done, the father decided to keep the boy's spirit and so announced it to the tribe. He requested a man whose record was without blemish to cut a lock of the boy's hair to be put in the spirit bundle. The man came at his request, and before going near the body of the boy, he purified his hands and also his knife with the smoke of sweetgrass. When about to cut the hair, he made three motions as if to do so and then cut it with the fourth motion. (See references on p. 74.) The lock cut was from over one eye. When the hair had been cut, it was wrapped in red cloth. (The remainder of the narrative is a compilation from several informants.) If desired, some article which had been worn next to the body of the child could be used instead of a lock of hair. Thus, Weasel Bear said that when keeping the spirit of his little girl, he used the ornaments which she had worn on her hair as the central article in the spirit bundle.

After wrapping this selected article in red cloth, the proposed spirit-keeper took the little packet in his arms as if it were the body of a child and rode around the camp circle, lamenting the child's death. This was his announcement to the tribe that he had taken upon himself the responsibilities of a spirit-keeper (<term>wana'ġi yuha'pi</term>) and wished to be considered as such. ...brought, and in this was placed the packet containing the hair, as well as sweet grass and the shed hair of the buffalo. This case was wrapped in red cloth. The spirit-keeper or his friends then selected the straightest pole they could find, with pine being preferred for the purpose. This pole was erected outside his door, and the spirit bundle was tied to it. The bundle was supposed to stay there for four days and nights before being taken down. During these four days, a special wrapping (<term>wi'ćaśke</term>) of soft-tanned hide was made for it, and feasts were given to those who had previously kept spirits. At the end of four days, the bundle was taken down by men who had kept spirits and was placed in its wrapping, which was elaborately decorated but had no sewing on it. Along with it were placed articles intended as gifts for those who took part in the ceremony. Small articles were placed in a decorated case, and large articles, such as pieces of red cloth, were folded smoothly.

Plate 6 shows a "spirit wrap" and a braid of sweet grass which was placed in the spirit bundle. Mrs. James McLaughlin said she "purchased it 30 years ago from Black Moon's mother, who said it was then about 80 years old and had been used in keeping the spirits of her grandfather, her mother, and other relatives." The porcupine quills on it were dyed with native dyes, and the wrap is so fragile that it had been used in recent years as an inner instead of an outer wrapping. A braid of sweet grass was usually placed in a spirit bundle, and an old one had been preserved with this wrapping. According to Mrs. McLaughlin, beads were seldom used on any of the wrappings of a spirit bundle, as beads were unknown among the Sioux when the White Buffalo Maiden came to them.

After the spirit bundle was complete, they prepared three stakes, painted red and decorated with quillwork, along with decorated thongs with which to fasten the bundle in place. Two of the stakes were tied together near the top, and the bundle was tied across them, with the third stake being used as a support for the other two, which faced the door of the spirit-keeper's tipi. The tripod was about 6 steps from this tipi, which was known as <term>wana'gi ti'pi</term>, or "spirit lodge."

When the tripod had been put in place, they made a decorated case (<term>paŋ</term>) of soft-tanned hide. In it were put gifts for the <term>itaŋ'ćaŋ</term> who would have charge of the final ceremony. These gifts, which were gradually collected, comprised needles, awls, knives, tobacco, and sometimes as many as 50 pipes. In the tipi, between the fire and the place of honor, a certain area of the earth floor was "mellowed." This was round, not square as in the <term>Hunka</term> and the Sun dance. In the center of this space was placed a buffalo chip, and beside it two implements (plate 7) made of wood, about 3 feet in length; one was broad at the end and the other was pointed. When sweet grass was to be burned, it was the custom to use the pointed stick in pushing a

<meta>This page continues the detailed description of the Spirit-keeping ceremony, specifically focusing on the daily conduct of the spirit-keepers, the ritual movement of the spirit bundle, and the specific protocols regarding sacred items like the white buffalo robe and communal property within the lodge.</meta>

<page-num>80</page-num>
<header>BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61</header>

The coal was placed on the other tool, which was used to lift it and lay it on the buffalo chip. The spirit-keeper and his wife wore no ornaments during this period, and their faces were painted at all times. Their behavior was always quiet and reverent, as if the body of the relative they mourned were present in the lodge. It was expected that those who kept a spirit would maintain charitable thoughts toward everyone in the tribe, and all unkind or harsh words were forbidden inside the spirit lodge.

The tripod and spirit bundle were brought into the lodge at night and also during bad weather. The bundle was placed in the position of honor and treated with great respect; no one was allowed to pass between it and the fire. Weasel Bear said: "In the evening, I burned sweet grass, and my wife passed her hands through the smoke, rubbing the fragrance onto her face, hair, hands, and neck. Then she took the tripod in her arms and carried it into the tipi, turning toward the left as she entered. In the morning, she again made herself fragrant and carried the tripod and its burden outside the lodge."

The thing most desired was for a man to have a white buffalo robe to spread in the place of honor. On this robe, the tripod and spirit bundle would rest when they were inside the lodge. Such a robe signified that the spirit being kept was pure and that all the articles connected with it had been purified. No one was allowed to touch the robe with bare hands or pass between it and the fire. The only person permitted to touch it was a medicine man known to be qualified for the task. Bear Face said that he had such a robe when he kept the spirit of his son, and the only person allowed to touch or move it was a man he hired who was noted for this ceremony. If that man needed help, he was required to call on someone as fully qualified as himself and give him half of the compensation for those services. The only exception was in favor of children who had been through the <term>Hunka</term> ceremony. These children could lift the white buffalo robe and carry it out of the lodge when the ceremony was finished.

Weasel Bear said further that during the period of keeping a spirit, the contents of his lodge were supposed to belong to the tribe. Thus, if a man came to his lodge saying, "I have come for some of my tobacco and red willow," he gave him what he required. Weasel Bear continued his narrative as follows:

> I selected a virtuous old man as one of the officers of the spirit lodge. He was called *waśpaŋ'ka ikpe'ya itaŋ'ćaŋ*, meaning "leader in charge of food." He came to the tipi for a short time every day, and if he wished to sleep there at night, he was at liberty to do so. Every morning, I put beef in a dish; he took a small piece of the meat, offered a prayer, and put it in a small dish provided for 그 purpose. This duty was never omitted. When the dish was full, he emptied it into the fire, saying, "Grandchild, this is our food, but we give it to you to eat before us." This continued from early winter, when my child died, until the next autumn, when we

...released her spirit. During that time, we collected many gifts for the final feast. Our relatives helped us with this, and the women made many items with their own hands. Because I was kept from the ordinary duties of life, I had a man called *wo' waśi itaŋ'ćaŋ* (literally "laborer leader") who carried messages for me, kept us supplied with wood and water, swept the lodge, and kept the area around the spirit bundle clean. He also cut and dried red willow <term>ćaŋsa'sa</term> so that I would have plenty to give away at the final feast.

The man who kept a spirit was frequently invited to feasts held by various societies and was expected to attend them. It was understood that if valuable presents were being given away, he would be the first to receive one. In return for these favors, he invited the societies to attend the feasts held outside the lodge when the time came to release the spirit. The length of time for keeping a spirit varied from several months to a year or even longer. At the end of this time, the final ceremony and feast were held. This was called <term>waki' ćaġa</term>, meaning the act of completing the undertaking. The entire band gathered for the event, and the various societies had their own special tents. The societies played a prominent role in the parts of the spirit-releasing ceremony that took place outside the lodge, but their members did not enter the lodge unless they were men who had kept spirits themselves.

If several spirits were to be released, the man who first announced his intention of keeping a spirit was considered the leader of the spirit-keepers. Early in the morning on the day the spirit was released, he sent a filled pipe to an old man who was to be the master of the entire ceremony and who was designated as the <term>a'taya itaŋ'ćaŋ</term>.

> Weasel Bear said: "On that day, I was to lay aside all signs of mourning, so I painted myself brightly and put on all my finest attire. I was only 28 years old, but I had won a war-honor feather, and I wore it that day. My wife dressed herself like a young girl." <note>See the reference to the bright adornments in the Ceremony of Restoring the Mourners in Bulletin 53, page 153.</note>

One man was selected for each spirit; he was known simply as an <term>itaŋ'ćaŋ</term>,<note>See page 70, footnote.</note> and he was a man who had previously kept the spirit of a relative. It was his duty to prepare the "spirit post" (<term>wana'ġi gele'pi</term>) and to perform other parts of the ceremony related to the individual spirit he had been employed to serve. The spirit post was crafted inside the spirit lodge. According to Weasel Bear, cottonwood was generally used for this purpose <note>compare pages 111 and 118</note>, and the man who made it always sat facing east and whittled upward, moving the knife away from himself. Before doing this, he purified his hands and knife with the smoke of sweetgrass. A spirit post for a child was smaller than one for an adult. The post represented the one used when the spirit of his little girl was released. The facial features are worked with beads on buckskin, and the paint lines are those that would be used for a girl who had gone through the <term>Alo'waŋpi</term> ceremony. The feather is the one worn by Weasel Bear's daughter when she was "sung over" in that ceremony. Both the lines and the feather belonged to a daughter who was somewhat older than the one whose spirit he kept. When the features had been depicted on the posts, each <term>itaŋ'ćaŋ</term> opened the case (<term>paŋ</term>) containing the articles of clothing to be placed on the posts. These garments, which had been previously displayed outside the lodge, were items worn by the person whose spirit was to be released. After the ceremony, these garments were given to the man who painted the post.

After the dressing of the posts, the woman in charge of the cooking brought food; she placed a plate of it in front of each spirit post after purifying the food in the smoke of sweet grass. Taking a round piece of pounded meat, each <term>itaŋ'ćaŋ</term> held it to the painted mouth on a spirit post. At this time, any orphan in need of help might appear and ask, in the name of the spirit to be released, to be fed and cared for. Such a request was never refused. Any others in need of help might also make an appeal at this time, as four opportunities were given during the "feeding of the spirits."

When this was finished within the spirit lodge, there was a distribution of gifts to the people in the camp. These gifts had been collected by the family of the spirit-keeper and had already been shown to the people. Weasel Bear said that his wife set up frames for this purpose, laying poles across forked stakes and hanging belts, moccasins, leggings, and other articles on the poles. At this time, the spirit-keeper sent gifts to the societies that maintained order in the camp. A gift to a society was said to be roughly equal in value to the gifts the spirit-keeper had received from that society, and it was something that could be divided among the members. Thus, Weasel Bear said that he gave a war bonnet to the <term>Tokala</term> society, and the feathers were distributed among the men. There was much feasting in the camp, and this was an occasion on which prominent families publicly announced the names they had given their children, or had their children's ears pierced in the same manner as at the Sun Dance. (See p. 137.)

The ceremony within the lodge was not studied in detail. Only former spirit-keepers were allowed to enter, and the man selected as the <term>a'taya itaŋ'ćaŋ</term> was "prepared with proper songs and prayers and was also qualified to offer lamentations for the dead."

If a white buffalo robe were used, song No. 1 was sung. Mention has been made of a filled pipe placed beside the round space of mellowed earth in the spirit lodge. A man was appointed to light this

He did not do this directly; instead, lowering the grass a short distance, he paused for a moment; then lowering it farther, he paused again, making four downward motions, after which he moved it four times in a circle, "with the sun," and placed it on the buffalo chip. The <term>a'taya itaŋ'ćaŋ</term> held the pipe in the rising smoke and repeated the words which the White Buffalo Maiden said to the Sioux when she appeared to them. <note>This ceremonial speech was not recorded, as none of the author's informants on this subject were able to repeat it.</note> The <term>a'taya itaŋ'ćaŋ</term> then turned the pipe and held it as if he would smoke it. Having done this three times, he put it to his lips, ready for lighting. More grass was put on the buffalo chip, and the man who was to light the pipe rubbed the fragrant smoke on his hands and face, after which he lit the pipe and the <term>a'taya itaŋ'ćaŋ</term> smoked it freely. Weasel Bear said:

> After he had smoked for a while, I sat down near him and he pointed the stem of the pipe toward me, saying, "Young man, you are going to smoke this pipe. It was brought to us by a woman, and smoking it will lead you to be as straight and truthful as the stem of the pipe." I smoked it without touching the bowl, and the old man, in taking it from me, passed his hand downward over my face. The pipe was then passed around the lodge, moving toward the left. When it was smoked out, the <term>itaŋ'ćaŋ iya'taŋ ki'yapi</term> took it and three times pretended to empty the ashes on the buffalo chip, emptying them with the fourth motion.

During the day of the ceremony, the spirit bundles lay beside their respective spirit posts. The actual release of the spirits occurred when these bundles were opened. This was done by the <term>a'taya itaŋ'ćaŋ</term>. Weasel Bear said:

> He did not take all the wrapping from a spirit bundle at once. He removed a portion and then gave a brief speech, doing this in such a manner that there were four acts of unwrapping, the last one occurring about an hour before sunset. Then he unfolded the final wrapping and let the spirit of my child depart.

The lock of hair, or other object which formed the nucleus of the spirit bundle, was kept by the family, and the <term>itaŋ'ćaŋ</term> kept such articles from the bundle as he desired, with the remainder being distributed among the people in the lodge. The spirit-keeper and his wife then gave away nearly everything they owned except for the clothing they were wearing.

If the principal spirit-keeper used a white buffalo robe in the spirit lodge, there was much interest at the close of the ceremony in seeing who would have the honor of carrying it out of the lodge. A man having the necessary qualifications might do this, and children who had been through the <term>Alo'waŋpi</term> ceremony might take hold of it and help him carry it. The qualifications included leading an upright life and having previously owned a white buffalo robe. Outside the lodge, a crude

An effigy of a buffalo had been built out of small trees. After being carried from the lodge, the white buffalo robe was laid over this framework, and valuable garments, such as an elk-tooth dress or an eagle war bonnet, were placed on it. The white buffalo robe, along with the articles placed upon it, were given to the society that had provided the most assistance to the spirit-keeper. In every society, there is one man who is qualified to take charge of such a robe if the society decides to keep it intact, and such a man may make drawings on it. However, the society is at liberty to cut it into pieces and divide it among the members, or to sell it if they so desire.

Weasel Bear said:

> When it was time for the people to depart, the <term>itan′can</term> went first, carrying his share of the bundle in which I had held the spirit of my little daughter for so long. My wife stood at the door of the <term>tipi</term> and said to the people, “If you have no leather, you may cut up this <term>tipi</term>.” The women came like a rush of wind and cut up the <term>tipi</term> very quickly. My wife even let them have a small <term>tipi</term> in which we kept our cooking utensils and other things not connected with the spirit-keeping. They even took away the <term>tipi</term> poles. Nothing was left except the grass on which we stood and the small spirit post. My wife and I had parted with everything. We walked side by side, and I thought with some regret about all I had given away. We went and sat down under a tree in deep reflection.

> That evening, one of our relatives came and pitched a <term>tipi</term>, led us to it, and said, “This is your home.” Others brought kettles, blankets, supplies, and clothing for us. Our relatives did all this for us so that we might begin our lives again.

> After a time, the camp moved to another place, and we left the spirit post standing there. No matter where we were, if a woman came and said, “I cleared the ground around your daughter’s post,” my wife would give her food. Sometimes, if there is a spirit post in the camp, a person who is hungry will go and clear the ground around the post. The relatives of the deceased person will see this and cook food, carrying the kettles to the spot so that the hungry person may eat and be satisfied. But if a spirit-keeper so desires, he may, after a certain time, take up the spirit post and bury it.

After finishing his narrative, Weasel Bear added: “All this came to us through the white buffalo and is one of the reasons why everything connected with the buffalo is so highly regarded by us.”

## THE SUN DANCE

In the myths of the Indians, as in the mythology of ancient peoples, the sun was a prominent figure. Doctor Swanton <note>1 Indian Tribes of the Lower Mississippi Valley and Adjacent Coast of the Gulf of Mexico, *Bulletin 43, Bureau of American Ethnology*, p. 174, 1911.</note> states that “the Natchez believed the universe to be filled with spirits in human forms, and that there were differences in power among these, the most powerful of all being a sky deity residing in or connected with the Sun.” Many other tribes held a similar belief, and the worship of such a deity was widespread among the Indians of North America. This worship assumed various forms, presenting contrasts in many important characteristics. The Sun dance was a

ceremony whose practice was limited to certain Plains tribes.<note>See bibliography, pp. 86, 87, footnote, of this work, also the article *Sun Dance*, by G. A. Dorsey, in *Handbook of American Indians*, pt. 2, p. 649.</note> In the Sun Dance, the Indian believed that he offered to Wakaŋ'taŋka<note>Throughout this work, the term Wakaŋ'taŋka will be used instead of the term "Great Spirit," which is commonly accepted as its English equivalent. The word Wakaŋ'taŋka is composed of *wa'kaŋ* (mysterious) and *taŋ'ka* (great). There is nothing in the term to suggest "spirit," as the Sioux have other words to express that idea. The statement has been made that the term Wakaŋ'taŋka, as well as the concept it is used to express, is a result of missionary teachings, and that the native religion was originally a worship of *Ta'kuwakan*, a *numen* (divine power) or a mysterious thing (hence a spirit or divinity). Rev. J. Owen Dorsey, who lived among the Siouan tribes first as a missionary and later as a philologist, wrote: "It is the missionaries, not the laypeople, who make positive statements about the absence of a belief in one Great Spirit." (See *Eleventh Rep. Bur. Ethn.*, p. 432.) During several seasons of work among the Teton Sioux, the writer has made careful inquiries concerning this matter, and the consistent opinion of the old men is that the Sioux have always believed in Wakaŋ'taŋka. The exact meaning of the term in the mind of the Sioux is as difficult to define as the exact meaning of the word "God" in the mind of Christians. (See p. 96.) In the past, the term Wakaŋ'taŋka was not used in ordinary conversation because it was held too sacred to be spoken except with due reverence and at an appropriate time. In this connection, it should be remembered that many Indian tribes avoid mentioning a man’s name, especially in his presence. What remains unspoken must be considered in the study of any deep aspect of Indian thought. A full and complete expression is not in accordance with Indian custom. The unspoken element may be a matter of mutual understanding, which does not appear in words, or it may be something indicated in such a way as to be intelligible only to those for whom it is intended. Thus, there is a "sacred language" used by medicine men in which familiar words take on a hidden meaning. (See p. 120, footnote.) In attempting to express the meaning of the word *wakaŋ*, the following statement was made to the writer by several elderly Indians after consultation: "An ordinary man has natural ways of doing things. Occasionally, there is a man who has a gift for doing extraordinary things, and he is called *wakaŋ*. Although this is a supernatural gift, he can use it only through effort and study. A man may be able to do things in a mysterious way, but no one has ever been found who could command the sun and moon or change the seasons. The most wonderful things that man can do are different from the works of nature. When the seasons changed, we regarded it as a gift from the sun, which is the strongest of all mysterious *wakaŋ* powers." (See p. 96.) In another discussion of the subject, it was said: "We use the words *taku wakaŋ* for anything we can see for ourselves has mysterious power. Thus, a pipe is *taku* (something) *wakaŋ*, for with it, prayers may be made and blessings obtained. We cannot see the thunder, and we say it is *wakaŋ*, but we see the lightning and we know that thunder and lightning are signs of rain, which does good to the earth. Anything that has similar power is *wakaŋ*, but above all is the sun, which has the most power of all." Other conversations, similar to those above, expressed the conviction in the minds of the Sioux that their people had always believed in a mysterious power whose greatest manifestation is the sun, and that Wakaŋ'taŋka was the name for that power. The belief in lesser "deities" will not be considered at this time.

The following citations indicate the way Wakaŋ'taŋka is regarded by the Sioux: He should be respected (p. 88); "I conquered by the help of Wakaŋ'taŋka" (p. 96); "Wakaŋ'taŋka, pity me" (p. 135); He is to be petitioned reverently (p. 184); He provides food (p. 185); He is the maker of all (p. 208); Wakaŋ'taŋka is represented by sacred stones (p. 214); medicinal herbs are a gift from Wakaŋ'taŋka (p. 268); He is all-powerful (p. 87); He is a help in sickness (p. 275); He gives success (p. 341). See also prayers to Wakaŋ'taŋka, p. 95, footnote.

The following experts on this subject may be consulted, though some hold opinions differing from the statement above: Rev. G. H. Pond, writing in 1866, said: "Evidence is also lacking to show that the Dakotas included in their religious beliefs the idea of one Supreme Existence, expressed by the term 'Great Spirit.'" (*Colls. Minn. Hist. Soc.*, vol. 2, pt. 3, p. 33, 1867.) Rev. S. R. Riggs mentions nine "Dakota gods," saying, "this list of Dakota gods is not intended to be exhaustive." (See Riggs, Stephen Return, *Tah-koo Wah-kan'*, pp. 61-75, Boston [1869]; also, by the same author, *The Theogony of The Sioux*, in *Amer. Antiq.* for April-June, II, No. 4, pp. 265-70, 1880, in which the elements of earth, air, and water each have a special deity.

Among certain Siouan tribes, the term *wakaŋ'da* was used. Regarding this word, Dr. W J McGee says: "The idea expressed by the term . . . cannot accurately be translated as 'spirit,' much less as 'Great Spirit' . . . It appears that, insofar as they grasped the concept of a god, the Sioux Indians were polytheistic; their mysteries or deities varied in rank and power; . . . and their temperaments and motives resembled those found among mankind." (McGee, W J, *The Siouan Indians*, in *Fifteenth Rep. Bur. Ethn.*, pp. 182-83.) Miss Fletcher states that among the Omaha and Ponca tribes, the word *wakaŋ'da* was used to designate a "mysterious power or permeating life," and that "this word is now used to designate the Deity." (Fletcher, Alice C., *The Emblematic Use of the Tree in the Dakotan Group*, in *Proc. Amer. Assoc. Adv. Sci.*, 1896, p. 193, Salem, 1897.) See also Fletcher and La Flesche, *The Omaha Tribe*, in *Twenty-seventh Rep. Bur. Amer. Ethn.* pp. 597-599, Washington, 1911; Fletcher, *Wakondagi*, in *Amer. Anthr.*, XIV, pp. 106-108, Lancaster, 1912.</note>

# BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY <note>Bulletin 61</note>

What was strongest in his nature and training—namely, the ability to endure physical pain—was demonstrated. He did this in fulfillment of a vow made in a time of anxiety, usually while on the warpath. Strange as it may seem, the element of pain, which ennobled the ceremony in the mind of the Indian, was a cause of its misunderstanding by the white man. The voluntary suffering impressed the spectator, while its deep significance was not apparent. It is probable that no Indian ceremony has been misinterpreted as widely and as persistently as the Sun Dance.

V. T. McGillicuddy, the agent at Pine Ridge, South Dakota, wrote in his report for 1882: “The pagan annual ceremony called ‘the Sun Dance’ will, I trust, . . . soon be a thing of the past.”¹ James G. Wright, the agent on the Rosebud Reservation in the same state, characterized the Sun Dance as an “original and uncivilized festival.”² The standpoint of the Sioux concerning the Sun Dance is indicated by the following statement from Red Bird, a thoughtful member of the tribe. In describing the Sun Dance to the writer, he said:

<margin>exclude</margin>
> There is a great deal in what a man *believes*, and if a man’s religion is changed for better or for worse, he will know it. The Sun Dance was our first and our only religion. We believed that there is a mysterious power greater than all others, which is represented by nature, one form of representation being the sun. Thus, we made sacrifices to the sun, and our petitions were granted. The Indians lived longer in the old days than they do now. I would not say this change is due to discarding the old religion; there may be other reasons, but in the past, the Sun Dance was held annually and was looked forward to with eagerness. I believe we had true faith at that time. But there came a year when “the sun died.” There was a period of darkness,<note>The Indians stated that this referred to a solar eclipse in 1868, but the reference is likely to the total eclipse that took place on August 7, 1869.</note> and from that day, a new religion came to the Indians. It is the white man’s religion. We are hesitant about it, just as we are about the other ways of the white man. In the old days, our faith was strong and our lives were cared for; now our *faith* is weaker, and we are dying.

The form of the ceremony presented here is that of the Sioux on the Standing Rock Reservation in Dakota, most of whom belong to the Teton division. In the past, the tribe was so large and so widely scattered that Sun Dances were held in more than one location; the Teton and Yanktonai usually united for a ceremony held on the western part of the Dakota prairie. Thus, their traditions of the ceremony have much in common, while the Sun Dance customs of the Santee, Sisseton, and other divisions of the tribe living toward the east present many fundamental differences.

### THE SUN DANCE OF THE TETON SIOUX

The author's study of the Sun Dance was conducted in 1911 among the Teton and Yanktonai Sioux on the Standing Rock Reservation in North and South Dakota. The principal part of the work was completed in a series of conferences covering a period of several weeks, which were held at the Standing Rock Agency. Fifteen men participated, and about 40 others were interviewed. These informants, who were carefully selected, lived within a radius of about 80 miles. Below is a brief sketch of each of the men who participated in the conferences. Ten are of pure Teton blood. Several of these men have been prominent in the history of the tribe and its negotiations with the Government. With one exception—a noted warrior who fought in the battle known as the Custer massacre—they were friendly to the white men during the troubled days on the frontier. Six of the men have consistently refused to be influenced by missionaries and still maintain their native religious beliefs.
