(1) <term>ITUN'KASAN-LU'TA</term> (RED WEASEL), a member of the Teton division of the tribe. Regarding the <term>Sun dance</term>, Red Weasel is considered the highest authority among the Teton Sioux. He served as the <term>Intercessor</term> four times, with the last occasion being the <term>Sun dance</term> of 1881, the final ceremony held by the Teton in Dakota. He also participated in the dance four times: once by being suspended from the pole and three times by receiving cuts on his arms. In earlier years, he was trained for the office of <term>Intercessor</term> (<term>Kuwa' Kiya'pi</term>) <sup>1</sup> by <term>Wi-ihan'bla</term> (Dreamer-of-the-Sun), who died around the middle of the last century. Before providing his information regarding the <term>Sun dance</term>, Red Weasel said:

> I am not boasting; I am telling you what I myself know, and I must speak for myself as there is no living man who can vouch for me. What I tell you is what I learned from Dreamer-of-the-Sun, who taught me as he was taught. Beyond that, I cannot tell you the history of the <term>Sun dance</term>. Dreamer-of-the-Sun was my uncle. He had many relatives, but he selected me as someone who was uniquely suited to succeed him if I lived to grow up. He thus decided to instruct me and began my training at an early age. One of the first and most important things I was taught was that I must have the greatest reverence for <term>Wakan'tanka</term>. Dreamer-of-the-Sun told me that if I would obey his instructions, I would be a help to the Sioux nation, and that, if properly prepared for the duties of the highest office in the <term>Sun dance</term>, I would have no anxiety when filling the office, as the proper thing to do would come to my mind at the time. Regarding the songs, Dreamer-of-the-Sun told me that I may pray with my mouth and the prayer will be heard, but if I sing the prayer, it will be heard *sooner* by <term>Wakan'tanka</term>. All the prayers which I offered in the <term>Sun dance</term> and which are still in my mind are prayers that were taught to me by Dreamer-of-the-Sun.

When Red Weasel shared his information regarding the <term>Sun dance</term>, he was about 80 years old and bowed with the weight of his years. He traveled 43 miles by wagon to confer with the writer. The sun shone in a cloudless sky while he was at the agency, and his presence was so highly valued by the elders that many said, "We have fine weather because Red Weasel is with us."

(2) <term>MATO'-KUWA'PI</term> (CHASED-BY-BEARS), a <term>Santee-Yanktonai</term> (plate 13), took part in the <term>Sun dance</term> twice as Leader of the Dancers and was present at the final <term>Sun dance</term> of the Teton. His first participation in the dance was in 1867 when, at the age of 24, he had "spoken the vow" of a war party. (See page 97.) On that occasion, as well as at other <term>Sun dances</term>, he cut the arms of the men, suspended them from the pole, or fastened buffalo skulls to their flesh, according to the nature of their vows. He said that he once saw a vision. He was dancing in the <term>Sun dance</term>, and as he looked steadily at the sun, he saw

(4) *<term>Peži'</term>* (<term>GRASS</term>), plate 73, also carries the name *<term>Mato'-wata'-kpe</term>* (<term>Charging Bear</term>); he is best known, however, as <term>John Grass</term>. When the Black Hills treaty and other treaties were made with the Government, he was the primary spokesperson for the Sioux tribe. Since then, he has consistently influenced his people to adopt civilized customs. He has traveled to Washington as a tribal delegate and for 30 years has been the presiding judge of the Court of Indian Offenses on the <term>Standing Rock Reservation</term>. As a young man, he was chosen to select the <term>Sun dance</term> pole, but he never made a <term>Sun dance</term> vow.

(5) *<term>Ituŋ'kasaŋ-mato'</term>* (<term>WEASEL BEAR</term>) is a Teton Sioux. He was once chosen to select the <term>Sun dance</term> pole but never fulfilled a vow at a <term>Sun dance</term>. While on a war party against the <term>Crows</term>, he vowed that if he was successful, he would give part of his flesh to *<term>Wakaŋ'taŋka</term>*, but he did not specify that he would do so at the <term>Sun dance</term>. As a young man, he was successful in war, a prominent member of the <term>White Horse Riders</term>, and a leader in the <term>grass dance</term>. (6) <term>WAKIN'YAṄ-WATA'KPE</term> (CHARGING THUNDER), plate 24, a Teton Sioux, is a hereditary chief of a band and a highly respected member of the tribe. He took part in the Sun dance four times, at the ages of 21, 23, 24, and 25. On each occasion, he had vowed that 100 cuts should be made on his arms, but the last time there was not enough room for all the cuts on his arms, so about 20 were made on his chest. He is a man of a genial countenance and powerful physique. In speaking of himself, he said, “My prayer has been heard and I have lived long.”

(7) <term>MAĠA'</term> (GOOSE), plate 31, was a member of the Teton division, and at the time of providing his information, he was 76 years of age. He still continued the practice of native medicine and was considered the best Indian doctor on the reservation. He took part in the Sun dance at the age of 27, being suspended from the Sun-dance pole. Goose served for a time in the United States Army. The records of the War Department show that he enlisted September 11, 1876, in Buffalo County, Dakota Territory, as a scout for the U.S.A., and served almost continuously in that capacity until July 10, 1882. He enlisted again on June 11, 1891, at Fort Yates, North Dakota, and was honorably discharged on April 30, 1893, as a private of Company I, 22nd United States Infantry. He was a corporal from October 16, 1891, to October 18, 1892. Goose died in September 1915.

(8) <term>ŚIYA'KA</term> (TEAL DUCK), plate 1, who also bore the name <term>Waṉbli'wana'peya</term> (EAGLE-WHO-FRIGHTENS), was a Yanktonai-Teton. Instead of being known by the English equivalent of his Sioux name, he was known as <term>Śiya'ka</term>, the name used in the present work. He was not a hereditary chief, but was elected chief of a band. He took part in the Sun dance twice as a young man and was also one of the four young men selected to choose the Sun-dance pole. The first time he took part in the Sun dance was at the age of 21 in fulfillment of a vow made on the warpath. He went with a party of 26 warriors on an expedition against the Mandan and Arikaree. About 20 of the warriors, including himself, vowed to take part in the next Sun dance by dancing, and the other members of the party vowed to participate in other ways. One battle was fought, and all members of the party returned home alive. His second participation in the Sun dance was at the age of 25, and he bore three long scars on each arm as evidence of the ordeal. He was once a tribal delegate to Washington. Śiya'ka died in March 1913.

(10) **HOGAN'-LU'TA** (**RED FISH**), plate 74, a Santee-Yanktonai, is a chief and a prominent man in the councils of the tribe. He took part in the Sun Dance twice: first when he was 26 years old, and the second time at the age of 40. (See song No. 192.)

(11) **IŚNA'LA-WIĆA'** (**LONE MAN**), plate 23, a Teton, took part in the Sun Dance when he was 20 and 31 years of age; he has 100 scars on each arm. He was chosen on one occasion to help select the Sun Dance pole and on another occasion to sing at the drum. He was prominent in tribal wars and took part in the Custer massacre.

(12) **MA'ZAKAN'-WIĆA'KI** (**SEIZES-THE-GUN-AWAY-FROM-THEM**), a Teton, took part in the Sun Dance by being suspended from the pole. He stated that when he was on the warpath, all the warriors made a Sun Dance vow, so he joined them, asking that he might conquer the enemy and capture horses, and also that he might find his friends alive when he returned home. In fulfilling this vow, he remained suspended for more than an hour, after which he was "jerked down," but the flesh still did not tear and only the sticks broke. The flesh was then cut, and the splinters of wood remaining underneath were removed; after this, a tiny portion of flesh was offered, just as in the case of the flesh cut from the arms.

(13) **TATAN'KA-HOKŚI'LA** (**BUFFALO BOY**), plate 9, is a Santee-Yanktonai. At the age of 30, he carried six buffalo skulls while fulfilling a Sun Dance vow. Ten years later, he took part in the dance again. He received his name from a dream in which he saw the buffalo.

(14) **ĆANȚE'-WANI'ĆA** (**NO HEART**) (plate 10), a Yanktonai, is a well-known medicine man of the tribe and is able to depict events through drawings. (See pl. 16.) He took part in the Sun Dance when he was 20 years of age and has 100 scars on each arm.

(15) **PTESAN'-MA'NI** (**WHITE-BUFFALO-WALKING**), plate 11, is a Teton and took part in the final Sun Dance in 1882.

---

The men mentioned above were the primary informants regarding the Sun Dance, with the work being conducted through a series of conferences. As already stated, about 40 additional men were interviewed. All were members of the Teton, Santee, and Yanktonai divisions of the tribe. The purpose of the interviews was to establish the facts concerning the ceremony as remembered by those who attended as spectators, and also to determine how the men who took part in the conferences were regarded by other members of the tribe. Thus, the importance given the opinions expressed by

<page-num>92</page-num>
# BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61

These men were influenced somewhat by the authority accorded them by these scattered members of the tribe. The facts brought out during these interviews did not conflict with statements made in the conferences, but served to corroborate them and to add minor details.

Not all the men in the foregoing list were present at every conference. Thus, on the first occasion, it was possible for only nine to attend. It was considered desirable that at least 12 people be present, and as no other elderly man was acceptable to the council, an invitation was extended to Thomas Frosted, a full-blood Santee-Yanktonai. He had witnessed several Sun dances when he was too young to make a Sun dance vow, and he has given much consideration to its history and beliefs. Robert P. Higheagle, the interpreter, also witnessed a Sun dance as a child. These men, with the writer, completed the desired number and no other persons were allowed in the room. Two days were occupied by the discussions, and several men remained longer to record songs.

Concerning these conferences, Iśna'la-wića' (Lone Man) said to the writer:

> When we heard that you had come for the facts concerning the Sun dance, we consulted together in our homes. Some hesitated. We have discarded the old ways, yet to talk of them is "sacred talk" to us. If we were to talk of the Sun dance, there should be at least 12 people present, so that no disrespect would be shown, and no young people should be allowed to come out of curiosity. When we decided to come to the council, we reviewed all the facts of the Sun dance and asked Wakaŋ'taŋka that we might give a true account. We prayed that no bad weather would prevent the presence of anyone chosen to attend, and look, during all this week the sound of thunder has not been heard, the sky has been fair by day, and the moon has shone brightly by night, so we know that Wakaŋ'taŋka heard our prayer.

Seated in a circle, according to the old custom, the Indians listened to the statements concerning the Sun dance as they had already been given to the writer. According to an agreement, there were no interruptions as the manuscript was translated. The man at the southern end of the row held a pipe, which he occasionally lit and handed to the man at his left. Silently, the pipe was passed from one to another, each man puffing it for a moment. The closest attention was given throughout the reading. A member of the white race can never know what reminiscences it brought to the silent Indians—what scenes of departed glory, what dignity and pride of race. After this, the men conferred together concerning the work.

That night, until a late hour, the subject was discussed in the Indian camp. The next morning, the principal session of the council took place. At this time, the expression of opinion was general, and after each discussion, a man was designated to state the decision through the interpreter. Sometimes one man and sometimes another made the final statement, but nothing was written down which did

did not represent a consensus of opinion. Throughout the councils, care was taken that the way questions were phrased did not suggest a specific answer to the Indians.

On the afternoon of that day, the entire party drove across the prairie to the location, about a mile and a half from the Standing Rock Agency, where the last Sun dance of these bands was held in 1882.

Most of the Indians who went to the site of the Sun dance with the writer were men who had participated in the Sun dance of 1882 and had not visited the place since that time. As they approached the site, they scanned the horizon, measuring the distance to the Missouri River and the buttes. At last, they signaled for the wagons to stop and, jumping to the ground, began to search the prairie. In a short time, they found the exact spot where the ceremony was held. The scars were still on the prairie, just as they were on their own bodies. A depression about 2 inches deep, still square in outline and not fully overgrown with grass, showed where the earth had been exposed for the <term>oway'ka wakaŋ</term> (“sacred place”); see page 122. Only 3 or 4 feet away lay a broken buffalo skull. Eagerly, the Indians lifted it and saw traces of red paint upon it—could it be anything other than the skull used in that ceremony? They looked to see if they might find a trace of where the pole was located. It should have been about 15 feet east of the “sacred place.” There it was—a spot of hard, bare ground 18 inches in diameter.

One said, “Here you can see where the shade-house stood.” This shade-house, or shelter made of boughs, was built entirely around the Sun-dance circle except for a wide entrance at the east. It was possible to trace part of it, with the outline being particularly clear on the west side of the circle; to the east, the position of the posts at the entrance was also recognized. The two sunken places (where the posts had stood) were about 15 feet apart, and the center of the space between them was directly in line with the site of the pole and the center of the “sacred place” to the west of it. <note>1 These measurements were verified by the writer at a later time.</note> More than 29 years had passed since the ceremony. It is strange that the wind had not sown seeds on those patches of bare earth.

The small party gathered again around the buffalo skull. Mr. Higheagle gathered fresh sage, which he placed beside the “sacred place”; he then laid the broken buffalo skull upon it and rested a Sun-dance pipe against the skull, with the stem pointing upward. He, too, had his memories. As a 6-year-old boy, he was present at that final Sun dance, wearing traditional Indian clothing and living the tribal life. Between that day and the present lay years of education in the white man’s way. Some of the Indians put on their war bonnets

The sky was blue above the little gathering, and all around the vast silent prairie seemed waiting, listening. The Indians were its children—would the white man understand them correctly?

A few weeks later, the material was discussed again point by point with men who traveled 40 miles for that purpose. Chief among these was Red Bird, who was being trained for the office of <term>Intercessor</term> when the <term>Sun dance</term> was discontinued. He was present at the first council, but some facts had come to his mind in the meantime, and he wished to have them included in the narrative. These men met four times to discuss the subject; the phonograph records were played for them and approved, and some ceremonial songs were added to the series. A few days later, a conference was held with five other men, most of whom were present at the council of August 28 and 29. The session lasted an entire day; the prepared narrative was translated into Sioux and the phonograph records were played for them, as they had been for the previous group of men. With one exception, all the men were chiefs.

Throughout this series of conferences, the principal points of the account remained unchanged. Each session added information, placed events in the proper order, provided descriptive details, and gave reasons for various ceremonial acts. The councils were not marked by controversy; a cordial spirit prevailed, and the open discussion helped in recalling facts. Nothing was recorded that was not pronounced correct by the council as a whole.

A message was then sent to Ituŋ'kasaŋ-lu'ta (Red Weasel), an elderly man who acted as <term>Intercessor</term> at the last <term>Sun dance</term>, asking him to come and give his opinion on the material. He came and, with three others, reviewed the subject in another all-day council. His training and experience enabled him to recall details concerning the special duties of the <term>Intercessor</term>, and he also sang four songs which he received from Wi-ihaŋ'bla (Dreamer-of-the-Sun), along with the instructions concerning the duties of his office. These songs are numbers 14, 15, 16, and 18 in the present memoir. Before

After singing the first song, the elderly man bowed his head and offered the following prayer,¹ which was recorded by the phonograph:

> Ho Wakan´tanka nama´h’on wo. Anp'e´tu le el ni´oië wan´zi´ ta´ku wo´wahtani wanil´ ya ´ obla´kin ktelo´. Oya´te wi´ca´ni´ waon´ tanyan´ ama´bleza yo. Mi´wankapatanhhan wanyang´ nan´jin yo. Wi´ca´yaka e´ce ki´n on tanyan´ ho ana´magoptan ye. Le mita´kuye yanka´pi kin ob tanyan´ to´ka e´wa´cin sniyan´ waon´ ktelo´. He´ce´ca kin toka´ta oi´najin wan onyeglepi kin ekta´ hountanin pi kta nu´nwe´.

->(Translation)<-

> Wakan Tanka, hear me. This day I am to tell your word. I shall speak without sin. The tribe shall live. Behold me, for I am humble. Watch me from above. You are always the truth; listen to me. My friends and relatives sitting here, and I, shall be at peace. May our voices be heard at the future goal you have prepared for us.

The preceding prayer was spoken in such a low voice that the phonograph record was transcribed with difficulty. It is uncertain whether the elderly man intended for it to be recorded; however, since he had seated himself before the phonograph in preparation for singing, it was possible to start the machine without attracting his attention. He began the prayer with his head bowed and his right hand extended, later raising his face and using the same gestures he would have used while performing his ceremonial duties.

The final work on this material was completed with Chased-by-Bears (Plate 13), a man who had twice served as Leader of the Dancers, had "spoken the Sun Dance vow" of a war party (see page 97), and had frequently administered the ordeals during the ceremony. He was a particularly thoughtful man, remaining steadfast in the ancient beliefs of his people. Few details were added to the description of the ceremony at this time, but its teachings received special attention. Chased-by-Bears’ account of his understanding of the Sun Dance was not given all at once, though it is presented here in a connected narrative. This material represents several conferences with the author, as well as conversations between Mr. Higheagle and Chased-by-Bears that took place during long drives across the prairie. To provide an opportunity for these conversations, the interpreter brought Chased-by-Bears to the agency every day in his own vehicle. Thus, the information was gradually gathered. When it was compiled into its current form, it was translated back into Sioux for Chased-by-Bears, who stated that it was correct in every detail.

The statement of Chased-by-Bears concerning the Sun Dance was as follows:

The Sun Dance is so sacred to us that we do not talk of it often. Before speaking of holy things, we prepare ourselves with offerings. If only two are to talk together, one

will fill his pipe and hand it to the other, who will light it and offer it to the sky and the earth. Then they will smoke together, and after smoking they will be ready to talk of holy things.

The cutting of the bodies in fulfillment of a <term>Sun dance</term> vow is different from the cutting of the flesh when people are in sorrow. A man’s body is his own, and when he gives his body or his flesh, he is giving the only thing which really belongs to him. We know that all the creatures on the earth were placed here by <term>Wakan’tanka</term>. Thus, if a man says he will give a horse to <term>Wakan’tanka</term>, he is only giving to <term>Wakan’tanka</term> that which already belongs to him. I might give tobacco or other articles in the <term>Sun dance</term>, but if I gave these and kept back the best, no one would believe that I was in earnest. I must give something that I really value to show that my whole being goes with the lesser gifts; therefore I promise to give my body.

A child believes that only the action of someone who is unfriendly can cause pain, but in the <term>Sun dance</term> we acknowledge first the goodness of <term>Wakan’tanka</term>, and then we suffer pain because of what he has done for us. To this day I have never joined a Christian Church. The old belief which I have always held is still with me.

When a man does a piece of work which is admired by all, we say that it is wonderful; but when we see the changes of day and night, the sun, moon, and stars in the sky, and the changing seasons upon the earth, with their ripening fruits, anyone must realize that it is the work of someone more powerful than man. Greatest of all is the sun, without which we could not live. The birds and the beasts, the trees and the rocks, are the work of some great power. Sometimes men say that they can understand the meaning of the songs of birds. I can believe this is true. They say that they can understand the call and cry of the animals, and I can believe this also is true, for these creatures and man are alike the work of a great power. We often wish for things to come, such as the rain or the snow. They do not always come when we wish, but they are sure to come in time, for they are under the control of a power that is greater than man.

It is right that men should repent when they make or fulfill a vow to <term>Wakan’tanka</term>. No matter how good a man may appear to others, there are always things he has done for which he ought to be sorry, and he will feel better if he repents of them. Men often weep in the <term>Sun dance</term> and cry aloud. They are asking something of <term>Wakan’tanka</term>, and are like children who wish to show their sorrow, and who also know that a request is more readily granted to a child who cries.<gloss>1</gloss> (See p. 185.)

We talk to <term>Wakan’tanka</term> and are sure that he hears us, and yet it is hard to explain what we believe about this. It is the general belief of the Indians that after a man dies his spirit is somewhere on the earth or in the sky; we do not know exactly where, but we are sure that his spirit still lives. Sometimes people have agreed together that if it were found possible for spirits to speak to men, they would make themselves known to their friends after they died, but they never came to speak to us again, unless, perhaps, in our sleeping dreams. So it is with <term>Wakan’tanka</term>. We believe that he is everywhere, yet he is to us as the spirits of our friends, whose voices we cannot hear. (See p. 85.)

My first <term>Sun-dance</term> vow was made when I was 24 years of age. I was alone and far from the camp when I saw an <term>Arikaree</term> approaching on horseback, leading a horse. I knew that my life was in danger, so I said, 

> “<term>Wakan’tanka</term>, if you will let me kill this man and capture his horse with this lariat, I will give you my flesh at the next <term>Sun dance</term>.”

I was successful, and when I reached home I told my friends that I had conquered by the help of <term>Wakan’tanka</term> and had made a Sun-dance vow. It happened that I was the first who had done this after the <term>Sun dance</term> of that summer, so my friends said that I should be the Leader of the Dancers at the next ceremony. (See p. 102.) In fulfilling this vow, I carried the lariat I had used in capturing the horse <note>Figure 21</note> fastened to the flesh of my right shoulder, and the figure of a horse cut from rawhide fastened to my left shoulder. <note>Figure 21 shows the lariat and whistle carried by Chased-by-Bears.</note>

Later in the same year, I went out with a party of about 20 warriors. As we approached the enemy, some of the men came to me saying that they desired to make <term>Sun Dance</term> vows and asking if I would “speak the vow” for the party. <note>See page 101.</note> Each man came to me alone and brought a gift with his request. He also stated what offerings he would make at the <term>Sun Dance</term>, but did not always say what part he intended to take in the dance. One man said, “I will give my whole body to <term>Wakan’tanka</term>.” I did not understand what he meant, nor was it necessary that I should, but at the time of the <term>Sun Dance</term> he asked that his body be suspended entirely above the ground.

Just before sunrise, I told the warriors to stand side by side facing the east. I stood behind them and told them to raise their right hands. I raised my right hand with them and said: “<term>Wakan’tanka</term>, these men have requested me to make this vow for them. I pray you take pity on us and on our families at home. We are now between life and death. For the sake of our families and relatives, we desire that you will help us conquer the enemy and capture his horses to take home with us. Because they are thankful for your goodness and will be thankful if you grant this request, these men promise that they will take part in the next <term>Sun Dance</term>. Each man has some offering to give at the proper time.”

We were successful and returned home victorious. Knowing that these men had vowed to take part in the <term>Sun Dance</term>, I saw to it that their vows were fulfilled at the next ceremony and personally performed the cutting of their arms and the suspension of their bodies. I did this in addition to acting as Leader of the Dancers and fulfilling my own vow.

The second time I fulfilled a <term>Sun Dance</term> vow, I also acted as Leader of the Dancers. At that time I carried four buffalo skulls. They were so heavy that I could not stand erect, but bowed myself upon a stick which I was permitted to use and danced in that position <note>page 133</note>.

When the work with Chased-by-Bears was finished, he went with the author and the interpreter to the spot where the final <term>Sun Dance</term> was held, a place which had been visited by the council of Indians a few weeks before. The purpose of this visit was so that Chased-by-Bears might arrange the ceremonial articles on the “sacred place” as would be done in an actual ceremony.

The outline of the “sacred place” was made clear, and intersecting white lines were traced on the exposed earth. <note>See page 122.</note>

A buffalo skull had been secured and brought to the place. Chased-by-Bears spread fresh sage beside the “sacred place” and laid the buffalo skull upon it. He then made a frame to support a pipe and placed in ceremonial position a pipe which had been decorated by the woman who decorated the <term>Sun Dance</term> pipe for the last tribal ceremony. The group of articles was then photographed. <note>See plate 20.</note> Suddenly, Chased-by-Bears threw himself face downward on the ground, with his head pressed against the top of the buffalo skull. This was the position permitted to a Leader of the Dancers when resting.

### DESCRIPTION OF A TETON SIOUX SUN DANCE

<image-desc>A rectangular photograph labeled FIG. 21. Lariat and whistle carried in Sun dance. It depicts a vertically hanging, long braided rope (lariat) with several loops at the bottom, and a thin, light-colored whistle made of bone or wood placed vertically to its right.</image-desc>

The Sun dance was called by the Sioux <term>Wi wan’yaŋg waćí'pi</term>, which is literally translated "Sun-watching dance." It was their only tribal gathering of a religious nature and was held every year at the full moon of midsummer, "when all nature and even men were rejoicing." The trees were in full leaf and the Juneberries were ripe. Furthermore, the wild sage was fully grown—a thing especially desired, as the sage was used in the ceremony.

The place where the Sun dance was held changed from year to year, but was known to all the tribe. Across the prairie came the small groups of Sioux, some traveling a long distance to attend the ceremony. One band after another arrived and set up its tipis in the customary part of the tribal circle. Each band constructed a vapor lodge ("sweat bath") near its camp for the use of those who took part in the dance, as well as a larger lodge in which the dancers gathered before and after the ceremony.

The Sun dance was held in the center of the great circle of tents. The opening of this tribal circle faced the East, and the tent of the <term>itaŋ’ćaŋ</term><note>The meaning of this word is "leader," and its exact significance is understood from the connection in which it is used. (See page 70, footnote.)</note> (Leader of the Dancers) was on the opposite side. A short distance in front of his tent was the council tent, larger than the others and without decoration. There the chiefs and leading men met to

<summary>This page introduces the Teton Sioux Sun Dance, or Wi wan’yaŋg waćí'pi, describing it as an annual midsummer religious gathering held in a large tribal circle. It details the preparation of the campsite, including the placement of tipis, vapor lodges, and the leader's tent.</summary>

<keywords>Sun dance, Teton Sioux, Wi wan’yaŋg waćí'pi, midsummer, Juneberries, tribal circle, vapor lodge, sweat bath, tipis, itaŋ’ćaŋ, council tent, lariat, whistle</keywords>

--- Page 153 ---
<meta>This page continues the description of the preparations for the Teton Sioux Sun Dance, focusing on the ritual placement of the buffalo skull and the ceremonies performed by medicine men to ensure fair weather.</meta>

DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC

conducted the business of the tribe, and from there the various orders pertaining to the ceremony were carried to the people by the Crier. Members of the tribe did not approach, and children and dogs were kept away from the area because the buffalo skull to be used in the Sun Dance ceremony lay to the west of this tent. During the four days preceding the ceremony, the skull lay on a bed of fresh sage outside the council tent, in a position corresponding to the place of honor inside the tent. The ceremonial lines of red paint had not yet been placed on the skull, but the openings in it were filled with sage. The use of sage around the buffalo skull was in accordance with the instructions given by the White Buffalo Maiden. (See p. 64.) It was said, too, that "the sage was used because the buffalo sought for it on the prairie and rolled their great bodies on its fragrant leaves." The sage used in this connection was identified as *Artemisia gnaphalodes* Nutt.

A month before the Sun Dance, the <term>wakaŋ'haŋ</term> (medicine men; see p. 245) prayed for fair weather by singing, burning sweet grass, and offering their pipes to the sky, the earth, and the cardinal points. Before burning the sweet grass, a medicine man prepared a spot of bare ground, placing a few coals in the middle of it. Then, taking a bunch of sweet grass, he offered it to the sky, the earth, and the cardinal points, after which he singed it over the coals. While it was smoking, he offered it again to the sky, the earth, and the cardinal points. It is said that the efforts of the medicine men were always successful, and that the oldest men cannot remember rain falling during a Sun Dance.

The following song was especially favored for securing fair weather; it is one of the songs which have descended from Dreamer-of-the-Sun, who died about the year 1845. (See p. 88.)

> hina'pa nunwe' .................... brightly shone upon

*Analysis.*—Like all the ceremonial songs of the Sun Dance, this song was sung with great flexibility in both timing and pitch; therefore, it cannot be fully represented by musical notation. However, the writer believes it is unnecessary to visually represent variations of less than a semitone, as these variations differ across several performances, while the primary features of the song remain consistent. The same words are always accented, and the general rhythmic ratios are steadily preserved. A comparison of several performances shows that the rhythm used for the word *hina'pa* can be accurately indicated by a sixteenth note followed by a dotted eighth. The E-flats both above and on the staff were sung with nearly perfect intonation, demonstrating an awareness of the octave interval. B-flat, the fifth of the key, was sometimes sung quite accurately and other times poorly; the same was true for F, the second of the key. It was previously noted among Chippewa songs that the octave and fifth were sung more accurately than other intervals <note>See Bulletin 45, p. 5</note>. The C-flat in the seventh measure of the present song was consistently sung too high. It might have been viewed as an accidental note, except that the intonation is flawed throughout that entire measure, with some progressions being *glissando*. Therefore, both the character of the song and, in many instances, the character of the singer must be considered when judging the significance of specific musical details.

About three-quarters of the intervals move downward, and the song is melodic in structure. It spans eleven tones and includes every note of the octave except the fourth.

Even during this time of celebration, the danger from enemies was not forgotten. Horses were herded near the camp, guarded by young men during the day, and brought closer to the tents to be tethered at night.

The people greeted one another warmly. They reviewed the events of the past year, and tales of war were told repeatedly. War was a primary focus, and the Sun Dance would witness the fulfillment of many warriors' vows.

DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC

When in danger, it was customary for an entire war party to vow that its members would take part in the next Sun Dance. The vow was usually made at sunrise and spoken by a warrior who had fulfilled a similar vow. <note>See p. 97.</note> If there was time to secure a proper offering, each man held this in his left hand, raising his right hand as the vow was spoken. It was a rite that could be varied by the individual. For instance, it was said that some made the vow more impressive by bowing their heads or lowering the right hand slowly toward the earth. A man’s spoken vow was only that he would take part in the dance, but deep in his heart was hidden a private vow concerning the specific role he would take.<note>¹ Among other instances see Red Fox (p. 376) and Jaw (p. 390).</note> Some had left little children at home, or sick relatives or friends whom they longed to see again. They vowed that at the next Sun Dance they would dance, or would be suspended by their flesh, or that many gashes would be cut in their arms; they felt that no extreme of heroic endurance would be too great an expression of thankfulness if they were reunited with their friends, yet they knew that their vow must be fulfilled even if they returned defeated or to an empty lodge.

During the months that passed between their return and the Sun Dance, they prepared for the fulfillment of their vows. They knew well that if they failed to do this of their own accord, it would be demanded of them by the forces of nature. More than one man who disregarded his vow to the sun had perished in a lightning flash; or if he escaped punishment himself, it was known that disaster had befallen his family or his horses. The old men knew of every vow and watched for its fulfillment.

The leading men of the tribe belonged to various military societies, such as the Strong Heart, the Crow-owners, the Wolf, Badger, and Fox societies, or the White Horse Riders. <note>See pp. 314–332.</note> During the four days immediately preceding the Sun Dance, these societies met together for the purpose of electing the <term>Kuwa' Kiya'pi</term> (Intercessor), the <term>Itaŋ'ćay</term> (Leader of the Dancers), the four young men who were to select the tree for the <term>caŋ wakaŋ'</term> (sacred pole), and the four young women who were to cut it down. The chiefs were also in the council tent whenever business was conducted. It was generally known in advance who would be chosen as Intercessor and Leader of the Dancers. The former office required long and special preparation and was repeatedly filled by the same man. His duties included the offering of prayers on behalf of the people, the singing of songs as he performed certain ceremonial acts, the painting of the <term>caŋ wakaŋ'</term> (sacred pole), and the preparation of the <term>owaŋ'ka wakaŋ'</term> (sacred place). The ceremonial songs had to be either composed by the man who sang them or purchased from someone who had previously

He held the office and instructed his successor in its duties. A significant payment was made for these instructions and songs. The tribe was aware when a young man aspired to this position, and if his training was complete, he was elected as soon as the opportunity arose.

Red Bird stated:
> "The tribe would never appoint an unworthy man to the office of <term>Intercessor</term>. In his prayers and offerings, he represented the people; if he were not a good man, <term>Wakaŋ'taŋka</term> might not answer his petitions or grant fair weather. He might even send disaster upon the tribe."

Chased-by-Bears said that no man who had committed a serious offense could serve as <term>Intercessor</term>, regardless of how deeply he had repented. The reputation of an <term>Intercessor</term> had to be completely flawless.

The <term>Leader of the Dancers</term> was usually the first warrior to return successfully from a war party, announcing that he had made a <term>Sun-dance</term> vow and wished to serve as <term>Leader of the Dancers</term> at the next ceremony. As with the office of <term>Intercessor</term>, the qualifications were so well known that a man who lacked them would not dare to seek the position. He had to have an irreproachable reputation and be able to fulfill the office with credit to himself and the tribe. He was required to provide the various offerings placed upon the sacred pole, as well as the buffalo fat used to set the pole in place. He was also expected to offer a <term>Sun-dance pipe</term> and provide the buffalo skull on which it rested during the ceremony—a flawless skull he selected from the many scattered across the prairie.

The <term>Sun-dance pipe</term> (plate 14), provided by the <term>Leader of the Dancers</term>, was decorated at his request by one of the tribe's most skillful women. Decorating this pipe, which was prepared some time before the ceremony, was considered a great honor. There was no required pattern, but the decoration consisted of porcupine-quill work and did not cover the entire stem. The men who fulfilled their vows also made certain offerings which they prepared before the ceremony; the value of these varied according to the man's wealth. For instance, a wealthy man might give a pipe, a quantity of tobacco, a buffalo robe, and other goods, while a man of limited means might give only tobacco. Like the offerings made by the <term>Intercessor</term> during the ceremony, these were regarded as gifts to <term>Wakaŋ'taŋka</term>. A difference between the two types of offerings was shown by the fact that the goods offered by the <term>Intercessor</term> were left untouched on the prairie, while those offered by the dancers were free for anyone to take. Red Bird explained the reason:
> "The <term>Intercessor</term> represented the entire tribe and his offerings were to <term>Wakaŋ'taŋka</term>, while the dancers were all equals and their offerings were shared among themselves."

The tobacco offered by the dancers was tied into small packets, each holding about one pipeful, and each attached to a stick (plate 15).

DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC

In the examples illustrated, the tobacco is wrapped in the dried bladder of a steer, whereas buffalo bladders were used in the past. The number of these packets varied; ten was the usual number, though a dancer sometimes gave one hundred. The sticks holding the packets were placed upright in the ground or left in any available place, and, like the other gifts of the dancers, were taken by the poor of the tribe.

If a man's vow involved the cutting of his flesh, he was permitted to offer a pipe similar to that of the Intercessor, filled with tobacco, sealed with buffalo fat, and placed beside the Intercessor's pipe during the ceremony. *Iśna'la-wića'* (Lone Man) stated that his Sun Dance vow included the offering of a pipe; he therefore offered a pipe when fulfilling his vow and had kept the pipe with the greatest care. This was smoked when the members of the Sun Dance council revisited the site of the final Sun Dance on August 29, 1911, and was again placed on the square of exposed earth, which was still visible on the prairie. (See page 93.)

Preparation for the Sun Dance included the choice of others who were to take part in the ceremony. It was required that the four young men who were to select the tree for the sacred pole should be unmarried, members of prominent families, and men of unquestioned integrity. The four women were selected from among the virgins of the tribe. Great care was exercised in these selections, and each choice could be challenged by the tribe. There was, however, no open rivalry at the time of the election, as it was generally known who would probably be chosen.

Twenty or more men were selected to carry the sacred pole to the camp and erect it in the Sun Dance circle; these men also sang at the drum, together with special singers, both men and women.

During the days before a Sun Dance, several begging dances were held. The begging dance, which was performed at every Sioux gathering, resembled a serenade rather than a dance. A party of men and women carrying a drum went from tent to tent, pausing before each and singing and dancing until food was given to them. A man went ahead of the party and placed a stick upright in the ground before each tent where the serenaders expected to sing. This was a signal to the occupants of the tent; the stick was removed by the singers after they had been supplied with food.<note>See Bulletin 53, pages 228–33; also pages 320, 327, 481 of the present work.</note>

To those who were to take part in the Sun Dance, the days preceding the ceremony were a season of preparation, including visits to the vapor lodges of their respective bands. During this time, the dancers usually made the arrangements for the painting of their bodies. The painting was done by men of known ability, who were paid by the individual dancers. Often there was some formality

connected with making this request, which was performed for the writer by *Zintka'la-lu'ta* (Red Bird), who represented the dancer, and *Iśna'la-wićá'* (Lone Man), who represented the man asked to apply the paint. Red Bird made the request, but his friend pretended to hesitate, finally holding out both hands tightly closed. Lone Man then tried to open his friend's hands. After succeeding with apparent difficulty, he placed a pipe in them, which his friend accepted and smoked. After a few moments, Red Bird asked for the pipe to be returned, but he was met with the same reluctance as before. Finally, he was forced to pry his friend's hands from the pipe, just as he had forced them open when the pipe was first offered. This was said to represent an agreement that one man would paint the body of the other, and it clearly illustrated the "artistic temperament" in an unmistakable way.

For four nights just before the Sun Dance, there were rehearsals for those who were to drum, sing, or dance, with each person being carefully instructed in their part of the ceremony.

Announcements were made by the Crier, who was a striking and important figure in every tribal gathering. An old man was preferred, as it was said that "the old men were more careful than the young men in making announcements."¹ Mounted on horseback and handsomely dressed, wearing a single eagle feather standing upright in his hair and carrying an eagle-wing fan, the Crier went around the camp circle, close to the tent doors, announcing the decisions of the council, the commands of the Intercessor, or the events of the day. He was also ready to answer any questions regarding the ceremony, as the Intercessor and the Leader of the Dancers were supposed to speak only when it was absolutely necessary.

During the days immediately preceding the Sun Dance, it was customary for each military society to hold one or more dances called braves' dances, which were followed by feasts. The term "braves' dances" is a general one, referring to the dances of the various military societies. It was said that a dance of the <term>Strong Heart society</term> might be announced by the Crier in the following words:

> *Ćante' Tiŋ'za waŋ! I'mnahan waya'tiŋ ktelo'. Hiyu' po!* (Strong Hearts! You are going to eat to your hearts' content. Come on!)

In response to this summons, the members of the <term>Strong Heart society</term> would arrive in their finest clothing. This society was composed of warriors, and the leaders of the tribe were usually among its members (See p. 329). They paraded around the camp circle before the dance, singing the songs they used when on the warpath.

BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61

Analysis—This <term>melody</term> is particularly forceful and direct. It is a song that would inspire confidence, and it is also <term>rhythmic</term> for dancing. The <term>tonic triad</term> is emphasized; the song consists only of the <term>tonic triad</term> and the <term>fourth</term>. In one instance, the <term>fourth</term> was accented and has no apparent chord relation to adjacent accented tones. The song is therefore classified as “melodic with a <term>harmonic framework</term>,” instead of “harmonic” in structure. Descending progressions are used effectively in this melody; the first <term>rhythmic unit</term> contains such progressions in duple time, and the second in triple time. It is interesting to note throughout these songs the effect produced by slight changes in rhythm. For instance, in the first occurrence of the second <term>rhythmic unit</term>, the second <term>measure</term> was sung in every rendition with two eighth notes on the second count. It will be seen that in other occurrences of this unit, the first note of this measure is a dotted eighth. In all renditions of this song, the <term>tempo</term> was increased with the introduction of the words, and the song closed in the original <term>tempo</term>. The return to this tempo was usually gradual, being made sooner in some renditions than in others. The timing of the drum did not change with the increased tempo of the voice; the <term>drum-rhythm</term> was continuous, as indicated. Similar instances were noted among the <term>Chippewa</term>; these are discussed in Bulletin 53, page 206. In the present work, the following instances of change of time are found:

Songs in which the voice changes <term>tempo</term>, while the song is recorded with a drum that is continuous and does not change in tempo—Nos. 5, 83, 114, 133, 188.

Songs in which the voice changes <term>tempo</term>, the song being recorded without a drum—Nos. 55, 58, 88, 137, 140, 145, 153, 156, 166, 170, 171, 174. In this song, there is one instance where a syllable is omitted: the third syllable of *bliheići̇ya* was left out by the singer. Among other songs containing this peculiarity are Nos. 17 and 38. The omission and addition of syllables was frequently noted in the <term>Chippewa</term> songs. Throughout the present work, all interpolated syllables are indicated by italics. These changes <note>OCR "cnanges" corrected to "changes"</note> in the lyrics of the songs represent an Indian custom and do not in any way affect the meaning.

The following song was also used in the <term>braves’ dance</term>; it is estimated to be about 180 years old, as the singer, who was a man past middle life, stated that his father said that his grandfather sang it. The age of a song can usually be determined in this manner with a fair degree of accuracy.

### No. 6. **Song of the Braves' Dance** (Catalogue No. 498)

->Sung by **RED BIRD**<-

<image-desc>A musical score for "Song of the Braves' Dance" written in bass clef. The transcription includes five staves of melodic notation and a separate line for "Drum-rhythm". The melody is characterized by frequent triplets and descending phrases. There are markings for repetition segments (1) and (2) above the staff. The time signatures change between 2/4 and 3/4. Analysis.—This song is in a minor <term>tonality</term> and contains all the tones of the <term>octave</term> except the sixth and second. In three instances, the seventh is raised a <term>semitone</term>. Twelve tones are included in the <term>compass</term> of the song, which has a steadily descending trend. The song contains two <term>rhythmic units</term>, each occurring twice. As is usual in such instances, the <term>rhythmic units</term> resemble each other, with the second seeming to be an “answering phrase.”

The tree to be used for the <term>sacred pole</term> was selected and cut, and the <term>sacred pole</term> was decorated and raised on the morning of the day preceding the <term>Sun dance</term>. All the tribe were present when the four young men set out from the camp to select the tree. For some time before their departure, the drummers and singers sang songs of war, for the tree was regarded as something to be conquered. The following song might be sung as the people assembled. This song was composed by the singer, a man who is known in the tribe as a composer of war songs.

**Analysis.**—The descending interval of a fourth makes up more than a third of the total number of intervals in this song. Three rhythmic units appear, and a comparison of them is interesting. The <term>count-divisions</term> of the first unit are reversed in the second. The third unit begins with two eighth notes, like the first, but these are followed by a reversal of the <term>count-division</term> found in the first unit. The ascent of a twelfth, which occurs with the introduction of the words, was performed quite accurately, but the intonation in the measure containing the words *waöŋ' welo'* was faulty, sounding almost like a glissando in the descent from one tone to another.

| ite'sabye ća | the black face-paint <note>see p. 359.</note> |
| owa'le | I seek |

*Analysis.*—The primary interest of this song lies in the number of <term>minor thirds</term> it contains. The song includes 23 intervals, 15 of which (about 54 percent) are minor thirds. The minor third E–G forms the framework of the opening measures, followed by the <term>minor triad</term> A–C–E. After a single measure of the <term>tonic triad</term>, there is a return to the minor thirds A–C and E–G, with the latter forming the closing interval of the song. The tones of the melody are those of the <term>fourth five-toned scale</term>, but the tonic triad appears only in the seventh measure. The song contains two rhythmic units; the <term>count divisions</term> of both are the same, but the accent is changed in the second unit. The first part of the song is based on the first rhythmic unit, while the latter part is based on the second unit.

<vocab>ŠIYA'KA, Teton Sioux, ethnomusicology, minor thirds, Lakota, rhythmic units, Frances Densmore</vocab>

A comparison of the phonograph record with the metronome shows the speed of the voice to be equivalent to 104 quarter notes per minute (♩ = 104), while the speed of the drum is equivalent to only 96 quarter notes per minute (♩ = 96). If there were no deviation from regularity, there would be a coincidence of the voice and drum at the fourteenth pulsation (quarter note) of the voice; this, however, is entirely theoretical, as a slight variation in either part would change the ratio between the two. In this and many similar instances, it appears that the voice and drum represent separate impulses, expressed simultaneously but having no rhythmic relationship to each other.

*Analysis.*—This melody contains only the tones A-flat, C, E-flat, and G-flat. These are not the tones typically included in the key of A-flat, as musicians usually define the term, but the sequence of the tones suggests A-flat as a satisfactory tonic. A test by ear seems permissible in an instance such as this, and the song is accordingly transcribed with A-flat as its tonic and G-flat as an accidental. The tonic triad makes up the first seven measures of the melody, while the descending fourth from the tonic to the dominant forms the outline of the rest of the song, with the flatted seventh as an accidental. A rhythmic unit occurs, forming part of both double and triple measures. It is varied slightly in repetition; the second count is in some instances a quarter note and in others two eighth notes. The triplet on the first count, however, is distinctive and is steadily repeated. Two-thirds of the progressions move downward.

Anyone who wished to accompany the young men was permitted to do so, but they had no part in choosing the tree. Upon arriving at the woods, the young men searched for a straight, slender tree. It was stated that cottonwood was preferred for the sacred pole and for all wooden articles used in the Sun Dance because the white down of the cottonwood seed resembles the downy eagle feathers used in the ceremony.<note>Cottonwood was also used for the post in the spirit lodge. (See p. 81; also in the offering placed on the Sun Dance pole, p. 118.)</note> If a cottonwood could not be obtained, elm was selected because the elm is the first tree to blossom in the spring. The tree for the Sun Dance pole had to be a standing tree and particularly fine in its straightness, branching, and fullness of leaves. It was required that the first tree selected be the one cut, with no change of choice allowed. It is interesting to note that all articles dedicated to ceremonial use had to be the best obtainable. A high standard of excellence prevailed among the Sioux, and this is especially shown in their ceremonies, which expressed their highest ideals.

When the young men had decided on a tree, they returned to make their report to the Intercessor. Their return had been anxiously awaited, and in response to their signal, a number of friends went on horseback to meet them, riding around them in wide circles and escorting them to the camp. There they found their friends dancing around the drum and singing the following song, which was also used to welcome a returning war party or men who had gone in search of buffalo. After the singing and dancing, a feast was provided by the friends of the young men. There was an abundance of food, and all were invited to partake.

->Sung by LONE MAN<-

Analysis—An unusual feature of this song is that seven of the 12 intervals it contains are fourths, with four being ascending and three being descending progressions. The tonic occurs only in the upper octave, and the song closes on the dominant. The seventh and second tones of the octave are not found in the song, which is major in tonality and harmonic in structure.

The announcement of a choice was followed by preparations for cutting the tree and bringing it to the camp. The cutting of the tree for the Sun Dance pole was an important part of the ceremony, and many went to witness it. Some went out of curiosity, and others wished to make offerings when the tree was cut. Even the children went to see the cutting of the pole. The young people, riding their swift ponies, circled around the party. The leading members of the company were the Intercessor (or, in his absence, one of the old medicine men), the four young men who selected the tree, the four young women who were to cut the tree, and the pole-bearers, who were to carry it to the camp. It was the duty of the Leader of the Dancers to provide the ax with which the tree was felled, but he did not accompany the party who went to cut it. In the old days, a primitive implement was used; in later times, this was replaced by an ax purchased from a trader, but it was required that the ax be a new one, never used before.

Great interest centered on the selection of the tree, and when it was indicated by the young men, the Intercessor raised his pipe, holding the stem toward the top of the tree and lowering it slowly to the earth while repeating a prayer in a low tone. When he held the pipe toward the top of the tree, he spoke of the kingbird; lowering it about one-third of the distance to the ground, he spoke of the eagle; lowering it half the remaining distance, he spoke of the yellow-hammer; and holding it toward the ground, he spoke of the spider. The tree was regarded as an enemy, and in explanation of the reference to these animals, it was said that “the kingbird, though small, is

"...feared by all its enemies; the eagle is the boldest of birds; the yellowhammer cannot overcome its enemies in an open fight but is expert at dodging them, darting from one side of the tree trunk to another; while the spider defeats its enemies by craftiness and cunning."

One of the four young women was selected to cut the tree, but she did not cut it down immediately. It was considered that she had been given the honor of conquering an enemy, and before she used the ax, a male relative was permitted to relate one of his brave deeds on the warpath. The young woman then lifted the ax and made a motion as if striking the tree. Each of the four young women did the same, with each person's action being preceded by a kinsman telling a story of victory. The ax was then returned to the first young woman, who swung it effectively, cutting the tree in such a way that it fell toward the south (see p. 78). While the tree was being cut down, no one was allowed near it except for those who used the ax, the Intercessor, those who wished to make offerings, and those who were to carry the pole. *Analysis.*—This melody consists of the tones of the fourth five-tone scale. In two instances, the sixth is lowered a semitone. A dotted eighth note, either preceded or followed by a sixteenth note, is a beat division that characterizes the song, though it contains no specific rhythmic unit. This song begins on the third above the tonic and ends on the third in the lower octave. A beginning and ending on the dominant occurs more frequently than on the third of the scale. A majority of both Sioux and Chippewa songs end on the tonic, which is also the lowest tone in the song. (See Table 3A, p. 27.)

Throughout this part of the ceremony, the tree was viewed as an enemy, and a shout of victory rose as it swayed and fell. Care was taken to ensure it did not touch the ground. The medicine men, some of whom usually accompanied the party, burned sweet grass, and offerings were presented. The branches of the tree were cut off close to the trunk except for one branch about one-fourth of the distance from the top, which was left a few inches long so that the crossbar of the pole could be fastened to it. In some cases, a small branch with leaves on it was also left at the top of the pole. From this time on, the pole was regarded as sacred, and no one was allowed to step over it, or over any of the branches which had been cut from it. Jealousy frequently arose among the women regarding the privilege of cutting the tree, and it is said that on one occasion a woman was so angry because she was not chosen for the purpose that she stepped over the pole. Half an hour later, she was thrown from her horse, dragged some distance, and killed. The horse was known to be a gentle animal, and the event was considered a punishment justly visited upon the woman.

Between 20 and 40 men were required to carry the sacred pole to the camp. These men walked two abreast, each pair carrying between them a stick about 2 feet long on which the pole rested as if on a litter. The pole was carried with the top end in front, and the <term>Intercessor</term> or his representative walked behind the bearers. No one was allowed to walk before the sacred pole.

The songs for carrying the pole home were songs of victory. The following song could be used at any time after the pole had been cut and was frequently sung as it was carried to the camp:

*Analysis.*—The rhythmic unit of this song is less interesting than the rhythm of the song as a whole, which has a decided "swing." The melody begins on the fifth above the tonic and ends on the third in the lower octave. Many songs have a greater range than this, but few have a compass of a tenth in three measures, as occurs in this song with the introduction of the words. This part of the song was sung quite accurately, but in the measures containing the last two words and in the corresponding measures of the first section of the song, the intonation was so unsteady as to make transcription difficult. It has been frequently noted among the <term>Sioux</term>, as among the <term>Chippewa</term>, that large intervals are sung with more accuracy than small ones. The drumbeat was in half notes, representing a very slow tempo. In the double measures, the drumbeat coincided quite regularly with the corresponding tone of the song.

The tribe’s young men and women on their ponies circled the pole-bearers. It was the custom for these young people to decorate their ponies with trailing vines and to wreathe the vines around their own bodies. They made hoops from slender branches with crossbars, similar to the frame of a shield, and draped vines and leaves over them, creating a striking contrast to the dignified procession of the pole-bearers.

The pole-bearers were allowed to rest four times on the way to the camp (see p. 74). The <term>Intercessor</term> gave the signal for each halt—a throbbing call that began on a high tone and descended like a wail. At this signal, the pole was lowered for a few moments onto forked sticks provided for that purpose.

The <term>sacred pole</term> was brought into the <term>Sun-dance</term> circle in the same way it had been carried, with the top end in front. As the pole-bearers walked across the circle, the <term>medicine-men</term> cried, "Now is the time to make a wish or bring an offering." The people crowded forward, shouting and offering gifts of various kinds. Such great excitement broke out that no one knew who had brought a gift, and a person could scarcely hear their own voice.

The <term>Intercessor</term> then prepared the <term>sacred pole</term>, first removing the rough outer bark, fragments of which were eagerly seized and carried away by the people. After the pole was made sufficiently smooth, the <term>Intercessor</term> painted it; native red paint or vermilion ¹ was used. The pole was painted in vertical stripes, beginning at the branch where the crossbar would be fastened and extending down to the base.

As the <term>Intercessor</term> painted the <term>sacred pole</term>, he sang the following song. Like the other songs related to his ceremonial office, he sang it alone and without a drum while the people listened attentively:

---

¹ <note>A yellow ocher substance is found on the Standing Rock Reservation. After being ground into a fine powder, the Indians use it to make yellow paint. When heat-treated, this substance yields the vermilion used on all ceremonial objects and for painting their bodies. The women perform the skilled process of baking this ocher. First, the substance is mixed with water and formed into a ball. A hole is dug in the ground where a fire of oak bark is made. When the ground is hot, the coals are removed, the ball is placed in the hole, and a fire is built over it. This fire is kept at a steady, gentle heat for about an hour, which is sufficient for the amount usually prepared. The heat changes the substance's color to red. When the ball is cool, it is pounded into powder. In the past, this red powder was mixed with buffalo fat to make paint, but now it is mixed with water. White, black, and blue paints were made by mixing colored earth with buffalo fat. The blue was found in southern Minnesota (this needed no heat treatment), and the white and black in Dakota (see p. 173). White paint was reportedly preferred for painting horses (see p. 353) because it was a "genuine color" and provided a good base for other colors. Brown earth is mentioned in song No. 62. The symbolism of various colors used in paint is noted on pages 77 and 124.</note>

The sustained tones were always held for the full indicated time. The words are continuous throughout the song. on the pole, being securely fastened to the short branch left for the purpose. At the intersection of the pole and the crossbar, a bag was tied with rawhide thongs; this bag constituted one of the offerings made by the <term>Leader of the Dancers</term>. This bag was about 2 feet square, made of rawhide decorated with beads, tassels, and fringe, and was wrapped in cherry branches 4 or 5 feet long which completely concealed it. Inside the bag was a smaller bag of tanned buffalo hide containing the offering, which consisted of a large piece of buffalo hump on a sharpened stick painted red. The stick was made of cottonwood and, according to Mato'-kuwa' (Chased-by-Bears), symbolized the arrow with which the buffalo had been killed and also the picket stake to which a horse stolen from an enemy was fastened when it was being brought to the camp. The additional offerings fastened to the crossbar were two effigies (see pl. 21) cut from rawhide, one in the form of an Indian and the other in the form of a buffalo, indicating that the enemy and also the buffalo had been conquered by supernatural help. To the crossbar were also fastened the thongs, or cords, by which the men would be suspended. One cord was made ready for each man, with the middle of it being fastened to the crossbar and the two ends hanging down to be fastened to the sticks passed through the flesh of the man’s chest. At the top of the pole, a tanned robe of buffalo calfskin was hung. In the later ceremonies, a banner of red list cloth was used instead of the buffalo robe.

After painting the <term>sacred pole</term>, the <term>Intercessor</term> examined the hole which had been prepared for its erection, in which he placed an abundance of buffalo fat. It was said that, while doing this, he “prayed and talked in a low voice.”

The command to raise the pole was followed by absolute silence on the part of the assembled people. Thus they watched the pole as it was raised slowly and carefully by the men who had brought it to the camp. The moment it was in place, everyone broke into cheers and rejoicing, and the three following songs were sung. These three songs were recorded by a man said to be the only <term>Teton Sioux</term> living (1911) who had filled the office of <term>Intercessor</term>. These songs comprised part of the instructions he received from the man who preceded him in that office. The singer was about 80 years of age when the songs were recorded. (See p. 88.)

*Analysis.*—The conciseness of this melody is interesting, especially considering that it was sung by an elderly man who said he learned it in his youth. The rhythmic units are clear-cut, and their repetitions make up the entire song except for two short parts that are somewhat similar to each other. The author has noted this to be common among old men who, in their younger days, were accustomed to addressing large numbers of people on the open prairie. Red Weasel, who had held responsible positions in tribal ceremonies, had developed this vocal quality. In this connection, the pitch of his songs should be noted.

This melody contains all the tones of the octave except the seventh. In structure, it is classified as melodic with a harmonic framework. About two-thirds of the intervals are <note>likely a printer error for "are"</note> downward progressions, with the principal accented tones being those of the descending series A, F sharp, D, B, and F sharp. Only two ascending progressions appear between accented tones.

<note>¹ This is an example of the "sacred language" mentioned on page 85. A language of this kind was said to be necessary so that people familiar with supernatural things could communicate without being understood by common people. The term "center of the earth" appears in a narrative on page 214 and also in song No. 137, which is translated as follows: "At the center of the earth I stand . . . at the wind center (where the winds blow toward me from every side) I stand." Songs No. 16 and No. 75 mention the places from which the winds blow. The first contains the words "at the places of the four winds may you be respected," and the second says, "At the four places . . . the places from which the winds blow . . . I was required to stand;" it also mentions "the homes of the four winds" on page 127. The following examples may also be mentioned: An expression similar to this appears in song No. 93 — *ćante' mato'kećaća*, also translated as "with a heart that is different," but carrying the idea of a bear's fierceness. The term *yatin'kte*, literally translated as "you will eat," is a phrase used only by medicine men when addressing the sick (song No. 57). The words "a scarlet relic" in song No. 1 refer to the custom of spirit keeping and would not be understood by those who were unfamiliar with that ceremony. The term "grandfather" is found in No. 21, which is the opening prayer of the Sun Dance. The word *tuŋkaŋ'*, "sacred stones," is said to be derived from *tuŋka'sila*, "grandfather." (See page 205.) In songs No. 41, No. 93, and No. 105, there is something approaching the personification of a wind and a rainbow, the idea being that these possess or wear the man who has dreamed of them and has not</note>

*Analysis.*—This song contains two rhythmic units, but the rhythmic structure of the song differs from most songs analyzed in that these two units appear to have no influence on each other. The first is in triple time, the second in double time, and none of the beat divisions are the same. The song is melodic in structure and contains the tones of the fourth five-tone scale. The descending fourth from the tonic to the dominant occurs frequently.

### No. 16. Song Sung after Raising the Sacred Pole (c) (Catalogue No. 630)

->Sung by RED WEASEL<-

->VOICE <note>quarter note</note> = 76<-
->DRUM not recorded<-

<image-desc>Musical score for a vocal performance, transcribed on a five-line staff with a bass clef and a key signature of three sharps (F#, C#, G#). the melody is divided into five systems. ->WORDS (NOT TRANSCRIBED)<-

| | |
|---|---|
| tuŋka′śila | grandfather |
| to′pakiya | at the places of the four winds (see p. 120, footnote). |
| wakaŋ′ nila′pi nuŋwe′ | may you be revered |
| ta′ku koyag′ mayaye′ | you made me wear something sacred |
| oya′te waŋ wakaŋ′yaŋ yaŋka′pi | the tribe sitting in reverence |
| niwa′ćiŋpi | they wish to live |

[the medicine man has] yet enacted his dream, just as a medicine man wears an object, or the symbol of an object, which is under his command. Thus, No. 41 contains the words, “a wind wears me”; No. 93, “a wind comes to get me;” and No. 105, “a hoop (rainbow) wears me.” The term *wahu′noŋ′pa*, or its abbreviation *hu noŋ′pa*, literally “two-legged object,” is used by those who treat the sick to refer to a human being (Nos. 76, 90), and the term *ćaŋte′to′keća*, ‘a heart that is different,’ is used by them to indicate anger (Songs Nos. 58, 93). The phrases “in a sacred manner,” or “I have made it sacred,” are not unusual and cannot be considered an adequate translation of the Lakota. In the Sioux mind, the meaning of the word *wakaŋ* involves more mystery and a greater supernatural element than we usually associate with the words “sacred” or “holy,” though these are used as its English equivalent. (See footnote, p. 88.)

<meta>This page continues the musical analysis of the Sun Dance songs and describes the physical preparation of the ritual space and the sacred pole.</meta>

*Analysis.*—Two intervals of a fourth form the structure of this melody: the first is C—F and the second is G—C. The tonic (the first note of the scale) is especially prominent, as it occurs in both of these intervals and is frequently repeated. The song is in a minor key and contains only the tones of the minor triad and the fourth. The melody's repetitive nature is shown by the fact that it contains 27 measures but only 12 progressions. It has been noted that the average number of progressions in this class of songs is 31.3. The rhythmic unit occurs six times, and its rhythmic divisions were clearly performed by the singer.

The sacred pole was positioned so that the crossbar pointed north and south, and the earth was packed firmly around its base.

The dance enclosure was about 50 feet in diameter, with a wide entrance on the eastern side. (See p. 93.) The sacred pole stood in the center of this circle. About 15 feet west of the pole, a square of earth was cleared; all plants were carefully removed, and the ground was ground into a fine powder. This square of earth was called <term>owaŋ'ka wakaŋ'</term>, or "sacred place," and no one was permitted to walk between it and the pole.<note>1 Miss Fletcher states (in *Peabody Museum Reports*, III, p. 284, note, Cambridge, 1887): "The softened earth space... has been present in every Indian religious ceremony I have seen or heard of. It represents the untapped life or power of the earth, which people can then receive."</note> Two intersecting lines were drawn inside the earth square to form a cross; these lines were parallel to the sides of the square but did not touch them.<note>2 Regarding this design, which is widely used by Native Americans, Mr. W. H. Holmes writes (in *Handbook of American Indians*, part 1, p. 366): "Early man aligns himself with his environment, both real and imagined, by keeping the cardinal directions in mind as he understands them. When the Indian considers the world around him, he thinks of it as divided into four quarters. When he communicates with the mysterious beings and powers his imagination sees there—the rulers of the winds and rains—he turns his face to the four directions in a specific order to make his appeals and offerings. Thus, his worship, ceremonies, games, and even his more common tasks are often arranged to match the cardinal points, and the various symbols associated with them take the form of a cross."</note> After drawing these lines in the soil, the Intercessor filled the grooves with tobacco that had been offered to the sky, the earth, and the four directions. He then covered the tobacco with vermilion paint-powder and spread sparkling white "mica dust" over it.<note>3 A sample of the "mica" was collected and identified as "Gypsum, variety Selenite," by Dr. G. P. Merrill, curator of the department of geology at the U.S. National Museum.</note> At the intersection and ends of the lines, he placed bunches of soft white eagle feathers. The contrast between the green grass, soft brown earth, shining white lines, and fluffy eagle feathers was very beautiful. To the west of this, a bed of fresh sage was placed, where the buffalo skull would rest during the ceremony. (Plates 16, 17.)

The Intercessor sang the following song while preparing the sacred earth square. Whenever the Intercessor sang this or similar songs, the large gathering of people remained in absolute silence.

#### WORDS

| | |
|---|---|
| to’pakiya maka’ta će’waki yelo’ | I prayed to the earth four times |
| owaŋ’ka | a place |
| waka’ġiŋ kta ća | I will prepare |
| oya’te | O tribe |
| waŋla’ka pelo’ | behold |

*Analysis*—Every tone of the octave except for the fourth occurs in this melody, which has a minor tonality and a melodic structure. A sense of the tonic triad is evident throughout the song, though there is more freedom in the progression than in many of the other songs being analyzed. The second degree of the key is unusually prominent, and the progressions in the sixth and seventh measures are interesting, as they include the tonic along with the tones immediately above and below it. About two-thirds of the intervals consist of downward progressions.

After the sacred pole was erected and the "sacred place" was prepared, a shelter, or "shade-house," was built entirely around the Sun Dance circle. Anyone who wished to help with this work was permitted to do so. Posts about 6 feet high were set up, and a light framework of poles was placed upon them. This framework was covered with buffalo hides and decorated with freshly cut branches. The elders, the relatives of the dancers, and anyone who attended the ceremony simply as a spectator sat beneath this shade.

On the morning of the Sun Dance, those who were to participate in the ceremony were allowed to eat a full meal. After this, they entered the vapor lodge while the following song was sung:

*Analysis.*—This song consists of 20 measures and contains only 15 progressions. In its limited melodic movement, it resembles songs 14, 15, and 16, which were performed by the same singer. (Refer to the analysis of No. 16.) Two-thirds of the progressions move downward; the song begins on the dominant note above the tonic and concludes on the dominant below the tonic. The melody utilizes the tones of the second five-tone scale and follows a melodic structure.

After their vapor bath, the dancers were painted by the men they had chosen for that purpose. A few of the author's informants stated that the bodies of the dancers were painted white on the first day of the ceremony, with colors added on the morning of the second day. However, others—including <term>Ituŋ'kasaŋ-lu'ta</term> (Red Weasel)—stated firmly that the color painting was completed before the dance began. <term>Red Bird</term> explained that every man who typically painted the dancers had a specific color "associated with his dream," and he used this color first during the painting. The colors used were red (the "tribal color"), blue, yellow, white, and black, with each color carrying symbolism related to the sky. For instance, it was said that red corresponds to the red clouds of sunset, which signal fair weather; blue represents the cloudless sky; yellow represents forked lightning; and white corresponds to the
