light; and black was used for everything associated with night, even the moon being painted black because it belonged to the hours of darkness. <note>See p. 77, footnote.</note>

Śiya'ka (Teal Duck) stated that when he took part in the Sun Dance, his face and body were painted yellow, with dark-blue lines extending down his arms and branching at the wrist into lines that ended at the base of the thumb and the little finger. Similar lines extended down his legs, branching at the ankles. There was also a dark-blue line across his forehead and down each cheek. A black deer's head was painted over his mouth; the man who painted him said he used this decoration because the deer could endure thirst for a long time without losing its strength. On his chest was painted a red disk representing the sun, and outlining this disk he wore a wooden hoop wound with otter fur and decorated with four white eagle feathers tipped with black. <note>See p. 139.</note> On his back was painted a dark crescent representing the moon. Bands of rabbit fur were worn around his wrists and ankles.

Those who took part in the Sun Dance wore their hair loose on their shoulders, in the style of men who had recently killed an enemy. A lock of hair was tied at the back of the head, and a white downy eagle feather was fastened upright to it. Small sticks about 8 inches long were also fastened in the hair, four being the usual number. These sticks were decorated with porcupine quills, beads, and tassels. (Fig. 22.) A dancer was not allowed to touch his body during the ceremony; the decorated sticks were taken from his hair and used for that purpose.

The dancers wore no moccasins. Each man wore a white deerskin apron (<term>nite'iyapehe</term>), which was fastened at the waist and extended below the knees in both the front and back; he also had a robe of buffalo skin in which he was wrapped while going to the Sun Dance circle and returning to his lodge. A whistle was hung around his neck by a cord. This whistle was made from the wing bone of an eagle, wound with braided porcupine quills and tipped with a downy white eagle feather fastened above the opening so that the dancer’s breath moved the snowy filaments. The mouthpiece was surrounded with fresh sage. The man blew this whistle as he danced. The instrument (illustrated in plate 18) was decorated by the woman who decorated the Sun Dance pipe.<note>The bone of this whistle was identified at the U.S. National Museum as the ulna of the golden eagle (*Aquila chrysaetos*). The specimen is described as follows by Mr. E. H. Hawley, curator of musical instruments: "Length, 8 inches; average diameter, 7/16 inch. It has a triangular sound hole, with its apex toward the lower or open end, which is 4 1/8 inches away. To the lower end of the whistle, a fluffy eagle feather 13 3/4 inches long is sewn with sinew. This feather grows under the tail feathers of an eagle." (Compare with p. 98.)</note>

After being painted and dressed, the men who were to take part in the ceremony assembled in the dancers' lodges of their respective bands and awaited the summons of the Crier.

The Leader of the Dancers was with the Intercessor in the council tent. His costume was not necessarily different from those of the other dancers. Chased-by-Bears stated that when he acted as the Leader of the Dancers, he was painted white with black streaks across his forehead and down his cheeks. The deerskin <term>nite'iyapehe</term> that he wore was elaborately crafted with porcupine quills by his female relatives, who wanted to do the work even though such decoration was not required.

The costume worn by an Intercessor was somewhat similar to that of the dancers, but on his wrists and ankles he frequently wore bands of buffalo skin on which the hair was coming loose, and his robe was the hide of a buffalo killed at the time when it was shedding its coat. Bits of hair shed by the buffalo were tied to his own hair (see pp. 64, 458), and he wore buffalo horns on his head, or he might wear a strip of buffalo skin fastened to his hair and hanging down his back. (See plate 19.) In contrast to the dancers, his hair was braided, but like them, he wore one white downy eagle feather. His face and hands were painted red. 

<image-desc>A drawing of a long, thin stick decorated for the Sun dance. The top of the stick features two tufts of light-colored downy feathers attached with dark bindings. The upper portion of the stick's shaft is decorated with many closely spaced dark rings or wrappings.</image-desc>
->FIG. 22. Decorated stick worn in Sun dance.<-

The costume of an Intercessor varied slightly depending on the individual; Red Weasel stated that he wore otter skin around his wrists and ankles, that his hair braids were wrapped with otter skin, and that he wore a shirt of buffalo hide trimmed with human hair, which was intended to represent the hair of an enemy.

On the morning of the day set for the Sun Dance, the Crier went around the camp circle, announcing the opening of the ceremony with the following words: 

> "Wana' u po. Wana' yuśtanpe. Inah'ni po!" ("Now everyone come. Now it is ready. Hurry!")

## CEREMONIAL GROUPING OF ARTICLES IN THE SUN DANCE

<summary>This page features a plate illustrating the ritual arrangement of sacred objects and a marked ceremonial site used during the Sun Dance.</summary>
<keywords>Sun Dance, ceremonial grouping, Bureau of American Ethnology, ritual objects, indigenous ceremony, sacred site</keywords>

--- Page 191 ---
<meta>This page continues the detailed description of the Sun Dance ritual, following the visual reference of Plate 20. It documents the ceremonial procession into the sacred circle and the specific ritual actions involving the buffalo skull and the sacred pipes.</meta>

<header>DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC</header>

The Sun Dance pipe would be smoked during the ceremony. The Leader of the Dancers walked beside the Intercessor, carrying the ceremonial buffalo skull, which had been painted with red stripes extending from the nostrils to the horns. Near him walked a close relative or friend, who carried the Leader's sealed pipe; this would later be placed with the buffalo skull beside the square of exposed earth. Those who were to fulfill their vows walked on either side of the Intercessor and the Leader of the Dancers, surrounded by the war societies and other organizations of the tribe. Upon reaching the entrance of the Sun Dance circle, the procession paused. The Intercessor directed the people's attention to the east, and it was understood that each man offered a silent prayer. This action was repeated toward the south, the west, and the north, after which they entered the enclosure. Amid an impressive silence, the procession passed along the southern "side" of the circle to the western "side." There, the Leader of the Dancers paused and laid the buffalo skull on the bed of sage, with its face toward the east. He then placed his sealed pipe in its ceremonial position, with the bowl resting on the buffalo skull and the stem supported by a small frame of sticks painted blue (see pages 64, 72). The mouthpiece of the pipe was pointed toward the Sun Dance pole (plate 20). When the Intercessor rose to sing or pray, he held this pipe in his hand, afterward replacing it in its ceremonial position. It was also pointed toward the sky, the earth, and the cardinal points, but the seal on it was not broken until after the ceremony.

The pipe which was smoked at the ceremony belonged to the Intercessor. He first burned sweet grass, the ascending smoke of which was said to symbolize prayer.<note>See the article on Incense by James Mooney in the Handbook of American Indians, part 1, page 604.</note> Then he lit the pipe and pointed the stem toward the sky, the earth, and the cardinal points. The following explanation of this action was given by <term>Wakin'yan-wata'-kpe</term> (Charging Thunder):

> "When we hold the pipe toward the sky, we are offering it to <term>Wakan'tanka</term>. We offer it to the earth because that is our home and we are thankful to be here; we offer it to the east, south, west, and north because those are the homes of the four winds. A storm may come from any direction; therefore, we wish to make peace with the winds that bring the storms."

After this action, the Intercessor, having first smoked the pipe himself, offered it to the Leader and all the dancers. This procedure was repeated at infrequent intervals throughout the duration of the dancing.

Beside the Sun Dance pole, the men who were to fulfill their vows stood facing the sun with their hands raised. The Intercessor cried, "Repent, repent!"<note>Certain features of the ceremony seem to show the influence of Christian teaching. See the footnote on page 88.</note> whereupon a cry of lamentation rose from the entire assembly.

<summary>This page describes the ritual procession into the Sun Dance circle and the symbolic presentation of the buffalo skull and sacred pipes to the four directions. It explains the spiritual significance of offering the pipe to Wakan'tanka and the winds to ensure peace and express gratitude.</summary>

<keywords>Sun Dance, Intercessor, buffalo skull, Charging Thunder, Wakan'tanka, ceremonial pipe, sweet grass, four winds, ritual prayer, Sioux music</keywords>

The opening song of the ceremony was sung three times with a tremolo drumbeat, after which the drum changed to a definite, even stroke, and the men began to dance with their faces still turned toward the sun and with hands upraised.

In songs expressing desire, it is common for the tempo to increase as the song is repeated (see page 481). Consequently, the second tempo in this instance is faster than the first. Comparing the two parts of the transcription, we see that important phrases remain consistent while minor changes occur in less important phrases—a characteristic that has been frequently observed in the musical performances of both the Chippewa and the Sioux. In contrast, there are other instances where multiple performances of a song are identical in every way.

This song is transcribed and analyzed in the key of D minor, though the second and fifth notes of that key are not present. The melody is broadly outlined by the descending intervals F–C, C–F, and F–D, with a return to F at the close. One accidental occurs—the fourth is lowered by a semitone. The number of downward and upward intervals is nearly equal, with 25 of the former and 22 of the latter in the song.

## No. 20. Opening Song of the Sun Dance (b) (Catalogue No. 479)

->Sung by LONE MAN<-

**VOICE** <note>quarter note</note> = 80
**DRUM** <note>quarter note</note> = 84
Drum-rhythm similar to No. 19

<image-desc>Musical notation for "Opening Song of the Sun Dance (b)" in bass clef. The key signature shows one flat (B-flat) and the initial time signature is 2/4. The melody is comprised of three staves of music featuring eighth and sixteenth note rhythms. There are mid-staff time signature changes to 3/4 and then back to 2/4. Brackets above several groups of notes indicate specific rhythmic units.</image-desc>

*Analysis.*—The rhythmic unit appears twice at the beginning of this song; the latter part of the song features an accented sixteenth note in several measures but offers little rhythmic variety. The purpose of this later section seems to be merely to carry the melody down to the final note. The melody spans a range of 13 tones. Only 11 percent of Chippewa songs have a range greater than 12 tones, and a similar range is found in only 10 percent of the current series (see Table 5A, page 28). This song has a minor tonality, missing only the sixth tone of the complete octave.

During the excitement of the opening dance, many gifts were given to the poor or exchanged among the people, and many individuals "paid their respects" to the parents of young men who were participating in the dance for the first time.

The drum used in the Sun Dance was placed south of the pole. It was a large dance drum of the typical style and was elaborately decorated; its sides were hung with beadwork and fur, and its supports were wound with beads and fur. In addition to the drum, a stiff rawhide was beaten. This gave the accompaniment of the songs a distinct tonal quality, which distinguished it from ordinary dances and marked it as a religious ceremony. The men who had carried the sacred pole were seated at the drum and the rawhide, along with special singers, both men and women. The women sat behind the men, forming an outer circle. The voices of the women singers were an octave higher than the voices of the men.

The Intercessor sat west of the "sacred place" during the entire ceremony. The Leader of the Dancers was with the others who were fulfilling their vows, but during the brief rest periods allowed to the dancers, he lay on the ground to the west of the "sacred place," face downward, with his head pressed against the top of the buffalo skull. (See p. 97.)

The man who had spoken the vow for a war party took on some responsibility for the correct fulfillment of their vows, and the dancers were attended by the men who had painted them. Everyone who participated in the dance was required to go without food and water during the entire period of dancing.

At the end of the opening dance, the Intercessor sang the following prayer while all the people listened reverently:

*Analysis.*—This melody is given unique strength because a quarter note is the shortest note appearing in the rhythmic unit. The timing of the sustained tones was accurate in every performance. Two-thirds of the progressions are downward; the melody begins on the fifth above the tonic and ends on the third in the lower octave. All the tones of the octave are found in the song, which has a minor tonality and melodic structure. The words are continuous. As already stated, continuous words are found most frequently in songs connected with “medicine.”

A man might take part in the Sun Dance in one of six ways, depending on the nature of his vow. The requirement of fasting was the same for every vow. The first way of taking part in the Sun Dance consisted merely of dancing; the second added a cutting of the flesh; and the other four required that a stick be thrust through the flesh and tension placed upon it until the flesh tore or was cut. The Indians stated that the stick, or skewer, was “put through the skin,” and it probably also pierced the subcutaneous fascia. <note>Since the word “skin” is commonly applied to the outer layer, the word “flesh” is used in this chapter to indicate more clearly the severity of the ordeal.</note> The two most common forms of this treatment consisted of piercing the flesh over the chest with skewers attached by cords to the crossbar of the sacred pole, and fastening buffalo skulls to the flesh of the back and arms. The two more severe and less frequent forms were the suspending of the entire body by the flesh of the back, and the fastening of the flesh of both the back and chest to four poles at some distance from the body, with the poles being placed at the corners of a square. <note>In this connection, it should be kept in mind that this account concerns only the customs of the Teton Sioux, as described by members of that tribe who took part in the dance.</note>

If a horse had carried a man on the warpath when his vow was made, the man might fasten the horse to the thong by which he was suspended from the pole, thus hastening his release; or he might fasten the bridle and whip which he carried on in a similar manner—

the warpath, or he might hold the bridle and whip in his hand as he danced. Chased-by-Bears stated that in fulfilling his first Sun Dance vow, he had a skewer put through the flesh of his arm; from it, he suspended the rawhide lariat that he carried when on the warpath, and with which he later captured a horse. (See p. 97.)

Women sometimes took part in the Sun Dance by fasting and standing beside a relative who was dancing, or by assuming part of the obligation of a vow made by a relative and allowing their own arms to be cut. (See p. 135.) The gifts distributed by the dancers' relatives and the feasts given in their honor were also the work of the women.

Even the simplest form of the Sun Dance was a severe test of a man's endurance. He was required to abstain from food and water, to dance with his face raised toward the sun from morning until night, and to continue dancing during the night and throughout the following day until he fell exhausted.<note>1 Intervals permitted for rest are noted on p. 134.</note>

If he had vowed to have his arms cut, he left the line of dancers and sat beside the pole for the procedure, after which he resumed his dancing. The number of cuts varied from 10 to 100 or even 200, according to the man's vow. However, if the vow required the larger numbers mentioned, part of that total was usually assumed by his relatives. The cutting was performed by an experienced man, to whom the dancer gave one or more horses. This man had an assistant who lifted a small portion of flesh on the point of an awl, and the man then severed it with a quick stroke of a knife. He lifted the first portion he cut toward the sky, saying, "This man promised to give you his flesh; he now fulfills his vow." (See p. 96.) The cuts were usually placed close together. The writer has seen the scars of a man whose arms were cut 100 times—small dots on the upper arm, about half an inch apart, in regular order.

Another method of cutting the arm was by gashes, which left broad white scars. As already stated, a man's relatives might assume part of the obligation of his vow by allowing their own arms to be cut. For example, Lone Man said that he vowed 200 gashes, but his relatives divided half the number among themselves.

If a man vowed that he would be suspended from the pole, the procedure for fastening the thongs to his chest was as follows: The dancer lay on the ground, and the man who performed the procedure, bending over him, lifted the flesh of the chest between his thumb and finger. Then, thrusting an awl through the flesh, he followed this by inserting a pointed stick. This stick was painted blue, and the man moistened it with his lips before inserting it into the flesh. He then lifted the dancer to his feet and tied the thongs hanging from the crossbar of the pole to the sticks in the man's flesh. Medicine was applied if the bleeding was excessive. In the old days, the awl used in this procedure was made of bone. Chased-by-Bears, who performed this—

<sig>4840°—Bull. 61—18——11</sig>

...ceremonial role many times in the <term>Sun dance</term>, stated that he used a knife with a blade sharpened to a point, and the handle and part of the blade were wrapped with <term>rawhide</term> (Plate 21).

The thongs by which a man was suspended were usually long enough to allow only his toes to touch the ground, though the height of the suspension depended somewhat on the man's physical strength. When first suspended, each man was given a stick he could use to raise his body slightly to ease the strain on the flesh of his chest. After discarding this support, any attempt to rest or any stopping of the dancing motion only increased the suffering.

The men were suspended soon after 9 o'clock in the morning on the north side of the pole, in a position where their upturned faces were in the full glare of the sun. It was expected that they would make an effort to free themselves as soon as possible. Sometimes this was achieved in half an hour, and according to <term>John Grass</term> and other informants, a man rarely remained in that position for more than an hour. If he was unable to tear the flesh in that time through the motion of dancing, he might offer horses for his release, or his relatives might offer them on his behalf. In that event, the man who had performed the cutting was allowed to cut through the flesh either partially or entirely. If a significant amount of time passed and the man could not free himself, and neither he nor his relatives could provide the required horses, he was jerked downward until the flesh gave way. While suspended, each man held his <term>eagle-bone whistle</term> in his mouth, blowing it from time to time.

If a man vowed to participate in the <term>Sun dance</term> by carrying <term>buffalo skulls</term>, the number varied from two to eight. If two were used, they were fastened to the flesh of the upper back near the spine. After the flesh was lifted with an awl, a small stick was inserted. A thong of buffalo hide was fastened to this stick, and the other end of the thong was passed through the nasal openings of the <term>buffalo skull</term>, suspending it some distance from the ground. The man then danced until the tearing of the flesh released the skull. If four skulls were used, the additional pair was fastened to the back, halfway between the spine and the point of the shoulder. With six skulls, the third pair was fastened to the upper arm. If more than six were used, the additional skulls were fastened anywhere on the upper back; it was also permitted to fasten more than one skull to a single thong. When several skulls were used, their weight made it impossible for a man to stand upright; therefore, the man had to lean forward on a stick, dancing in a bowed position. The scales showed a weight of 25 pounds for a <term>buffalo skull</term> obtained by the writer. The skull was shown to <term>Chased-by-Bears</term>, who, after lifting it, said that although the specimen was a large one, it was not unusual for men to carry such skulls in the <term>Sun dance</term>.

<meta>This page continues the detailed description of the physical trials and spiritual motivations associated with the Sun Dance ritual, specifically detailing the various forms of suspension and the communal nature of the dancers' prayers.</meta>

### BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61

Buffalo Boy stated that he carried six buffalo skulls for four or five hours, after which he was set free when the flesh they were hanging from was cut. This occurred after the required number of horses were given for his release.

A more severe form of torture involved hanging the body entirely off the ground using leather thongs passed through the flesh on each side of the lower back. Seizes-the-Gun-away-from-Them described an instance where a man rode a horse to the sacred pole and was suspended by his back, after which the horse was led away. The most extreme form of torture was suspending the body between four poles using thongs passed through the flesh of both the chest and the back. The body hung in such a way that only the toes touched the ground. Under these conditions, the flesh did not tear as easily. John Grass stated that a man was known to remain in that position from one morning until the evening of the next day, until gifts were given for his release.

While the men were dancing, they "prayed for everyone in the tribe, especially the sick and the elderly." Red Bird said:

> The warriors went to war to protect the tribe and its hunting grounds. All the people shared in this benefit, so when the warrior fulfilled his vow, he wanted the whole tribe to share in its rewards. He believed that <term>Wakan'taŋka</term> is more ready to grant the prayers of those who make and keep their vows than of those who are careless about their duties. He also believed that an act performed in public is more effective than the same thing done in private. So, when a man was fulfilling his vow, he prayed for all the members of the tribe and for all branches of the tribe, wherever they might be.

As soon as a man enduring torture was set free by the tearing of his flesh, it was customary to apply a powdered medicine to the wound. It was said that the wounds healed quickly, and infections or even swelling were unknown. The author saw many <term>Sun-dance</term> scars, which appeared slight considering the severity of the ordeal.

After the medicine was applied, the man returned to his place with the dancers, continuing his fast and dancing until he was exhausted. During the dancing, the men who painted the dancers would occasionally offer a pipe, holding the bowl while the dancer puffed; they also placed the dancer's whistle into his mouth, as participants were not allowed to touch any objects while they were dancing.

Each man stayed in one place as he danced, simply turning so that he constantly faced the sun, toward which he raised his face. While dancing, he raised himself on the balls of his feet with rhythmic regularity. Every few hours, the men at the drum were allowed to rest, and the dancers could stand in their places or even sit down and smoke for a short time. However, if they showed any hesitation in starting the dance again, they were forced to their feet by the men who performed the cutting and oversaw the fulfillment of the vows.

<summary>This page describes various methods of ritual suspension during the Sun Dance and explains that the participants' suffering and prayers were intended to benefit the entire tribe. It also details the post-ritual care for wounds and the strict rules dancers followed regarding physical contact and facing the sun.</summary>

Women whose relatives were fulfilling vows frequently danced beside them for part of the time. White Robe (Taśi'na-skawiŋ), the singer of the following song, stated that she composed it while taking part in a Sun Dance in which her brother was fulfilling a vow. As the result of a successful raid against the Crow Indians, he brought home many horses, which were divided among his relatives; she received a portion of them. He had vowed that if he were successful, he would be suspended from the pole and would also have 200 cuts made on his arms. She and her sister took on half of this number, each having her arms cut 50 times. She and his other female relatives danced while he was dancing, and she sang this song spontaneously; it was quickly learned and sung by all the women:

<page-num>136</page-num>

This is one of the songs in the group that was composed or sung by a woman. One accidental note occurs—the fourth is raised by a semitone. The way this accidental is used introduces two intervals, one of which seems particularly difficult for a native singer: the minor second. The other interval is the augmented fourth, heard in the descent from D-sharp to A. All these intervals, as well as the octave ascent, were sung with good intonation. The song has a minor tonality and a free melodic structure.

The elderly members of the tribe sat comfortably in the "shade house" on the outer edge of the dancing circle. There, they listened attentively to everything that took place; indeed, everyone who attended showed the greatest reverence and respect for the ceremony. The spectators realized that when prayer was offered by the Intercessor, "it was their duty to join in his prayer with their hearts."

Meanwhile, many events were occurring throughout the great tribal gathering. Those who were happy invited others to rejoice with them, while others joined their friends in mourning chiefs who had died during the year or warriors who had been killed by the enemy. The relatives of those who took part in the <term>Sun Dance</term> provided feasts, and small groups could be seen feasting here and there in the camp while, at the same time, songs of lamentation could be heard. The following song was used at a <term>Sun Dance</term> to commemorate <term>Kaṅġi'-iyo'take</term> (Sitting Crow), a <term>Sioux</term> warrior who was killed in a fight with the <term>Crows</term>. The words of this song are a warrior's best memorial.

->Sung by LONE MAN<-

### WORDS

| | |
|----------|----------|
| <term>Kaṅġiʹ-iyoʹtake</term> | Sitting Crow (man’s name) |
| heʹc'el yuṅkiṅʹ kte hícin | that is the way he wished to lie |
| ec'el yuṅkaʹ he | he is lying as he desired |

*Analysis.*—Five renditions of this song were recorded, and they are entirely uniform. The upward progressions in the measure containing the first word are interesting, as is the upward progression necessary when beginning a repetition of the song. These intervals were sung with good intonation. From the author’s observation, an Indian singer may vary the pitch of unimportant intervals but very rarely loses the pitch of what might be called the “outline” of a melody. In structure, this song is freely melodic, yet the tonic triad is felt throughout. The minor third occurs frequently and constitutes 37 percent of the total number of intervals. The melody tones follow the second five-toned scale.

Even children had a part in the <term>Sun Dance</term>, which involved the piercing of their ears. This was frequently done to fulfill a vow made by their parents; for instance, if a child was ill, the parents might vow that if the child lived until the next <term>Sun Dance</term>, their ears would be pierced. This was considered an honor, and the required gifts made it impossible for poorer members of the tribe to participate. The piercing of the ears was done publicly by any experienced person—in some instances by the <term>Intercessor</term>, assisted by those who cut the arms of people fulfilling vows at the ceremony. The parents of the child gave gifts to those who pierced the ears, with the gifts varying according to their means. Some gave one horse, some ten horses, and wealthy individuals added large and valuable presents of goods to show their affection for the child. A wealthy family also provided rich furs on which the child was laid during the operation—soft robes of otter, beaver, or buffalo, elaborately decorated on the inner side with beads or porcupine quills. They also brought a pillow filled with the soft hair scraped from a deer’s hide or the down of cat-tail reeds that grow in the marshes. All these articles were left in place after being used and were collected by the poor of the tribe.

The piercing of the ear was originally done with a bone awl, which was later replaced by a metal one. After the puncture, a piece of copper was inserted so that the wound would heal rapidly. One or both ears might be pierced, and if desired, more than one hole was made in each ear.

The children whose ears were pierced in this way were considered to have a status similar to the men whose flesh was lacerated in the <term>Sun Dance</term>, and their relatives gave feasts in honor of the event.

It details the musical structure of the song and the social and material aspects of the childhood rite, including the distribution of gifts to the poor.</summary>

The following song was sung by the <term>Intercessor</term> during one of the periods when the drummers rested; the people listened attentively. In explanation of this song, Red Bird said:

> This is a song concerning a dream of an <term>Intercessor</term>. In his dream, he saw the rising sun with rays streaming out around it. He made an ornament which represented this. At first, he alone wore it, but afterwards others wore the same ornament. <note>See p. 89.</note> It is a hoop with feathers fastened lightly to it. The hoop represents the sun, and the feathers fastened to it are feathers of the eagle, which is the bird of day, the crane, which is the bird of night, and the hawk, which is the surest bird of prey.

*Analysis.*—In many songs, the rhythmic unit is merely a short phrase that is incomplete by itself, but which appears frequently throughout the melody and influences the rhythmic divisions of the entire piece. The song currently being analyzed, however, contains a rhythmic unit that is complete in itself and was sung with a clear "phrase perception." Repetitions of this unit make up the entire song except for the closing measure. The melody tones belong to the fourth five-toned scale. The only intervals found here are the major second and minor third. Descending intervals make up about two-thirds of the total number.

The songs performed during the hours of dancing are particularly rhythmic; the following are examples. These songs were not used exclusively in the Sun Dance; some of them were songs belonging to various War societies.

*Analysis.*—The distinct minor character of this song is interesting. The fourth and seventh tones of the octave are missing from the melody. Note that these are the same tones omitted from the fourth five-toned scale, which has a major tonality; in contrast, this song has a minor tonality, as the third and sixth are minor intervals. This tonal material is found in four Chippewa songs (see Table 6A) and is discussed in Bulletin 53 (p. 188). Similar songs in this current series are numbers 73, 89, 115, 126, and 194. The interval of the fourth is prominent, making up about one-quarter of the total number of intervals. Two rhythmic units occur, but they do not resemble each other. It has been noted that when several rhythmic units appear in a song, they usually share some common characteristics.

*Analysis.*—An interesting feature of this song is the E–D–E progression, which shows a whole tone between the seventh and eighth notes of a minor key. ### No. 29. Dancing Song (a) (Catalogue No. 499)

->Sung by Red Bird<-

Voice <term>♩</term> = 80
Drum <term>♩</term> = 60
Drum-rhythm similar to No. 6

<image-desc>Musical notation for "Dancing Song (a)" written in bass clef. The key signature has two sharps. The score consists of two systems of melody lines. *Analysis.*—A notable feature of this song is the difference in tempo between the voice and the drum. Occasionally the two coincided on the first beat of a measure, but this appears to have been accidental, as the two parts are entirely distinct. (See the analysis of No. 8.) The vocal timing is not strictly maintained, though the variations are neither significant nor regular enough to be indicated except on the E, which was shortened in every performance and is marked as such in the transcription. The structure of the melody is more regular than that of most of the songs being analyzed. It consists of three periods of four measures each, with one additional measure after the second period. The melody tones belong to the fourth five-toned scale, and two-thirds of the progressions are downward.

### No. 30. Dancing Song (b) (Catalogue No. 505)

->Sung by RED BIRD<-

**VOICE** <term>♩</term> = 80
**DRUM** <term>♩</term> = 80
Drum-rhythm similar to No. 8.

<image-desc>A musical score for a "Dancing Song" written in five staves of bass clef. The key signature contains two sharps (F# and C#). Time signatures vary between 2/4, 3/4, and 4/4 throughout the piece. Small numbers in parentheses — (1) through (5) — are placed above the staff to denote specific rhythmic units. The score consists of melodic phrases with repetitive rhythmic patterns, primarily eighth and sixteenth notes.</image-desc>

*Analysis.*—The rhythmic division that characterizes this song consists of two sixteenth notes followed by an eighth note. This is combined with other divisions of a quarter note to form five distinct phrases of one measure each. The repetition of these short phrases, or <term>rhythmic units</term>, makes up the entire song except for the closing measure. The first rhythmic unit occurs twice, the second three times, the third three times, the fourth six times, and the fifth twice. The irregular order of these phrases prevents them from being grouped into musical periods, but the rhythm of the song as a whole is complete and interesting. In structure, the song is harmonic, with the principal tones being those of the <term>tonic triad</term>. All the tones of the octave except the fourth are found in the melody. An ascent of 11 tones in two measures is noted in the seventh and eighth measures before the end. The small rhythmic divisions were clearly produced by the unique throat technique that characterizes Indian singing. <note>See Bulletin 53, p. 13.</note> Half of the intervals (19) are <term>major seconds</term>, and all but two of these occur in a descending progression.

## No. 33. **Dancing Song (e)** (Catalogue No. 457)

->Sung by ŚIYA'KA<-

**VOICE** <term>♩</term> = 176
**DRUM** <term>♩</term> = 176
Drum-rhythm similar to No. 6

<image-desc>A musical transcription of "Dancing Song (e)" presented in four staves. The music is written in bass clef with a key signature of one flat (B♭). The time signature alternates between 2/4 and 3/4. Rhythmic units within the melody are identified with horizontal brackets above the staff, numbered (1), (2), and (3). The melody consists of eighth, quarter, and dotted quarter notes.</image-desc>

*Analysis.*—This melody is transcribed in the key of <term>D minor</term>, but in the opening phrases and also near the end of the song, there is a feeling of “<term>interval formation</term>” <note>the specific arrangement of musical intervals to build a melody</note> which is stronger than the feeling for a <term>keynote</term> or its related <term>chords</term>. These parts of the song are based on the descending <term>interval of a fourth</term>. (See p. 418 of this work, and also Bulletin 53, p. 99.) Two <term>rhythmic units</term> occur in the song, with the second reversing the beat divisions of the first. The <term>drumbeat</term> in this song, as in the preceding one, is a rapid <term>tremolo</term> during the opening measures, before changing to the rhythm indicated in the transcription. About 45 percent of the intervals are <term>major seconds</term> <note>a musical interval of a whole tone, such as the distance between C and D</note>.

On the second day, the men were allowed a brief intermission; they could even return to their lodges, but they were not permitted to take food or water. During this day, the men fell from exhaustion one after another. Red Bird (Plate 22) said that he had a vision during the <term>Sun Dance</term>. On the second day, while he was dancing, he noticed that the <term>Intercessor</term> held a small mirror in his hand and that he reflected the light from this mirror into the face of one dancer after another, with each man falling to the ground when it flashed into his eyes. At last, Red Bird felt the flash of light in his own face and fell unconscious. Then he saw something in the sun; it was a man’s face, painted, and as he looked at it, he saw that the man in the sun was the <term>Intercessor</term>. It was said that this vision was sufficient to entitle Red Bird to act as <term>Intercessor</term> himself, after he had received the proper instructions concerning the duties of that office.

As soon as a man fell from exhaustion, he was carried into the shade, where he gradually regained consciousness.

Those who had taken part in the <term>Sun Dance</term> returned to their respective lodges at the close of the dancing. Before consuming food or water, they spent some time in the <term>vapor lodge</term> <note>a ceremonial sweat lodge</note>. Their first sip of water was taken in the following manner: a large bowl was filled with water, and a bunch of sweetgrass was placed beside it. After dipping this into the water, the dancer placed it to his lips. He was then given a small piece of cooked buffalo meat and later sat down to a meal that was spread in his own lodge.

When the entire ceremony was finished, the <term>Intercessor</term> took the pipe given by the <term>Leader of the Dancers</term> from its ceremonial position and carried it to his own lodge. There, he broke the seal of buffalo

Among the Indians discussed here, the camp had to be broken before the evening of the second day. The sacred pole and its offerings, the red-painted buffalo skull, and the bits of white eagle down remained on the prairie. As the last man left the camping ground, he looked back and saw them in their places. Then he left them with Wakaŋ'taŋka and the silent prairie.

After the people reached their homes, the boys of the tribe began a childish enactment of the Sun Dance, which continued at intervals during the entire summer. Boys whose fathers or grandfathers had taken part in the ceremony were given preference in the assignment of roles. Mr. Robert P. Higheagle, the interpreter, stated that he well remembered the gravity with which the grandson of an <term>Intercessor</term> imitated the actions of that official. A fine was required from any boy who failed to do his part in the proper manner, or who showed disrespect toward the performance. Whistles in imitation of Sun Dance whistles were made of reeds (see fig. 23), the plumy blossom representing the eagle down, and long red and green grasses being wound around the reed in imitation of the porcupine-quill decoration.

Through the summer woods, the boys searched for wild grapes and berries with which to color their bodies and their decorations.

Removing the outer bark from trees, they took long, thin layers of the inner bark for streamers, coloring them with the juice of grapes and berries. The tree for their sacred pole was carefully selected and was brought home with much pomp and ceremony. Boys with good voices were assigned the role of singers and sat around an old pan. A hoop was sometimes covered with a bright handkerchief or cloth; this more closely resembled the Sun Dance drum in appearance, but the pan was considered more satisfying. The ritual torture was imitated by thrusting a stiff cactus spine through a boy's skin; this was fastened to the pole with a very fragile thread. When his dancing movements broke this thread, the boy was considered released.

In this way, the boys of the tribe were trained through play to become the men of the future.

The children's desire to imitate the actions of their elders is further illustrated by the children's Games of War found in Bulletin 53, pages 137–139. These games included a mock fight by the boys, while the little girls sang of relatives who had been wounded while on the warpath.

<summary>Teton Sioux children performed a detailed imitation of the Sun Dance and "Games of War" to prepare for their future adult roles in the tribe. These activities included creating ceremonial objects from natural materials and mimicking the ritual's physical trials and songs of warfare.</summary>

## DREAMS AND THEIR OBLIGATIONS

The obligation of a dream was as binding as the necessity of fulfilling a vow, and the disregard of either was said to be punished by the forces of nature, usually by a stroke of lightning. Dreams were sought by the Sioux, but it was recognized that a dream would correspond to the character of the man. Thus, it was said that "a young man would not be great in mind, so his dream would not be like that of a chief; it would be ordinary in kind, yet he would still have to do whatever the dream directed him to do." The first obligation of a dream was usually its announcement to the tribe. This was done by means of a performance which indicated the nature of the dream and allied the man with others who had similar dreams. If the dream was connected with the sacred stones, or with herbs or animals concerned with the treatment of the sick, it was considered mandatory that the man use the supernatural aid granted to him in the dream and arrange his life in accordance with it.

Below are three groups of dream songs which, as noted among the Chippewa as well as the Sioux, are songs believed to be received supernaturally in dreams. The first of these groups comprises the songs of the Heyo'ka (dreamers of the thunderbird) and songs of those who dreamed of birds or animals. The numbers of these songs are 37–58, inclusive; with few exceptions, they were recorded by the men who received them in their dreams. Two other groups follow; these comprise songs of the sacred stones and songs connected with the treatment of the sick.

### HEYO'KA KA'GA (FOOL IMPERSONATION)

A dream of the thunderbirds <note>1</note> was considered the greatest honor which could come to a man from a supernatural source, and for this reason, the obligation of the dream was heavier than that of any other.

The manner in which the thunderbirds are regarded was indicated by Shooter, who said:

> Dreamers have told us of these great birds in the sky, wrapped in the clouds. If the bear and other vicious beasts are regarded as dangerous, how much more should we fear the thunderbirds that cause destruction on the face of the earth. It is said that the thunderbirds once came to the earth in the form of giants. These giants did

---

<note>1: The thunderbirds (*wakin'yan*) are defined by Riggs as "the cause of thunder and lightning, supposed by the Dakota to be a great bird." (See *Contr. N. Amer. Ethn.*, vii, p. 514, 1890). Compare the article "Thunder-bird" by Dr. J. R. Swanton, in *Handbook of American Indians*, part 2, 1910.</note>

<summary>This page explains the spiritual obligations the Sioux attached to dreams, noting that dreams must be publicly performed and obeyed. It introduces the Heyo'ka, or those who dream of the thunderbirds, as having the highest and most serious supernatural obligations.</summary>
<keywords>Sioux, dream songs, Heyo'ka, thunderbirds, wakin'yan, Shooter, spiritual obligation, dream performance, Dakota, supernatural aid</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Heyo'ka Ka'ga, moving from the general obligation of dreams to the specific mythology of the thunderbirds and the social role of the "fool" or "clown" in Teton Sioux culture.</meta>

# BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61]

amazing things, such as digging the ditches where the rivers run. At last they died of old age, and their spirits returned to the clouds and resumed their form as thunderbirds. While they were on earth, the rain fell without the sound of thunder or the flash of lightning, but after their return to the sky the lightning came—it is the flash of their eyes, and the thunder is the sound of their terrible song. When they are angry, the lightning strikes a rock or tree as a warning to men. The bodies of these giants turned to stone, and parts of them are found in many places; in fact, the entire bodies of more than one of these giants have been found in the land of the Dakotas.

The *Heyo'ka Ka'ga* was a ceremony of public humiliation in which the man who had been selected by the thunderbirds to receive a manifestation of their presence in a dream voluntarily exposed himself to the ridicule of the lowest element in the tribe. <note>1</note> His self-abasement was exaggerated to the greatest possible degree. The superficial and unthinking heaped their scorn and derision upon him, but the wise members of the tribe understood that, for the rest of his life, that man could command the powers of the sky to help him in his undertakings. In the opinion of the author's informants, acting the part of a fool in connection with a thunderbird dream was an example of the antithesis through which Indians sometimes disguise their meaning. In this, it might be said to resemble the "sacred language" (see p. 120, footnote), which is incomprehensible to those who are not initiated into its mysteries.

Several of the author's informants, after consultation, gave the following meanings (or uses) for the word *heyo'ka*: A man who has dreamed of the thunderbirds; a person who does things contrary to the natural way of doing them; and, in some instances, a joker. Regarding the ceremony to fulfill a thunderbird dream, the word is translated as "fool," because only a foolish or half-witted person would behave, under such circumstances, in the manner assumed by the dreamer, while the merriment provoked by the action gives rise to the term "clown." The author's informants stated that in their youth they had never heard of *heyo'ka* being regarded as gods by the Teton Sioux. In their opinion, the *heyo'ka* resembled characters in the field of folk tales rather than in religion. Holding the opposite view, both Riggs and Pond enumerate *heyo'ka* among the Dakota gods. <note>2</note> The reason for the author's informants not regarding *heyo'ka* as gods seemed to be that they are not credited with supernatural power. Writing on this subject, J. Owen Dorsey says: <note>3</note> "Dr. Brinton has confused the Heyoka with the Wakinyan. <note>4</note> The two are distinct classes of powers, though there is some connection between them, as may be inferred from the

Dorsey then relates the story of a *heyo'ka* man who predicted the time of his death and was killed by lightning as he rode on his horse pointing the stem of his pipe toward the clouds; also the story of a *heyo'ka* woman who was killed by lightning. Further, he quotes Bushotter as saying—

> Women used to dream about the Thunder-beings, just as the men did, and in those dreams the *heyo'ka* man or woman made promises to the Thunder-beings. If the dreamers kept their promises, it was thought that the Thunder-beings helped them to obtain whatever things they desired; but if they broke their promises, they were sure to be killed by the Thunder-beings during some storm.

Riggs states further that—

> The nature of the *Ha yo'-ka* is the very opposite of nature. He expresses joy by sighs and groans . . . and sorrow and pain by the opposite sounds and looks. Heat causes his flesh to shiver . . . while cold makes him perspire. In the coldest weather, when the mercury freezes, these gods seek some prominence on the prairie, where they put up bushes to shield themselves as they swelter with heat. . . . They feel perfect confidence when beset with dangers, and quake with fear when safe.

In his Dakota Dictionary, Riggs (under *Heyo'ka*) says: "*Heyo'ka* is represented as a little old man with a cocked hat on his head, a bow and arrows in his hands, and a quiver on his back. In winter he goes naked, and in summer he wraps his buffalo-robe about him." "The little hills on the prairie are . . . the houses of *Heyo'ka*." Mythical "little men" enter into the beliefs of many tribes of Indians. Thus among the White River Ute, on the Uinta Reservation in Utah, the writer was informed of "little green men," who lived in the mountains and often appeared to the Indians, telling them of "medicines" and teaching them songs. <note>1</note>

Two dreams of the thunderbirds were related to the writer, one by Lone Man (pl. 23); followed by an account of the *Heyo'ka* ceremony in fulfillment of his dream, the other by Charging Thunder (see p. 170), this dream being the source of his name, which is literally translated "Charger-of-the-Thunderbird." In describing his dream Lone Man said:

"One day when I was on the warpath I sat down to rest and was at some distance from the other members of the party. I looked up at the sky and the rolling clouds. I fell asleep, and while I slept I had a dream. My face was toward the west, and I heard thunder in that direction. There was a sound of hoofs, and I saw nine riders coming toward me in a cloud, each man on a horse of a different color. Then I heard a sound in the north and saw nine riders coming toward me from that direction, each on a white horse. They joined the riders from the west and came toward me. One of them spoke to me, and said they had appointed me to make the first attack upon the enemy. He said the man to be attacked was painted red and was standing in the water, and he said that if I could conquer that man I would gain something which would be useful to me all the rest of my life. Then a voice from among the company of riders said that, having been appointed to make this attack, I would be considered

> Ho tuŋka’śila ake’ nita’olo’waŋ waŋźi’ awa’hiyayiŋ kta éa taŋyaŋ’ an’am ag’optaŋ yo. Lena’ aŋpe’tu iyo’hi waŋźig’źi kiksu’ye mayaśi’ koŋ lehaŋl’ aŋpe’tu kiŋ waŋźi’ wek’suyiŋ ktelo’.

Analysis.—The opening of this melody is unusual, consisting of a descent from the fifth to the second of a minor key. In the third measure, the third of the key appears; the tonic enters in the sixth measure, followed by five measures in which the tonic and third are emphasized. Two descending fourths (A–E and E–B) carry the melody down toward the tonic in the lower octave, which is given as the closing tone. The melody includes all the tones of the octave except the seventh. It will be noted that the opening tones of the song contain the beginning of the rhythmic unit, which appears in complete form in the succeeding measures and occurs three times in the song.

### Continuing his narrative, Lone Man said:

Before the riders in the cloud went away, they gave me a charm (*<term>wo'tahe</term>*), which I always carried. If I were in great danger and escaped alive, I attributed it to the charm and sang a song in its honor. The song relates to the swallow, whose flight precedes a thunderstorm. When I sang the song of my charm, I fastened the skin of a swallow on my head. This bird is so closely related to the thunderbird that the thunderbird is honored by its use. The movements of a swallow are very agile. The greatest aid to a warrior is a good horse, and what a warrior desires most for his horse is that it may be as swift as the swallow in dodging the enemy or in direct flight.<note>See footnote 3, page 71.</note> For this reason, my song is in honor of the swallow as well as of my charm.

*Analysis.*—The rhythm of this song shows remarkable clarity of concept. There are two rhythmic units, and the entire song is composed of their repetitions. The order of their occurrence is irregular, but this feature seems to give an interesting unity to the rhythm of the song as a whole. The tones of the melody are those of the fourth five-toned scale. The tempo of the drum indicates four drumbeats to one melody note, and this proportion was maintained during most of the melody, with the drum and voice coinciding on the first part of each count. As in many other melodies of the present series, the downward progressions comprise about two-thirds of the total number.

Resuming the story of his dream, Lone Man said:

> After my return to the camp, I wanted to do something to show that I realized I was unworthy of the honor given to me by the thunderbirds. No one told me that I ought to do this, and yet all who dream of the thunderbirds in any of their forms have a deep sense of their own unworthiness. I knew that I was only an ordinary mortal and had often done wrong, yet the riders in the air had disregarded this. By appearing to me, they had given me a chance to redeem myself. I wanted to perform an act of public humility to show how deeply I realized my unworthiness. I wanted to do as others had done who saw the thunderbirds in their dreams, so I composed the following song.

*Analysis.*—This song contains several points of unusual interest. First among these is its range of 14 tones, beginning on the fourteenth above the tonic and ending on the tonic. (See Table 5.) We also note the upward progression of a tenth, which is found midway through the song and again at the beginning of the repeated part. The low tone at the close of the song (G-flat) was sung accurately in some instances, while in others the singer found difficulty in reaching it and sang it slightly sharp. It is strange that a song characterized by a range of almost two octaves and by one particularly large interval also contains an unusual number of minor seconds—the smallest interval recognized in these analyses. Many songs do not contain even one minor second, but in this melody 18 (44 percent) of the total number of intervals are minor seconds. The song contains all the tones of the octave and is melodic in structure.

As already stated, the ceremony called *Heyo'ka Ka'ga* is a ceremony of public humiliation and is performed chiefly by those who have dreamed of the thunderbirds. A man is required to be the leader in only one such ceremony, but when other thunderbird dreamers are performing the ceremony for themselves, he is expected to join them. If a man who has seen the thunderbird in a dream becomes arrogant or fails to express his unworthiness, it is said that Wakaŋ'taŋka would punish him through the power of some of the great forces of nature. Thus, every man who has been favored with this wonderful dream tries to demonstrate that, in his own estimation, he is the humblest in the tribe. A man signals his intention of performing this ceremony by placing a decorated robe, tobacco, or some other offering to the thunderbirds high on the poles of his tent. All who see such offerings know that the man intends to fulfill the obligations of his dream at the earliest opportunity, after which he will feel free to mingle with his relatives and friends.

The ceremony may be held at any time after the thunderstorms begin in the spring. In fulfilling the obligation of his dream, Lone Man set up a tent within the tribal circle that only the poorest member of the tribe would use; in this, as in other ways, he followed the custom of the ceremony. The tent was often ragged, and its furnishings were always of the lowest quality. On the day of the ceremony, he dressed himself in the poorest garments.

        ### Lone Man said:
        A man performing this ceremony often tied a bundle of grass or sage to the lock of hair over his forehead, wearing this just as a warrior would wear his medicine. Some were so humble that they covered their faces. It was the custom for a man to go with his head bare, and he often had his face painted in black and white, or blue and white, with his arms and legs painted with streaks of lightning. If a man wished to express the greatest possible humiliation and did not feel that he could even go through the ceremony, he cut off part of his hair and placed it with the entire body of a dog that had been killed for the purpose; both were placed on a pole beside his lodge.

        The man who was to show his humiliation hired a medicine man to be in charge of the ceremony. For this, he selected a man who had had many dreams of the wolf, horse, and other animals, and compensated him generously, probably by giving him a horse.

        On the appointed day, the Crier announced to the tribe that a certain man (giving his name) had had a dream of the thunderbird and wished to fulfill the dream, and that he requested all who had had similar dreams to join him in the ceremony of humiliation. Sometimes women also had these dreams, and they were under the same obligations as the men.

        The medicine man led the dreamer, who wore tattered clothes, out of his tent. If the man were rich, a horse was ready for him to ride, one was provided for the medicine man, and his relatives accompanied him on horseback as he went around the tribal circle, followed by a jeering crowd who treated the matter as a joke. On their return, they dismounted, sang, and told their dreams. A fire was burning in front of the specially built tent, and a pot of boiling water was hung over the fire. For this pot, the man provided as valuable an offering of meat as he could afford; this might be a buffalo tongue, and sometimes a dog was given. He did not put this into the pot himself, but gave it to the medicine man, who held it toward the west, then toward the north, east, and south as he sang of his own dreams and also told the dreams of the man who was expressing his humiliation. He then turned toward the pot and pretended that he would throw the meat into it. He did this three times, and the fourth time he released the meat <note>see p. 74</note>, which sped through the air, falling into the pot without splashing the water. All who joined him in the ceremony put some meat in the pot. These constituted an offering to the thunderbird and were symbolic.

### Lone Man said:

A man performing this ceremony often tied a bundle of grass or sage to the lock of hair over his forehead, wearing this just as a warrior would wear his medicine. Some were so humble that they covered their faces. It was the custom for a man to go with a bare head, and he often had his face painted in black and white, or blue and white, with his arms and legs painted with streaks of lightning. If a man wished to express the greatest possible humiliation and did not feel that he could even go through the ceremony, he cut off part of his hair and placed it with the entire body of a dog that had been killed for the purpose; both were placed on a pole beside his lodge.

The man who was to show his humiliation engaged the services of a <term>medicine man</term> to be in charge of the ceremony. For this, he selected a man who had had many dreams of the wolf, horse, and other animals, and compensated him generously, probably by giving him a horse.

On the appointed day, the Crier announced to the tribe that a certain man (giving his name) had had a dream of the <term>thunderbird</term> and wished to fulfill the dream, and that he requested all who had had similar dreams to join him in the ceremony of humiliation. Sometimes women also had these dreams, and they were under the same obligations as the men.

The <term>medicine man</term> led the dreamer, dressed in tattered clothes, out of his tent. If the man was wealthy, a horse was ready for him to ride, one was provided for the <term>medicine man</term>, and his relatives accompanied him on horseback as he went around the tribal circle, followed by a jeering crowd who treated the matter as a joke. On their return, they dismounted, sang, and told their dreams. A fire was burning in front of the specially erected tent, and a pot of boiling water was hung over the fire. For this pot, the man provided as valuable an offering of meat as he could afford; this might be a buffalo tongue, and sometimes a dog was given. He did not put this into the pot himself, but gave it to the <term>medicine man</term>, who held it toward the west, then toward the north, east, and south as he sang of his own dreams and also told the dreams of the man who was making his humiliation. He then turned toward the pot and pretended that he would throw the meat into it. He did this three times, and the fourth time he released the meat <note>see p. 74</note>, which sped through the air, falling into the pot without splashing the water. All who joined him in the ceremony put some meat in the pot. These constituted an offering to the <term>thunderbird</term> and were symbolic.

which were rubbed on the hands and arms. A specimen of the herb most often used for this purpose was secured by the writer and was identified as *Malvastrum coccineum* A. Gray <note>commonly known as scarlet globe mallow</note>.

The man for whom the ceremony was given was the first to put his hand into the boiling water, and it was expected that he would try to take out the piece of meat he had put into the pot. He did not eat it himself but gave it to someone in the assembly. The other dreamers followed him, and the meat was distributed. No other food was eaten at the time, and the occasion was not regarded as a feast. It was a ceremony enacted to teach a great lesson. Ignorant persons or children laughed at the tattered garments and the actions of the dreamers, who in every movement attempted to imitate persons not only poor but lacking in judgment. All intelligent members of the tribe, however, regarded the ceremony with greatest reverence.

This and the following song were sung by Lone Man when enacting his part in this ceremony. The words of the song require explanation. From the time of a dream until the time when the dreamer has fulfilled its requirements, he regards himself as belonging to the elements and under an obligation of obedience to them. A medicine man may wear the head of a bird as a sign of his power, indicating that bird to be subject to his commands. So in this song, the elements are said to be "wearing" the singer, who has not yet fulfilled his obligations to them. In the second rendition of the song, the word meaning "wind" was replaced by *wasu'ća* <note>hail</note>; in the third by *wakaŋ'glića* <note>lightning</note>; and in the fourth by *mahpi'ya* <note>clouds</note>.

*Analysis.*—This song contains only the tones B-flat, C, and F and is transcribed in the key of B-flat, as the sequence of tones, especially at the end of the song, suggests B-flat as a keynote that is pleasing to the ear. Sixteen progressions occur in the song, seven of which are fourths and eight of which are major seconds. This melody is an excellent example of how a rhythmic unit influences parts of the song where it is not actually found, as the count divisions of the second measure of the unit appear frequently throughout the melody.

Charging Thunder (plate 24) recounted his dream of the thunderbirds, in which, as in Lone Man's dream, they took the form of men riding horses. From this dream, he received his name *Wakiŋ'yaŋ wata'kpe*. This is literally translated as "Charger-of-the-Thunderbird," though he is commonly called Charging Thunder. His earlier dreams about the wolf and the buffalo are described on pages 181–184.

In telling his dream of the thunderbird, Charging Thunder said:

> Shortly after the Standing Rock Agency was established, I asked the agent (an Army officer) if I might go hunting. I said that before I settled down and adopted the ways of the white man, I would like to go hunting for an unspecified amount of time. Permission was granted, and I went out alone. As I was traveling north, near Timber Lake, I saw a deer coming toward me from the north. I wanted to shoot the animal but decided to wait until it came closer. The deer must have been moving very slowly, for while I was waiting, I fell asleep and dreamed. In this dream, I saw the deer still coming toward me, and behind it were several men riding painted horses with grass tied on their forelocks. The riders seemed to be chasing something. I became one of these riders, and they told me to lead the group. Then they told me to charge at the object they were pursuing. At first, I was not sure what it was, but I soon saw it was a wolf standing toward the west with its face toward the north. I was chosen to do this because one day I would need the protection of these riders, who were thunderbirds that had taken human form. They told me that because I had

*Analysis.*—This song contains only the tones B-flat, C, and F. It is transcribed in the key of B-flat because the sequence of tones, especially at the end of the song, suggests B-flat is a keynote that is pleasing to the ear. Sixteen progressions occur in the song, seven of which are fourths and eight of which are major seconds. This melody is an excellent example of how a rhythmic unit influences parts of the song where it is not actually found, as the count divisions of the second measure of the unit appear frequently throughout the melody.

### DREAMS CONCERNING ANIMALS

A dream concerning an animal was greatly desired by the Sioux. Brave Buffalo (see pp. 207 and following, 248 and following) said:

> I have noticed throughout my life that all men have a liking for some special animal, tree, plant, or spot of earth. If men would pay more attention to these preferences and seek the best way to make themselves worthy of that toward which they are so attracted, they might have dreams which would purify their lives. Let a man decide upon his favorite animal and make a study of it, learning its innocent ways. Let him learn to understand its sounds and motions. The animals want to communicate with man, but <term>Wakaŋ'taŋka</term> does not intend for them to do so directly—man must do the greater part in securing an understanding.

This suggests that a fondness for a certain animal preceded a dream concerning it.

Shooter, a thoughtful man and well-versed in the old customs, made the following statement, given in the words of Mr. Higheagle, the interpreter:

> All living creatures and all plants derive their life from the sun. If it were not for the sun, there would be darkness and nothing could grow—the earth would be without life. Yet the sun must have the help of the earth. If the sun alone were to act upon animals and plants, the heat would be so great that they would die, but there are clouds that bring rain, and the action of the sun and earth together supplies the moisture that is needed for life. The roots of a plant go down, and the deeper they go the more moisture they find. This is according to the laws of nature and is one of the evidences of the wisdom of <term>Wakaŋ'taŋka</term>. Plants are sent by <term>Wakaŋ'taŋka</term> and come from the ground at his command; the part to be affected by the sun and rain appears above the ground and the roots press downward to find the moisture which is supplied for them. Animals and plants are taught by <term>Wakaŋ'taŋka</term> what they are to do. <term>Wakaŋ'taŋka</term> teaches the birds to make nests, yet the nests of all birds are not alike. <term>Wakaŋ'taŋka</term> gives them merely the outline. Some make better nests than others. In the same way, some animals are satisfied with very rough dwellings, while others make attractive places in which to live. Some animals also take better care of their young than others. The forest is the home of many birds and other animals, and the water is the home of fish and reptiles. All birds, even those of the same species, are not alike, and it is the same with animals and with human beings. The reason <term>Wakaŋ'taŋka</term> does not make two birds, or animals, or human beings exactly alike is because each is placed here by <term>Wakaŋ'taŋka</term> to be an independent individual and to rely on itself. Some animals are made to live in the ground. The stones and the minerals are placed in the ground by <term>Wakaŋ'taŋka</term>, with some stones being more exposed than others. When a medicine-man says that he talks with the sacred stones, it is because of all the substances in the ground, these are the ones which most often appear in dreams and are able to communicate with men.
> 
> Not all animals have the same disposition. The horse, dog, bear, and buffalo all have their own characteristics. This is also true of the birds of the air, the living creatures in the water, and even the insects; they all have their own ways. Thus a man may enjoy the singing of all the birds and yet have a preference for the melodies

of certain kinds of birds. Or he may like all animals and yet have a favorite among them.

From my boyhood I have observed leaves, trees, and grass, and I have never found two alike. They may have a general likeness, but on examination I have found that they differ slightly. Plants are of different families, each being adapted to growth in a certain locality. It is the same with human beings; there is some place which is best adapted to each. The seeds of the plants are blown about by the wind until they reach the place where they will grow best—where the action of the sun and the presence of moisture are most favorable to them—and there they take root and grow. All living creatures and all plants are a benefit to something. Certain animals fulfill their purpose by definite acts. The crows, buzzards, and flies are somewhat similar in their use, and even the snakes have a purpose for being. In the early days, the animals probably roamed over a very wide country until they found their proper place. An animal depends a great deal on the natural conditions around it. If the buffalo were here today, I think they would be different from the buffalo of the old days because all the natural conditions have changed. They would not find the same food nor the same surroundings. We see the change in our ponies. In the old days, they could stand great hardship and travel long distances without water. They lived on certain kinds of food and drank pure water. Now our horses require a mixture of food; they have less endurance and must have constant care. It is the same with the Indians; they have less freedom and they fall easy prey to disease. In the old days, they were rugged and healthy, drinking pure water and eating the meat of the buffalo, which had a wide range, not being shut up like cattle of the present day. The water of the Missouri River is not pure as it used to be, and many of the creeks are no longer good for us to drink.

A man ought to desire that which is genuine instead of that which is artificial. <note>See pages 205, 330.</note> Long ago there was no such thing as a mixture of earths to make paint. There were only three colors of native earth paint—red, white, and black. <note>See page 116, footnote, which includes blue, obtained from blue clay found in Minnesota. The above list evidently includes only those colors found in the country of the Teton Sioux.</note> These could be obtained only in certain places. When other colors were desired, the Indians mixed the juices of plants, but it was found that these mixed colors faded, and one could always tell when the red was genuine—the red made of burned clay.

Four men told their personal dreams of animals and sang the songs which, they said, were received by them in these dreams. Brave Buffalo related his dreams of the buffalo, elk, and wolves; Charging Thunder, his dream of the wolves; and **Śiya'ka**, his dream of the crow and the owl. (Dreams of the thunderbirds by Lone Man and Charging Thunder are contained in the preceding section on the **Heyo'ka**.) The following group comprises, in addition to narratives by the dreamers, certain accounts of dreams and their songs which were given by men who had heard them related by others, and also a few dream songs whose history is unknown.

When I was 10 years old, I dreamed a dream, and in my dream a buffalo appeared to me. I dreamed that I was in the mountains and fell asleep in the shade of a tree.

Something shook my blanket. It was a buffalo who said, “Rise and follow me.” I obeyed. He took a path, and I followed him. The path was above the ground; we did not touch the earth. The path led upward and was smooth like polished black rock. It was a narrow path, just wide enough for us to travel. We went upward a long distance and came to a tent made of buffalo hide, its door facing us. Two buffalo came out of the tent and escorted me inside. I found the tent filled with buffalo and was placed in the middle of them.

The chief buffalo told me that I had been chosen to represent them in life. He said the buffalo play a larger part in life than men realize, and so that I might understand the buffalo better day by day, they gave me a plain stick (or cane) and told me that when I looked at it, I should remember that I had been appointed to represent them. The cane was like the one I carry now and have carried for many years. I would not part with this cane for any amount of money. <note>See plate 25, in which Brave Buffalo is depicted leaning on his staff.</note>

<header>DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC</header>

*Analysis.*—This song is made up of five sections; four of these use the same rhythmic pattern, while one uses a different rhythm. Looking at the structure of the melody, we see that the first section has three measures and is built on the minor triad of B-flat, D-flat, and F, with the notes appearing in descending order. In the fourth measure, the accidental B-double-flat leads down to A-flat. For several measures, the melody stays within the descending minor third of A-flat to F. This is followed by a return to the minor triad in the higher octave, a descent to A, and a reappearance of the accidental note. The song ends with the descending minor third of A-flat to F. There are five different tones in the melody, and the tonality is clearly major. The way the tones are arranged suggests D-flat as the keynote; therefore, the song is written down and analyzed in the key of D-flat with one accidental—the sixth note of the scale lowered by a half-step. It is worth noting the intervals used in this song. The number of times they occur is as follows: minor sixth, 1; major third, 3; minor third, 9; major second, 7; and minor second, 9—making a total of 29 intervals. It is clear that about 65 percent of the intervals are minor. We have often noticed a high number of minor intervals in songs with a major tonality. <note>See Bulletin 53, page 263.</note> It should be remembered that the minor second is a relatively rare interval in Sioux songs. <note>Compare with the analysis of Song No. 40.</note> The pitch of the notes written as B-double-flat and A-flat was not always perfectly exact, but the singer clearly distinguished between the tones in every performance. Three versions were recorded, and all showed the same carefulness found in the singer's next song. The drum and the voice did not hit the beats at the same time, even though they shared the same basic tempo.

Continuing his story, Brave Buffalo said:

> The buffalo in my dream told me that I would live to be 102 years old. Then they said: “If you are to show people the great value of the buffalo, one proof you must give them is a demonstration of your endurance. After properly preparing yourself, you will be able to show that weapons cannot harm you. You may then challenge anyone to shoot you with arrows or with a gun.”

Brave Buffalo said that when he woke from his dream, he went home and thought about the matter seriously. After preparing himself for the trial, he asked his relatives to set up a very large tent of buffalo hide. Inside, he would give his demonstration and challenge anyone to shoot him with arrows. He dressed himself in an entire buffalo hide, including the head and the horns. The whole tribe came to see if anyone could wound him. Many tried with arrows, but they could not hurt him; the arrows did not pierce his skin. Several years later, the test was repeated with guns, and Brave Buffalo stated that they were still not able to injure him.

## DREAMS CONCERNING THE ELK

A dream of the elk has a peculiar significance. The elk is a favorite animal among the young men. Shooter explained this as follows:

> The best part of a man’s life is between the ages of 18 and 33. During this time, he is at his peak. He has the strength and ability to achieve his goals. He is brave enough to defend himself and others and is free to do much good. He is kind to everyone, especially to the poor and needy. The tribe looks to him as a protector, and he is expected to shield the women. His physical strength is at its greatest. He is light on his feet and can cover long distances quickly. He is taught true politeness and is very gallant. What animal has these traits more than any other? It is the elk, which is the emblem of beauty, gallantry, and protection. The elk lives in the forest and is in harmony with all his beautiful surroundings. He moves easily through the thickets, despite his broad, branching antlers. In observing the remains of an elk, it is found that two teeth remain after everything else has crumbled to dust. These teeth will last longer than the life of a man, and for that reason, the elk tooth has become the emblem of long life. We desire long life for ourselves and our friends. When a child is born, its parents desire a long life for it, and for that reason, an elk tooth is given to a child if its parents can afford the gift.

Brave Buffalo gave the following narrative regarding his dream of the elk:

When I was about 25 years old, I was able to think for myself. I was not afraid to go into the woods, onto a mountain, or into any dangerous place. At that time I was at my
