I was at my best in health and worthiness, for I had behaved correctly in my youth, fulfilling everything required of a boy and young man and living in a way that honored my parents and grandparents. I had a clean record when I dreamed of the elk.

The dream came to me while I was asleep in a tent. Someone came to the door of the tent. He said he had come for me, and I rose and followed him. It was a long and difficult journey, but eventually he led me to a beautiful lodge. All the surroundings were beautiful. The lodge was painted yellow on the outside, and the door faced the southeast. Upon entering the lodge, I saw drawings on the walls. To the right of the entrance was a drawing of a crane holding a pipe with the stem pointing upward, and to the left was a drawing of a crow holding a pipe with the stem pointing downward. I could see that the inhabitants of the lodge were living happily and in luxury. I was guided to the seat of honor across from the entrance and reached it with difficulty, as the lodge was filled with brush and I was not accustomed to making my way through thickets. <note>At this point the inhabitants of the lodge seem to have been recognized as elks.¹</note> The elks in the lodge watched me with interest and encouraged me to go on, saying they had something they wanted to tell me. Finally, I managed to reach the seat assigned to me, and when I was seated, the elks rose and said they had heard that I was a great friend of the buffalo and that they wanted me to be their friend as well. They said they had tested me by requiring me to reach this difficult place, and since I had succeeded in doing so, they were glad to receive me. They then said that they were going to sing a song and wanted me to learn it. They sang the following song, which contains no words.

### No. 46. Song of the Elks (Catalogue No. 609)

->Sung by BRAVE BUFFALO<-

<image-desc>Musical score for "Song of the Elks" set in the bass clef with a key signature of B-flat major. The melody is presented in four systems of notation. The time signature alternates between 3/4 and 2/4. The piece features many descending melodic figures using eighth and sixteenth notes, with several instances of fermatas over sustained notes. Rhythmic variations include triplets in the third system.</image-desc>

*Analysis.*—The descending fourths E-flat—B-flat and B-flat—F are prominent in the framework of this melody, though the interval is usually broken, with the progressions being a major second followed by a minor third. The interval of a fourth in songs concerning animals has been frequently noted. (See Bulletin 53, p. 101.) One interval of a minor second occurs in the song, but it was sung too wide. It has been observed that the minor second is found less frequently than

The song is in a major second and seems to be sung with difficulty. The melody contains all the tones of the octave except the sixth and seventh.

After teaching Brave Buffalo this song, the elks gave him many instructions. He noticed that every elk had a soft white eagle feather tied to its right horn to show that it could run as fast as an eagle flies. He was told to wear a similar feather on his head, and at the time of giving this account, he had a soft eagle plume fastened to the right side of his felt hat. (See p. 248.) The elks told him to paint his tipi in a way similar to theirs: yellow on the outside with drawings of the crane and the crow on its inner walls, saying that these birds would protect him. He has always followed this style of painting his tipi. The elks further told him that before he would be fully entitled to ask them for help, he must perform a ceremony he devised himself to show the people that he was acting under their protection.

On reaching home, Brave Buffalo made a mask of elk hide, using the skin from the head along with the horns. He then painted himself yellow and held a hoop in each hand, which was wound with elk hide and decorated with an herb that elks like very much. <note>This hoop is mentioned in Song 105, and its symbolism is described there.</note> A specimen of this herb was collected and identified as *Monarda mollis L.*, commonly known as wild bergamot. This was used by the young men mainly because of its fragrance. Another variety of this "elk herb" was used by Eagle Shield in his medical practice. (See p. 270.) Brave Buffalo also made a hoop (pl. 26), which he said was similar to the one he carried when performing his dream. Since the flowers of the "elk herb" were not then in season, he used flowers that looked as much like them as possible, as well as whatever fur was available.

Brave Buffalo said that after dressing himself as described, he went around the camp, passing close to the tents. Two young women walked ahead of him, carrying his pipe. As he was making this circuit and imitating the actions of the elk, a thought occurred to him:

> "Now I have done everything as I was directed to do, and I wish I might show these people that I have the power of the elk. There is a spot of damp ground before me. I wish that when I step on this damp ground, I may leave the footprints of an elk."

A crowd of people followed him, and after he had passed over this spot, they saw the footprints of an elk instead of those of a man.

He was not required to repeat this proof, but if another elk dreamer were giving a similar performance and asked him to join, he would do so, wearing the same mask as on the first occasion. (See p. 166.) During a performance of an elk dream, no woman is

Brave Buffalo stated that after this demonstration, the elks gave him the power to find medicinal herbs. At the present time, if he is in doubt about what herb to use in treating a sick person, he appeals to the elks, and they tell him what to use and where to find it.

The emblem of the elk is a circle, exemplified by the hoop which an elk dreamer carries in his hand when “acting out his dream.” The young men wear a hair ornament consisting of a small hoop wound with porcupine quills and having a downy white eagle feather suspended in the center. The fastening is from the center of the hoop so that the ornament hangs lightly above the ear.

### DREAMS CONCERNING THE WOLF

Brave Buffalo stated that about two years after his dream of the elk, he had a dream of a wolf. This dream came to him as he was hunting alone. He had been wandering for several days in search of game when he met a pack of wolves. They formed a circle around him, and as they stood looking at him, he noticed that their nostrils and paws were painted red. They came toward him, at which point he grew dizzy. When they reached him, he was unconscious. They stood around him until he regained his senses; then they moved on, telling him to follow them. They led the way to a wolf den on top of a high hill. While he was there, more wolves came out of the hole, painted like the others. The wolves have always been wanderers, not knowing where they would find food. They knew he had been hunting and had had much difficulty in finding game, and they wanted to help him. They said there was a certain herb which, if dried, would enable him to catch all kinds of snakes. He was told to dry this herb and put it on the ground where the snakes are accustomed to come. He did so and caught a live rattlesnake. The wolves told him to carry this live snake when giving the demonstration of his wolf dream. Instead of the mask of elk hide which he wore in his former demonstration, he used a similar mask of wolf skin, wearing practically the entire hide <note>Compare with the wearing of a wolf hide by warriors, page 388.</note> and carrying in his hand a bent stick somewhat resembling a bow, which was painted red. A duplicate of this stick made by Brave Buffalo for the author is shown in plate 28. Brave Buffalo stated that he carried this and the snake in the same hand, with the snake coiling itself around the bow. He held the snake close to its head during the demonstration and let it go after the demonstration was closed. The

*Analysis.*—This melody as a whole is of unusual interest. Three performances were recorded on one cylinder; these show no variations. Three performances recorded at a later time were found to be identical. The intonation is not as good as in other songs by the same singer; an uncertainty, or wavering of the tone, occurs at the same point in all the performances. The customary “calls” or “cries” were given between the repetitions of the song. About one-fourth of the intervals are minor seconds which, as already noted, are found less frequently than major seconds in both Chippewa and Sioux songs.

Some medicine-men consider the owl especially sacred among birds. Two reasons were given for this by an Indian, who said:

> The owl moves at night when men are asleep. The medicine-man gets his power through dreams at night and believes that his dream is clear, like the owl’s vision. So he promises that he will never harm an owl. If he did so, his power would leave him. For this reason, some medicine-men wear owl feathers. The medicine-man also regards the owl as having very soft, gentle ways, and when he begins to treat sick persons, he is supposed to treat them very gently. So in night wisdom and in the manner of carrying itself, the owl is greatly respected by the medicine-men of the tribe.

Charging Thunder had three dreams of animals. The first was the dream of the thunderbirds, from which he received his name (see pp. 170, 171); the second was a dream of wolves, which is described here; and the third was a dream of buffalo. This last dream occurred about a year after his dream of the wolves. He did not tell the dream of the buffalo, but said that because of it he was often sent to look for buffalo; the leaders would send him alone instead of a searching party, as described in the account of the hunt on page 439. Charging Thunder said that he had faithfully fulfilled all the obligations of his dreams and believed that he had received great benefit from them, but that none of his dreams required him to engage in the practice of medicine. They required other acts, which he had duly performed.

In describing his dream of the wolves, Charging Thunder said:

> When I was about 22 years of age, I dreamed that I came to a wolf den and found the little wolves unprotected by either father or mother. They seemed to say, “We are left here helpless, but our parents will soon return.” <note>[¹ A dream similar to this is recorded by J. Owen Dorsey in *Eleventh Rep. Bur. Ethn.*, pp. 478–479.]</note> I learned their song, which was as follows:

> Soon I saw the old wolf returning, and a buffalo calf came behind him. This old wolf told me how to make a pipe, instructing me to smoke it when I was on the warpath. He said that the smell of the pipe would be so strong that the enemy would not detect my approach, and thus I would be able to steal their horses. The old wolf said that with the help of this pipe, I would be able to outwit the wisest and most cunning of my enemies. I made the pipe exactly as he directed and carried it on the warpath, where I had great success. It did not look any different from an ordinary pipe, but it had been "made sacred" by a medicine man.<note>The ability to make objects "sacred," thereby giving them mysterious power, was said to belong only to men who had the ability to talk with such objects and understand what they said. *Analysis.*—Three renditions of this song were recorded, with an interruption of the time between the repetitions. In this, as in many similar songs, the tempo was not strictly maintained. From the beginning of the song to the fifth measure before its close, the melody is framed on the chord F-sharp—A—C-sharp—E, a minor triad with a minor seventh added. Other tones occur, and the descending fourth C-sharp—G-sharp is noted, but this chord is felt as a framework. The song closes with a repetition of the descending minor third E—C-sharp. The song is melodic in structure, and about two-thirds of the intervals are descending progressions.
See the plot of this melody on page 204.

### DREAM OF THE CROW AND OWL

Śiya'ka in his youth dreamed of a crow and an owl. His narrative as given here reveals the manner in which a dream was sought and also the importance attached to it:

> All types of people know that when human power fails, they must look to a higher power for the fulfillment of their desires. There are many ways in which the request for help from this higher power can be made. This depends on the person. Some like to be quiet, and others want to do everything in public. Some like to go alone, away from the crowd, to meditate upon many things. In order to secure a fulfillment of his desire, a man must prepare himself to make his request. A lack of preparation would mean failure to secure a response to his petition. Therefore, when a man makes up his mind to ask a favor of Wakaŋ'taŋka, he makes due preparation. It is not fitting that a man should suddenly go out and make a request of Wakaŋ'taŋka. When a man shuts his eyes, he sees a great deal. He then enters his own mind, and things become clear to him, but objects passing before his eyes would distract him. For that reason, a dreamer makes his request known through what he sees when his eyes are closed. It has long been his intention to make his request of Wakaŋ'taŋka, and he resolves to seek seclusion on the top of a butte or other high place. When at last he goes there, he closes his eyes, and his mind is upon Wakaŋ'taŋka and his work. The man who does this usually has in mind some animal which he would like for protection and help. No man can succeed in life alone, and he cannot get the help he wants from men; therefore, he seeks help through some bird or animal which Wakaŋ'taŋka sends for his assistance. Many animals have ways from which a man can learn a great deal, even from the fact that horses are restless before a storm.

> When I was a young man, I wanted a dream through which I could know what to depend upon for help. Having this desire, I went to a medicine man <gloss>[¹]</gloss> and told him about it. He instructed me on what to do, and I followed his instructions in everything. He told me to get four well-tanned robes, with one for my own use, as well as a decorated pipe and offerings of tobacco, and to appear before him on a certain day prepared to seek my vision. I prepared the articles as he directed and went to him on that day. He painted my face white, and before leaving him, we went together into the sweat lodge; while we were there, he told me of his own dream and gave me an idea of what a dream was like. I had already selected a hill on which to await my dream, and after leaving him, I went to this hilltop to follow his instructions.<gloss>[²]</gloss>

---
<note>[1] Similarly, Lone Man consulted a medicine man in his youth. (See p. 214.)</note>
<note>[2] Compare Old Buffalo's fasting vigil on a hilltop, pp. 274-275.</note>

Śiya'ka details his own experience consulting a medicine man and undergoing rituals like the sweat lodge before his hilltop vigil.</summary>

--- Page 263 ---
<meta>This page continues the narrative of Śiya'ka, who is describing his personal experiences and the specific rituals he performed while seeking a vision, focusing on the preparation of his hilltop site and the spiritual symbolism of his offerings.</meta>

185
DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC

I was not required to fast before seeking the vision, but of course, I took no food with me when I went to the hilltop. In the middle of this hilltop, I dug a hollow about two feet deep and large enough so that I could crouch against its side when I grew weary of standing. At each of the four cardinal directions, I placed one of the robes and some of the tobacco. These offerings were to show that I desired messages from the directions of the four winds and was waiting anxiously to hear the voice of some bird or animal speaking to me in a dream.

After placing these offerings in position, and according to the medicine man's advice, I stood facing the west and watched the sun disappear. As soon as the sun was out of sight, I closed my eyes and turned my face toward the east, standing there for a while, then facing the north and the south. I stood there, wrapped in a buffalo robe. I was not exactly singing, but more like lamenting, like a child asking for something. <note>Compare with page 96.</note> In the crying or lamenting of a young man seeking a vision, two things are especially desired: first, that he may have a long life, and second, that he may succeed in taking horses from the enemy.

Beside me, to the north, was placed a buffalo skull, its face painted with blue stripes. <note>1</note> The openings of the skull were filled with fresh sage, and it was laid on a bed of sage. The skull was placed with its face toward the south. The reason for this was that when the buffalo come from the north, traveling toward the south, they bring news that Wakaŋʹtaŋka has provided food for the Indians and there will not be a famine. During part of the time, I rested my pipe against the buffalo skull, with the stem pointing toward the north. Part of the time, I held the pipe in my hands, with the stem pointing away from me. The pipe was filled but was not to be lit until I returned to the medicine man after my dream. <note>Compare with the sealed pipe in the Sun dance, pages 149 and 150.</note>

As I continued to face the west after the sun had set and when it was almost dark, I heard a sound like a bird flying around my head, and I heard a voice saying, “Young man, you are recognized by Wakaŋʹtaŋka.” This was all the voice said.

All night I stood with my eyes closed. Just before daybreak, I saw a bright light coming toward me from the east. It was a man. His head was tied up, and he held a tomahawk in his hand. He said, “Follow me,” and in an instant, he changed into a crow. In my dream, I followed the crow to a village. He entered the largest tent. When he entered the tent, he changed back into a man. Opposite the entrance sat a young man, painted red, who welcomed me. When I was received like this, I felt highly honored, for as this was the largest tent, I knew it must be the chief's tent. The young man said he was pleased to see me there. He further said that all the animals and birds were his friends and that he wished me to follow the way he had used to secure their friendship. He told me to lift my head. I did this and saw dragonflies, butterflies, and all kinds of small insects, while all kinds of birds flew above them. As soon as I cast my eyes down again and looked at the young man and the man who had brought me there, I saw that the young man had been transformed into an owl, and my escort had changed back into a crow. The following is the song of this part of my dream.

---

<note>1 It will be recalled that the stripes on the buffalo skull used in the Aloʹwaŋpi ceremony and in the Sun dance were red, and that in the Huŋka ceremony the skull was laid facing the west and in the Sun dance facing the east. In both these instances, the skull was laid on a bed of fresh sage. In a narrative concerning the “calling of the buffalo” by a medicine man, it is stated that a buffalo skull was painted with both red and blue stripes. (See pages 72, 127, 444.)</note>

The owl said, “Always look toward the west when you make a petition, and you will have a long life.” After this, the owl commanded me to look at him. <header>BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61</header>

*Analysis.*—Two versions of this song were recorded. The principal difference between them was that in the second version, the half note at the end of the third measure was sung as a quarter note, and the last note of the following measure was a half note; this resulted in five counts across the two measures but distributed them differently. The intonation wavered throughout the performances, making the song especially difficult to transcribe. This was undoubtedly due, in part, to the presence of the accidental. It was clearly the singer's intention to differentiate between the tones transcribed as D-sharp and D-natural, but the interval between the two was not always an exact minor second. As already stated, the minor second does not occur frequently. It is often sung too small, but not with enough consistency to justify the belief that the singer had a definite interval smaller than a semitone in mind. The measure transcribed in 3/8 time was sung consistently in all the performances. The melody tones follow the second five-tone scale, with the fourth note raised a semitone as an accidental. The song is melodic in structure and has a range of 12 tones.

Śiya'ka said further:

> The hilltop where I had my dream was quite a distance from the camp. My friends knew I had gone there, and in the early morning they sent a man with my horse. I came home, and the first thing I did was to take a sweat bath. In the lodge with the medicine man, I told him my dream.
> 
> I was a young man at that time and eager to go on the warpath and make a name for myself. After this dream, my stronghold was in the east, but the west was also a source from which I could get help. All the birds and insects I had seen in my dream were things I knew I should focus on and learn their ways. When the season returns, the birds and insects return with the same colors as the previous year. They are not all on the earth, but are *above* it. My mind must be the same. The elk is brave, always helping the women, and in that way the elk has saved a large portion of his tribe. In this, I should follow the elk, remembering that the elk, the birds, and the insects are my helpers. I never killed an elk or ate its meat. I would not kill the birds that fly continually in the air. I may kill water birds and grass birds if they are suitable for food, but only those.

Śiya'ka was deeply moved by the telling of this dream and the singing of the songs. Shaking hands with the writer, he said that he had given her his most cherished possession.<note>1. Śiya'ka's narrative was given in November 1912; he died in March 1913.</note>

Two Shields related the following dream, which is a tradition in the tribe, and sang the song which is said to have been received in the dream:

> Many years ago, a war party was in their camp when they heard what they believed to be the song of a young man approaching them. They could hear the words of the song and supposed the singer was one of their party, but as he came nearer, they saw that he was an old wolf—so old that he had no teeth, and there was no brush on his tail.

*Analysis.*—One interesting feature of this song is the difference in tempo between the voice and the drum, with the drum being slightly slower. The song remained consistent across its several performances. The melody tones follow the fourth five-tone scale. Major seconds make up 52 percent of the intervals, and minor thirds account for 35 percent; the remaining three intervals are upward progressions of a major third, a fourth, and a fifth. The song has a lively character and is completely different from the earlier songs in this group.

*Analysis.*—The tones included in this song belong to the second five-tone scale, with A as the keynote. The A minor chord forms the framework of the entire melody except for the closing measures, which consist of the minor third E—G. The minor third is prominent throughout the melody, making up 41 percent of the total number of intervals. Two rhythmic units are found in the song. The duration of the sustained tones was consistent in all the performances. In this song, as in most such instances, the long-held tones contain an uneven number of beats.

> The reference to the deer and the scarlet object is because venison is red and is the bait used to catch the eagle. The reference to blue is because, when trying to catch an eagle, we look at the sky so steadily that everything appears blue.

*Analysis.*—The range of this song covers 17 tones. Among the Chippewa, no songs were recorded that had a range of more than 14 tones, yet three songs in the present series have a range of 17; the others are No. 196 and No. 202. The final tone is faint, but it can be heard on the phonograph record. The rapid tempo and wide intervals cause more uncertainty in pitch than is usual in these songs. However, in this case, as in No. 58, the precision of the smaller intervals is less important than the fact that 27 of the intervals (37 percent) are larger than a major third. An equal number of intervals are major seconds, and the remaining 15 intervals are minor thirds. Changes in time occur as indicated. (See song No. 5.)

No narrative was provided with this song. Four dream songs concerning deer were recorded among the Chippewa—Nos. 95–98 in Bulletin 53.

See the plot of this melody on page 204.

## SONGS CONCERNING THE BEAR

Two Shields said:

The bear is the only animal dreamed of as offering herbs for the healing of man. The bear is not afraid of either animals or people and is considered ill-tempered, and yet it is the only animal that has shown us this kindness; therefore, the medicines received from the bear are supposed to be especially effective.

In a similar way, Śiya'ka said:

The bear is quick-tempered and is fierce in many ways, and yet he pays attention to herbs that no other animal notices at all. The bear digs these for his own use. The bear is the only animal that eats roots from the earth and is also especially fond of acorns, Juneberries, and cherries. These three are frequently compounded with other herbs in making medicine, and if a person is fond of cherries, we say he is like a bear. We consider the bear as the chief of all animals regarding herbal medicine, and therefore it is understood that if a man dreams of a bear, he will be an expert in the use of herbs for curing illness. The bear is regarded as an animal well acquainted with herbs because no other animal has such good claws for digging roots.

---

<note>1. This animal was mentioned by Lewis and Clark in the account of their journey on the upper Missouri. In September 1804, Clark wrote, "I walked on shore and saw goats, elk, buffalo, blacktail deer, and the common deer." (*Original Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition*, vol. 1, p. 155.) A footnote on this passage in the Coues edition is as follows: "*Cariacus macrotis*, also called mule deer. The tail is mostly white, but tipped with black." (*History of the Expedition under the Command of Lewis and Clark*, edited by Elliott Coues, vol. 1, p. 122, footnote, 1893.) The common deer is mentioned in Śiya'ka's song, No. 55.</note>

## PLOTS OF SONGS (DREAMS ABOUT ANIMALS)

Four plots from the preceding group of songs are presented here. No. 56 is an example of Class A (see fig. 19) and contains no ascending intervals. No. 49 resembles it but contains short intervals that frequently occur in songs concerning animals or suggesting motion, as shown in Class D. We note that the title of this song is "Song of the old wolf," but no suggestion of motion is found in the words. No. 55 has the wide compass and "rambling" outline that characterize songs of Class D. The title

Top left: "No. 56" depicts a descending sequence of dots.

of this song is "An Eagle nation is coming." No. 58, although it was said to have been received in a dream of an animal, is a song used in the treatment of the sick; in it, one can observe the emphasis on the keynote, which characterizes Class C, as well as the divergence which characterizes Class D.

## THE SACRED STONES (TUŊKAŊ')

Songs relating to the sacred stones constitute the second group of songs received in dreams. To dream of a small stone was regarded by the Teton Sioux as a sign of great importance, indicating that the

<summary>This page analyzes the melodic contours of several Teton Sioux dream songs, specifically comparing those related to animals and healing. It also begins a new section on songs inspired by dreams of sacred stones, which were considered highly significant signs.</summary>
<keywords>melodic plots, dream songs, Teton Sioux, Tuŋkaŋ', sacred stones, Song of the old wolf, An Eagle nation is coming, ethnomusicology, melodic analysis</keywords>

--- Page 283 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Sacred Stones" (Tuŋkaŋ') introduced at the end of page 204, detailing their physical characteristics, their spiritual symbolism according to Chased-by-Bears, and their linguistic origins.</meta>

<page-num>205</page-num>
<header>DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC</header>

A dreamer, by fulfilling the requirements of his dream, would become possessed of supernatural power; in exercising this power, he would use the sacred stones. This power would be demonstrated by an ability to cure sickness, to predict future events, and to reveal the location of objects beyond the range of his natural vision. The stones were native brown sandstone, usually spherical in shape, though oval stones and slightly flattened stones were also used; the principal requirement was that they should be regular in outline and untouched by any tool. The symbolism of the stones was given by Chased-by-Bears<note>¹ See Chased-by-Bears' account of the meaning of the Sun dance on page 95. Other symbolisms are noted on page 77, footnote.</note> as follows:

> The outline of the stone is round, having no end and no beginning; like the power of the stone, it is endless. The stone is perfect of its kind and is the work of nature, with no artificial means used in shaping it. Outwardly it is not beautiful, but its structure is solid, like a solid house in which one may safely dwell. It is not composed of many substances, but is of one substance, which is genuine and not an imitation of anything else.<note>² An emphasis on genuineness is also found on pages 173 and 330.</note>

The term used by the Sioux when speaking of these stones is *tuŋkaŋ'*, which is said to be an abbreviation of *tuŋka'śila*, "grandfather." The word *tuŋkaŋ'* is an example of the "sacred language" mentioned on page 120. Riggs (in the Dakota Dictionary) gives the meaning of this word as, "In the sacred language, a stone, and the moon." Thus, it is seen that the term "sacred stones," used in the present work, is not a direct translation of *tuŋkaŋ'*, but is a term expressing more nearly the idea in the mind of the Sioux. (Compare footnote, page 88.)

It is said that a medicine man, in demonstrating his power to acquire information by means of the sacred stones, sends them long distances. After a time, the stones return and give him the desired information. He is the only person who can understand what they say, and therefore he repeats their message to the man who requested him to make the inquiry. During a demonstration for curing the sick, it is said that the stones, flying through the air in the darkened tent, sometimes strike those who have refused to believe in them. This power of the sacred stones to move through the air is connected in the mind of the Sioux with *Ta'kuśkaŋśkaŋ'*; this term is composed of *ta'ku*, "something," and *śkaŋśkaŋ'* (defined by Riggs as the reduplicated verb form of *śkaŋ*: "to stir, move about, or change place"). Several of the writer's most reliable informants, after consultation, expressed the opinion that *Ta'kuśkaŋśkaŋ'* could correctly be said to be one of the native Dakota gods. Pond regards this as one of the native gods and writes: "The significance of the term 'Takuśkaŋśkaŋ' is 'that which stirs.' This god is too subtle in essence to be perceived

by the human senses. . . . His symbol is the boulder. . . . He also lives in what is called ‘the four winds.’ ” $^1$ Dorsey writes:

> Takuśkaŋśkaŋ, the moving deity . . . is the most powerful of their <note>the Dakota</note> gods; the one most to be feared and appeased, since, more than all others, he influences human well-being and woe. He is believed to live in the four winds, and the four black spirits of night do his bidding.$^2$

Miss Alice C. Fletcher uses the term “Something that moves,” and a connection between this mysterious power and the small stones appears in her article on “The Religious Ceremony of the Four Winds.” $^3$ Miss Fletcher says:

> An intelligent Santee Indian said to me: . . . “The Four Winds are sent by ‘the Something that moves’. There is a ‘Something that moves’ at each of the ‘Four Directions or Quarters’. . . . Among the Santee (Sioux) Indians the Four Winds are symbolized by the raven and a small black stone, less than a hen’s egg in size.

The desire for a dream of this small black stone and the way it is treated, as described by this author, are similar to those connected with the sacred stones that are the subject of the present discussion.

Distinct from these small stones, which were carried on the person, were the large stones or rocks in the field that were “objects of worship.” Riggs says, “Large boulders were selected and adorned with red and green paint, where the devout Dakota might go to pray and offer his sacrifice.” $^4$ An interesting account of such a stone, known as Eyay Shah, “Red Rock,” is given by Hovey. This stone was situated near the site of St. Paul, Minnesota, and was last visited by the Sioux shortly before their outbreak in 1862.$^5$ Many stones on the Dakota prairie are said to have been similarly regarded by the Sioux.

To talk of these stones is “sacred talk” to the Sioux, and the material included in this chapter was treated with the same reverence as that relating to the dream of the thunderbird or the ceremony of the Sun Dance.

Songs and information concerning the sacred stones were obtained from men who, in their relation to these objects, may be said to represent five different perspectives, as follows:

(1) Men who have dreamed of the sacred stones, possess one or more of them, and have used them successfully in treating the sick or in locating lost articles. Those of this class who provided information were Brave Buffalo (Tataŋ'ka-ohi'tika) and Goose (Maġa').

(2) Men who possess sacred stones and believe they have been helped in various ways by their presence. Chased-by-Bears (Mato'-

kuwa) had owned a sacred stone for more than 40 years, which he had acquired by purchase. He called upon it when in danger and anxiety, but he never attempted to secure benefits through its use for anyone other than his immediate family. Lone Man (*Iśna'la-wića'*) owns one stone and believes he has been greatly helped by wearing it on his person.

(3) A man who owns a stone but does not use it. Charging Thunder (*Wakin'yan-wata'kpe*) has had a sacred stone for many years, but has not been able to command it as the medicine men do. He attributes this lack of efficiency to the fact that he "does not place his faith entirely in it, but believes in the help of many other agencies." The stone was given to him at a time when he was sick, in the belief that it would restore him to health and also act as a charm. His father was skilled in the use of the stones, and Charging Thunder recorded songs which he said were composed by his father.

(4) A man who has not used the sacred stones, but who was one of the singers when White Shield (*Waha'ćanka-ska*) gave his wonderful demonstrations with them. It was customary for six or eight singers to sit at the drum and sing with the man who was giving the demonstration. Two Shields (*Waha'ćunka-non'pa*) recorded two of White Shield's songs which had been used on such occasions. Two Shields is a strict follower of the old beliefs, the missionaries having made no impression on him (*pl. 47*).

(5) Men who have witnessed demonstrations with the sacred stones in the camp, on the hunt, and on the warpath, and were familiar with the songs used at such times. Songs were recorded by Gray Whirlwind (*Wamni'yomni-ho'ta*), Shooter (*Oku'te*), Teal Duck (*Śiya'ka*), and Bear Eagle (*Mato'wanbli*). Additional information, as well as confirmation and personal memories, was provided by Buffalo Head (*Tatan'ka-pa*) and Standing Soldier (*Aki'ćita-na'źin¹*).

Among the informants mentioned above, the man whose use of the sacred stones is most active at the present time is Brave Buffalo, a prominent medicine man of the Standing Rock Reservation. He was born near the current site of Pollock, North Dakota, and at the time he provided his information, he was about 73 years of age. His father <note>see page 250</note> was a leading medicine man of the tribe. In describing his dream of the sacred stone, Brave Buffalo said:

> When I was 10 years of age, I looked at the land and the rivers, the sky above, and the animals around me, and I could not help but realize that they were made by some great power. I was so eager to understand this power that I questioned the trees and the bushes. It seemed as though the flowers were staring at me, and I wanted to ask them "Who made you?" I looked at the moss-covered stones; some of them seemed to have the features of a man, but they could not answer me. Then I had a

<header>BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61</header>

Dream. And in my dream one of these small round stones appeared to me and told me that the maker of all was Wakaŋ'taŋka, and that in order to honor him I must honor his works in nature. The stone said that by my search I had shown myself worthy of supernatural help. It said that if I were curing a sick person I might ask for its assistance, and that all the forces of nature would help me perform a cure.

Soon after this dream, Brave Buffalo found his first sacred stone on the top of a high butte; it is still in his possession. About a month later he found several others, one of which is in the possession of the writer (pl. 29). This stone is almost a perfect sphere. On one side there are a number of dots, the grouping of which suggests a tiny face, a characteristic pointed out by Brave Buffalo. The stone is dyed red with native dye. This color, which is a favorite of Brave Buffalo, has no specific religious significance. The stone, surrounded by eagle down, is kept in a wrapping of red cotton cloth. It was said that “there is something between the eagle down and the stone, because when surrounded by eagle down, it cannot get away.” The stone can be sent on errands of observation by its owner, and when not in use, it is imprisoned by the downy eagle feathers.

Brave Buffalo said that he had cured many illnesses by means of this stone, which he said is “a brother of the first stone” he found. He said further that he “had no authority to secure its sisters, but that it was good to have several brothers of the original stone to cooperate with it.” He “can feel if he is near a relative of the original stone” and always secures it. These relatives he may give away if he so desires, but the original stone has been seen by very few except the sick persons in whose treatment it has been used. (See p. 211.)

Concerning the nature of the sacred stones, Brave Buffalo said:

> It is significant that these stones are not found buried in the earth, but are on the top of high buttes. They are round, like the sun and moon, and we know that all things which are round are related to each other. Things which are alike in their nature grow to look like each other, and these stones have lain there a long time, looking at the sun. Many pebbles and stones have been shaped in the current of a stream, but these stones were found far from the water and have been exposed only to the sun and the wind. The earth contains many thousand such stones hidden beneath its surface. The thunderbird is said to be related to these stones <note>see p. 158</note> and when a man or an animal is to be punished, the thunderbird strikes the person; if it were possible to follow the course of the lightning, one of these stones would be found embedded in the earth. Some believe that these stones descend with the lightning, but I believe they are on the ground and are projected downward by the bolt. In all my life I have been faithful to the sacred stones. I have lived according to their requirements, and they have helped me in all my troubles. I have tried to qualify myself as well as possible to handle these sacred stones, yet I know that I am not worthy to speak to Wakaŋ'taŋka. I make my request of the stones and they are my intercessors. <note>See p. 88, footnote.</note>

<summary>Brave Buffalo recounts a dream that granted him the power to use sacred stones for healing and describes finding his first stone on a high butte. He explains the spiritual significance of the stones' round shape, their connection to the sun and the thunderbird, and their role as intercessors between him and Wakaŋ'taŋka.</summary>

*Analysis.*—This melody is in a minor key and contains all the notes of the octave except the seventh and second. In its structure, it is classified as a melody with a harmonic framework; the E-flat in the third and eleventh measures are the only accented tones other than those of the tonic triad. The major second and major third make up 80 percent of the intervals, even though the song's tonality is distinctly minor. The drumbeat is so fast that it is essentially a tremolo. The melody’s form is regular, consisting of four periods. One rhythmic unit appears in the first and third phrases, and a second rhythmic unit appears in the second and fourth phrases. These units show a similar division in the opening measure, followed by slightly different divisions. It is as if the second phrase acts as an "answering phrase," with the two combining to form a satisfying whole.

->See plot of this melody on page 245.<-

Goose, a prominent medicine man, also had dreams about the sacred stones <note>See p. 251</note>. He said that he had two of these stones in his possession for some time before he tested his power over them. One day, a fur trader mocked the medicine men within his earshot. This white man claimed that everything the medicine men did was just sleight of hand and said he would have to see an instance of their power before he would believe it. Goose spoke with the trader on the subject, and the trader offered him ten articles, including cloth and blankets, if he could call a buffalo to the spot where they were standing. Goose sent both sacred stones to summon a buffalo. The trader brought his field glasses and looked across the prairie, saying mockingly, "Where is the buffalo you were supposed to summon?" Suddenly, the trader saw a moving object far away. It came closer until they could see it without the help of the glasses. It was a buffalo, and it came so near that they shot it from the very spot where they stood.

At a later time, Goose found a rifle that had fallen into the water. This happened near the current site of Pierre, South Dakota. Some horses were being taken across the river on a ferry, while others were forced to swim. In the confusion, a white man dropped his rifle into the river. The man was sorry for his loss but made no effort to recover the rifle. After the man had gone, Goose decided to try to find it with the help of the sacred stones. Accordingly, he took the stones with him and rowed on the river until the stones told him to dive. Doing so, he found the rifle on the riverbed; an unusual detail was that while he was in the water, it appeared clear instead of murky as it usually was. Goose later had an opportunity to return the rifle to its owner, who rewarded him generously.

DENSMORE]                              TETON SIOUX MUSIC                              211

The stone is smooth and not dyed. It was wrapped in a piece of deerskin and surrounded by the finely powdered root of an herb. Chased-by-Bears said that he used this herb as a "charm" and also took it internally. When parting with the stone, he refused to give the writer any of this herb, but it was secured and identified later.

This stone had been in the possession of Chased-by-Bears for 40 years, and during that time he had faithfully fulfilled its requirements of character and action. Throughout this period, moreover, he had not lost one of his children; illness was almost unknown in his family, and he had suffered no great misfortune from any cause. In times of anxiety, whether through fear of sickness or disaster, he had carried the stone in his medicine bag. Chased-by-Bears was 64 years old when he gave this information and seemed to be in perfect health. He said that the stone formerly belonged to a very powerful medicine man named White Shield, who then lived at Standing Rock but had since moved to Poplar Creek, Montana. He warned the writer that the stone was still subject to a summons from White Shield and that at some time it might disappear from its wrappings, but that if such were the case she need feel no anxiety, as it would return. He said that White Shield had many such stones, one of which was for his personal use; this was always worn in a buckskin bag around his neck. The others were the "helpers" of this stone, and he could sell them, though he retained the right to recall them if he so desired. White Shield had dreamed of the sacred stones, had qualified himself to use them in treating the sick and in other ways, and had composed many songs concerning them.

White Shield's stone came into the possession of Chased-by-Bears in the following manner: About 40 years before giving this information, a daughter of Chased-by-Bears was ill, and he sent for White Shield to treat her. White Shield showed him the sacred stone, then it disappeared and the tent was darkened. After a time the light was restored, whereupon the stone was found on the person of the girl, who at once began to recover. Chased-by-Bears then asked for the stone which White Shield had used in performing the cure, and White Shield transferred it to him together with the song which he sang at the time and which he said should always be sung when any request was made of the stone. In exchange for these, Chased-by-Bears gave a horse. The song, which follows, is believed to have been composed by White Shield.

*Analysis.*—This melody consists of 32 measures, which group themselves into four periods of eight measures each. The first and third of these periods are based on the triad of F minor, and the second and fourth periods on the minor third C–E flat. The song is transcribed and analyzed in the key of C minor, although the fifth of that key does not occur. The rhythm of the first and second halves of the song is the same except for slight changes in the part containing the words. The rhythmic unit is short and occurs frequently. Two performances, recorded on separate cylinders, show no significant points of difference.

understand the native religious ideas which had governed his life, and that the white man might better know the mind of the Sioux. But misfortune followed his action. After a few weeks, the writer, upon returning to the reservation, was informed that Chased-by-Bears had suffered a stroke,¹ which was attributed to his sale of the sacred stone and its song. Mr. Higheagle was asked to visit Chased-by-Bears and find out whether the report was correct. It was found that Chased-by-Bears seemed to be in danger of death. Mr. Higheagle was then instructed to tell him that the stone would be returned to him as soon as it had been measured, weighed, and photographed. Every effort was made to ease the nervous tension that the elderly man was suffering. After a time, Chased-by-Bears was well enough to come and camp near the agency. He walked with difficulty, leaning on his cane. Food was sent to his camp, and when he was able to come to the writer’s office, she played for him the phonograph records of sacred-stone songs which others had sung, trying to convince him that he had not sinned more than they had. Finally, the subject of the herb used with the stone was brought up, and it was suggested that if the stone were to be returned, perhaps he would be willing to lend a portion of the herb for identification; this herb, along with the stone, would later be given back to him by Mr. Higheagle. After several meetings, Chased-by-Bears brought the plant, which was identified in Washington as *Aster sp.* Along with this, he had in his medicine bag a root which, he said, he powdered and mixed with the root of the first plant. It was a pithy root, but as none of the upper part of the plant was available, it could not be identified. Chased-by-Bears was encouraged to be present when other Indians were recording songs, and it was observed that his health steadily improved. When the writer left the reservation a few weeks later, he had almost regained his strength, and a year afterward, he appeared to be in his usual health.² Both the stone and the herbs were returned at the earliest opportunity, but it is interesting to note that the man’s physical recovery began before these were actually restored to his possession. Chased-by-Bears’ misfortune did not seem to cause any resentment toward the writer or her work. In conversation with those who were considered authorities on the subject, it was said that he “should have known better than to sell a stone when he had only one.” A medicine man could sell the “helpers” of his special stone, but even a medicine man would not part with the stone which was the center of his power.

Thus, the writer saw at a remote Chippewa village on the northern shore of Lake Superior a man who had suffered paralysis on one side of his face and body, and whose personal reputation was not good. The Chippewa say that many offending members of the Midé'wiwin become paralyzed.</note>

<note>2 Chased-by-Bears died in February 1915, more than two years after the stroke.</note>

# BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61

As an introduction to his narrative concerning the sacred stones, Lone Man said:

Ever since I have known the elder Indians and their customs, I have seen that in any great undertaking it is not enough for a man to depend simply upon himself. Most people place their reliance on the medicine-men, who understand this life and all its surroundings and are able to predict what will happen. They have the right to make these predictions. If, as we sit here, we should hear a voice speaking from above, it would be because we had the right to hear what others could not hear, or we might see what others did not have the right to see because they were not properly qualified. Such are some of the rights and privileges of the medicine-men, and those who desire to know mysterious things must seek their aid. If a man desires success in war or the hunt, or if he wishes to make the greatest of all requests—the request for long life—he should make it through a medicine-man. The medicine-man will give him a charm, probably a root or herb wrapped in buckskin, and he will wear this charm. <note>See p. 161.</note> It is not enough for a man simply to make his request known. There is a way that has been found best to follow, which is to make an offering along with the request.

When I was a young man, I went to a medicine-man for advice concerning my future. The medicine-man said: "I do not have much to tell you, except to help you understand this earth on which you live. If a man is to succeed on the hunt or the warpath, he must not be governed by his own whims, but by an understanding of the ways of animals and of his natural surroundings, gained through close observation.<note>In this connection, it is interesting to note the following statement by Father De Smet, a native of Belgium, who came to America in 1821 and for many years worked as a Jesuit missionary among the Sioux, writing extensively of their conditions and needs. He says: "Some writers have supposed that the Indians are guided by instinct, and have even ventured to assert that their children would find their way through the forests as well as those further advanced in age. I have consulted some of the most intelligent Indians on this subject, and they uniformly told me that they acquire this practical knowledge by long and close attention to the growth of plants and trees, and to the sun and stars. . . . Parents teach their children to remark such things, and these in their turn sometimes add new discoveries to those of their fathers." (*Life, Letters, and Travels of Father Pierre-Jean De Smet, S. J., edited by Hiram Martin Chittenden and Alfred Talbot Richardson, III, p. 1016, New York, 1905.*)</note> The earth is large, and many animals live upon it. This earth is under the protection of something which at times becomes visible to the eye. One would think this would be at the center of the earth <note>see p. 120</note>, but its representations appear everywhere, in large and small forms—they are the sacred stones. The presence of a sacred stone will protect you from misfortune."<note>To the Sioux, carrying a sacred stone to secure a benefit from its presence is on an entirely different level than wearing a "charm" (*wo'tahe*). This is one of many instances in which the English language lacks a brief equivalent for the nuances of meaning in an Indian language.</note> He then gave me a sacred stone which he himself had worn. I kept it with me wherever I went and was helped by it. He also told me where I might find one for myself. Wakan'taŋka tells the sacred stones many things that may happen to people. The medicine-man told me to observe my natural surroundings, and after my talk with him, I observed them closely. I watched the changes of the weather, the habits of animals, and all the things by which I might be guided in the future, and I stored this knowledge in my mind.

The medicine-man also told me that the sacred stone may appear in the form of a person who talks and sings many wonderful songs. Among these was the following song, in which the sacred stone says that all living creatures look to him for protection. This song and the one following it were composed and used by Ite'-oksaŋ-lu'ta [Red-Streaked-around-the-Face], a man who dreamed of the rainbow and therefore painted his face with an arch of color. He used red for this arch, as red was his favorite among the colors of the rainbow.

<summary>Lone Man explains the essential role of medicine-men and sacred stones in Sioux life, emphasizing that success and protection come from spiritual guidance and a disciplined observation of nature. He recounts receiving a sacred stone and learning that these stones act as protectors and messengers of Wakan'taŋka.</summary>

After singing this song, Lone Man bowed his head and reverently offered the following prayer. It was not his expectation that this and the prayers which preceded two other songs (Nos. 53, 55) would be recorded, but as he was seated at the phonograph, it was possible to secure the recordings without attracting his attention, and the records were later translated. His prayer was as follows:

> Maka'taŋhan wićá'śa waŋ wićo'haŋ waŋ awa'hiyaya tka hena' oŋ oŋ'śimala yo, tuwa' waŋka'taŋhaŋ in'itaŋćaŋ he'ćina.

->(Translation)<-

> I am a man from the earth; I have sung concerning an event, for which have compassion on me, whoever is from above, you [who are] the supreme ruler.

Continuing his narrative, Lone Man said:

Another instruction given to me by the medicine man was that all herbs and roots are made for the benefit of animals or man. Some herbs and roots vary in color according to the season of the year, while others do not. All are carefully tested, and if one is found to be a cure for a certain disease, it should be regarded as a gift from Wakaŋ'-taŋka, intended especially as a remedy for that disease. It should be revered, and this reverence should be closely observed, as without it, the herb will have no effect. Because of the reverence due to these medicinal herbs, certain songs are used to express this feeling. This, like the preceding song, was used by the man who dreamed of a rainbow. It may have been used when painting a horse on the warpath. <note>See pp. 350, 353.</note>

*Analysis.*—Four versions of this song were recorded. In the first and fourth versions, the word <term>peźu'ta</term> was sung, as shown in the transcription. This is an abbreviation of <term>peźi'huta</term>, meaning "a root or herb," but it is commonly used to mean "medicine." In this context, the herb possesses either a curative power or a mysterious power to provide benefits simply by its presence. In the second version, this word was replaced by <term>maka'ġi</term>, or "brown earth," and in the third by <term>maka'to</term>, or "blue earth." Both of these earths were used to make paint, which was applied to horses as well as to the bodies and possessions of men (see p. 116). This song begins with an upward progression of a fifth, which is somewhat unusual; however, only about one-fourth of the intervals in the song are upward. The song is in a minor key and has a melodic structure. The seventh and second tones of the octave are not found in the melody. The song lacks a strong rhythmic quality and contains no specific rhythmic unit.

In closing, Lone Man said:

> After the medicine man had given me this advice and instruction and had taught me the songs, he told me how to act in various emergencies. Afterward, I realized that I must depend on myself, and that if I failed, I must seek help from other sources, as he did not expect me to return to him.

(3) Charging Thunder recorded four songs concerning the sacred stones. He does not use the stones himself, but he learned the songs from his father, Bear Necklace (<term>Mato'napin</term>), who was a prominent medicine man. The first of these songs was received in a dream about the sacred stones.

Charging Thunder said that his father, while on a buffalo hunt, was thrown from his horse, falling on a pile of stones and injuring his head. He lay unconscious for almost the entire day and was found in the evening. His wound was dressed, and when he regained consciousness, he said that all the rocks and stones "were people who had been turned to stone."

BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61
page 218

After this, he found some stones (similar to those in plates 29 and 30). He could talk to them and depended on them for help. Once, a war party had been gone for two months; no news of them had been received, and it was feared that all had been killed. In their anxiety, the people appealed to Bear Necklace, asking him to determine, by means of the sacred stones, what had become of the war party. Bear Necklace requested them to tie his arms behind him, then to tie his fingers and toes, interlacing them with twisted sinew. He was then wrapped in a buffalo robe and tied with ropes. His medicine drum, medicine bag, and a bell were hung high on the tent poles, and he was laid on the ground beneath them. The tent was darkened; he sang the following song and told his dreams. Then the tent began to tremble, the articles hanging from the pole dropped to the ground, his cords loosened, and he stood entirely free. As soon as the medicine articles fell to the ground, there appeared a row of four or five small round stones ready to tell him what he wanted to know. Sitting Bull was present and made an offering of a buffalo robe to the sacred stones and asked that he might become famous.<note>See the account of Sitting Bull, page 458; also songs numbers 91 and 92.</note> Bear Necklace wrapped one of the stones in buckskin and gave it to him. Sitting Bull wore it in a bag around his neck until the time of his death, and it was buried with him.

Bear Necklace then gave correct information concerning the absent war party. At that time, he proved his power to provide information with the help of the sacred stones, and afterward, the stones always told him the names of those who were killed in war, the names of the survivors, and the day on which they would return. This information was always correct.

The following song was composed by Bear Necklace at the time he was injured, and was sung by him when demonstrating his power. The words refer to the passing of the stones through the air in the darkened tent while an exhibition of his power was in progress. It is said that a person who did not believe in the power of the stones was frequently struck by them, or by other objects hurtling through the air in the spirit-filled darkness.

<summary>Bear Necklace demonstrates his spiritual power by using sacred stones to locate a missing war party, a ritual witnessed by Sitting Bull. These stones provided accurate prophecy regarding war and were kept by Sitting Bull as a sacred charm until his death.</summary>
<keywords>Bear Necklace, Sitting Bull, sacred stones, war party, divination, medicine ritual, buffalo robe, Lakota spirituality</keywords>

BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61

*Analysis.*—This song, like the one before it, is in a major key and contains every note of the octave except for the seventh. The repetitions begin without any break in the tempo. In this song, as in many other instances, the note marked with a fermata <note>the symbol .)</note> was consistently shortened in every performance. Although the song's structure is melodic, the first six measures are based on an F-sharp minor triad; the melody then rises to E, and the tonic chord appears during the downward progression. The prominence of a minor submediant triad at the beginning of a song in a major key was also observed in Chippewa songs and occurs frequently in this series.

*Analysis.*—Almost two-thirds of the intervals in this song are minor thirds. In the first part, the descending minor third E-flat to C forms the basis of the melody. In the eighth measure, the descending minor third D-flat to B-flat is introduced and continues for several measures, followed by the minor third A-flat to F. The song ends with D-flat to B-flat, making a satisfactory close on the tonic. All the tones of the octave are present in this song and the feeling of a keynote is well established, yet it is observed that the tones are not grouped along the lines of triad chords, but of single intervals. This "interval formation" was given extended consideration in Bulletin 53, pages 7–8.

(4) In giving a complete demonstration of the sacred stones, it was customary for the man who was proving his power to tell his dreams and sing the songs of the dreams, as these served as his credentials. The two following songs were used in this manner by White Shield and recorded by Two Shields. The words are obscure, as they are in the majority of dream songs.

In songs Nos. 70, 71, and 72, the sacred stones address their owner as "father" or "grandfather."

*Analysis.*—It is common to notice a song in a major key starting with a submediant chord, which is minor. In this instance, however, a song in a minor key begins with the submediant triad, which is major. The eighth measure introduces the descending minor third A to F-sharp, which forms the framework of the melody until the sixteenth measure. This is followed by a return to the submediant triad, with the song closing on the descending minor third A to F-sharp. If these tones (F-sharp, A, C-sharp, E) were used consecutively, one might say that the melody is based on a minor triad with an added minor seventh, but the melody's framework does not suggest this chord relationship. This song is melodic in structure and lacks the sixth and second tones of the complete octave. The

*Analysis.*—This is one of the songs in which a single change in the time signature seems to give a certain "swing" to the entire rhythm. This rhythmic peculiarity was frequently observed among Chippewa songs. For example, in two out of three performances of this song, the fourth measure was sung exactly as transcribed. In the third performance, however, an additional measure was inserted: the first two beats of the fourth measure formed a measure in double time, followed by B-flat (the final beat of the fourth measure) which was prolonged into a triple measure. Adding an extra measure does not seem to trouble a Native singer, as the overall form of a song seems to be less rigid among Indigenous people than among Western musicians.

This melody has a major tonality and a harmonic structure. The tonic triad forms the framework of the first four measures, after which the descending minor third B–G sharp appears; the song closes with a descent to the third of the key. This melodic outline is unusual and interesting. The opening of the song has force and definiteness, and the prominence of the fourth in the latter portion

*Analysis.*—All the accented tones in this song are those of the <term>tonic chord</term>, showing the song to be strongly harmonic in structure. The melody tones are those of the fourth <term>five-tone scale</term>. The interval of a fourth is prominent in both ascending and descending progression, as has often been noted in songs concerning motion. About two-thirds of the intervals in this song are downward progressions.

Śiya′ka (see pl. 1 and pp. 184 et seq., 439 et seq.) sang three songs of the sacred stones and recounted instances where he had heard of them being used to locate buffalo and find the enemy. He first described a performance by Crooked Foot (Siha′limin), who died in 1877. Crooked Foot was asked to determine, by using the sacred stones, where buffalo could be found. The stone which he used was egg-shaped, and he was said to have found it on top of the highest butte near his home. When giving this performance, Crooked Foot had the stone encased in a bag. He said: “The stone has now gone to look for the buffalo, but when it comes back you will see it.” The people then prepared a place where they expected the stone to appear. This was done by pulverizing the earth for a space about a foot square and covering this area with buffalo hide or with part of a red blanket. Everyone watched this place, and after a time, the stone appeared upon it. Crooked Foot questioned the stone concerning the location of the buffalo, and the tribe, acting on his advice, found the herd as he

had indicated. If an individual had employed him to locate lost horses or other property, the man who employed him would have lit a pipe and offered it to the stone as soon as it appeared. Before passing the pipe to the rest of the group, this man would have questioned the stone. The replies were given by the owner of the stone, as he was supposed to be the only person present who understood what the stone said. He repeated what the stone said to him, and the man who employed him accepted it as the message of the stone. *Analysis.*—This song is in a minor key and lacks the seventh and fourth tones of the complete octave. (See song No. 26.) The rhythmic unit is long and repeated continuously, providing little opportunity to take a breath. Between the performances of the song, the high calls or cries that frequently interrupt Indian singing were given; however, the tempo of the song was maintained in these calls, so there was no break in the timing during the entire performance. This song begins on the twelfth interval and progresses steadily downward to the tonic note at the close.

When Śiya'ka was on the warpath, the <term>sacred stones</term> were invoked by Heha'ka-na'źiŋ (Standing Elk), who sent them on their customary search and then said to the warriors:

> In the early morning, you will meet one man and kill him. You will meet a wolf coming from the north before you see this enemy. Let each man pray to the wolf, calling him "grandfather" and asking that he may get a count.<note>The right to wear a war-honor feather in the hair.</note> You will also meet a large crow flying toward you from the north. Let each man make the same prayer to the crow. After seeing the crow, you will see one enemy also coming from the north.

Everything happened just as the stone had predicted. They met the wolf and the crow; then they saw one man and killed him. The man was a scout, but the Sioux did not know this at the time. The enemy's war party, following the scout, charged the Sioux. There were 19 men in the enemy's party, and four brave Sioux stood against them and drove them back. The enemies were Arikaree and Mandan. After peace was established, the Sioux spoke with them about this battle and learned that the scout's name was One Feather. Śiya'ka was one of the four men who drove them back and won a count at that time. He said that Standing Elk used the following song when making his request to the stones. No drum was used with this song.

Red Horn then offered the pipe to the little red stone and asked it to go before them as a scout. Eagle Man sang his song again, and the stone disappeared. The war party went on and made a camp for the night. Toward morning, Eagle Man said that the stone had returned, and that, when questioned concerning the enemy, the stone had stated that they would meet the enemy the next day, but did not name the hour, adding that there would not be more than 10 men in the enemy's party. The stone was left on the red blanket where it appeared after its quest.

That morning the war party went on again, and Śiya'ka and another man were chosen to act as scouts. They found six men drinking at a water hole, whereupon they immediately returned and reported this to the war party. They tried to surround the men but failed, and the six escaped. However, they met one man—an Omaha—coming to join this party and killed him. Red Horn shot him, thus securing the first "count" <note>This refers to the practice of counting coup</note>, and Śiya'ka secured the fourth count.

Eagle Man sang the following song during this demonstration by the sacred stones:

*Analysis.*—The rhythmic unit of this song consists of five measures, and, as in the previous song, its repetitions make up the entire melody. The first note in the second measure of the unit was always shortened, as shown. Four versions were recorded, separated by calls or short spoken sentences. In its tonality, the song is minor; the melody tones are those of the minor triad and fourth.

*See plot of this melody on page 245.*

Śiya'ka shared a remarkable demonstration of the sacred stones performed by White Shield. Three of White Shield's sacred-stone songs have already been provided (see numbers 67, 68, and 69). Śiya'ka said that on one occasion he had lost two horses and asked White Shield to find them. Before being bound with sinews (see page 218), White Shield asked, "What sign shall the stone bring to show whether your horses are by a creek or on the prairie?" Śiya'ka replied: "If they are by a creek, let the stone bring a small turtle and a piece of clamshell, and if they are on the prairie, let the stone bring a meadowlark."

White Shield then sent the stone on its quest. While the stone was away, the people prepared a square of finely ground earth as previously described. It was evening when the stone returned. The tipi was dark, as the fire had been put out, but there was dry grass ready to be placed on it when White Shield called for light. At last, the stone appeared on the spot prepared for it, and beside it was a small turtle with a small piece of clamshell in one of its claws. Then White Shield said to Śiya'ka: "Your horses are 15 miles west of the Porcupine Hills at a fork of Porcupine Creek. If you do not want to go for them, there is a traveler coming that way who will find them and bring them to you." This proved true. One of Śiya'ka's neighbors had been out looking for wild fruit, and on his way home, he saw the horses at the fork of Porcupine Creek; recognizing them as Śiya'ka's, he brought them back.

^1^ <note>The full form of this expression is *wahu' non'pa*, meaning "two-legged object," which was used by medicine men to refer to a man (see page 120, footnote). The full form occurs in song number 78.</note>

<meta>This page continues the ethnographic record of Teton Sioux spiritual practices, moving from Śiya'ka's account of White Shield on the previous page to a new narrative by Mato'-waŋbli' (Bear Eagle) regarding the medicine man Shell Necklace and his use of sacred stones during a war party.</meta>

<header>BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61</header>

Mato'-waŋbli' (Bear Eagle) said that he was once the leader of a war party against the Crow people. One member of the party was Paŋke'-ska-napin' (Shell Necklace), who was able to consult the sacred stones. One night in the camp, Eagle Man asked Shell Necklace to obtain news of the enemy. A spot on the ground was prepared and covered with a red blanket. When the stone returned, Shell Necklace covered himself entirely with a buffalo robe, including his head, and asked what news it brought. When the customary pipe was offered to the sacred stone, a wolf was heard howling in the distance. Shell Necklace said the stone reported that the next day they would meet two men on horseback and see a large enemy camp. The stone told the men to be ready, and that they would kill the enemy, who would fall on "prepared" or soft ground. Then the stones said that they wanted a buffalo as a reward in the morning; they said the men would kill the buffalo with an arrow, and that it would fall with its head pointing toward the south. The next morning, the men killed a buffalo just as the stone had predicted and placed fresh sage in the wound. Beside the prepared ground where the stone had rested was a painted gift-stick with tobacco tied at the top (see plate 15). They laid this stick at the head of the buffalo they had killed, leaving it on the prairie as an offering. That day they encountered two enemies and killed them both.

The following two songs were said to have been sung by Shell Necklace while giving this demonstration. The first concerns himself, establishing his qualifications to ask favors of the sacred stones. The second concerns his power as a medicine man, which enables him to control people at a distance.

*Analysis.*—The structure of this song is interesting. With one exception, all the accented tones belong to the minor triad B-flat–D-flat–F; accordingly, the song is analyzed as being in the key of B-flat minor. However, the progressions in the last four measures suggest the relative major chord. There are sixteen intervals in the song, only five of which are upward progressions.

*Analysis.*—This song begins on the <term>dominant</term> above the <term>tonic</term> and ends on the <term>dominant</term> below the <term>tonic</term>, with two-thirds of the progressions moving downward. All the tones of the <term>octave</term> except the seventh are present in the melody. One <term>accidental</term> appears—the fourth raised a <term>semitone</term>.

The following account of a performance by White Shield differs from preceding narratives in that it took place in a house, and the stone was held in White Shield's hand instead of being laid on the ground. The narrative was given by Bull Head, who witnessed the performance. He said it occurred when the Government first issued harnesses and wagons to the Indians. At that time, the old people "kept close track" of everything which was issued to them by the Government and prized it very highly. One old man lost part of a harness. Knowing that White Shield often recovered lost articles with the aid of the sacred stones, he appealed to him, asking him to find the missing part of his harness and also a handsome tobacco bag and pipe. White Shield came, and during the performance, he held the stone in the palm of his hand, saying, "This will disappear." Bull Head said that though he watched it very closely, it suddenly vanished from before his eyes. The length of time that a stone is absent depends on the distance it must travel to find the lost object. In this instance, the stone was gone for a long time. At last, a rattle was heard at the door. White Shield stopped the singing and said, "The stone has returned; be ready to receive it." He then opened the door, and the stone was found on the doorstep. White Shield brought it in and heard its message. The stone said that the missing articles had been taken by a certain man who, for fear of being caught, had thrown them into the river. The stone said further that the articles would be brought back that night and left where they had been last seen. The next morning, all the missing articles were found in the place where they had been last seen. Their appearance indicated that they had been under the water for several days.

The following is the second analysis group of dream songs, comprising those concerning the sacred stones (Nos. 59–78, inclusive). The aid of the sacred stones was invoked to locate the camp of an enemy (p. 348); also in finding a missing man (p. 496). Other analyses of dream songs are on pages 198 and 278.

## PLOTS OF SONGS (THE SACRED STONES)

The songs concerning the sacred stones contain no examples of a song without ascending progressions (Class A, fig. 19). Song No. 59 is the closest to this type and contains one ascending interval. No. 71 has a strongly descending trend but contains three ascending intervals. No. 68 is an example of Class B, and Nos. 76 and 74 have the same general outline. No. 70 suggests Class D, though it has the descending trend that characterizes Class A. The title of this song is "I am required to roam." It should be remembered that songs of Class D concern animals or contain the idea of motion.

## TREATMENT OF THE SICK

This is the third of the groups of songs received in dreams. All treatment of the sick was performed in accordance with dreams. No one attempted to treat the sick unless he had received a dream instructing him to do so, and no one ever disregarded the obligations of such a dream. Each man treated only the diseases for which his dream had given him the remedies. Thus, Shooter said:

> In the old days, the Indians had few diseases, and so there was not a demand for a large variety of medicines. A medicine man usually treated one special disease and

<summary>This page analyzes the drum tempo and melodic structure of songs related to the sacred stones and begins a discussion on how healing practices were strictly dictated by individual dreams.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Treatment of the Sick," specifically focusing on the specialization of medicine-men based on their dreams and the three primary methods of Sioux healing.</meta>

treated it successfully. He did this in accordance with his dream. A medicine-man would not try to dream of *all* herbs and treat *all* diseases, for then he could not expect to succeed in all of them, nor could he properly fulfill the requirements of the dream of any specific herb or animal. He would depend on too many things and fail at them all. That is one reason why our medicine-men lost their power when so many diseases arrived among us with the coming of the white man.

The Sioux used three methods for treating the sick: the use of sacred stones, "conjuring," and the administration of herbs. The first kind of treatment could be given by a <term>wakaŋ'haŋ</term>. This term was applied to the highest class of medicine-men—those qualified to command the sacred stones, to bring fair weather, or to fill

<image-desc>Figure 25 contains six rectangular melodic plots on grid backgrounds, arranged in two columns of three.
