->FIG. 25. Plots, Group 3.<-

such important ceremonial positions as that of <term>Intercessor</term> in the <term>Sun dance</term>. A man who "conjured" the sick was called a <term>wapi'ya</term> ("one who repairs"), and a man who treated the sick using herbs was called a <term>peźu'ta wića'ku</term> ("one who places his confidence in the roots of herbs"). It was not unusual for the same man to use more than one of these methods, but he was best known by the one he employed the most.

Treating the sick with sacred stones and conjuring has been forbidden by the Government in recent years, but certain elders are allowed to continue treating the sick by administering herbs. Four such men described the method they

were using at the time they provided the information; one (Used-as-a-Shield) gave an account of "conjuring" from the patient's perspective; another (Old Buffalo) narrated his fasting prayer for a sick relative; and additional information was received from other informants.

When a man skilled in using the sacred stones was called to attend to a sick person, he was expected to give a demonstration of his supernatural power. Many were invited to witness this exhibition, and it is said that harm would come to those who did not "believe in the sacred stones." The sick person filled a pipe and gave it to the medicine-man. After smoking it, the man was bound tightly with thongs—even his fingers and toes were interlaced with sinews like those used for bowstrings—after which he was firmly tied in an animal hide. The tent was dark, and the medicine-man sang songs addressed to the sacred stones; he also sang his own dream songs. Strange sounds were heard in the darkness, and objects were felt flying through the air. The voices of animals could be heard speaking. One said, "My grandchild, you are very sick, but I will cure you." Frequently a buffalo appeared, and those who did not believe in the sacred stones were kicked by the buffalo or struck by a flying stone or a bundle of clothing. At last, the medicine-man called out, "Hurry, make a light!" Dry grass, which had been prepared, was placed on the fire. In its light, the man was seen wedged between the poles near the top of the tipi, with all the restraining cords cast away from him.<note>Similar demonstrations were performed by the medicine-men of other tribes. A description of the custom among the Chippewa is provided in Bulletin 45, pages 123–25. (Compare also page 218 of this work.)</note>

Brave Buffalo said that when treating a person using the sacred stones, he rolled a stone on the person's body "to locate the ailment," and if the sick person wished to hold the stone in his mouth, he was allowed to do so, as this produced an internal effect.

In many instances of treating the sick by "conjuring," no medicines were given, as the conjuror claimed that he removed the disease from the person's body by sucking it out. Mrs. James McLaughlin, who witnessed such a performance on the Devils Lake Reservation in North Dakota, described it to the writer. Regarding this Santee demonstration, Mrs. McLaughlin said:

> I saw a conjuror named Śip'to (Beads) give a performance in an attempt to cure a boy who was suffering from lung hemorrhages. Śip'to was an old man. He wore nothing but his breechcloth; his entire body and face were painted red, and his hair was short and loose. The boy lay in a tipi. If a conjuring performance was held in a log house, it was necessary to remove a portion of the floor, as the conjuring had to be done on bare ground. I have seen a house where a large part of the floor had been cut away for this purpose.
>
> When I entered the tipi, the conjuror was in the place of honor, opposite the door. This area was cleared of turf, and the bare ground had been made very smooth. The boy lay with his head near the conjuror. In the middle of the lodge was a fire with many red coals. A young girl brought water and placed it beside the conjuror. When

After this had been done, the conjurer rinsed his mouth, put a piece of root in his mouth, and chewed it. Removing a coal from the fire with a stick, he picked it up in his hands and put it in his mouth. He then dropped on all fours and began to tear up the ground with his fingers and toes, as if they were claws. He made a cry like an animal and approached the boy as if he were a wild beast. With the coal still in his mouth, he stooped over the boy’s chest and sucked so violently that the blood came to the surface. Then he made a whistling, puffing sound <note>see p. 254</note> and spat into a dish which was partly filled with water. When this performance was completed, he sat down, dripping with perspiration, and the boy immediately suffered a hemorrhage from the lungs.

The same performance was repeated four times, and after each time, the boy had a hemorrhage. Then the boy complained that the treatment was making him worse, and the boy’s father asked the conjurer not to work over the boy any longer. The boy’s father gave the conjurer a horse, as it is the belief of the Santee that sickness will return if the “doctor” is not paid.

The following is an account of a somewhat similar treatment, which included the administration of medicine. This account was given by Used-as-a-Shield, a reliable informant who sang a number of songs in the present work and took part in several discussions of serious topics by the old men. He described his own experience in receiving treatment from a conjurer, saying:

The first thing done in summoning a medicine man to treat a sick person was to put black paint on the stem of a pipe. Charcoal was ordinarily used in making this paint, which was smeared on the stem of the pipe, with an eagle feather being tied next to the mouthpiece. A messenger took this painted pipe to the medicine man’s lodge, carrying it with the bowl toward himself. If the medicine man was at home, the messenger entered the lodge, turning toward the left. Without speaking, he handed the pipe to the medicine man, who smoked it as a sign of his agreement. A request to visit a sick person was never refused unless the medicine man was physically unable to go. If the man was not at home, the messenger left the pipe in the place of honor, with the bowl toward the door.<note>1. Compare the position of the pipe on pages 72, 127, and 185.</note> The relatives of the medicine man then made an effort to find him as soon as possible.

It was in this manner that many years ago, I sent for a medicine man to treat me. When he entered my lodge, he seated himself behind the fire. After a time, he came and sat by my head, examining me. He then took up a lock of hair on my forehead and tied a wisp of grass around it, letting the rest of my hair hang loose. Then he had me placed so that I lay facing east, and he began his preparations for the treatment. Opening a bundle, he took from it a whistle (<term>śi'yotaŋka</term>), a small drum (<term>ćaŋ'ćeġa</term>), and a rattle (<term>wagmu'ha</term>) which he used in beating the drum. He also took out a black cloth, which he tied over his eyes. Then he dropped on one knee, facing me, holding the drum in his right hand and the rattle in his left hand. Beating the drum rapidly with the rattle, he said: “Young man, try to remember what I tell you. You shall see the power from which I have the right to cure sicknesses, and this power shall be used on you this day.” Then he told the dream by which he received his power as a medicine man. When he rose to his feet, I noticed that a horse’s tail hung at his side, fastened to his belt. Standing, he offered his drum to the cardinal points, then beat it as hard as he could, sometimes louder, sometimes softer. A wooden bowl which he carried was placed next to my head. Then he came toward me, still beating his drum. As he came near me, his breath was so forceful it seemed as if it would blow me away. Just before he reached me, and while blowing his breath so strongly, he struck his body on the right side and on the left side. He was still telling his dream—

and singing, but when he paused for an instant, I could hear the sound of a red hawk; some who were there even said they could see the head of a red hawk coming out of his mouth. He bent over me and I expected that he would suck the poison from my body with his mouth, but instead, I felt the beak of a bird over the place where the pain was. It penetrated so far that I could feel the feathers of the bird. The medicine man kept perfectly still for a time; then he got up with a jerk to signify that he had removed the trouble. I still felt the beak of a bird. A boy stood near, holding a filled pipe. It was soon apparent that the medicine man had swallowed the poison. He took four whiffs of the pipe. Then he had to rid himself of the poison. This part of the performance was marked by great activity and the pounding of the drum. At times he kicked the bare ground in his effort to get rid of the poison; he paced back and forth, stamped his feet, and used both the rattle and the drum. Finally, he ejected the poison into the wooden bowl. Then he told the people that he had sucked out all the poison, that none remained in my body, and that I would recover.

Opening his medicine bag, he took some herbs and placed them in a cup of cold water. He stirred it up and told me to drink it and to repeat the dose the next morning, and that in less than ten days, I would be well. I did as he told me, and in about ten days, I was entirely well.

Brave Buffalo is considered one of the most powerful medicine men on the Standing Rock Reservation and was actively engaged in the practice of native medicine when he held his conferences with the writer. In describing his treatment of the sick, he said:

<image-desc>A line drawing of a mirror design used in healing. On the left is a large downward-curving crescent shape. To the right is a smaller symbol consisting of an 'X' crossed over two parallel horizontal lines. Below the crescent is the caption: ->FIG. 26. Drawing on mirror used in treatment of the sick.<-</image-desc>

> Some people have an idea that we medicine men, who get our power from different sources, are the worst of human beings; they even say that we get our power from the evil one, but no one could disregard such dreams as I have had, and no one could fail to admire the sacred stones. <term>Wakan'tanka</term> is all-powerful, and if we revere his work, he will surely let us prove to all men that these things are indeed his doing. It is a very strict requirement that a medicine man must act out his dream <note>see p. 157</note>, and that he maintain absolute integrity of character. If he fails to do this, he will be punished and will not live long. I am not required to fast, only to smoke, showing that I am at peace with all men. Dreams come to me now in a natural way. Often during the day when I am alone on a journey, and my mind is on many things, I stop to rest for a while. I observe what is around me, and then I become drowsy and dream. Often I see the sacred stones in my dreams.

Brave Buffalo’s conference with the writer was interrupted by a call to visit a sick person many miles away. On his return several days later, he said that he left his patient recovering. He had with him a bag containing articles which he had used in treating this sick person, and on his hat, he wore a bone about five inches long instead of a feather, which had been fastened to his hatband on his previous visit. In describing his treatment, he said that he “sucked out the disease” through the bone and ejected it from his mouth into a bowl of water. Opening his bag, he took from it a small mirror enclosed in a flat frame

One of the songs Brave Buffalo used in treating the sick was recorded. Before singing this, he said: "Some diseases are affected by the day and others by the night. I use this song for cases that are worse at night. I composed it myself and always sing it at night, whether or not I am treating a sick person. I offer smoke to the four winds and sing this song." Brave Buffalo received this song in his dream of a wolf. (See Song No. 47.)

Brave Buffalo also sang one of his father’s medicine songs. Crow Bear (Kanġi-mato), the father of Brave Buffalo, was a famous singer and medicine man who lived to the age of 80 years. In one of his dreams, he saw a bear, and a majority of the songs he composed concerned or were addressed to the bear. The song recorded by Brave Buffalo was not one of those, but was a song that his father sang every morning, as required by one of his dreams. In a dream, it was also required that anyone who passed him—even if he was smoking or eating—must pass in front of him. If anyone accidentally passed behind him, the physical effect was immediate: his teeth chattered and he became unconscious, with much effort being necessary to restore him.

**Analysis.**—Three performances of this song were recorded, and they show no differences. Between the performances, the singer gave sliding "calls" or "cries," but the repetition began on the same tone as the original performance. No change in tempo occurs in the song—an unusual feature—and the rhythmic unit is repeated more continuously than in a majority of the songs. The first tone of the rhythmic unit was strongly accented. The only tones present are those of the minor triad and fourth, and the structure of the song is melodic with a harmonic framework; the accented G prevents it from being classified as strictly harmonic in structure. Two-thirds of the progressions move downward, with the melody descending steadily from the tenth interval to the tonic.

See the plot of this melody on page 283.

Goose (plate 31), a widely-known <term>medicine-man</term>, is what might be called a specialist in the treatment of consumption <note>Historically used to refer to tuberculosis.</note> and is said to have had a significant degree of success in his work. He also provided information concerning the <term>Sun dance</term> and the sacred stones. (See pages 90, 210.) Goose narrated the dream through which he felt authorized to undertake the treatment of the sick. It was impossible to record the songs when he first told the story of his dream, and unfortunately, another opportunity did not arise. In describing the dream, Goose said:

> When I was a young man, I was an excellent marksman with bow and arrows. After coming into contact with the Army, I was given a rifle and cartridges and never missed my aim. One morning, I woke up before daybreak to go on a hunting trip. As I went around a butte, I saw an antelope, which came toward me and stood still a short distance away. The antelope looked at me and then began to graze. I took my rifle and fired several shots with no effect. I fired 16 cartridges and wondered what could be wrong. I put in four more cartridges and fired again, but with no effect whatever. Then the animal stopped grazing and began to move slowly away. Then I heard a voice speaking three times, and then a fourth time; the voice said it was going to sing something, and I must listen. The voice was above me and commanded me to look at the sun. I looked and saw that the rising sun had the face of a man and was commanding all the animals and trees and everything in nature to look up. In the air, in front of the sun, was a booth made of boughs. In front of the booth was a very bright object, and between this and the booth was a man, painted and wearing an eagle-down feather, while all kinds of birds flew around him. The bright object was a <term>sacred stone</term>, and it was heated red-hot. After seeing this, I heard another voice telling me to look and receive what would be given to me. Something in the form of a bird came down, and where it touched the ground, an herb sprang up. This happened three times. The voice above me said that I was to use these three herbs to cure the sick. The fourth time, the descending object started in the form of a bird, but a human skeleton came to the ground. Then the voice above me told me to observe the structure of the human body. I then saw blood run into the skeleton, and a <term>buffalo horn</term> appeared on the back, between the shoulders, and drew the blood out of the skeleton. The voice above me said this was a sign that I would have more power than any other to cure diseases of the blood. The voice came from the sacred stone and said I must use the buffalo horn in curing diseases of the blood, a practice which I have followed ever since. I do not consider that I dreamed this as one dreams in sleep; it appeared to me when I was early on the hunt.

<summary>This page analyzes a song by the medicine man Goose and recounts his foundational vision quest, which took place during a hunt. In his vision, Goose received the power to heal blood diseases and tuberculosis using specific herbs and a buffalo horn.</summary>

<keywords>Goose, medicine man, Teton Sioux, song analysis, vision quest, consumption, tuberculosis, sacred stone, buffalo horn, healing rituals</keywords>

--- Page 336 ---
<meta>This page continues the narrative of the medicine man Goose, focusing on his medical philosophy, his specific treatments for consumption, and the sacred objects used in Sioux healing practices.</meta>

One of the greatest lessons it taught me is that the first thing a sick person should do is take a sweat bath to remove all impurities, so that the body will respond to remedies. The vision of the booth showed how the sweat lodge must be built, and the hot stone demonstrated the use of heated stones within the lodge. The hot stone is brought into the lodge, and water is sprinkled upon it. The more often this bath is taken, the healthier a person will be. In case of illness, the sick person must take this bath first, and as frequently afterward as the medicine man directs. I always prescribe the sweat bath first. I also maintain that a sick person cannot recover unless their diet is changed. Certain kinds of food and wild fruit are harmful in certain illnesses, and certain types of game or venison are injurious to a sick person. The food must be lighter than usual, and the person must avoid unnecessary exertion. My requirements are the sweat bath, a light diet, and rest. I have treated <term>consumption</term> <note>Historically used to refer to tuberculosis.</note>, and if the disease is not too far advanced, the person usually recovers. The treatment depends on the severity of the case. All three herbs which I saw in my dream were prepared in a certain way and were intended for use in treating consumption, which is caused by improper blood circulation. I do not want the patient to make any unnecessary effort, but I try especially to maintain their circulation. The sweat bath improves circulation. In the old days, a person did not catch a cold after a sweat bath. The sick person did not jump immediately into cold water, as is sometimes claimed, but was covered with furs and allowed to cool off gradually.

Many years ago, a <term>medicine man</term> named *Ćeha'kiŋ* (Carry-the-Kettle) lived among the Sioux; he was said to possess *wakaŋ'* <note>Sacred or spiritual power.</note> power to a remarkable degree. A gourd rattle^1 (pl. 32) used by him in treating the sick came into the author's possession.

The Sioux call such a rattle a *wagmu'ha*.^2 This is not the only type of rattle used among the Sioux in treating the sick, however, as the form of the rattle depends on the medicine man's choice.

Every medicine man had a bag or case in which he kept his supply of herbs and the items he used in treating the sick. In some instances, the outer case was made of decorated rawhide. A man's medicine bag was hung on a pole outside the lodge and was usually brought in at night; it was often purified with the smoke of burning sweetgrass. It was believed that the presence of "the wrong kind of person" in the lodge would affect the medicine's effectiveness, and if it were exposed to such influence for any significant time, its power would be entirely destroyed. The author obtained three of these medicine bags. One (pl. 33) belonged to a medicine man named *Waŋbli'iyo'take* (Sitting Eagle), who lived many years ago. The bag is made of four antelope ears. When Sitting Eagle died, the medicine bag and its contents passed into the possession of his niece, who emptied most of the small bags contained in the pouch, but kept the pouch and two of the

---

^1 This specimen is described as follows by Mr. E. H. Hawley, curator of musical instruments at the U.S. National Museum: "Total length, 10 inches; body length, 6 inches; diameter, 5¾ to 6 inches. This is an irregular gourd shell with a short neck. A wooden handle enters the neck and emerges at the blossom end. 3/16-inch holes are made in the neck, and a strip of leather is sewn to the neck through these holes; this leather is brought down over the handle and bound to it by a strip of bright cloth. This provides a firm attachment between the gourd and handle. Near the outer end of the handle, a groove is cut; a strip of twisted cloth is tied in it so it can be worn on the arm or hung up. remedies. The niece’s name was Maka'-peźu'tawin (Earth-medicine Woman). One of her songs (No. 146) is included in this work. In the pouch were seven empty medicine bags, the entire foot of an eagle, and a small piece of an elk bone. On the inner edge of each medicine bag was a small mark by which the contents could be identified. Earth-medicine Woman said that her uncle used the eagle claw in treating scrofulous sores, especially on the neck. For this purpose, he scraped the surface of the claw, mixed a small quantity of the scrapings with hot water, and applied the mixture to the skin. The elk bone was said to be an effective remedy for broken bones. It was prepared in the same way as the eagle claw, but the mixture was taken internally.

A medicine pouch made of badger's paws is shown in plate 34; this was obtained among the Teton Sioux, but its history is unknown.

<image-desc>FIG. 27. Bear claw used in treatment of the sick. A scientific line drawing of a bear claw, showing the curved keratinous sheath attached to a fragment of the digit's bone structure.</image-desc>

Eagle Shield said that he received his knowledge of herbs from the bear and the badger; the former gave him instructions concerning most of the remedies which he used for adults, and the latter told him of remedies for children. As already noted, those who dreamed of the bear were supposed to have particularly effective remedies. (See p. 195.) Like others who gave valuable information, Eagle Shield hesitated at first, but later became interested, expressing a desire to make his part of the work as complete as possible.<note>The material furnished by Eagle Shield and White-paw Bear in this section was interpreted by Mrs. James McLaughlin.</note> For this reason, he sold his medicine bag and four small bags containing herbs which he always took with him when visiting the sick. He also secured fresh specimens of many medicinal herbs which he used in his practice. These were sent to Washington for identification, with a view to determining whether any of them are used in the medical practice of white people. Furthermore, Eagle Shield permitted the photographing of a bear claw which he said had been in his possession for 48 years and was constantly used by him in treating the sick. (Fig. 27.)

Eagle Shield's medicine bag (pl. 35) was made of the entire skin of an animal called by the Sioux *i'kusana*, or "white chin."<note>On examination of this specimen at the U.S. National Museum, the animal was identified as a mink, subspecies *Mustela vison lacustris*.</note> He said that he killed this animal 44 years ago, on the present site of Fort Keogh, Montana. He was hunting large game in the autumn, after the leaves had fallen, and had two antelopes on his horse when he killed this little creature near the water. Ever since that time, he had used the hide as a medicine pouch. The matted fur around the neck shows the manner in which it was carried. In this pouch were placed

small buckskin packets of herbs. The large supply was kept in a bundle that was placed outside his lodge during the day and brought inside every night, being treated with great respect. The number of small packets in a medicine pouch varied according to the man who used them. For example, the medicine pouch belonging to Sitting Eagle contained seven small packets, which were said to be only part of the remedies he used. Eagle Shield had four principal remedies, the most important of which was contained in a beaded case. This herb is described in connection with song No. 81. His four medicine packets, together with a small spoon of white bone used for giving medicine to children, are shown in plate 36.

As already stated, an Indian doctor in the old days did not pretend to have a remedy for every disease. Thus Eagle Shield said that if an Indian were suffering from a malady, he would go to a doctor and say, "Have you a remedy for such and such an ailment?" The doctor did not hesitate to say he lacked the remedy if that were the case, as he was not expected to have any remedies except those that various animals had revealed to him, unless he had acquired a few from other medicine men.

The herb kept by Eagle Shield in the decorated bag (pl. 36) was called <term>*taö'pi peźu'ta*</term>, "herb for the wounded." Many remarkable cures are said to have been performed by Eagle Shield through the use of this remedy. A fresh specimen of the herb was obtained and identified as <term>*Achillea lanulosa*</term> Nutt. (yarrow). It was said to "grow on hills and in the Bad Lands." The entire plant was dried, and instead of being prepared as a tea, the patient was required to chew it. Eagle Shield said that he had treated men shot through the body and they had recovered. One man treated this way was personally known to the writer. The man had attempted suicide by shooting himself in the left side; the bullet passed through his body and broke the edge of the shoulder blade. As a result of the wound, his arm was paralyzed, and two white doctors said that it must be amputated. Eagle Shield undertook the treatment of the case and did his work so effectively that the man appears to have as much use of one arm as the other. For this treatment, Eagle Shield received a fee of $100, a new white tent, a revolver, and a steer.

Eagle Shield said that he sang the following song when treating wounded people with this herb. Between the performances of all these songs, he gave deep groans, like those of a man in extreme distress, frequently interspersing these with a hissing exhalation of his breath. (See Bulletin 53, p. 264; also p. 247 of this work.)

*Analysis.*—More than 60 percent of the intervals in this song are larger than a minor third. This is an unusual proportion of large intervals. Fifteen of these intervals are fourths, nine are fifths, and one is an octave. Two performances were recorded, and they show no differences. The melody has a minor tonality and contains every tone of the octave except the sixth and seventh.

See the plot of this melody on page 283.

The following song was used with the same herb as the previous one and was sung when the patient began to improve.

The first half of this song is based on the triad C—E-flat—G. This part includes the repetitions of the rhythmic unit. The latter part contains only the tones of the minor third G—B-flat, and the song is considered to be in the key of G minor, even though the fifth of that key does not appear. The rhythmic unit of this song is longer than those of many other songs and is interesting. The rhythm of the latter part of the song is somewhat similar but does not duplicate any of the count-divisions of the unit. The song begins and ends on the same tone, a peculiarity occurring in only 11 Chippewa songs <note>See Bulletin 53, page 222.</note>. The following other songs in the present series have this structure: Nos. 97, 99, 207, 212, 220, 221, 234, 238. Five renditions of this song were recorded. There was no break between the first and second rendition, but a short pause was made between the others.

A remedy used by Eagle Shield for those suffering from a loss of appetite was called *loćé' pi śni peźi'huta*. The plant was said to grow "near creeks and in gravel." Only the root was used. This herb was identified as *Astragalus carolinianus* L. (loco weed). The following song was sung in connection with its use. In a short speech before singing the song, Eagle Shield said that it was the song of a bear.

<page-num>259</page-num>
<header>DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC</header>

*Analysis.*—This song is characterized by the interval of the fourth, which makes up 18 percent of the total number of intervals. It appears in the first part of the song as the descending progression E–B, and later as A–E; the ascent of an octave brings a return of the interval E–B, followed again by A–E, descending to the tonic. The melody tones consist only of the minor triad and the fourth, and the song is harmonic in structure. The rhythmic unit is short and consists of a phrase that is common in these songs.

Eagle Shield had a special remedy for those suffering from headaches—an herb called *nasu'la yazan'pi ipi'ya*, or "no appetite medicine," which grew on the prairie. The root was dried, powdered, and sprinkled on hot coals so the patient could inhale the fumes. This plant was identified as *Artemisia frigida* Willd. (Colorado sage).

Before recording the song, Eagle Shield spoke the following sentences:

*Pežu'ta čiču' ktelo' tka wašte' ča yani' ktelo' lena'ke wašte' ke'yape.*
*(Translation)* I shall give you herbs, and they are good, so you shall recover; they say all of these are good.<margin>1</margin>

The following song was sung during the treatment.

<header>BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61</header>

*Analysis.*—Few songs in this series have upward and downward intervals as nearly equal as this song, in which 27 progressions move upward and 32 move downward. The major second occurs 11 times in upward and 11 times in downward progressions, and the minor second is found 10 times in upward and 10 times in downward progressions; yet the melody is not monotonous, and the intonation on these small intervals was better than in most similar cases. The song begins on the octave and ends on the tonic. All the tones of the octave are present except the sixth. It is interesting to observe that the interval between the seventh and eighth is in some instances a semitone and in others a whole tone. The transcription is from the first performance, which gives the entire song, while the second and third performances omit the first four measures. This is in accordance with a custom observed among both the Chippewa and Sioux, where the first phrase of a song seems in many instances to serve as an introduction to the performance.

An herb called *cante' yazaŋ'pi iću'wa* was prepared as a tea and used for those suffering from “heart trouble or pain in the stomach.” This plant was identified as *Astragalus* sp. (loco weed).

Before singing, Eagle Shield said:

> *Te'han mawa'ni kte śni ećaŋ'ni ķe'yaśi to'kśa eća'na maya'ni ketlo'.*
> (*Translation*) You may think it will be a long time before I can walk, but in only a short time you shall be able to walk.¹

The following song was sung as the herb was administered.

Analysis.—The interval of a fourth is prominent in the first part of this melody. It appears in the opening measures as the descending interval E-flat to B-flat; the tone A also occurs, and the descent from B-flat to A-flat introduces the tonic chord. The fourth then appears as the descending interval A-flat to E-flat. The subdominant of the key occurs twice, and in both instances, it was sung slightly sharp, as indicated in the transcription. The song is major in tonality and contains all the tones of the octave except the sixth and seventh. Four renditions were recorded, which are uniform in every respect.

Eagle Shield could be called a specialist in the treatment of broken bones. In this treatment, he used an herb identified as *Allionia nyctaginea* Michx., called by the Sioux *hu'huwehañkañ peźu'ta*,¹ which was said to grow in the woods. The dried leaves and root of this plant were mixed with soft grease. When treating a fracture, Eagle Shield covered his hands with this mixture; after holding them over the coals until they were warm, he rubbed the flesh above the broken bone. He said the patient was often so relieved by this treatment that he fell asleep. The treatment was repeated three times a day and continued "until the fracture was healed." He said that when an arm or leg was first broken, he "pulled it until the bone slipped into place," then covered it with a parfleche case laced together with thongs. This case was removed for the treatment described above, but he emphasized the need of keeping the case firmly laced and of tightening it whenever the thongs seemed to be loosening. He said the purpose of the rubbing was to keep the muscles from becoming stiff. He added that he had treated four cases in which the large bone of the leg was broken, and in each instance, the patient was able to walk in a month. One was a fracture near the hip. It had been put in iron braces by a white doctor, but the patient, unable to endure the treatment, came to him.

Eagle Shield made a small "splint" of parfleche, 8 inches in length, saying this was the size he would use for a broken wrist. In it, with Indian accuracy, he put a piece of old, soft flannel, saying that was what he "would put next to the person's arm." He sold to the author a matted portion of soft hair, which he said was the shed hair of a deer; this was thick with grease. Eagle Shield said he had used this in treating fractures for more than forty years, holding it in his hand as he rubbed the flesh (see pl. 37).

The song used by Eagle Shield in treating fractures was sung four times "while getting ready to apply the medicine."

*Analysis.*—Three versions of this song were recorded, and in all of them, the changes in measure lengths occur exactly as shown in the transcription, with the tempo being remarkably well-maintained. It is impossible to use an eighth note as the metric unit for the first and similar measures, because 6/8 time implies two groups of triplets, whereas the three beats in these measures are distinctly defined. The rhythmic unit is interesting, and fragments of it appear in parts of the song that do not contain the full unit. The song is in a minor key and lacks the seventh and fourth notes of the complete octave. (See song No. 26.)

The fourth interval makes up 37 percent of the total number of intervals in this song, a proportion even higher than that in the previous song. In the descending fourth from D to G, the lowest note was consistently sung slightly sharp in this song, providing a contrast to the previous song, where the fourth was sung with accurate intonation.

Eagle Shield shared the following story about his dream of the badger, through which he obtained his remedies for children. As previously mentioned, the remedies for adults were received from the bear.

->Eagle Shield said:<-

> A man appeared to me in a dream, showed me a plant, and said, "My friend, remember this plant well. Be sure to get the right one, as this is effective." It was a badger who appeared to me in human form and said this. This was the first time the badger visited me, but later he brought me other herbs. There were no songs associated with any of the herbs the badger brought me. To repay the badger’s kindness, I took tobacco, chopped it finely, and dug a hole in the ground. I buried the tobacco and said, "Badger, I give you this in return for what you have told me." When the badger is alive, he eats this herb. Any herb introduced by the badger is especially good. Some believe his medicine is stronger than that of the bear because he digs deeper and further into the ground.

Eagle Shield said that he buried a small amount of tobacco as an offering to the badger whenever he dug up any of these roots. He also said that before administering these remedies to a child, he always made a prayer similar to the following: "Wakan Tanka, you created these herbs. We are going to give them to this child. We hope you will make the child well, and we hope nothing will interfere with the effectiveness of these herbs."

The first remedy given to Eagle Shield by the badger was a plant identified as *Leptilon canadense* (L.) Britton (horseweed). This was used as a treatment for intestinal pain and diarrhea. Since it is a mild remedy and the size of the plant varies, it was difficult to specify the exact amount to be used for a dose. Eagle Shield said that if a plant were small, it would be necessary to use the entire root and a few inches of the stalk, but if the plant were large, half the root would be sufficient for a dose. A decoction <note>a medicinal preparation made by boiling a plant in water</note> was prepared, and he said it was "good to smell the tea to judge its strength, as it should smell of the root to be right." He said it "should be taken before meals, in the morning

...the dose being the largest. If a person should take this after a meal, it would cause distress, but when taken before a meal, it prepares the stomach to receive and digest the food." A small spoon made of white bone was used when giving medicine to children. (See Plate 36.)

The second of Eagle Shield's remedies for children was identified as *Chenopodium album* L. (lamb's-quarters). A decoction of the entire plant was used in cases of bloody dysentery. It could be administered from the time a child was old enough to drink water, with the dose being increased according to the age of the child.

The third remedy was for diarrhea and was seemingly stronger than the others, as the dose was about a teaspoonful and only two or three doses were usually given. The herb was not boiled; instead, hot water was poured over it to make a tea. This was identified as *Aquilegia canadensis* L. (wild columbine).

The fourth remedy was for fever and headache. In this instance, the herb was to be steeped. Some was given internally, and the child's entire body was rubbed with it. This herb was identified as *Rumex* sp. (dock).

Mato'-nape'-ska (Bear-with-White-Paw) (Plate 38) was a man who showed great seriousness in describing his medical practice. He said that when treating the sick, he wore one side of his hair unbraided, as shown in the illustration. (See p. 64.) The drum he holds is the one he used when singing his medicine songs. The term <term>ċaŋ'ċeġa</term> <note>the Sioux name for drums</note> is applied by the Sioux to all drums, including both the large dance drums and the hand drum. The specimen shown here (Plate 39) has a single head made of rawhide and is held by two iron wires at the back, which are passed through a short section of iron tubing to form a handle. Thongs or strips of stout cloth are also used as handles on these drums, which are common to many Indian tribes. (See Bulletin 53, p. 62.) Drums of this type appear in the hands of members of the <term>Kaŋġi'yuha</term> <note>Crow Owners society</note> in a native drawing by Eagle Shield (Plate 40). The drumstick used by Bear-with-White-Paw is elaborately decorated with porcupine quills and could be used with a large dance drum as well as with a hand drum. Such a stick might be carried to a gathering by a man who expected to sing at the drum.

A "necklace" which Bear-with-White-Paw said he had worn for many years when attending the sick is shown in Plate 41. He said that when summoned to visit a sick person, it was his custom to put on this "necklace," which consists of a strip of hide with two small bags of "medicine" and a bear's claw attached to it. He further stated that he pressed this claw into the patient's flesh so that the medicine might enter more easily and be more effective. Eagle Shield also used a bear's claw in treating the sick (p. 253).

BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61

Like Eagle Shield, Bear-with-White-Paw received his knowledge of healing herbs from the bear. He said, "The bear is very truthful. He has a soul like ours, and his soul speaks to mine in my sleep and tells me what to do."

Six herbs were described to the author by Bear-with-White-Paw, and fresh specimens were provided for identification.

Before beginning his account of the herbs and their uses, he offered the following supplication to the bear—a prayer which he said he would use when treating the sick:

> Ho mita'kola oŋ maśi'ke taŋyaŋ' ana'maġoptaŋ yo. Aŋpe'tu kiŋ lehaŋl' ta'ku waŋźi' awa'ćaŋ mi he oći'ćiyakiŋ ktelo'. Peźu'ta lena'ke ślolye' mayaki'yiŋ na ta'ku ećoŋ' maya'śi na wo'yazaŋ waŋ'źigźi api'ye ma'yaśi na hena' iyo'kihe kta ke'he koŋ wana' lehaŋl' iya'hpe wa'yiŋ kta tka he'će iyu'ha owa'kihi kta. Wo'yazaŋ hena' heyab' iya'yiŋ kte.

Translated as follows by Mr. Higheagle:

> My friend, I am poor and needy. Listen well to me. Today I have something in mind, and I wish to tell you. You have made all these medicines known to me, and you have commanded me to perform certain actions in order to treat specific illnesses. You have told me that these medicines possess certain powers within them. Now I wish to use them effectively. I want these illnesses to go away.

Bear-with-White-Paw said that he had only one song, which he sang while using all these herbs. The song is as follows:

*Analysis.*—This is the only song recorded by this singer. It is an interesting melody and was sung twice. There is no difference between the renditions, and the singer’s performance was characterized by a marked degree of carefulness, similar to that of Brave Buffalo when singing similar songs. The tonic chord (D minor) is evident throughout this song; however, it is classified as melodic with a harmonic framework because of the accented G, which appears four times. The last tone of the rhythmic unit was slightly shortened in every instance, as indicated in the transcription. The song contains 32 intervals, only two of which are larger than a minor third.

The herbs provided by Bear-with-White-Paw, along with the directions for their use, are as follows:

(1) Identified as *Cheirinia aspera* (DC.) Britton (western wallflower). This was said to be a very rare plant among the Sioux, though it can occasionally be found on level ground or along a river. It was used as a remedy for cramps in the stomach or bowels. The plant has long, slender seed pods, somewhat resembling pine needles. In preparing the medicine, these seed pods are opened and the seeds are removed and crushed. Warm (not hot) water is poured over them, at which point the water becomes yellow. This mixture is taken internally and also applied externally. It is a very strong medicine, and if the person has been sick for only one day, a single dose of the remedy is usually sufficient.

(2) Identified as *Heuchera hispida* Pursh (alum root). This plant was said to grow on high ground. Only the root was used; this is so strong that a fragment of a small root about half an inch long was a sufficient dose for a child. It is a powerful astringent and was used as a remedy for chronic diarrhea. Usually, only two or three doses were given.

(3) Identified as *Lithospermum linearifolium* Goldie (puccoon). This was used as a remedy for hemorrhages from the lungs. The

<meta>This page continues the descriptions of medicinal herbs provided by Bear-with-White-Paw and other Sioux healers, following the analysis of their ceremonial songs.</meta>

# 270
## BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61

The plant grows on the hills and has fragrant white flowers. Bear-with-White-Paw said, "The scent of these flowers reaches every plant that brings healing to people. It makes them sweeter and strengthens them as they grow in the field." He also said that the medicine men keep this or another fragrant herb in the bundle with their roots during the winter. (Compare p. 79.)

(4) Identified as *Echinacea angustifolia* DC. (“nigger head”). A specimen of this herb was also provided by Jaw (pl. 59), who, like Bear-with-White-Paw, said that he used it as a remedy for toothache. Bear-with-White-Paw provided other uses for it, saying that he used it also for pain in the bowels; that it would cure tonsillitis, and was frequently used in combination with other herbs. Only the root of this plant was used.

(5) Identified as *Monarda fistulosa* L. (horsemint). This was said to be an “elk herb” but is not the same variety of plant as the one called the “elk herb” in the description of Brave Buffalo’s dream, which was identified as *Monarda scabra* Beck. (See p. 178.) This remedy was used to reduce fever and was also said to be “good for a severe cold.” Only the blossoms were used, and Bear-with-White-Paw said they were so strong that “only a little” should be used when making the tea.

(6) This herb, identified as *Allionia nyctaginea* Michx. (umbrellawort), is the same as the specimen provided by Eagle Shield and used externally by him in the treatment of broken bones. Bear-with-White-Paw gave the following directions for its use: “Grate the root, moisten it, and rub it on the skin wherever there is a swelling.” He said it grew close to the water and was intended only for external use.

The account concerning these medicines was given at intervals over a period of several weeks, as much time was required to find suitable specimens of the herbs. Bear-with-White-Paw understood the purpose of the study, and the plants he brought were especially large and representative. When the work was completed, he assured the writer of the sincerity with which he had done his part, saying again, “These are the medicines which I use for the purposes I have told you, and the song which I sing when I use them.”

In addition to the herbs obtained from Eagle Shield and Bear-with-White-Paw, two plants were obtained from Jaw: one mentioned above and another which was said to be an unfailing cure for rheumatism; this was identified as *Parmelia* sp. (a lichen). No songs were recorded by Jaw in connection with the use of these herbs.

**Analysis.**—This melody contains 23 measures but only 11 progressions, 6 of which are downward and 5 upward. It has a <term>compass</term> of only 6 tones. Among 340 Chippewa songs, 7 percent have a range of 6 or fewer tones, and in the present series, 5 percent have this range. The <term>rhythmic unit</term> is long and interesting, possessing a completeness which is frequently lacking in such units. The melody tones are those of the fourth <term>five-tone scale</term>. The <term>tonic chord</term> is clearly felt throughout the melody, which would be classified as <term>harmonic in structure</term> except for the accented C, which occurs once in the song.

BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61 NARRATIVE OF A VIGIL AND PRAYER FOR THE SICK

## By TATAŊK'-EHAŊ'NI (OLD BUFFALO)

It was with considerable hesitation that Old Buffalo told this story and depicted the event in a drawing (pl. 42). It is an account of a prayer vigil which he kept for a niece who was very ill and who, he believed, recovered because of this action on his part. Such a vigil is called by the Sioux *haŋble'ćapi*, 'prayers offered standing.' <note>¹Compare the vigil by Śiya'ka (pages 184-188)</note>

This narrative is given in the present tense, as it was related, and the words of the interpreter (Mrs. James McLaughlin) are followed as closely as possible. Old Buffalo said:

I have a sister older than myself. We are children of one father and one mother. As my sister's child is growing up to be a young girl, she falls ill, and is so thin that there is no flesh on her bones. She cannot rise from her bed. I sit beside her. She asks me to bring her a drink of water. My heart is very sad. As I see her, I think, "I will call on Wakaŋ'taŋka for help." I had heard that when men reached a point of helplessness in sickness they did this. I could not bear the thought of going many miles barefoot, but I wanted the girl to recover.

I go up a high hill and make a vow, saying, "Wakaŋ'taŋka, I call upon you. Have pity on me. My niece is on her deathbed. Have pity on her, so she can live on earth and see you. Give me strength to do what is right and honest. I will give you four sacrifices. I will smoke a fine pipe. It is a Chief's pipe, so you can bless it. I will do this in your honor if you will spare her life."

The girl recovers. She drinks water and eats a little food.

Now I am going to fulfill my vow to Wakaŋ'taŋka. It is July, and the weather is very hot. They make a lodge for me at some distance from the village. It is a lodge of branches. Several men take the big-leaf sage and spread it on the ground in the lodge, then they bring hot stones and pour water on them. As I sit in the lodge, it is filled with steam. When I am wet with sweating, the men rub me with sage. They take a buffalo robe, put it around me with the fur outside, and tie it across my chest. The discomfort of wearing this heavy robe is part of my sacrifice, as well as the disgrace of being dressed like a woman. I have no moccasins on my feet. So I start for the distant hill where I am to offer my prayer. I carry a pipe decorated with ribbons and mallard-duck feathers, holding the stem upward in front of me as I walk. The sun has not been up long as I leave the village, and I reach the hill before noon. There I find a buffalo skull, which a man has brought from the village. It is a large skull with horns on it. My friends have also prepared a soft place on the ground for me and covered it with sage leaves, so that I may rest when I am too weary from standing. That afternoon I hold the pipe and follow the sun with it. At night I lie face down on the sage.

Now the sun has risen. I stand up again, facing the east and holding the pipe. All day I follow the sun with the stem of the pipe. The second night I stand up all night, until the daylight appears. Then I put my pipe against the buffalo skull and lie down with my head near it. When the sun has fully risen I stand up again and cry, saying "Give me strength for long life, and strength to be right and honest in all I do." On the third day I put a piece of red cloth [*waöŋ'yapi*] at each of the four directions.

Just as the sun is going down on this day, they come for me. I leave the buffalo skull, the pipe, and the four offerings of red cloth on the hill. Now I am going back

<summary>Old Buffalo recounts a personal narrative of a three-day prayer vigil and ritual sacrifice he performed to save his niece from a terminal illness. The ritual involved fasting, enduring the heat of a steam lodge, and standing on a hill with a sacred pipe and buffalo skull.</summary>

...with my friends, still walking with bare feet. They have made a new sweat lodge near the old one, and I am the first to enter it. Again they bring hot stones and pour water on them, and again they rub me with the sage leaves. After this I put on moccasins and leggings, and go away.

This is the means by which we prolonged our lives in the old days. My niece recovered.

The writer then asked a question about the care given to the girl by the medicine-man (or doctor), and Old Buffalo replied indignantly:

> “It was Wakaŋ'taŋka who saved her life; not the doctor. She lived in answer to my prayer.”

This song is commonly used by medicine-men of the tribe:

*Analysis.*—This song contains the tones of the fourth five-toned scale. In structure, it is melodic with a harmonic framework, and the tonic chord is strongly evident throughout the melody. Regarding the change in tempo, see song No. 5. In this instance, the phrase indicated as the rhythmic unit of the song is long and is not accurately repeated. Three reasons seem to justify this: (1) the phrase forms the rhythmic divisions of the entire song; (2) the phrase opens with the same measure-divisions in every instance; and (3) the note values of the phrase were necessarily changed in some instances to conform to the words. Two-thirds of the progressions are downward, and the song contains only three intervals larger than a minor third. See the plot of this melody on page 283.

In this song, we encounter a strange phase in the life of a <term>medicine-man</term>. Two Shields, who recorded the song, said that “White Shield used to sing this song when he was worried or disappointed.” This little melody is strangely human. Two Shields also said that when singing the song, he would mention the direction from which the wind was blowing that day, as “every man who performs ceremonies respects the various winds.”

## SOCIETIES (OKO'LAKIĆIYE)

Two classes of societies existed among the Sioux—dream societies and military societies. Both classes are mentioned by Hayden, one of the earliest writers on the Indians of the upper plains. Hayden lists the Sioux societies as the "Bull Head, Elk, and Bear" (the first being correctly translated as "buffalo" and all being dream societies); he also lists the "Scalp, Strong Heart, Fox, Big Owl, and Soldier."<note>Hayden, F. V., *Ethnography and Philology of the Indian Tribes of the Missouri Valley*, p. 281, Philadelphia, 1862.</note> In every instance, the Sioux equivalent name is given, identifying the societies with organizations of relatively recent times.

Societies based on dreams (known as "dream societies") were composed of men who, in their fasting visions, had seen the same animal. The common experience of the vision bound the men together, and societies were thus formed. These societies held meetings to which only those who had dreamed of the animal for which the society was named were admitted. Concerning these societies, Miss Fletcher writes:

> Among the Siouan family of Indians, there are societies, religious in character, which are distinguished by the name of some animal. . . . Membership in these societies is not confined to any particular <term>gens</term> <note>a group of families with a common ancestor</note>, or grouping of <term>gentes</term>, but depends upon supernatural indications over which the individual has no control. The animal which appears to a man in a vision during his religious fasting determines to which society he must belong.<note>Fletcher, Alice C., *The Elk Mystery or Festival. Ogallala Sioux*, in *Reps. Peabody Museum*, III, pp. 276, 277, Cambridge, 1887. Cf. also Wissler, Clark, *Societies and Ceremonial Associations of the Teton-Dakota*, *Anthr. Papers, Amer. Mus. Nat. Hist.*, XI, pt. 1, pp. 81-98, New York, 1912.</note>

Among the Teton Sioux, there are some societies which belong unmistakably to one of these groups and others which, according to the writer's informants, probably originated in a dream of the name-animal but are now open to men who have distinguished themselves in war. Thus, the Elk and the Buffalo are distinctly dream societies, and the Strong Heart, Miwa'tani, and White Horse Riders are distinctly military in character, while the great military society of the Kaŋġi'yuha is said to have originated in a dream of an owl. The writer obtained an account of a dream of a wolf, but the terms "Wolf society" and "Fox society" seem to some extent interchangeable at the present time. Mention was made of a Horse society, but no dream of a horse was recorded; it was, however, a dream society and is included by Wissler in his list of "dream cults."

<summary>This page explains the structure of Sioux societies, categorizing them into dream societies based on shared animal visions and military societies based on bravery in war. It highlights that dream society membership was determined by supernatural fasting visions rather than kinship.</summary>

It is probable that these societies held no regular meetings and that no new members of the military organizations had been elected for about 30 years before this material was collected. Therefore, it is impossible to obtain much reliable information on the history of these societies among the Teton Sioux.

### DREAM SOCIETIES

#### BUFFALO SOCIETY

Regarding the Buffalo society, Dr. Lowie writes:

> Among the Santee, the men performing the Buffalo dance <term>Tatanⁿk watcīpi</term> had seen visions of the buffalo, although it seems the sons of such men were also entitled to join. One man might dream that he . . . had been shot by an arrow so that he could barely get home. . . . Such a man painted himself vermilion to represent blood trickling down. Another man dreamed of being shot with a gun. He would act out his dream during a Buffalo dance.³

Catlin mentions the Buffalo dance in one of his letters,⁴ stating that he witnessed it at Fort Snelling, Minnesota. The author saw a Buffalo dance at Bull Head, South Dakota, on July 4, 1913. In this dance, it is customary for the dancers to wear headdresses decorated with buffalo horns and to imitate the movements of buffalo. A shield used in the buffalo dance is shown in plate 43.

The following songs were reportedly sung in the Buffalo society. Some of these songs were said to have been received or composed during a dream about buffalo, but the story of the dream has been forgotten, leaving only the songs as a tribal tradition.

### No. 103. Buffalo Society Song (c) (Catalogue No. 577)

->Sung by SHOOTER<-

VOICE <term>♩</term> = 112

<image-desc>Musical notation for the "Buffalo Society Song (c)". The score is written on three staves. It begins in 2/4 time with a key signature of two sharps. **Analysis.**—This song is based on the second five-tone scale and has a melodic structure. Its range is small, spanning only six tones. Two-thirds of the melodic progressions move downward, and two intervals occur that are larger than a minor third. Several performances were recorded, and all were consistent. The rhythmic form of the song is interesting. The rhythmic unit appears twice, followed by a one-beat pause, after which the unit appears twice again; the remainder of the song resembles the unit but does not repeat it. Such precision of form suggests that the song is clear in the singer's mind and is being performed correctly. The interval between B and A-sharp was not always an exact half-step, but the A-natural in the third measure from the end was consistently performed as a much larger interval. This shows that the singer intended to sing a different tone than the one used in the preceding measures.

## ELK SOCIETY

The men who had dreamed of the elk (see page 176 and following) banded together and called themselves the Elk Society. Two Shields was one of the singers and drummers in this society, the last meeting of which was held about 30 years ago. He sang the following song, which was used in this society and which he said had been passed down for many generations. He stated that the song is still performed at dances and must always be paid for by the person who requests that it be sung. Such a person is usually an elk dreamer.

DENSMORE]   TETON SIOUX MUSIC

The hoop carried by an elk dreamer is mentioned as "a rainbow" in the following song. The following explanation was given for the use of this term: 

> "Part of the rainbow is visible in the clouds, and part disappears into the ground. What we see is in the shape of a hoop. This word is used by medicine men and especially by those who dream of the elements of the air and the earth." 

(For songs of a man who dreamed of a rainbow, see Nos. 61 and 62.) The hoop of an elk dreamer was considered sacred, and the dreamer took great pride in it. When carrying it, he sometimes put it around his neck or thrust one arm through it and carried it on his shoulder. Such a hoop is shown in plate 26 and is described in connection with Brave Buffalo's dream of the elk.

DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC [297]

*Analysis.*—The first four measures of this song are based on the tonic chord. Among both the Chippewa and Sioux, it is unusual for the tonic chord to be presented at the opening of a song. In this instance, these measures serve as an introduction to the performance of the song, being sung only once while the repeated part was sung six times without a break in the tempo. The high tones in this song, especially the accented tones, were delivered with a sharp attack, which began slightly above the tone and immediately descended to it. This was a personal style of the singer that is impossible to indicate in musical notation. An augmented second is found in the song; this, as well as the minor second, was performed with particularly good intonation. An augmented second also occurs in songs No. 63 and No. 225. This song contains the tones of the fourth five-toned scale and is melodic in structure. Only two intervals larger than a minor third appear in the song.

BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61]

*Analysis.*—The fourth makes up 55 percent of the intervals in this song, a characteristic frequently seen in songs concerning animals. Many other intervals in this song are seconds, which form part of the descent of a fourth. An ascent of an eleventh is achieved in two intervals with the introduction of the lyrics. This represents the entire range of the song, which contains the tones of the fourth five-toned scale and is melodic in structure. Two distinct rhythmic units occur. It is often noted that two rhythmic units in a song share one or more identical measure divisions.

### HORSE SOCIETY

No dream of a horse was shared with the writer, but the Teton Sioux have an organization called the Horse Society. It was said that some of the songs in the following group were used in this society and were also used on the warpath to make a horse swift and reliable. The high regard in which the Sioux hold the horse is shown by a speech from Brave Buffalo. This speech was made before the singing of his first song and was recorded by the phonograph. Freely translated, it is as follows:

> Of all the animals, the horse is the Indian's best friend, for without it he could not go on long journeys. A horse is the Indian's most valuable piece of property. If an Indian wishes to achieve something, he promises his horse that if the horse will help him, he will paint it with native dye so that everyone may see that help has come to him through the aid of his horse.

Śiya'ka said that on one occasion when he was hard-pressed on the warpath, he dismounted, and standing in front of his horse, spoke to him, saying—

> We are in danger. Obey me immediately so that we may conquer. If you have to run for your life and mine, do your best, and if we reach home, I will give you the best eagle feather I can get and the finest <term>sina' lu'ta</term>, and you shall be decorated with the best paint. <note>The eagle feather was tied to the horse's tail, and the sina' lu'ta was a strip of red cloth fastened around the horse's neck. (See p. 388.)</note>

<summary>This page analyzes the musical structure of animal-themed songs and introduces the Teton Sioux Horse Society, emphasizing the spiritual and practical importance of horses. It includes speeches by Brave Buffalo and Śiya'ka regarding the bond between a warrior and his horse.</summary>

<keywords>Horse Society, Teton Sioux, Brave Buffalo, Śiya'ka, sina' lu'ta, musical analysis, rhythmic units, warpath, ethnomusicology</keywords>

**Analysis.**—This is one of the instances in which the key signature indicates the pitch of the tones as performed by the singer but does not imply a "key" in the technical musical sense of the term. The song is classified as "irregular" (see the table on page 305). It should be noted that the progressions of the first 12 measures are based on the major triad of B—D-sharp—F-sharp, yet the presence of E-sharp makes it impossible to consider that part of the song to be in the key of B. The remainder of the song suggests the key of B minor. In the first part of the song, Brave Buffalo sang E-sharp and D-sharp, and in the latter part he sang E-natural and D-natural; these tones were delivered clearly and unmistakably. A comparison of the tone C, recorded at the beginning of the cylinder, with C on a piano, shows that the phonograph was properly adjusted when the record was made. Therefore, the change of pitch is not due to any slowing of speed in the recording machine, which might have been the case if the machine's mechanism had partially run down. Two performances were recorded, with a pause and some conversation between them, and the unique characteristics of the first performance were repeated exactly in the second. The personality of the singer should be taken into account when considering a song of such marked eccentricity, and Brave Buffalo, who made this recording, was not a man given to

seeking effects, as some of the young men occasionally do. He recorded nine songs, and his manner of singing was marked by more than usual carefulness. This was the first song he recorded and he did it quite reluctantly. The transcription has been compared with the phonograph record many times at long intervals so that the test of the ear might be renewed. It is, therefore, the writer’s opinion that the transcription indicates as nearly as possible the song as it was sung by Brave Buffalo. It is a peculiar melody, but the purpose of the present work is to ascertain what the singer sang, not to adapt his song to a white musician's standard of either time or key.

Of the intervals in the song, 60 percent are major seconds, and the song contains only two intervals larger than a minor third. It has been noted frequently that an Indian has great difficulty in maintaining the adjustment of a melody in which a majority of the progressions are small intervals.

*Analysis.*—It is interesting to compare this with other songs about horses, not only in this group but also in the war songs (Nos. 138, 139, 140, 145). The tempo is slower, and the rhythm does not have the galloping feel found in some of the other songs. It possesses some of the dignity and solemnity that always seems present in the mind of the Sioux when they sing of the dawn. The drum follows a rapid tremolo. Two performances were recorded, which are identical in all respects. The song contains only the tones of the minor triad and the fourth. Of the intervals, 65 percent are major seconds, and the melody trends downward from the twelfth to the tonic.

*Analysis.*—Two performances of this song were recorded; these are identical except that the second is slightly lower in pitch. It has been noted that some singers will pause after the first performance of a song and then begin a second performance on exactly the same pitch as the first, while others will begin slightly higher or lower. This song contains no rhythmic unit, but the song as a whole has a rhythmic completeness that is interesting. The first and last phrases resemble each other in some of the count-divisions, particularly in the first triple measure.

*Analysis.*—The words of this song refer to the free, almost playful movements of a herd of horses. This melody is notably rhythmic. Before starting to sing, Two Shields beat the drum in a rapid tremolo; the indicated tempo of the drum was not fully established until the first few measures of the song had been sung, after which it was steadily maintained.

In its tonality, the melody is clearly minor, but it contains only one interval of a minor third; a descent from E-flat to C occurs several times, but always with D as a passing tone. The song contains only the tones of the minor triad and the second—a somewhat unusual set of tones. The interval of a second is especially prominent in the melody. Two recordings were made; they are identical in every way.

This group includes the songs of societies made up of men who have had similar dreams, with the name of the society indicating the animal that appeared in the dream (songs Nos. 95–113). Undoubtedly, many of the songs in this group are songs that were "received in dreams," but the names of the original owners have been forgotten, and the songs are now the common property of the societies.

# MILITARY SOCIETIES

Warrior organizations existed among all the Plains tribes. The term "wolf" was applied to the warriors of several tribes, while among others the term "dog soldiers" was used. W. P. Clark¹ provides a condensed account of the military organizations of the Plains Indians, identifying 11 societies among the Siouan peoples. Authors writing about specific tribes have described their customs; the following are representative citations.

## Among the Kiowa:

The Kiowa have an elaborate military organization, which is now rapidly becoming obsolete, known as the *Yä’pähe*, or "Warriors." A similar organization is found among most of the prairie tribes and is commonly known to white people as the Dog Soldier society, a name derived from an inaccurate translation of the name of one of the principal bands. The Kiowa organization consists of six orders, each having its own dance, songs, insignia, and duties.²

---

<note>¹ W. P. Clark, *The Indian Sign Language*, p. 355, Philadelphia, 1885.</note>
<note>² James Mooney, *Calendar History of the Kiowa*, Seventeenth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, part 1, p. 229, Washington, 1898.</note>

### Among the Arapaho:

Among the Arapaho, the organization was called *Běni'něna*, "Warriors," and consisted of eight degrees or orders, including nearly all the men of the tribe above the age of about 17.¹

### Among the Cheyenne:

The Great Prophet grouped these warriors into five societies who, along with the chief, were responsible for the conduct of the tribe. The societies were named the Red-Shield, Hoof-Rattle, Coyote, Dog-Men's, and Inverted or Bow-String.²

### Among the Omaha:

There were two classes of societies among the Omaha—social and secret. Membership in the social class was open to those able to perform the acts required for eligibility. To this class belong the warrior societies, as well as those for social purposes only. [This is followed by an extended consideration of the war societies.]³

### Among the Blackfeet:

The association of the All Comrades consisted of a dozen or more secret societies, graded according to age; the whole group formed an association that was partly benevolent and helpful and partly military, but its main function was to punish offenses against society at large.⁴

This association appears to resemble that of the Aki'ćita among several other tribes. (See pp. 313, 314.)

Lewis and Clark made what is probably the first recorded mention of societies among the men of the Sioux tribe. Under the date of August 30, 1804, their Journal contains the following section written by Clark:⁵

> I will note here a SOCIETY which I had never before this day heard existed in any nation of Indians; four of its members are present at this time, and they are all who remain of this band. Those who become members of this society must be brave, active young men who take a *vow* never to retreat, regardless of the danger. In war parties, they always go forward without sheltering themselves behind trees or anything else; they strictly adhere to this vow throughout their lives. An instance of this happened not long ago: while a party was crossing the Missouri River on the ice, there was a hole in the ice directly in their path which could have been easily avoided by going around it. The lead man went straight ahead and was lost; the others were dragged around the hole by the rest of the party. In a battle with the Crow (Kite) Indians who inhabit the *Cotes Noires* or Black Mountain, 18 out of 22 members of this society were killed; the remaining four were dragged away by their party. These men are capable fellows; they sit together, camp together, and dance together. This society is an imitation of the societies of the *De Corbeau* or Crow (*De Corbeau*, Kite) Indians, whom they imitate.

This evidently refers to one of the military societies of the tribe, and the action described is that of the Aki'ćita. An old man on the Standing Rock Reservation said to the writer, "Many military soci-

[Soci]eties had their origin in a dream, but the organization of these societies and their meetings were more public than those of the regular 'dream societies.'"

In his study of the Oglala Sioux, Dr. Clark Wissler divided the men’s societies into *Aki'ćita* societies, Headmen's societies, and War societies.<gloss>1</gloss> He listed six *Aki'ćita* societies as existing at the time of his observation among the Oglala on the Pine Ridge and Rosebud Reservations in South Dakota: the *Toka'la* (Kit Fox), *Kaṅgi'yuha* (Crow Owners), *Čante'-tinza* (Strong Heart), *Ihio'ka* (Badgers), *Sotka'yuha* (Bare-lance Owners), and *Wi'ćiska* (White-marked). Only the first four of these societies were found by the author among the Teton Sioux on the Standing Rock Reservation.

Another society mentioned by the author's informants was said to be known by two names: the Silent Eaters (*A'inila wo'ta*) and Strong Heart at Night (*Ahe'pi čante'tinza*). This was a secret society, entirely distinct from the Strong Heart society described in this section. No songs and no further information regarding this society were obtained.

Before proceeding to a consideration of these societies and their songs, it may be helpful to briefly consider the meaning of the term *aki'ćita*.

The word *aki'ćita* is commonly translated as "soldier," but its meaning is closer to "guard" or "police." The proper word for "warrior" is *iki'ćize*. Thus, the *Aki'ćita* societies were those whose members could be required to act as guards or marshals when the tribe was moving, or as "police" in the village. The *aki'ćita* were primarily associated with the buffalo hunt, in which they ensured that no one disregarded the laws of the chase (see p. 442); they also maintained order in the camp and punished all offenders. They were primarily civil officers, though *aki'ćita* might also be appointed to act in connection with a large war party. Hennepin records an instance of punishment by *aki'ćita* among the Santee, or eastern Sioux. In 1680, Hennepin and his party were traveling down the Mississippi River and were "in the Islands of the River," not far below the Falls of St. Anthony (probably near the site of St. Paul, Minnesota). The Indians set food before them, but while they were eating, other Indians arrived, took the food from them, and plundered the tipi. Hennepin says:

> We did not know who these people were at first; but it appeared they were some of those we had left upstream at the Falls of St. Anthony. One of them, who called himself my uncle, told me that those who had given us food had acted dishonorably by going ahead and getting the jump on the others in the hunt; and that according to the laws and customs of their country, it was legal for them to plunder them, since they had been

Lewis and Clark refer to these men as follows:

> These people have some brave men whom they use as soldiers; these men attend to the policing of the village and correct all errors. I saw one of them today whip two women <note>The original text uses the term "squars" (squaws).</note> who appeared to have had a quarrel; when he approached, everyone nearby appeared to flee in great <note>terror</note>. At night they keep two, three, four, or five men at different distances walking around the camp, singing about the occurrences of the night.<sup>2</sup>

The <term>aki'ćita</term> are mentioned also by many writers on the tribes of the Plains. Reverend J. Owen Dorsey states that "The <term>Akitcita</term>, soldiers or guards (policemen), form an important body among the Assiniboin as they do among other Siouan tribes."<sup>3</sup>

Wissler states that the manner of selecting <term>aki'ćita</term> was as follows: The chiefs chose the four "head <term>aki'ćita</term>" from one society, who in turn chose their assistants from the society to which they themselves belonged. Thus, the choice of the four head <term>aki'ćita</term> was practically the choice of a certain society for this duty. The selection was usually made at the beginning of the summer hunt, and service continued to the close of the season. It seems to have been customary, but not obligatory, for the chiefs to choose from the societies in rotation.<sup>4</sup>

Concerning the organizations of these societies, Wissler states:<sup>5</sup>

> We find a surprising degree of uniformity in details. All were liable to be called into <term>aki'ćita</term> service, while other societies never rendered such service. . . . The scheme of officers is practically the same. All have from four to six lance bearers, who are the most conspicuous, if not the most important personages in the society. They are usually grouped in pairs, as in fact are nearly all the other officers; . . . Next in rank to the two leaders stands another pair; among the <term>cante tinza</term> and the <term>wiciska</term> they are known as bonnet bearers, and among the others as pipe bearers, but their functions are much the same. These two ranking pairs are sometimes spoken of as the four chiefs in charge of the organization. There are two whip bearers in all <note>the societies</note> except the <term>kanǵi'yuha</term>. . . . As to food passers, drummers, and singers, there is general uniformity throughout. It is thus clear that whatever may have been the origin of these societies, they were all brought to an approximation of the one type.

To the nose part, some small bags of medicine are attached. [See p. 389.] The edges, feet, and ears may be decorated with porcupine quills and hung with bells according to the tastes of the individual owners. They take the jawbones of the <term>toka'la</term>, paint them red or blue (the old native colors), fasten them on a strip of otter skin or some similar material, and wear the bones on the forehead. On the back of the head, a bunch of crow tail feathers is fastened sideways, and two eagle feathers stick up. . . . When participating in a dance, the officers paint their bodies yellow.

The teachings of the society instilled "bravery, generosity, chivalry, morality, and fraternity for fellow members." Men who joined the society were required to promise obedience to these teachings, and the whip bearers had whips of a unique kind with which they lashed those who disregarded their vows. One of the officers of the society was the custodian of the drum.

The "kit-fox dance" as performed by the Santee Sioux is described by Dr. Lowie;<note>1. Ibid., p. 155.</note> Some of the songs of this society are still sung at Fort Berthold, North Dakota, and have been recorded by the writer.

Miss Fletcher mentions the <term>Toka'lo</term> (<term>Toka'la</term>) among the Omaha as one of two "social societies that were borrowed or introduced from the Dakota. . . . There are no words to the songs—a fact which makes it probable that the music was adopted from another tribe, the foreign words being dropped."<note>6. Fletcher, Alice C., and La Flesche, Francis, *The Omaha Tribe*, op. cit., p. 486.</note>
