### KANǦI'YUHA (CROW-OWNERS)<note>The author's informant regarding the Kaŋgi'yuha was Eagle Shield (Waŋbli'-waha'ćunka), who was a member of the society. In plate 43, he is shown wearing the "crow-skin necklace" (*kaŋgi'waná'pi*), which was the insignia of the society.</note>

This society, like other military and social organizations, was widespread among the tribes of the Plains. Miss Fletcher states that, among the Omaha, "the wolf and the crow were not only connected with carnage, but they had a mythical relation to the office of 'soldiers,' the designation given to certain men on the annual tribal hunt who acted as marshals."<note>Fletcher and La Flesche, in the previously cited work, p. 442.</note> A full description of "the crow" worn by the Omaha, with an account of its symbolism, is given by Miss Fletcher.<note>Ibid., p. 441.</note> Among the northern tribes, the crow and the raven appear to be connected exclusively with success in war, with the skin of the bird being worn around the neck or attached to the spear that was carried in battle. A "Crow or Raven society" was noted among the Mandan and was mentioned by Maximilian.<note>*Travels in the Interior of North America in the years 1832 to 1834*, by Prince Maximilian of Wied, ii, p. 140, Coblenz, 1841. "The second class or band is the... Crow or Raven band (*La bande du corbeau*), young people from 20 to 25 years old."</note>

The Crow-owners society of the Teton Sioux and the Raven-bearers society of the Mandan, as studied by the present author, appear to be similar in essential features. Lowie, however, uses the term "Crow society" in his list of Mandan organizations.<note>Lowie, Robert H., *Societies of the Crow, Hidatsa and Mandan Indians*, in the previously cited work, p. 309.</note> A Crow-owners society is noted by the same authority among the Crow Indians.<note>Ibid., p. 199.</note> The Raven-owners society is mentioned by Lowie in his observations among the eastern Dakota,<note>Lowie, Robert H., *Dance Associations of the Eastern Dakota*, in the previously cited work, p. 109.</note> and the Raven-bearers by Wissler among the Blackfoot Indians.<note>Wissler, Clark, *Societies and Dance Associations of the Blackfoot Indians*, Anthropological Papers, American Museum of Natural History, xi, part 4, p. 392, New York, 1913.</note>

The full organization of the Crow-owners society is given as follows by Wissler:<note>Wissler, Clark, *Societies and Ceremonial Associations in the Oglala Division of the Teton-Dakota*, in the previously cited work, p. 23.</note>

> The <term>Kaŋgi' yuha</term> (those who have the crow) was an organization similar to the <term>Toka'la</term>, with the structure as follows:

| | |
|---|---|
| 2 leaders | 4 lance bearers |
| 2 rattle bearers | x lay members |
| 2 pipe keepers | 4 drum bearers and singers, two of whom |
| 2 short-lance bearers | carry rattles and sit around the drum |
| 2 crow-skin bearers | 1 herald |

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Crow-Owners society (Kaŋgi'yuha), transitioning from the visual reference of the crow-skin necklace on the previous page to Eagle Shield's explanation of the society's spiritual beliefs, origins, and ritual practices.</meta>

<page-num>319</page-num>
# DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC

When asked why the crow was honored by the society, Eagle Shield said:

We want our arrows to fly as swiftly and straight as the crow. The crow is always the first to arrive at the gathering of the animals in the Black Hills. The reason why the Black Hills remained unknown to the white man for so long was that Wakan'taŋka created them as a meeting place for the animals. The Indians had always known this and respected the law of Wakan'taŋka concerning it. By this law, they were forbidden to kill any of the animals during their great gatherings. In the Black Hills, there is a ridge of land surrounded by a smooth, grassy place called the "race course."¹ This is where the animals have races during their gatherings. Even small animals like the turtle are there. The crow is always the first to arrive, and the other birds come before the animals, while insects and creatures like the frog travel slowly and arrive last. Sometimes it takes 10 years for all the animals to arrive, as they come from long distances and camp wherever winter overtakes them.

Eagle Shield further said that among the Teton of Standing Rock, the Crow-owners society originally had only 10 members, but it later became a large organization that only successful warriors could join. Such distinguished men could be admitted by requesting entry from the leader and hosting a feast for the society members.

The society used a special tent in the village as its meeting place. Eagle Shield said, "the village was full of noise, with children shouting at their games and women singing and dancing, and the members of the Kaŋgi'yuha liked to spend the evenings in their lodge, singing and enjoying themselves." The "Crow lance" hung in its wrappings over the door of this lodge. According to Eagle Shield, this lance was decorated with a crow skin next to the lance head. Before a fight, the lance was unwrapped and passed over the smoke of burning sweet grass. When stuck in the ground during a fight, it marked a place from which the members of the society could not retreat unless they took the lance with them.²

When going to war, each man carried his crow-skin "necklace" in a rawhide case (plate 44), and before putting it around his neck, he passed it over the smoke of burning sweet grass. Feathers for head

---

<note>¹ This is undoubtedly the mound referred to by Clark in the *Original Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition*, vol. 1, pp. 121–123. Clark writes, under the date of August 25, 1804, as follows: "Captain Lewis and I decided to go and see the mound . . . which the Indians call the Mountain of Little People or Spirits. . . . The surrounding plains are open, devoid of timber, and level to a great extent; therefore, the wind, from whatever direction it may blow, drives with unusual force over the naked plains and against this hill. Various kinds of insects are thus involuntarily driven to the mound by the force of the wind, or fly to its leeward side for shelter. The small birds that feed on them consequently gather in great numbers at this place in search of them, particularly the small brown martin, of which we saw a vast number hovering on the leeward side of the hill as we approached, busy catching those insects. They were so tame that they did not leave the place until we had arrived within a few feet of them. One piece of evidence the Indians give for believing this place is the residence of some unusual spirits is that they frequently discover a large assembly of birds around this mound. In my opinion, this is sufficient proof to produce in the native mind a confident belief in all the properties they attribute to it."</note>

items for decoration were also carried in this case. Eagle Shield said that before a battle, the warriors always put on their finest regalia so that, if they were killed, they would die in a manner worthy of their position. The sleeves of the war shirts were not sewn, but were tied together along the length of the arm. Before a fight, the warrior untied these fastenings and threw back the sleeves to allow his arms to move freely.

Regarding the "<term>aki'ćita</term> duties" of this society's members, Eagle Shield said: "These men were among those who protected the people and watched for buffalo when the camp was moving, and who helped select suitable places for winter camps."

One Feather sang a "praise song," <term>iwa'ki'cipi olo'waŋ</term> (No. 158), of this society; this song was in honor of Sitting Crow, a member of the society. Eagle Shield sang one of the dancing songs (No. 164); this is presented alongside a narrative of his personal experience on the warpath.

### ĆAŊTE' TIŊŹA (STRONG HEART)

Bushotter translates this term as "Stout-hearted ones,"<note>1 See Dorsey, James Owen, A Study of Siouan Cults, Eleventh Rep. Bur. Ethn., p. 463.</note> while Wissler translates it as "the dauntless" and "the braves."<note>2 Wissler, Clark, Societies and Ceremonial Associations in the Oglala Division of the Teton Dakota, op. cit., p. 25.</note> In this work, it will be translated as "Strong Heart," according to the explanation provided by the author's interpreters on the Standing Rock Reservation. Lowie does not include this society in his list of eastern Dakota societies.<note>3 Lowie, Robert H., Dance Associations of the Eastern Dakota, op. cit., p. 104.</note> However, Wissler provides a full account of its organization.<note>4 Wissler, op. cit., pp. 25-31.</note>

A Sioux man once said to the author, "Indian patience and philosophy are results of long training." This was a training that began in childhood. For instance, Red Fox said that when he ran away with a war party, the men frightened him "to make his heart strong." (See p. 375.)

It was said that the Strong Heart society among the Teton Sioux, as it existed within the memory of the author's informants, was organized by Sitting Bull, Gall, and Crow King—prominent chiefs who were effectively in command of all the warriors. They desired to have a body of fearless warriors to meet any emergency, and the society was organized for that purpose. If a man was known to be fully qualified for the honor of membership, it was not necessary for him to undergo any tests. Upon initiation, all he had to do was promise to be brave in defense of the tribe, to care for the poor and needy, and to maintain a high moral character. The

<summary>This page describes the battle preparations and civic duties of the Crow-Owners society and introduces the Strong Heart society, founded by notable chiefs to develop fearless, moral warriors.</summary>
<keywords>Eagle Shield, aki'ćita, Strong Heart society, Ćaŋte' Tiŋźa, Sitting Bull, Gall, Crow King, Teton Sioux, war regalia, tribal virtues</keywords>

--- Page 423 ---
<meta>This page continues the description of the Strong Heart society, focusing on its specific regalia—including the horned eagle-feather war bonnet—and the "waving banner" carried by members and certain female relatives.</meta>

<page-num>321</page-num>
<header>DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC</header>

The society’s distinctive headdress was a war bonnet made of eagle tail feathers, with a pair of horns attached to the front. Every member owned one of these headdresses and wore it only when setting out on the warpath or during actual combat. If a man was consistently successful and had never shown any sign of cowardice, he might be buried wearing this bonnet; however, if he showed cowardice while on the warpath, he was punished upon his return by being

->FIG. 29. Woman with banner of the Strong Heart society.<-

severely reprimanded in front of all the members; his headdress was taken away, and he was expelled from the society.

Members of this society were permitted to carry a banner made by attaching feathers to a long strip of flannel, which was fastened to a pole. This was called *<term>wapa’ha kamini’mini</term>*, or ‘waving banner.’ Women whose relatives had been members of the society and were killed in war were allowed to carry this banner. *<term>Pahii’wiŋ</term>* (Yellow Hair) stated that six of her uncles had been members of this society, and because of this, she was entitled to carry the Strong Heart society banner.

(fig. 29). A similar custom was noted at White Earth, Minnesota, among the Chippewa. In plate 16 of Bulletin 53, a Chippewa woman, the daughter of a chief, is shown carrying such a banner, which belonged to her father.

The distinctive rattle of the Strong Heart society is shown in plate 45. This consists of a rawhide container on which the lines of a turtle are traced. It contains a few small stones or lead shot. This rattle was used by the dancers.

One of the customs of this society seems to have been designed to increase the self-control of its members. An informant said:

> In the old days, there were four lodges of the Strong Hearts in the center of the village. Every morning the Strong Heart men met in one of these lodges and sang their songs. Then two young men with rattles and two with bows and arrows went around the village and killed dogs which were to be eaten in their lodge. Some Indians are short-tempered, and the Strong Hearts did not kill their dogs. They killed the dogs of prominent families, and when the dog was shot, they shouted and shook their rattles. It strengthened a man's heart to have his dog killed and not show anger. The women singed the dogs, cooked them, and took them to one of the Strong Heart lodges. There they all sang and danced, and the dogs were part of the feast.

*Analysis.*—This melody has a range of 12 tones. This range is not as unusual as the frequency with which large intervals are spanned. For example, an ascent of 12 tones is achieved in two progressions at the introduction of the words, and in two instances, a descent of a seventh is made in two progressions. Of the intervals, 22 percent are fourths. The song contains all the tones of the octave except the fourth, and in structure, it is classified as melodic with a harmonic framework.

### BADGER SOCIETY

The fourth <term>Aki'ćita</term> society, according to Wissler, was the Badger society. He noted this among the Oglala Sioux,¹ as did Lowie among the eastern Dakota² and the Mandan.³ It is said to have become extinct about 20 years ago. Two songs from this society were recorded at Standing Rock.

### <term>MIWA'TANI</term>

The <term>Miwa'tani</term> was an important military society among the Teton Sioux, whose members were exempt from <term>aki'ćita</term> duty. Charging Thunder said that he belonged to this society and that it was originated long ago by a man who dreamed of an owl; he noted that the society was sometimes mistakenly called the Owl society. The word *miwa'tani* cannot be fully explained, as it is not found in the common speech of the Sioux. Two informants said it is not a Sioux word and that they thought it meant "owl feathers." Wissler says: <note>1 Societies and Ceremonial Associations in the Oglala Division of the Teton-Dakota, work cited, p. 42.</note>

According to one informant, this society—which, by the way, is regarded as a very ancient one—was so named because an owl-being, while conferring the ritual, said, "My name is <term>Miwa'tani</term>." . . . Our informants all agree that the term is associated with no concept other than that of a particular society. It is also their name for the Mandan, the tradition being that the latter were named because of some resemblance to the <term>Miwa'tani</term> society.

The Omaha word for Mandan is <term>Mawa'dani</term>, <note>2 Fletcher and La Flesche, The Omaha Tribe, work cited, p. 102.</note> and a "Mandan dancing society" among the Omaha is mentioned, and one of its feasts described, by the Reverend J. Owen Dorsey. <note>3 Omaha Sociology, Third Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, p. 273. See also Dorsey, Eleventh Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, p. 463.</note>

Wissler<gloss>1</gloss> states that the organization of the *Miwa'tani* consisted of:

| | |
|---|---|
| 2 leaders | x lay members |
| 2 sash bearers, or bonnet men | 1 drum bearer |
| 2 whip bearers | 8 singers |
| 1 food passer | 1 herald |

Charging Thunder said the *Miwa'tani* society, besides being one of the most difficult to join, was one of the most demanding in its requirements. Each member pledged to sacrifice his own life to defend a wounded member if such a sacrifice became necessary on the warpath. When the society needed anything, the principal officer appointed someone to collect what was required, and the request was never refused. This collection was usually done at a public meeting of the society and served as one of the tests by which the tribe's leaders determined which men were qualified to be useful to the tribe.

If an officer of this society saw a supply of provisions in the camp that should have been donated to the society, he could take it, either for the use of the medicine men who conducted the ceremonies or for the use of the organization as a whole. He had the right to do this, and he was even expected to do so if donations were intentionally withheld.

According to Charging Thunder, the purpose of this society was to promote friendship and helpfulness among its members. Its more important meetings were for the initiation of new members. Any member of the tribe could apply for membership, and if his application was accepted, he was notified by the crier.

Before an initiation meeting, the candidates and the members of the society were required to fast partially for four days. They gathered in their lodge, and once each day the leader brought in a pail of water; after dipping a bunch of sweet grass into it, he handed the grass to each member along with a very small piece of buffalo meat. This was all the nourishment they were allowed; therefore, the end of the four days found them greatly weakened.

After consulting together, two elderly men described the initiation to the author. On the day of the ceremony, the society officers—wearing headdresses made of owl feathers (*hinhay' śun wapa'ha*)—took their positions in the place of honor opposite the lodge entrance. In their hands, they held the owl-feather headdresses that the new members were to receive. All the members of the tribe gathered to witness the installation of the new members. The newly elected men were required to show that they were qualified for the honor bestowed upon them. Behind the fire was a

The candidates gathered around the "mellowed-earth space" <note>See p. 122, footnote.</note>, and the men were required to carry live coals in their hands and place them on the earth. Each man, rising from his seat, took coals in the palm of his hand and, turning to the left, walked slowly around the lodge. After the first circuit of the lodge, pausing at the <term>mellowed-earth space</term>, he pretended that he would place the coals upon it. This was done three times, and after the fourth circuit of the lodge, slowly lowering his hand, he gently rolled the coals onto the softened earth <note>See p. 74.</note>. If he could do this without being burned, he was considered qualified to be a member of the society.

As already stated, a headdress of owl feathers had been prepared for each of the new members. These headdresses were long, like war bonnets, but were made of owl feathers instead of eagle feathers. A significant heap of coals lay on the mellowed earth after all the men had completed the circuit of the lodge. Sweet grass was placed on this heap, and the headdresses were held in the fragrant smoke, after which they were placed on the heads of the newly installed members.

The following ceremonial song was sung as the headdresses were placed upon the heads of the men, who were then understood to be fully received into the society.

After a man was admitted to this society, he donated his best horse to the group, regardless of its value. He also hired a man to make his paraphernalia, usually giving a horse as payment for this service. One of the items he provided for himself was a whistle made from the wing bone of an eagle; this whistle was intricately decorated with beads (fig. 30) and hung around his neck. Each member also had a rattle fastened to a wand (pl. 46), which he carried during the society's dances. This rattle was made by boiling a deer's hoof and cutting the hard outer part into pieces of the desired shape and size. All the feathers used for decoration by members of this society were owl feathers tipped with red down. Owl feathers were also used on their arrows.

A rattle of dewclaws (pl. 46) was used in many Sioux dances.

### WHITE HORSE RIDERS
### **(ŚUŊK'SKA-AKAŊ'YAŊKA)**

The White Horse Riders were not considered a tribal society like those already described; instead, they were an old organization that, in the opinion of some informants, was local in character. The term "white horse riders" is not an exact translation of the Sioux name, the first word of which means "white horse,"

<summary>This page details the ritual equipment of the Miwa'tani society, including eagle-bone whistles and owl-feather decorations, and introduces the White Horse Riders as a localized Sioux organization.</summary>
<keywords>Miwa'tani, eagle bone whistle, owl feathers, deer hoof rattle, Eagle Shield, One Feather, White Horse Riders, Śuŋk'ska-akaŋ'yaŋka, Sioux societies</keywords>

--- Page 436 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the White Horse Riders, specifically focusing on their horse-painting traditions and social customs.</meta>

while the second is a compound word indicating age and experience. One informant said:

> The White Horse Riders were primarily the older warriors. These older people had a particular preference for painting their horses for parades or on the warpath, as by that means they could show that the horse's owner had performed some brave deed. They rode white horses for two reasons. They liked the white color because it was considered a *genuine* color [see pp. 173, 205], and also because a white horse was the only one on which the paint would show up clearly. The usual decoration was a horse's hoofprint and a hand, with the hand being understood to represent the hand of the enemy. To people with an understanding of these marks, the arrangement of these designs told the story of the man's brave deeds. (See p. 77, footnote.)

The parade of the White Horse Riders was greatly admired in the camp. It is said that if the White Horse Riders came to the tent of a man who had been wounded in war, they fired their guns into the air, after which the women of the family cooked a large amount of food and placed it in the middle of the camp circle. The custom was that "those who had no one to cook for them went and ate this food."

The songs of the White Horse Riders were favorites among the Sioux, and the lyrics of these songs were often changed. For instance, No. 225 is a song of this society in which the name Ptesan'-non'pawin has replaced another name.

Analysis.—This song contains an unusual number of progressions. There are 52 intervals in the song. It has been stated that the average number of progressions in relatively modern songs is 31.3. Thirty (58 percent) of these intervals are thirds, with 18 being major and 12 being minor thirds. It is interesting to note the large number of minor thirds in a song which is distinctly major in tonality; these intervals, however, are usually part of the tonic triad, which forms the framework of the melody. Two rests are found in the song (see No. 79). The two performances show no points of difference, and the small beat-divisions were clearly given. The drum and voice have the same metric unit and were played together.

### WAR SONGS (OZU'YE OLO'WAN)

#### CONSECUTIVE SONGS OF A TYPICAL WAR EXPEDITION

War expeditions were of two kinds: tribal and individual. In the former, the tribe acted as a single unit, just as they did during a buffalo hunt. For instance, if the tribe as a whole needed horses, the only way to obtain them was by stealing them from the enemy. The matter was discussed in either the tribal council or the council of chiefs. Scouts were selected by the council, or each military society could choose some of its members to serve in that role. The process of selecting and sending the scouting party was similar to the one used before searching for the pole for the Sun Dance or for a buffalo hunt. (See pages 109 and 439.) The scouts set out at night, having received instructions on where to go and what to do if they encountered the enemy. Once the scouts returned and made their report, the tribe began its journey. The organization was similar to that of a buffalo hunt, with the men being restrained by the <term>akí'ćita</term> from taking any individual action until it was time for the tribe to act as a unit.

An individual war party could be organized at any time when the tribe was not involved in a general expedition. A man who wished to organize an individual war party visited his relatives and friends at night, explained his purpose, and invited them to join him. If they were willing to participate, they smoked a pipe as a sign of their acceptance. Such an invitation could hardly be refused, and the man who issued it became the leader of the party. Every detail concerning the expedition was carefully discussed before setting out. The warriors were somewhat familiar with the terrain they would pass through and the enemies they might encounter, so the leader could verbally explain the route he proposed they take. However, it was not uncommon for a map to be sketched on the bare ground, and it was quite customary for a war party to leave behind a "map" on buckskin showing the hills and streams they expected to pass, so that other parties could find them if necessary.

# DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC

It was not considered a great honor to be asked to join a war party, and no demonstration was made when they left the village. As an old warrior said, 

> “The honor was in coming home victorious, and the demonstration was reserved to see whether it would be needed when we returned.”

The following section presents in consecutive order certain songs which might be sung on a war expedition. Many details of description are omitted, as they are included in the personal narratives which follow this section.

The next 10 songs are common war songs, or “wolf songs,” which were sung in the societies or other gatherings before the departure of a war party. Many of them mention the wolf, as the life of a warrior was supposed to be like that of the wolf. Two Shields (plate 47), who recorded several of these songs, is a leading singer at every tribal gathering.

### WORDS

| | |
|---|---|
| kola'pila | friends |
| epe'ćon ¹ | I have said |

*Analysis.*—This song was recorded by the same singer on two separate occasions. The duplication was accidental, and a comparison of the results is, therefore, more interesting. Both versions were transcribed and are presented here. It is easy to see that the differences are slight and unimportant. This is usually the case when a song is repeated by the same singer or sung by two equally talented singers. The rhythm, which is unique, was exactly repeated. It has been frequently noted that the rhythm of a song is more accurately repeated than the melodic progressions. The previous transcription was from the second "recording," in which the song was sung three times, while in the first recording it was sung only once, with a repetition of the first part. The transcription following this analysis is from the first recording of the song, in which the pitch was slightly lower and the tempo slower than in the second. It was probably because of this low pitch that the singer closed both parts of the song on the third instead of on the tonic. The drumbeat was the same in both recordings but was especially clear in the second, as shown in the previous transcription. It is not customary to vary the rhythm of the drum as in this instance, but Two Shields is a particularly skilled singer at the drum during large gatherings, and such "leading drummers" frequently elaborate on their part, especially in songs of this kind. It is probably unnecessary to state that writing the drum part on a staff does not imply pitch. Drum and voice coincided throughout the performance. Between the three versions recorded at this time, the drumbeat was continuous. The pause in the voice was about equal to two measures, but was not exact; in one instance, it was interrupted by shrill cries. The time in the five-eight and three-eight measures was absolutely exact, and the triplet and couplet groups are indicated according to the rhythm in which the passage was sung. The melody contains the tones of the second five-toned scale. About one-fourth of the intervals are minor thirds, but the melody progresses mainly by whole tones, with the major second forming 49 percent of the total number of intervals.

*Analysis.*—This song was recorded by the same singer on two separate occasions. The duplication was accidental, and comparing the results is, therefore, more interesting. Both versions were transcribed and are presented here. It is easy to see that the differences are slight and unimportant. This is usually the case when a song is repeated by the same singer or performed by two equally talented singers. The rhythm, which is unique, was repeated exactly. It has been frequently noted that the rhythm of a song is more accurately repeated than the melodic progressions. The previous transcription was from the second recording, in which the song was sung three times, while in the first recording it was sung only once, with a repetition of the first part. The transcription following this analysis is from the first recording of the song, in which the pitch was slightly lower and the tempo slower than in the second. It was probably because of this low pitch that the singer closed both parts of the song on the third instead of on the tonic. The drumbeat was the same in both recordings but was especially clear in the second, as shown in the previous transcription. *Analysis.*—The framework of this melody is one that is familiar in these songs. The submediant chord forms the basis of the opening measures, followed by a descent from the dominant to the mediant—a descent of a minor third; after this, the melody returns to the submediant chord, and the song closes on the mediant. A comparison with the preceding song will show the same outline in that melody. About half of the intervals in this song are minor thirds. The intonation is good, and the melody contains all the tones of the octave except the seventh. The rhythm of the drum is one found frequently in Chippewa songs but is much less common among the Sioux.

->WORDS<-

| | |
|---|---|
| Wakaŋ'taŋka | Wakaŋ'taŋka |

| awa'ku we | bringing home |
| taśuŋ'ke | his horses |
| ko | also |
| ma'ku welo' | (he) granted me |

*Analysis.*—When determining the keynote of a song, an ear test seems permissible; by this test, the song under analysis is transcribed as being in the key of A, although the seventh and third tones of that key do not appear in the melody. The omission of these tones places the song in the <term>first five-tone scale</term>, according to the system of pentatonic scales provided by Helmholtz (see p. 7). One instance of a song on the first five-tone scale is found in the analyzed Chippewa songs (see song No. 116, Bulletin 53). A descending fourth characterizes this melody. It appears as E–B in the first two measures, followed by D–A and A–E; these progressions are repeated in the latter part of the song, which contains the words. The tonality of the song is major, even though more than half the intervals are minor thirds.

*Analysis.*—The lyrics of this song are the same as those in the first version of No. 129, expressing an idea that was commonly associated with the warpath—that the life of a warrior was like that of a wolf. This song is not entirely like the preceding ones, as it is a personal song rather than a society song. BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULLETIN 61]

song. Comparing the two transcriptions, it is noted that 53 percent, rather than 75 percent, of the intervals are thirds, with the major and minor thirds being equal in number. The rhythmic unit is shorter but features the same division of the first count. The compass is the same, but song No. 134 contains all the tones of the octave except the seventh and second, while song No. 155 contains only the major triad.

The warriors carried extra moccasins, and each man took his own cup or cooking utensil; these features of the preparation are indicated in the personal war narratives that follow. The war party also took a supply of medicines for the treatment of the wounded.

The leader usually carried the skin of a wolf with the head pointing in the direction they were going. When the party camped, he laid the wolf skin on the ground with its head toward the enemy's country, and when they resumed their journey, the head still pointed the way. No drum or rattle was used, as the men walked silently. If there happened to be a man in the party who had dreamed of a wolf, he was asked to perform certain ceremonies. For instance, as the warriors approached the enemy's camp, they desired bad weather—especially a drizzling rain—to cover their attack. Then the medicine man would sprinkle water on the wolf hide, sing his personal song, and offer a prayer, saying that the warriors wished for a storm in which to attack their enemies. It is said that a storm usually followed this procedure by the medicine man. If they had difficulty in locating the enemy because the enemy's camp had been moved, they again called on a medicine man to search for the enemy using his power. If he was able to command the sacred stones, he would use them for that purpose.

From an old warrior, the author obtained a decorated shield which the man said he had carried in wars against the <term>Crows</term> (plates 48 and 49). The shield is made of rawhide stretched over a hoop and laced with a strip of hide. The greatest diameter is 16 inches. The decoration on the shield was said to refer to a dream of a bear. The eight segments were painted alternately red and yellow; the painting on the yellow segments, in black, represented bears' paws, while the space below the paws was white. The warrior said that the decoration commemorated a fight with the Crows and that certain features of the painting showed that the fight, though fought in the Black Hills, took place in a level, open area. He said that he was "in the middle of the shield and the enemies were all around him, but the claws of the bear were on every side to protect him"; therefore, he was not hurt in the battle.

A typical <term>Sioux</term> war bonnet is shown in plate 50. These headdresses were made of the tail feathers of the eagle, and many of them were tipped with horsehair or white down.

[DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC

Men on the warpath searched for the highest points to scout for the enemy and estimate distances; they often piled up stones to hide themselves from the enemy's view. Many of these stone heaps can still be seen in Sioux country. Some are said to have been built as landmarks to guide war party members back to their meeting place. However, this claim is incorrect. The time and location of the meeting were agreed upon before an attack was made, but the men had to find their way back to the site as best they could.

Dog Eagle (Śun'ka-waŋbli <note>The word "śuŋ'ka" can be translated as either "wolf" or "dog," but in proper names, the latter meaning is usually used.</note>) stated that when he went on the warpath, this song was sung at night in the camp to "strengthen their hearts." They sang very quietly and sometimes imitated the sound of an owl.

# BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61]

*Analysis.*—This song contains only the tones of the minor triad and fourth. The melody moves mostly by whole tones, as 56 percent of the intervals are major seconds. The interval of the fourth is also prominent, making up 20 percent of the progressions. Several versions were recorded, and these are consistent in every way. The rhythm of the song suggests a rhythmic unit, but it is notable that no rhythmic phrase repeats within the melody.

When warriors acted as scouts or wanted to remain unseen for any reason, each wore a white cloth draped like a blanket, often with eagle feathers fastened at the shoulders. Sometimes a separate cloth covered the head, as shown in the drawing by Jaw (plate 59), but the hands were always covered. It was said that upon seeing an enemy in the distance, the warrior would string his bow, preparing to shoot. As he drew closer to the enemy, he took an arrow from his quiver; he then tucked the quiver tightly under his armpit and held the bow below it with the arrow in place. This allowed him to throw open his blanket and release the arrow in an instant. Plate 51 shows two Sioux men in this attire, performing the role of scouts. This was part of a Fourth of July celebration in 1913 at Bull Head, South Dakota.

If an open fight was expected, the warriors put on their finest regalia. Feather ornaments were carried in rawhide cases, and these, along with decorated war shirts, were put on by the warriors. Sometimes the men wore very little clothing and rubbed "war medicine" on their bodies. It was said that they mixed soil that a mole had "dug up" with a powdered herb, rubbing it on themselves and their horses. A sample of this herb was obtained and identified as *Gutierrezia sarothrae* (Pursh) B. & R. <note>Commonly known as broomweed or snakeweed.</note> This specimen grew near one of the old buffalo wallows on the prairie.

Some warriors preferred to be painted by the medicine men.

Little Buffalo (Tatan'ka-ćika'la) was a man who "made medicine" for the warriors. Using blue clay mixed with "medicine," he painted a band across the man's forehead with a branching end on each cheekbone; this specific painting was done only during war. Additionally, the "medicine" was rubbed on the warrior's body and limbs.

Bear Eagle (Mato'-waŋbli'), who had been painted in this manner by Little Buffalo, recorded the following two songs. He said that Little Buffalo sang the first one alone while painting them, and the warriors sang the second one after the painting was finished. He further noted that they did not sing loudly, but after mounting their horses, they sang this song belonging to the man who had painted them.

*Analysis.*—This melody is based on the minor triad A–C–E, although D and G frequently appear as accented tones. The song has a range of 12 tones, beginning on the twelfth and descending steadily to the tonic along the tones of the second five-toned scale. It is minor in tonality, and about one-third of the intervals are minor thirds. The singer's pitch accuracy was particularly good in this and the following song. Three versions were recorded, and they are consistent throughout.

A somewhat similar description of war painting was given by Śiya'ka, who said that he and four others were in a war party and that their horses were painted by a man named Holy Horse (Taśuŋ'kawakan'). He painted the horses with white clay, drawing zigzag lines from the mouth down the front legs, branching at the hooves, and the same on the hind legs; there was also a band across the forehead and spots on the chest. All the horses were painted alike.

The four men had their faces painted brown with a white line across the forehead extending down the cheeks and forked at the end. Their hair was tied in a bunch on the forehead and in it was tied some of the same <term>medicine</term> which had been put on their bodies.

When the men were ready to start, they mounted their horses with their faces toward the east and walked single file in a great circle, Holy Horse following close behind them. The three following songs were said to have been sung by Holy Horse and the men whom he had thus painted. It seems probable that, as in the preceding narrative, the first song was sung by Holy Horse alone as he painted the men and their horses, and the others by the warriors after the painting was finished.

*Analysis.*—This song is divided into three rhythmic periods, the third of which differs slightly from the others in the division of the opening measure. The tempo was slightly slower on the word *sito'mniyan*, but not enough to be indicated. Three renditions were recorded, which are identical in every respect. The melody tones are those of the minor triad and fourth, and the song has a range of 12 tones. Only five intervals occur that are larger than a minor third, yet the melody is interesting and full of vigor.

*Analysis.*—In every rendition of this song, the tempo was hastened in the latter part. (See song No. 5.) The song is minor in tonality and contains all the tones of the octave except the sixth. In structure, it is harmonic, with the accented tones descending along the intervals of the chord of B-flat minor. One-third of the progressions are minor thirds.

Before entering the enemy's camp, a warrior might strike another member of the party as a sign that he was willing to die in that man's place if such a sacrifice became necessary.

# DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC
## 359

The latter, however, is such a short phrase and is used in such diverse ways that it cannot be said to constitute a unit of rhythm. A triple measure followed by a double measure is an interesting peculiarity of this song.

A man’s purpose in going to war was to gain honor and to capture horses. This honor could come to him either through loyalty to his comrades or by conquering the enemy. If a man carried either a wounded friend or a captive on his back, upon his return he could place a specific decoration on his tobacco bag or his blanket. (Fig. 31.) <image-desc>A simple line drawing, labeled FIG. 31, representing a "Decoration denoting bravery." It consists of a vertical line with pointed ends intersected by a horizontal line that has thickened, blunt ends.</image-desc> By this sign, everyone knew of his deed. If two relatives were together in a war party, and one was wounded and deserted by his kinsman, a stranger who saved him was granted special honor. From then on, he was called <term>Wawo'kiyapi</term>, or "Helper of the Helpless." Deserting a wounded friend on the warpath was considered the greatest act of betrayal. (See song No. 167.)

The custom of wearing feathers and painting the face, as well as the practice of "counting coup," likely varies among different tribes or bands. The following information was provided by the author's informants as the custom of the Teton Sioux on that reservation. It was said that if a party of warriors attacked the enemy and killed several men, the first warrior to kill an enemy had the right to wear "black face paint"; thus, many of the war songs include the words "the black face paint I seek." (See songs Nos. 8, 11, 27, and 171.) A man wore this paint during the dances that followed his return from war. Usually, it covered only the face, although a man might paint his entire body if he wished. The second warrior to kill an enemy might "strike the enemy"; for doing so, he could let his hair hang loose upon his return, but he could not paint his face. The duration of this practice varied by individual, but it usually lasted about a month. If a war party defeated the enemy without any losses of their own, the first four men who killed enemies, as well as their female relatives, were permitted to use the black face paint. In such an event, special songs would be sung; at any large gathering, these four men would appear, as the tribe considered them all equally entitled to the honor of using the black paint.

If a man killed an enemy without being injured himself, he was entitled to wear a feather upright at the back of his head. If he killed two or more, he could wear a corresponding number of feathers, provided the enemies were all killed in the same battle. If he succeeded in striking an enemy, he could wear a feather horizontally at the back of his head. Four men could "count coup" by striking the same enemy. (See an instance of striking an enemy on page 376.)

BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61
360

At the final camp, a returning war party prepared the scalps they had taken for use in the victory dance. Eagle Shield said:

If such a man were in the party, they selected one who had dreamed of a carnivorous animal that attacks human beings. This man scraped the flesh from the inside of the scalp and, having mixed the fat from it with gunpowder, rubbed it on his face and hands. He did this because of his dream of an animal that devours human beings. Then, after making a small hoop, he sewed the scalp inside it and fastened it to the end of a pole.¹

Plate 52 shows a scalp captured by a Sioux warrior. This does not seem to have been placed in a hoop, but was dried by stretching it with two short sticks; the mark of one is clearly visible. The texture of the skin allowed this specimen to be fully identified at the United States National Museum as a human scalp. A dance ornament made of human hair (plate 52) was obtained from the Sioux, but it does not represent a custom of that tribe. It is said that this ornament was worn by the Crow people while dancing. It was later used by the Mandan and Hidatsa, with whom the Sioux were frequently at war and from whom this item was undoubtedly taken. While among the Mandan at Fort Berthold, the author was told that ornaments of this sort were frequently seen in the old days, and that they were made, not from the scalps of an enemy, but from hair that had been cut or had fallen out and been kept for making the ornament. The strands of hair were secured at intervals with spruce or other gum, and the ornament was fastened to the wearer’s head, with the hair hanging down his back.

On its return, a victorious war party approached the village carrying the scalps high on poles. Dog Eagle said that he sang this song when he came in sight of the camp on his return from war. It was also used in the dances that followed.

¹ Regarding the customs of the Chippewa in preparing a scalp, see Bulletin 53, page 118; for the Menominee, see Alanson Skinner, *War Customs of the Menomini Indians*, *American Anthropologist*, Vol. 13, No. 2, page 309, Lancaster, Pa., 1911; and for the Osage, see *Eleventh Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*, page 526.

*Analysis.*—This song is rhythmic and lively, yet very simple. The only tones used are those of the major triad and the second, with the tonic triad forming the framework of the melody. The song has a compass of one octave, and the intonation wavered in all the performances. Nearly two-thirds of the melodic progressions move downward.

As the warriors approached the village, the women came out to meet them. War was conducted for the defense of the home and the helpless, and a man usually gave the scalps he had taken to the women of his immediate family (Compare Bulletin 53, pages 118–126). The return of the war party was followed by preparations for the victory dances. Songs in honor of victorious warriors were sung during these dances, and the women carried the scalps on poles. When the celebration was finished, it was the custom to take the scalps to the top of the highest butte, where the poles were set upright in the ground and food was placed beside them. Neither the food nor the scalps were ever disturbed.

At subsequent tribal gatherings, a woman was allowed to carry evidence of her husband's success in war. Such a privilege as this was highly prized by the women. Plate 53 shows a gathering at Bull Head, South Dakota. In the foreground, a woman is seated, holding a pole displaying the trophies of her husband's success in war; the wisp of horsehair represents a scalp. (See also fig. 29.)

If a young man was successful on his first war party, it was expected that at the first large gathering after his return, he would give away many horses and receive his manhood name, reflecting his deed of valor. After that, he discarded his childhood or boyhood names. If he went on the warpath again and surpassed his first achievement, he could be given another name upon his return to correspond with his second victory.

A man who captured horses usually gave some of them to the women in his family. This custom is expressed in the following song:

*Analysis.*—This is a particularly lively melody and is unique because all the downward progressions are minor thirds and major seconds. These descending intervals comprise more than 76 percent of the intervals. Concerning the change of tempo, see song No. 5. The song is melodic in structure and contains all the tones of the octave except the second. See the plot of this melody on page 419.

The songs of the victory, or scalp dance, were many. These were known as *iwa'kići'pi* (scalp dance); the equivalent term for "songs" is unexpressed, according to Sioux custom. This term, however, is applied to a large number of songs where the lyrics do not involve the killing of an enemy, and in this context, the term is translated as "praise song." The lyrics of many praise songs deal with a man's generosity, and the adaptation of the term *iwa'kići'pi* is clear: the man is praised in the scalp dance for his bravery, and the song is later used as a means of obtaining gifts from him. After he has proved his generosity as well as his bravery, another set of lyrics expressing that fact could be composed. In this manner, the term *iwa'kići'pi* became applied to a wide range of songs.

The following song, in both lyrics and melody, is a typical *iwa'kići'pi* in the original meaning of the word.
Maka'-peźu'tawiŋ (Earth-medicine Woman) sang this about her cousin, Peźu'ta-wakaŋ' (Holy Medicine). <note>2 As already stated (p. 217), the full form of "Pezu'ta" is Pezi'huta, meaning literally "a root or herb," but it is commonly translated as medicine, understood to refer only to preparations of roots and herbs.</note> She said that when she was 13 years old, he went in the middle of winter to "look for Crow horses." Thirty Crows met them, one of whom he killed, bringing home the scalp. <note>3 Regarding the manner of removing a scalp, see Bulletin 53, page 86.</note>

The men thrust skewers through the flesh on the outside of their legs. It was the custom for them to go around the village circle displaying these signs of mourning, and as they went, they sang a song in which they inserted the name of their dead relative; alternatively, they might compose an entirely new song in his honor.

The following song was sung by Mrs. Hattie Lawrence (plate 54), whose Sioux name is *Caŋku'lawiŋ* (Road). Mrs. Lawrence was a student at Carlisle, but she retains an unusually clear knowledge of old war customs. She assisted the author at McLaughlin, South Dakota, by acting as an interpreter for part of the material provided by Jaw, Old Buffalo, and Swift Dog. Mrs. Lawrence said that when she was 10 years old, her cousin, named *Kimi'mila-ska* (White Butterfly), was killed by the Crows, and she remembered hearing her aunt sing this song when the war party returned with the news of his death.

*Analysis.*—This is a strange melody. The tonality of the song as a whole is minor. The tone most satisfactory to the ear as a keynote is C-sharp, yet the major third occurs six times and the minor third only twice. A wailing effect is created by the prominence of the minor second, which appears 18 times, making up 46 percent of the intervals. It will be recalled that this interval is entirely absent from a large majority of these songs. All the tones of the octave except the fourth are found in the melody, with the seventh being sharpened as an accidental. Two renditions were recorded. In both, the accidental was clearly performed, but the overall intonation was somewhat wavering, undoubtedly due in part to the large proportion of semitone progressions.

Mrs. Lawrence said that her aunt lost another son in addition to White Butterfly, and that she sang this song as she went around the village, mourning his death:

he iyo'taŋ................... is foremost

*Analysis.—*In many respects, this song is like No. 149. It is in the same key and has the same compass and tonal material. Like song No. 149, it begins with an ascending fifth and contains no rhythmic unit. This song, however, contains fewer progressions, and the singer performed the lowest tone with less clarity. The minor second occurs with about the same frequency as in the latter, but the proportion of minor thirds is larger in this melody. Both features are characteristic of the songs which are sung by women.

The following song was sung by Ini'laoŋ'wiŋ (Silent Woman) about her younger brother, who was killed by the Crow Indians. This singer is shown in plate 54 in a pose often assumed by women singers when they wish to "throw" their voice. By placing the hand beside the mouth, they are able to make the sound carry a long distance. In this picture, she is shown wearing a decorated dress (pl. 55), the use of which was permitted only to those whose relatives had been killed in battle. This dress is a type of costume worn in the old days, but the history of the exploits pictured on the garment is lost. It was in a collection of Sioux articles owned by Mrs. James McLaughlin and was photographed with her permission.

*Analysis.*—This song has a range of 13 tones, with both the highest and lowest tones being clearly produced. Like song No. 147, this melody is full of semitone progressions, which create a peculiar, wailing effect. About 13 percent of the progressions are semitones, an interval that is completely absent from a large majority of these songs. The minor third constitutes about 24 percent of the intervals. An ascent of 13 tones is achieved in three measures with the introduction of the words. The intonation was good throughout the song.

*Analysis.*—This is a relatively simple melody based on the second pentatonic scale, with the minor third making up one-third of the intervals. The rhythmic unit is brief but serves as the foundation for the rhythm of the entire song. The range of 11 tones is reached in two progressions as the lyrics of the song are introduced.

The following four songs could be called "love songs connected with war." <note>1</note> It was said that in the past, all love songs were associated with a man’s eligibility for marriage, which was determined by his success in war or in the buffalo hunt. (See the duplicate of song No. 133.) No stories concerning these songs were obtained.

Two versions of the following song were recorded, one by Two Shields and the other by Śiya'ka. This unintentional duplication provides an opportunity for comparison, as Two Shields and Śiya'ka were both excellent singers, and neither knew that the other had performed the song. (See song No. 133.) The lyrics are slightly different but express the same idea. It is common for the words of a song to vary in this way when performed by different singers. Both recordings are transcribed, and it can be seen that the melodic progressions are the same in both.

In structure, the song is melodic. It is a lively melody and particularly rhythmic, though the rhythmic unit is found only twice.

DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC

### PERSONAL NARRATIVE BY RED FOX

Red Fox (Tokala-lu'ta), shown in plate 56, provided the following account of how he began his career as a warrior:

My mother was a kind and beautiful woman. She wore her hair in long braids, and I still remember how she looked when she said, "If my son ever goes on the warpath, I will take a lariat and hang myself." I was a very small boy then, and her words left a deep impression on me, just as she intended. Of course, she did not actually mean it, but she did not want me to run away to join a war party. Yet, that is exactly what I did.

One day, when I was about 12 years old, I took my bow and arrows to go hunt birds. My arrows were the blunt-tipped ones used by children. I noticed a group of men leaving the village, dressed in their finest clothes and followed by young boys carrying packs. I asked another boy, "Where are they going?" He answered, "They are heading north on the warpath." This was the first time I had ever seen a war party. The other boy said, "Our friends are the ones carrying those packs; let’s go too." So, we followed the war party. We did not go home first or take any extra moccasins; we had only the small calfskin robes we were wearing and the blunt arrows we had intended for birds. Nevertheless, we caught up with the war party and joined them. Of course, the boys who had originally set out with the warriors were well-supplied with clothing and food.

In every war expedition, there is an advance party that travels ahead of the main group of men. My father was one of the warriors in this group, and I later learned that my cousin Hairy Chin was also in the advance party. We had traveled a long distance before any of the older members of the group noticed me. Then, one of them called out to my father, "Here is your boy." My father told me to sit down beside him and questioned me, asking, "Do you have your mother's permission?" I said, "No; we were hunting birds and just came along to join you." He said, "You had better camp with the advance party when we catch up to them; you will have better food and a better bed than if you stay with us." I learned that the advance party always keeps a good camp, while the others sleep however they can. On the day we left home, the rear party killed a buffalo and shared the meat with the advance party, who were waiting for them on a butte.

When my cousin saw me, he came over and said, "Why did you come, brother-in-law?" <note>A term used in casual speech that does not necessarily imply a family relationship.</note> I replied, "We were hunting birds." He said, "Come with me," and took me to his camp. When we entered, all the men said, "What a small boy to be going on the warpath!" I leaned over my dish and began to cut and eat my meat. While I was eating, I heard the men say, "Someone is coming on horseback, singing." As the man came closer, we could hear him saying, "The news is spreading through the camp that a little boy ran away with the war party, and that his mother took a lariat and hung herself." Then I began to cry, saying, "That must be my mother; she said she would do that if I ever ran away with a war party."

One man said, "They are only saying that to toughen your spirit. They are just teasing you. You will be fooled many times while you are on the warpath." But that did not matter to me. I thought of my mother and continued to cry.

After a ten-day journey, we came across a previous war party of six Sioux men, all of whom had been killed by the Crow Indians. I only remember the names of four: Mato'-ina'pa (Bear Appears), Kaŋgi'-śuŋka' (Crow Dog), Ma'za-ska (White Metal), and E'gna-in'yaŋke (Runs Amidst). When I saw the dead bodies lying there with their heads scalped, I asked, "What are these?" The reply was, "These are our friends who went on the warpath." I asked, "Who killed them?" The reply was—

<summary>Red Fox recounts running away at age twelve to join a Sioux war party, describing the journey, a psychological prank played on him by the men, and the grim discovery of six slain Sioux warriors.</summary>
<keywords>Red Fox, Tokala-lu'ta, Sioux warriors, warpath, Lakota childhood, Hairy Chin, Crow Indians, Mato'-ina'pa, Kaŋgi'-śuŋka', Ma'za-ska, E'gna-in'yaŋke</keywords>

--- Page 500 ---
<meta>This page continues Red Fox's personal narrative, moving from the discovery of his relatives' bodies during his first unauthorized war party to his later career and ritual vows as a seasoned warrior.</meta>

"By our enemies," they said. I asked, "What will you do with these bodies?" The men replied, "We will wrap them up and take them home with us." Then I exclaimed, "When I grow up, I will have my revenge, and I will slay the Indians who killed my people." So I became a warrior.

Our expedition was away from the village for 20 days. My mother did not say a word when I came back. She did not scold me nor tell me how anxious she had been. While the men were away on the warpath, the women made moccasins. While I was gone, my mother continued making moccasins. When I returned, she gave me the moccasins, and I wore them, but I could scarcely move because I was so closely watched. For a long time, whenever I left the lodge, she asked me where I was going.

### Continuing his narrative, Red Fox said:

I went on 45 war parties. I even followed the west branch of the Missouri River to the place where the snow never melts on the mountains. I will tell you of the war party on which I first killed an enemy. On this expedition, I rode a beautiful white horse with brown ears. Just before we started, there was a <term>Sun dance</term> in the village, and the leaders said, "If anyone wants to be successful in war, let him come and join the Sun dance." There were a hundred men standing abreast in the circle. We were asked, "What offering will you make to the great sun shining over your head? Will you give him tobacco? Will you give him your flesh and blood?" When the <term>Intercessor</term> came to me and asked these questions, I said in reply, "I will give my flesh and blood so that I may conquer my enemies." I fulfilled this vow at a <term>Sun dance</term> when I returned victorious from war. My arms were cut 7 times below the elbow and 2 times above the elbow, making 18 wounds in all. <note>[Compare the description on p. 91.]</note>

After making my <term>Sun-dance</term> vow, I started on the warpath. We had traveled five days and had reached the end of the Missouri River when the scouts said, "The Crow Indians are having a great buffalo hunt." We went where they directed and saw three Crows: one had a gun, one had a bow and arrows, and the third had a revolver. The first two pointed their weapons at us, and the third brandished his revolver, but we were able to go up to them and strike each of them with a <term>coup stick</term> while they were still alive. We killed those three and also two more. Then we went further and saw another Crow party, but they did not see us. They went into the timber, made a fire, and cooked some meat. After a time, one of them came out and pointed his gun in every direction. I rode up and hit him with a club. My <term>Sun-dance</term> vow made me fearless. This was the fourth coup I counted on that expedition. We watched for the man and afterward killed him. From there, we went on until we came to a village of the Blackfeet. The banks of the river were heavily timbered, and the Blackfeet were camped there. This was beyond the country of the Crows. When the Blackfoot village was in sight, I put on my war bonnet, mounted my white horse, and ran toward the village. I charged them and captured about 50 horses from the center of their herd. They shot and shot at me, but they did not hit me.

On the second night of our homeward journey, we camped at a place called Bear Butte.<note>[1]</note> Some of our horses were exhausted, and when the rest of the war party continued on their way, I stayed behind with two young men. We traveled more slowly than the others, and as we were going along the side of a foothill, I saw four Crow warriors coming toward us. I said to the young men: "Come near and stand by me. Four warriors are coming." The young men said, "Let us run and hide." I said: "<term>Wakan'tanka</term> has but one path. No matter how or where you die, you must go by that path. Let us stand together and fight."

---

<note>[1 It was said that there were two or more places called Bear Butte. One of these, located in Montana and likely referred to in this account, was said to be higher than the one in South Dakota, which is probably referred to in song No. 82, p. 256.]</note>

<summary>Red Fox recounts his development as a warrior, detailing his vow of flesh and blood during a Sun Dance and his subsequent bravery in battles against the Crow and Blackfeet. He describes counting coups, capturing horses, and his stoic philosophy regarding death as he faces an ambush near Bear Butte.</summary>

<keywords>Red Fox, Sun Dance, warpath, Crow Indians, Blackfeet, counting coup, Missouri River, Bear Butte, Wakan'tanka, ritual sacrifice</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Red Fox's narrative of his war expeditions, detailing a specific encounter with Crow Indians where his bravery and mercy led to his appointment as a chief.</meta>

DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC

I had a gun and two revolvers, one of the young men had a quiver of arrows, and the other had a double-barreled gun. I sang my death song <note>A song sung under these circumstances indicated that the man realized the probability of death and was ready to meet it. Red Fox’s song is given as number 155.</note> because I felt certain that I was soon to die. I sang as I pointed my gun. I said to my companions, “I will see which of the four has a gun, and I will fire at him; then our numbers will be even.” They all said, *ho*. There was an immense rock in front of us, and in a crack of the rock grew a cherry tree. It was through this crack that I watched the warriors. One had his hair combed high and carried a gun; the others had bows and arrows, and as they came nearer, I saw that one of them was only a boy. I said to my companions: “Now work and be brave. We have only three to fight, as one of them is a boy.” When they came opposite the crack in the rock, I fired, but my gun snapped and did not go off. A branch of the cherry tree interfered with it. The man with the gun saw me and aimed at me, but I grabbed his arm so he could not fire. My companions chased the others, and I fought hand-to-hand with the man for an hour. Then I called my companions; they succeeded in taking the gun from the man, and I had the satisfaction of killing him.

The boy ran away, but my companions brought back the two Crows whom they had taken captive. One of them said: “We are Crow Indians. We want to live. We give you our bodies, and we give you the right to wear the feathers, if only you let us go.” So we gave them back their lives. Because of that act, I was appointed a chief, for it was considered a brave deed to spare the lives of two enemies.

Red Fox then recorded the song which he said he sang when he fired at the Crow. The words are those of a boy who wishes to go on the warpath but is opposed by older brothers. He is divided between obedience and ambition, and while he shows no sign of yielding, he finds his difficulties increased by this opposition. This recalls the story of Red Fox’s first war expedition, when he was a boy.

---

<summary>Red Fox describes a battle against Crow warriors where his gun misfired, leading to a hand-to-hand struggle. After killing one enemy and capturing two others, he spared the captives' lives, a deed for which he was made a chief.</summary>

*Analysis.*—This song contains only the tones of the major triad, a tonal material found in only five Chippewa songs within a series of 340. This is its only occurrence in this specific series. Three-fourths of the intervals are thirds, with half being minor thirds and a quarter being major thirds. The song has a range of an octave, extending from the dominant above the tonic to the dominant below it. In the latter part of the song, the division of the final beat in the rhythmic unit is altered to match the words. The song contains no changes in time signature. Compare this with the analysis of Song No. 134.

DENSMORE]                                    TETON SIOUX MUSIC

->PERSONAL NARRATIVE BY EAGLE SHIELD<-

Eagle Shield described a specific war expedition, with Mrs. Jas. McLaughlin acting as his interpreter. Eagle Shield said:

Many years ago, in the middle of winter, I wanted to organize a war party, so I cooked food and invited some men to a feast. While they were eating, I said, “I want to go somewhere; that is why I invited you here.” They asked where I wished to go, and I replied, “On the warpath.” “Why are you going on the warpath?” they asked; and I answered: “It is winter. The Crow do not tie their horses as close to the tipis as they do in summer, so we can capture them more easily. We will ask the women to make moccasins for us all day tomorrow, and we will start in the evening.”

The next day, toward evening, three men came to my lodge, and then more arrived until there were 16 men, even though I had only invited 10. We sat in a circle and smoked in my lodge until the village was asleep. Then we set out. The snow was deep, and walking was slow and difficult. At our first camp, we cut low plum trees and made a bed of branches in the snow. As we traveled, we sometimes saw a herd of buffalo. Then we would kill one for food, cooking the meat on pointed sticks. We used the hide for a bed but left it behind when we continued our journey.

After camping on the tenth night, I said, “Two of us will go ahead to see if we can spot the enemy’s village.” A third man asked to go with us, and early the next morning we started out. We had traveled some distance when my companion said, “Let us climb that butte and look over.” We climbed the butte, and looking over the top, we saw a very large Crow settlement; beyond the tipis was a herd of horses that looked like a cloud. My companion said, “Let us take two horses and go back.” But I replied: “No. The Crow will follow us, and since we would be the only ones on horseback, the others would be killed.”

We immediately turned back toward our camp, traveling a little way at a dogtrot, then stopping to rest, and then resuming the dogtrot again. It was just daybreak when we approached the camp. I gave the wolf howl that a war party uses to announce its return, and I heard our friends cry: “The scouts are coming back. The scouts are coming back. Come and meet them.”

The people stood in a line to receive us. In front of them, a stick was placed upright in the ground, and I knocked down this stick as a guarantee that I would tell the truth. <note>See page 441.</note> My companions joined me in the long, drawn-out wolf howl. After I had knocked down the stick, everyone sat down. Then a man filled a pipe, offered it to the four directions, to the sky, and to the earth, and gave it to me and my companion. He did this four times, and then we smoked together for a while.

At length, the man who had offered the pipe asked: “What have you done? Have you looked across the prairie or climbed a butte? Did you see a four-legged animal <note>meaning a wolf</note>? Do not deceive me, but tell the truth.”

I said: “I went up a butte, looked over, and saw nothing. Then I went farther, and what should I see but buffalo coming toward me. I looked again, and it was a Crow village that I saw. There were many horses. I beg that you give us something to eat, for we must start at once and travel far. We must reach there at night and take the horses in the dark.”

They hurried and brought us food. We kept our blankets tied down as we ate and only waited long enough to put on dry moccasins. As we journeyed toward the Crow village, we hung food in trees so that we could find it on our return. We could see our tracks in the snow when we started, and we came in sight of the Crow village at daybreak. All that day, we stayed on the butte. We had no food that day. When night came, we went in and out of a creek and so reached a second butte, from which we had a full view of the Crow camp. The smoke was thick above the tipis. We put on fresh

<summary>Eagle Shield narrates the beginning of a winter war expedition against the Crow, detailing the recruitment of his party, the journey through deep snow, and the discovery of a large Crow village and horse herd.</summary>
<keywords>Eagle Shield, war party, Crow Indians, scouting, winter warfare, horse raiding, ritual, wolf howl, Teton Sioux</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Eagle Shield’s narrative of a winter war expedition against the Crow, picking up as the party prepares to raid the camp for horses and then detailing their escape and subsequent skirmish.</meta>

BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61

...moccasins and tied them very firmly. We fastened our belts tight and arranged our buffalo-hair lariats so they could be released very easily. As we started for the Crow camp, I said, "Do not take too many horses, or they will make a wide track in the snow and we shall be followed. Whoever reaches the trees where the food is stored first must wait for the others."

Although the snow was deep, we captured 21 horses. I had six horses and no colts, so I could travel rapidly. The man with me rode one horse and led four. I heard a sound, and looking back, I saw a mule following us. The mule came up and joined us, as he had probably been raised with the horses. Mules were highly valued by the Sioux, and I claimed this mule as mine.

A few of our men reached the meeting place before my companion and I arrived. We waited for the rest, but two men did not appear. We fastened our moccasins and were about to go back for them when they came into sight. "Hurry!" they cried. "There is excitement in the Crow camp. They have seen us and are mounting their horses." Some of us were eating when the alarm came, but we prepared to start at once. Four went ahead so the horses would follow, and the rest of us drove the herd. The cold was extreme. We traveled all that night, and I often went back to see if we were being pursued. The next morning, we made a fire and put on dry moccasins. We were afraid that if we traveled slowly we would be caught and killed, so we hurried. That day, we let the horses trot for a while and then walk for a while, but we did not dare stop to rest. On the second night, a man who had been acting as a lookout said, "The Crows are after us; they are right on our trail."

I said, "We are not cowards. We must stand our ground and not run away." My companions cried, "What shall we do?" I said, "We will go to that little rugged ravine and take the horses down there." It was a "draw" on the prairie, and at the end of it were some large rocks. It was a moonlit night, as bright as day. We got the horses into the ravine and could hear the voices of the Crows. Evidently, there were many of them. I made up my mind that we had a difficult time ahead of us, but we had good guns and plenty of bullets. I said: "We will crawl up on top of the ridge and lie flat in a line, far apart. We can see them on the prairie, and as soon as they are in range, we will fire." We threw off our blankets and wore only our calfskin shirts. So we lay in a row, watching for the Crows. I said, "Be ready with your guns."

There was a great crowd of Crows. They were following the horses' tracks, and when they came near us, we sprang up, yelled, and fired at random. The Crows turned and ran, leaving behind one man who was dead and whose horse had run away, and one horse whose rider was fleeing on foot. We all gathered together and ran a short way after them, firing as fast as we could reload our guns. We shot from above their heads so they could not tell where to shoot back at us, and only once in a while did they shoot in our direction. I said to my companions: "The Crows outnumber us. If we go out on the prairie to run away, they will see how few of us there are. We will keep on shooting and stay out of sight. Then they will think there are a great many of us."

We could see the Crows. They were still there, like a large scorched patch on the prairie. Every so often, one of our men went toward them and shouted: "Come and fight! It is good to fight!" <note>Compare to song No. 157.</note> This continued all day, and the Crows thought there were a great many of us because we called for them to come back and fight. At last, our scouts reported that the Crows had given up and gone away. I said, "Hurry; let us start for home." We rode our fastest horses, drove the herd before us, and went as fast as we could across the prairie. We camped for three nights before we reached home with our horses.

The Sioux occasionally sent a man ahead of a returning war party to give a false report to the village. Thus, when an old man came forward to receive his report, the man might say, "Everyone was killed except me." Then great wailing would follow in the—

Some of the people were among those who were easily deceived, but most of them understood the trick. The war party arrived immediately afterward, so the people were not left in uncertainty for long.

On the expedition I have told you about, my brother-in-law was the one who made the report, and he said, "Eagle Shield was the very first one killed."

I suspected that he would do this, so I said to my companions, "Hurry, before my friends harm themselves with grief." So we fired our guns, whipped up our horses, and came dashing into the village with not even one man wounded, driving a fine herd of captured horses before us.

Eagle Shield said that on one of his war expeditions, he and his companions were five days without food, except for a few roots which they gathered. He said, further, "We were all so very sleepy." When they finally secured food, they ate only a little at a time, and even that caused them great distress.

The singer of the following group of songs is ***Wi'yaka-waŋżi'la*** (One Feather), shown in plate 57, who is well known as one of the old warriors of the Standing Rock Reservation. He was 57 years old when giving these songs in 1913. On the warpath in the old days, he wore the skin of a wolf on his head (pl. 58). Attention is called to the upright feathers on the head of the wolf, which were said to resemble the ears of the animal. A man lying in the grass on a rise of ground could lift his head to spy on the enemy, and the feathers would look like the ears of a prowling wolf. The quills are very light, and the feathers tremble with every motion of the wearer.

The narrative concerning the first song of the group is as follows: When One Feather was 18 years of age, he went with a war party against the Crows. It was winter, and they traveled as far as the Rocky Mountains. There were 22 Sioux in the party, three of whom were sent in advance as scouts. He was one of these scouts, and when coming near the Crow country, he saw a Crow man butchering a buffalo. Pursuing the man, he killed him close to the Crow camp. One Feather said that he sang the following song as he ran back to his comrades after killing the Crow. It was said to be a dancing song of the <term>Miwa'tani</term> society. (See p. 326.)

Analysis.—This melody serves as an example of interval formation rather than key relationships between tones. All tones of the octave are present in the song, which is transcribed and analyzed in the key of D major, although D is not a completely satisfactory keynote. The progressions move mainly through small intervals; about 54 percent of the intervals are minor thirds and 36 percent are major seconds. The other intervals include an ascending ninth and four fourths. The A major triad is prominent in the melody. It is interesting to compare this with songs No. 108 and No. 166, in which the final interval is also a descending fourth. These songs are classified as "irregular."

*Analysis.*—Three performances of this song were recorded; in all of them, the intonation was wavering. The song has a range of 12 tones, is melodic in structure, and contains the tones of the second five-toned scale. Only four intervals larger than a minor third are found in the melody. This fact may partially account for the uncertain intonation, as the Indian singer usually finds it difficult to accurately sing a long succession of small intervals. The total number of minor thirds and major seconds in this song is 32.

One Feather said the following song was sung in connection with a fight against the Assiniboin in which he took part. The "spotted horses," which were heavily mottled with black and white, were highly prized by the Sioux, and a few of these are still seen among them today.
