*Analysis.*—This is a pleasant rhythmic melody on the <term>fourth five-toned scale</term>. The song is based on the <term>tonic triad</term>, but the second note is accented twice, classifying the song as melodic with a harmonic framework. The eighth rest in the third measure from the end was clearly performed in all three renditions. The intonation was good on everything except the highest tones. As frequently occurs in songs on the <term>fourth five-toned scale</term>, the <term>minor third</term> is prominent, in this instance forming one-third of the total intervals. An ascending <term>minor sixth</term> is found in the early part of the melody. It is interesting to note that the <term>minor sixth</term> appears much more often than the <term>major sixth</term> in the Sioux songs under analysis. (See Tables 11 and 12, pages 16 and 17.)

### SONGS ACCOMPANIED BY NATIVE DRAWINGS

Four men contributed their drawings to this section of the work. Their names are Jaw, Eagle Shield, Swift Dog (Suŋ'ka-lu'zahan), and Old Buffalo. The work of each man has certain characteristics besides the specific outlines of his sketches of men or horses. Thus, in the drawings of Jaw, most of the incidents concern the capture of horses, and the numbers of the enemy are not shown, while in those of Eagle Shield, the latter feature is clearly indicated; his work includes more detail than the drawings of any other native artist except perhaps Old Buffalo. Several rescues are shown in Eagle Shield's work, but none in the work of the others. The coup stick appears frequently in Swift Dog's drawings, but not in any of the others.

There is a difference in the part of the sheet where the drawing "begins." This is determined by the narrative, as an observer would not know which sketch the artist regarded as the opening of the series.

The manner of depicting the Crows and the Assiniboine is similar in all the drawings; they are distinguished by the upright hair on top of the head.

The man who provided the material in the following pages is commonly known as Jaw (Čehu'pa), plate 59, a name which he received from a white brother-in-law. His childhood name was Ma'za-ho'waśte (Loud-sounding Metal), and at the age of 17, he was given the name Oki'ćize-ta'wa (His Battle), which is his true name at the present time. He was given this name after taking part in a fight for the first time. He had been out with a war party once before and had stolen horses, but this was his first experience in actual warfare. When asked about his connections within the tribe, he replied: "I am of two bands. My mother was a Gi'gilaś'ka, a division of the Hunkpa'pa band, and my father was a Sans Arc, of the Te'toŋwaŋ." He said that he was 63 years old at that time (1913), and when asked the year of his birth, he said that he was born in the year known as *Ke woyu'spa ta wani'yetu*, "the winter that Turtle Catcher died." Upon consulting the picture calendar (see page 69), this year was found to be 1850.

As a further test of his memory, Jaw was asked to name several succeeding years of the picture calendar of the Standing Rock Sioux. He did this accurately except for giving a different name to one year. Upon reaching the name of his seventh year, he added,

BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61

"that was the year I killed the bird." In explanation of this, he said that the people were moving camp and he was with his grandmother, who had taken care of him since his infancy, when his mother died. He said, "I killed the bird and took it to my grandmother." (See plate 60, *B*.) "If I killed many, she would carry them all, and when we camped at night, she would eat my hunting, and I would eat some too." He said that his father first called him <term>Ma'za-ho'waśte</term> when he killed the bird. His name before that time is not recorded.

In his young manhood, Jaw was known especially for his success in stealing horses from the enemy. In addition to his narratives of expeditions for this purpose, he gave general information concerning war customs. Among other things, he recalled that in the old days each warrior carried his own wooden bowl (plate 61), hung by a cord from his belt. It is said that "A man on the warpath always ate and drank from his own dish. When he returned home, the dish was put away with other articles which he used on the warpath, and sweet grass was put with it." ^1

Jaw's manner of painting himself and his horse when going on the warpath was as follows: He painted a red crescent over his mouth, the points of the crescent extending upward halfway to his cheekbones. His hands were painted red from the wrists, and his feet from the ankles. A large crescent like that on his face was painted on his horse's chest, and a smaller one on the animal's left hip, while the entire end of the horse's nose was painted yellow. If a horse succeeded in some difficult undertaking, it was his custom to reward the animal by putting a feather in its mane or tail, or a band of red list-cloth around its neck. (See page 298.)

Jaw had two medicine bags containing the same 'medicine,' one for his horse and one for himself. The horse's medicine bag was tied to the bit of his bridle. He said that if his horse "had a headache," he chewed a certain herb and put it into the horse's mouth, whereupon the trouble was relieved at once. This was probably the herb numbered 4 in the component parts of his war 'medicine.' Jaw said that when going to steal horses, he often went to the windward of them and chewed this herb, at which the horses at once "pricked up their ears," being attracted by it.

When on the warpath, Jaw carried a leather pouch containing vermilion paint mixed with grease, for applying to his face and body. This pouch is shown in plate 61, together with Jaw's war whistle and a warrior's bowl. On his shoulder he wore a wolf skin, to the nose of which was tied his war whistle ^2 and to this whistle was

DENSMORE]   TETON SIOUX MUSIC

fastened the medicine bag, which he tied to his horse's bridle when on the warpath. According to Jaw, these medicine bags contained a mixture of four herbs, dried and powdered. It was said that they could be used singly, as indicated, or in combination, as in his war medicine, which had power as a charm in addition to its effectiveness as a curative agent. He secured fresh specimens of the herbs, which were identified as follows:

(1) *Echinacea angustifolia* DC. (nigger head <note>An archaic common name for the purple coneflower</note>). Jaw said: "The root of this plant, when dried, is good for toothache. The person should chew it. The top is also good, but not as strong."

(2) *Cheirinia aspera* (DC.) Britton (western wall flower). This was said to be "bitter and good for stomach trouble. The whole plant is dried and chewed, or a tea may be made if preferred."

(3) *Erigeron pumilus* Nutt. (daisy). A decoction of this was used for rheumatism and lameness, and it was also used for disorders of the stomach.

(4) *Laciniaria punctata* (Hook.) Kuntze (blazing star). A decoction of this was given to people with heart pain, the entire plant being used for this purpose. The root was also dried and powdered. This medicine, either in a dry powder or in the form of a decoction, was also given to horses.

An herb used by Jaw in the treatment of rheumatism is included in the list of medicinal herbs on page 270.

A successful war expedition by Jaw is shown in a drawing by himself (plate 62), the same drawing appearing in the background of his portrait (plate 59). Jaw said that before any important undertaking he smoked a certain pipe in a ceremonial manner and "offered prayers to Wakan'tanka." Instead of attempting to describe this, he enacted it for the writer as follows:

(1) With the bowl of the pipe in his left hand and the stem in his right hand, he held the pipe upright in front of and close to his body, saying rapidly in a low tone: 
> "Wakan'tanka, behold this pipe, behold it. I ask you to smoke it. I do not want to kill anybody; I want only to get good horses. I ask you to help me. That is why I speak to you with this pipe."
(See p. 66.)

(2) Changing the position of his hands, placing his left hand on the stem of the pipe and holding the bowl in his right hand, he pointed the stem toward his left shoulder, saying: 
> "Now, wolf, behold this pipe. Smoke it and bring me many horses."

(3) He then placed his right hand once more on the stem of the pipe and his left hand on the bowl, and pointing the stem upward and forward while holding the pipe level with his face, he said: 
> "Wakan'tanka, behold this pipe. I ask you to smoke it. I am holding it for you. Look also at me."

<sig>4840°—Bull. 61—18—27</sig>

(4) After placing the stem of the unlit pipe in his mouth (while still holding the bowl in his left hand), he said again, "Wakaŋ'-taŋka, I will now smoke this pipe in your honor. I ask that no bullet may harm me when I am in battle. I ask that I may get many horses."

(5) After raising the pipe as described in section 3, he lit and smoked it, holding it firmly in both hands. Then he said (referring to his participation in the Sun Dance): <note>¹ Jaw had scars on his chest and back, as well as small scars along the entire length of his arms, showing that he fulfilled his Sun Dance vow.</note> "Wakaŋ'taŋka, behold this pipe and behold me. I have let my breast be pierced. I have shed much blood. I ask you to protect me from shedding more blood and to give me a long life."

When this ceremonial act was completed, Jaw filled another pipe—one that he commonly used—and smoked it. He said: "It is the role of a certain pipe to be smoked when making a request of Wakaŋ'taŋka. I always did what I have now performed for you, and my blood was never shed after I took part in the Sun Dance. This was because I asked Wakaŋ'taŋka to give me success."

At that time the following song was sung:

*Analysis.*—The character of this melody seems to indicate that it is an old song and is correctly sung. The rhythmic unit is well-defined and has an evident influence on the rhythm of the song as a whole. More than half the intervals are minor thirds, and only four intervals larger than a minor third appear in the song. The ascent of a seventh is somewhat unusual. This ascending interval is found only 9 times in the 2,864 intervals of Chippewa songs and 13 times in the present series. This song is melodic in structure, has a range of nine tones, and contains all tones of the complete octave.
See the plot of this melody on page 419.

BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61

*Analysis.*—The second part of this song, containing the words, is an exact repetition of the first part, which is a somewhat unusual feature. The form of the song is simple. It has a range of an octave and ends on the tonic. The melody tones are those of the minor triad and fourth, but only the tones of the tonic triad are accented. The size of the intervals varies more than in many of the songs, with one-third of the intervals being larger than a minor third. The song contains no rhythmic unit, but the rhythm of the song as a whole is interesting and distinctive.

When night came, the goal of the expedition was carried out. Under cover of darkness, Jaw succeeded in capturing seventy horses on this occasion. (See plate 62.) In referring to this exploit, he said:

> “I did not wake or kill any of the Crows; I just took their horses. No Sioux ever took more horses than that in one night.”

As Jaw and his party approached their village, they gave the long wolf howl, at which the people came out to meet them. The following song celebrated the victory, with the women singing along with the men:

[DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC

*Analysis.*—Four performances of this song were recorded. In all the versions, the accidental G-flat appears, though the pitch of the tone varies slightly; the interval between G-flat and F is usually sung too small. The song is based on the fourth five-toned scale and is melodic in structure. Although the song is major in tonality, 44 percent of the intervals are minor thirds.

Events similar to those in the preceding narrative are shown in plate 63, but no songs were recorded about them.

The following pages contain narratives of personal experiences on the warpath by Eagle Shield, illustrated by his own drawings. With few exceptions, a song is associated with each drawing. Plate 64, *A*, depicts his first fight, which took place when he was 14 years old. As he was so young, he had no song to sing in this fight, nor did he commemorate it in a song, as he might have done had it occurred later in his life. His second drawing (plate 64, *B*) represents the members of the <term>Kaṅġi'yuha</term> society (see page 318 and following). The customs of this society among the Teton Sioux are described by Wissler. Regarding this, Eagle Shield said, "I am leader of the dancers, and when I rise to dance the singers begin to beat their drums," while Wissler states that "the two rattle-bearers gave the signal for the dancing," and, further, that "the four drummers each carry a small hand-drum." (See plate 64.)

The following was said to be a characteristic song of the <term>Kaṅġi'yuha</term>. The words express a rebuke.

*Analysis.*—The upward and downward progressions in this song are more balanced than in many others, as it contains 25 ascending and 28 descending intervals. The primary progressions are major seconds (48 percent) and fourths (22 percent). The intonation was somewhat wavering throughout the performances, but the tones transcribed as C-sharp and C-natural were clearly distinct. This was the first song recorded by Eagle Shield, and his voice became steadier as he grew accustomed to singing into the phonograph. This song is melodic in structure and contains every tone of the octave except the seventh. Shrill war cries were given during the rest that precedes the lyrics of the song.

*Analysis.*—The rhythmic structure of this song is interesting. The two rhythmic units are almost alike, yet their difference provides variety to the rhythm of the song as a whole. With the exception of the octave ascent at the beginning of the words, there are only three intervals in the song—the fourth, the minor third, and the major second—the last of which makes up 60 percent of the total number of intervals. The song has a major tonality, yet 28 percent of the intervals are minor thirds. The only tones in the melody are those of the major triad and second. This suggests that the

The song might be harmonic in form, but the second part is frequently accented, causing the song to be classified as melodic with a harmonic framework. The melody has a range of eight tones, extending from the dominant above the tonic to the dominant below the tonic.

During the season of ripe cherries <note>The Sioux call the month of July *Ćanpa' sa'pa wi*, or the 'black-cherry moon.'</note>, a party of Sioux was in the territory of the Assiniboine. There they found a small group of cherry pickers and attacked them. This act was witnessed by the Assiniboine in the camp, who charged the Sioux in a futile attempt to save the cherry pickers. All the men were killed, but the women escaped, except for one whom Eagle Shield captured and carried away on his horse, as shown in plate 65, *B*. Eagle Shield took the captured woman to the Sioux camp, but the following autumn she escaped and returned to her own people.

The following song celebrates this victory:

*Analysis.*—Regarding a keynote, this melody is classified as irregular. (See analysis of No. 108.) For this reason, the signature should be understood as indicating only the pitch of the notes. Of the intervals, 45 percent are minor thirds, and the minor second appears six times. The descending fourth at the end of each part of the song is distinctive and was clearly performed in every rendition of the song. The song contains a change of tempo. (See No. 5.)

A memorable incident is depicted in plate 66, *A*. The Sioux attacked a Crow camp, capturing 80 horses. This was not the entire number of horses owned by the Crows, but the expedition was considered a success. The Sioux killed three Crows. On their way home, they sang this song, the melody being the same as that of the preceding song.

*Analysis.*—Several versions of this song were recorded, and in every one, E-flat was sung. This suggests the key of B-flat, but the melody's progressions follow the D minor triad; the song is therefore analyzed as being in the key of D minor. The song has a range of nine tones and lacks the sixth and seventh tones of the complete octave. Two rhythmic units are found in the song, and the division of the last beat is the same in both.

Eight of Eagle Shield's companions made a stretcher of poles and placed the wounded man on it. They were 50 miles from home and were forced to cross the Missouri River with their burden. After traveling about 25 miles, they made a camp and also killed a buffalo. Food for a war party was obtained from the land through which it passed. Mention is frequently made of the killing of buffalo, with the meat being used for food and the hide for robes or for making

Plate 67 also shows a skinning knife made from the shoulder blade of a buffalo, with the handle wrapped in buffalo hide. The wounded man wanted soup, but the party carried no vessel large enough for boiling meat. However, Eagle Shield remembered his grandfather telling him how the warriors of his day cooked meat in the stomach casing of a killed animal, and he decided to try the experiment. The casing, suspended on a tripod, was filled with water into which heated stones were placed (see figure 32).

<meta>This page continues the description of traditional cooking methods used by Eagle Shield, transitioning from the preparation of the stomach casing to the recovery of a wounded man and the introduction of a related war song.</meta>

When the water was boiling, the meat was put into it, and the cooking process was finished without any trouble.<note>1 The author saw a cooking setup of this kind prepared and used in a Sioux camp at Bull Head, South Dakota, on July 5, 1913. The stones were heated in a fire near the tripod; each stone was lifted with a forked stick and placed in the water. A blunt stick was used to push the heated stones onto the forked sticks, and a short stick was used for stirring the boiling meat. All of these items (shown in figure 32) are now in the U.S. National Museum in Washington.</note>

The wounded man was refreshed by the broth. After making him comfortable and cooking a good amount of meat, the war party left him in the care of a young man. Eight days later, another war party passing through found that the wounded man was able to travel. He and his companion joined this party and reached home safely.

Since Eagle Shield, who provided this narrative, is a medicine man who specializes in treating wounds and fractures, his account of the man's injury was somewhat professional. He said the injury was so severe that at first the bones protruded and buckshot continued to come out of the wound for some time. After that, the flesh began to heal, and within one month and the first quarter of the next month, the leg was completely healed.

Eagle Shield said that on one occasion he was pursued by Crow Indians while he was carrying a friend whose horse had been shot. This incident is shown in plate 68, *A*.

The following song was reportedly sung at this time, though the meaning of the words in this context is not clear:

### WORDS

| | |
|---|---|
| Psa'loka kin | the Crow Indians |
| natan' hi'yelo | come attacking |
| kići' yaŋka' yo | sit with them |
| waŋźi' | one of them |
| kte'pi ktelo' | will be killed |

*Analysis.*—The rhythmic form of this song is interesting. Two rhythmic units appear, which are used alternately in the middle of the song. In the second complete measure containing words, the rhythmic unit begins on the second beat of the measure, while the singer clearly accents the first beat. The progressions of the melody are primarily by whole tones, with 60 percent of the intervals being major seconds. The other intervals vary and range from a minor third to a tenth. The song is based on the second five-tone scale and has a range of 12 tones. In its structure, the song is melodic with a harmonic framework.

On one occasion, when Eagle Shield led a war party against the Crows, they found that the Crows had tethered their horses within the circle of tents. Eagle Shield and a companion saw these horses after entering the village as scouts (Plate 68, *B*). Eagle Shield said to his companion, "Let's go and get some of the horses." His companion replied, "No; if we do that, the rest of the party will be angry." Eagle Shield then said, "Let's each take *one horse*." His companion replied, "*You* do it." Thereupon Eagle Shield, creeping into the circle of tents, took two horses—a black one and a brown one—and escaped without being detected. Each riding a horse, he and his companion reached their camp around daybreak.

The Crows soon discovered the loss of the horses and increased their watchfulness, so that the other members of the Sioux war party were unable to secure any horses. So it happened that Eagle Shield and his companion were the only ones who returned on horseback, while the rest were forced to walk.

*Analysis.*—The tempo of this song speeds up slightly in the first measure containing words, but the change is not steadily maintained. The 5–8 measures, however, are clearly performed and are accurate in time. (See song No. 64.) The triad of D major is strongly suggested by the melody progressions; however, F, the third note of that chord, does not appear. Nevertheless, the song is analyzed as being in the key of D major. The third is absent from 12 songs in the series of 340 Chippewa songs; this distinctive feature was considered in the analysis of song No. 53 in Bulletin 53 (p. 140). In this study, the third is absent from only five songs. (See p. 135.) The interval of the fourth is remarkably prominent in this song, making up more than half of the total number of intervals.

...get my fame. My father’s name was Running Fearlessly (*Kaġi’-śni-in’yaŋka*). When he went to Washington long ago, he was given one of the first medals that were ever made. In his portrait, Swift Dog is shown wearing a headdress known as a “four-horned bonnet.” He said that the Sioux once killed an enemy who wore a headdress similar to this and imitated the design for their own use. This incident occurred in the year 1852, designated in the Sioux picture calendar as *He-to’pa uŋ’waŋ kte’pi*, “the winter when the four-horned enemy was killed.”

Several of Swift Dog’s war exploits are shown in his own drawing (plate 70), and the songs accompanying these exploits are provided here. In this drawing (*A*), Swift Dog has shown the first encounter in which he killed a man. He was then 24 years old and had been to war several times. This expedition was to the country of the Assiniboin, and the man whom he killed was a member of that tribe. In describing the event, he said that the enemy was on foot, while he was on horseback on higher ground. On this expedition, he sang the following song:

*Analysis.*—Half-step (semitone) progressions characterize this melody; 55 percent of the intervals are minor seconds. Surprisingly, the major third is the next most frequent interval, constituting one-fourth of the total, even though the song has a minor tonality and the F-minor triad forms the melody's framework. The trend of the melody suggests that F is the tonic, so the song is analyzed in the key of F minor, although E and B are always sung as natural notes rather than flats. This is one of many instances where the term "key" is used for convenience, rather than to indicate a formal tonal system where all notes have an established relationship to a central tonic. In every performance of this song, the tempo began as indicated, but after 10 or 12 measures, it began to slow down, while the words were sung in the specified time. A division of the beat into dotted eighth and sixteenth notes characterizes the song's rhythm and appears in both rhythmic units. The upward and downward progressions are more balanced than usual, with 20 ascending intervals and 25 descending intervals. A tempo change occurs within the song. (See No. 5.)

While Swift Dog was chasing the Assiniboin, they ran and hid in a white man’s house. The Sioux fired at anyone who approached the windows of the house. Meanwhile, Swift Dog stole one of the Assiniboin horses and rode away. He took a white horse that was already saddled. (See plate 70, *B*.) He said that he used a bow and arrows and shot them as fast as he could, though he did not know if he hit anyone. At that time, he sang the following song:

Analysis.—This song was recorded twice; the duplication was accidental. Both recordings were transcribed and are provided here. The first was by Swift Dog, and the second by Kills-at-Night (Haŋhe'pikte) and his wife Wita'hu (Woman's Neck), as women are accustomed to joining in these songs. In both instances, the melody tones are the major triad and the sixth, but it can be seen that the note values differ slightly according to the differences in the words. In the second rendition, the words are placed so as to repeat the rhythmic phrase of the previous measures. This seems to indicate a sense of a rhythmic unit. The first rendition is by an old singer, and the second is by a comparatively young man who usually "sits at the drum" during current tribal gatherings. His wife is considered one of the best among the younger singers. The first rendition is more complete, as it includes a significant part of the song before the words are introduced. In both renditions, about 28 percent of the intervals are minor thirds. The song has a range of 12 tones and is melodic in form.

*Analysis.*—This is a duplicate of the previous song, and its structure is discussed in the analysis of that song. The performances by Kills-at-Night and his wife were recorded on two phonograph cylinders, each containing four versions of the song. In every instance, her voice was silent during the opening measures, with her point of entry varying by one or two measures. The transcription shows the earliest point where she entered. The words, of course, are the same in both parts.

The reason for recording this song twice with Kills-at-Night and his wife was that the first performance suggested "part singing," as the wife held a tone while he sang several notes, then sang the delayed words rapidly to catch up with him. The author questioned the singers about this and asked if they could repeat it. The woman said it was unintentional on her part, caused by a "catch in her throat," and the seven other versions showed no trace of it. The author has heard many instances of group singing. In these, the women invariably sing an octave above the men, with the note values being identical.

*Analysis.*—In this melody, it will be noted what is often referred to as “the influence of the rhythmic unit on parts of the song in which it does not occur in its entirety.” Thus, in the measure following the third occurrence of the rhythmic unit, we have one quarter note followed by a group of four sixteenth notes, which is a reversal of the count divisions appearing in the unit. The tempo quickens with the introduction of the words, a feature often found in Sioux war songs but not noted among the Chippewa. The song is major in tonality and progresses largely by whole tones, with the major second constituting 46 percent of the total number of intervals. With the

### OLD BUFFALO’S WAR NARRATIVE

In August 1913, Old Buffalo (*Tatan'k'-ehan'ni*) (see plate 41) came with Swift Dog to McLaughlin, South Dakota, to meet with the author. They took this meeting very seriously. Old Buffalo said, “We come to you as if from the dead. The things you are asking us about have been dead to us for many years. By bringing them to mind, we are calling them back from the dead; and once we have told you about them, they will return to the dead to remain forever.”

Old Buffalo was born in 1845, a year recorded in the Sioux picture calendar as *Titaŋ'ka oble'ća kaha'pi kiŋ wani'yetu*, or the ‘Winter in which lodges with roofs were built.’ When he was 28 years old, he

<image-desc>A line drawing depicting a scene from a war party incident. In the center, a dark figure on horseback is being pursued or surrounded by several smaller, lightly drawn figures on foot and horseback, representing an engagement between Old Buffalo and the Crows.</image-desc>

->FIG. 33. Incident in the life of Old Buffalo (drawing by himself).<-

led a war party against the Crows. On this expedition, he and his comrades were entirely surrounded by the Crow warriors, an event that Old Buffalo depicted in a drawing (Fig. 33). Old Buffalo said that at the time of this expedition, his band of Sioux were living in the “Queen’s Land” (Canada), but had come down to the United States for a buffalo hunt. The expedition started from this temporary camp under his leadership.

Old Buffalo further said: <note>This narrative was interpreted by Mrs. Hattie Lawrence (see page 365), and is given as nearly as possible in her own words. Another narrative by Old Buffalo appears on page 274.</note>

> One night the Crows came and stole our horses. I had an older sister of whom I was very fond. The Crows stole her horse, and she cried for a long time. This made my heart very heavy. I said, “I will go and pay them back.” A friend said that he would go with me. I told my friend, “We will go and look for the Crows. Wherever their horses are corralled, we will find them.” Eleven others joined us, so there were 13 in the party, and I was the leader. It was during the coldest part of the winter, in the moon the Sioux call *Caŋ napo'pa wi*, the ‘Wood-cracking moon’. The

<summary>Old Buffalo shares a personal narrative about leading a war party against the Crows to recover stolen horses, reflecting on the emotional weight of recounting these long-past memories. He describes the origins of the expedition from a camp in Canada and identifies the specific winter of the event through the Sioux calendar.</summary>

<keywords>Old Buffalo, Tatan'k'-ehan'ni, Sioux history, Crow Indians, war narrative, Queen's Land, Canada, horse raiding, Sioux calendar, Wood-cracking moon, Hattie Lawrence</keywords>

The snow was deep, and I was lame in one leg, but I was angry, and I went. I thought, "Even if I die, I will be content." The women made warm clothing and moccasins for us to wear, and we started away. We carried no shelter. When night came, we shoveled aside the snow and laid down brush, on which we slept. At the fork of the Missouri River, we took the eastern branch and followed its course. It was 11 nights from the fork of the river to the enemy's camp, and every night we sang this song. It is one of the "wolf songs." (See p. 333.)

### Old Buffalo continued:

As we approached the end of our journey, a terrifying blizzard overtook us. We found a sheltered spot in a butte and stayed there for two days because my leg was very painful. After the storm died down, we looked around and could see the enemy's village. Night fell again, but my leg was so painful that we rested for another day. The next afternoon, as the sun was getting low, I tightened my belt and prepared for whatever might happen. We walked toward the enemy village and entered a rocky region, like the Badlands. Then it became dark.

A large number of Crows were camped at this place, and there was dancing in two parts of the village. We were close to the village, but no one saw us. Only the dogs barked. We went up to the edge of the village and reached a spot where many horses were gathered in a bunch. We drove the herd in front of us, and they trotted along quietly. After reaching a safe distance from the camp, we mounted some of the horses and drove the rest ahead of us. We did not stop but kept the horses at a fast trot all night. When daylight came, we counted the horses and found there were 53. We traveled all that day, and as the sun set, we rested. We were tired because we had no saddles, and we slept that night.

The next morning, another terrible blizzard arrived. My eyelashes were so frozen that I could barely see. I went back a short distance to see if we were being followed, then I returned to my companions. I realized that the horses' tracks left a clear trail, and I saw that the enemy was pursuing us. This was my war party, and I felt a great responsibility for its safety.

The Crows caught up with us and recovered most of the horses we had captured from them. We jumped down a steep, rocky ledge, and soon the Crows entirely surrounded us. A Sioux boy, about 15 years old, was with us, and he was shot in the back. We fought for as long as the sun remained in the sky. It was a hard struggle. Every time we fired a gun, it turned white with frost. During this fight, I sang a very powerful song of the Fox society, to which I belong. <note>Regarding the Fox society, see page 314 and following.</note>

->WORDS<-

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| toḳa'la koṇ | the fox |
| miye' yelo' | I am |
| ta'ku | something |
| ote'ḥika | difficult |
| owa'le yelo' | I seek |

*Analysis.*—This is a particularly interesting melody. It contains only the tones A, B, C, and E, which are the tonic triad and the second in the key of A minor; the song is analyzed as being in that key. The melody is built around the interval of a fourth, with almost half of the total intervals being fourths. The major third appears four times, but the minor third does not appear at all; there are, however, four minor seconds, or semitone progressions. In structure, the song would be considered harmonic except for the accented B near the end; it is therefore classified as melodic with a harmonic framework. Songs containing only one accented nonharmonic tone are frequently noted in both Chippewa and Sioux music. At the beginning of the song, there is a repeated phrase that is not considered a rhythmic unit because it seems to have no influence on the rhythm of the song as a whole. Its repetition on the same tone suggests that it may simply be an introductory phrase. The final tone is immediately preceded by a tone a major third lower, a conclusion that is somewhat unusual in the songs being analyzed.

Old Buffalo resumed the account of his exploit as follows:

> The Crows took the saddles from their horses and charged back at us, but our gunfire was more than they could stand, and they finally retreated, leaving their saddles on the ground. We captured these saddles and took them back to the place where the Crows first overtook us. There, we found only four horses alive. We put one of the captured saddles on a horse and lifted the wounded boy onto the horse’s back. I held the reins and walked beside the horse all through that night. When daylight came, we rested. The boy had no pillow, so I lay down and he rested his head on my body. There was timber near that place, and the next day we made a travois for the boy, and I rode the horse that pulled it. That night we traveled on, and about midnight we reached a certain place and set up camp. We had occasionally killed a buffalo for food, and since the men on foot had worn out their moccasins, we took fresh buffalo hide and tied it around their feet. The three horses ran away, but we caught them.
>
> All the following night we traveled, and the next day we reached the fork of the Missouri River, where we stayed for two nights.
>
> While we were on the warpath, our friends had finished their buffalo hunt and returned to Canada. I kept four men and the sick boy with me, and I sent the others home to report on the expedition. We kept the horses with us and followed slowly. The boy was thirsty, and since there was no cup, I took the hide from a buffalo head, put snow in it, and then placed a hot stone in the snow. In this way, the boy had hot water to drink. He wanted soup, so I took the buffalo tripe and boiled meat inside it. Thus, the boy had soup. (See p. 399.)

We camped for a time beside a creek, and as we came near the "Queen’s Land" <note>Canada</note> we camped again. There, the father and mother of the boy met us. They had heard the news from the other members of the party and started at once to meet us. After we had given the boy to his parents, we went on with the horses, leaving them to travel more slowly. It was dark when we reached home, and we fired our guns to let the people know of our coming. The next day the boy arrived. For two days and nights I stayed with him constantly. I did this because I felt that I was the cause of his misfortune. The boy had come to call me "father," and at the end of this time he said, "Father, you can go home now to your own lodge." I went to my own lodge and slept that night. The next morning the boy died. He is always spoken of as <term>Wana'gli ya'ku</term>, ‘Brings the arrow,’ because he brought home the arrow in his body.

I did not keep any of the horses for myself, because I was the leader of the war party.

Another expedition was described by Old Buffalo and illustrated by a drawing (fig. 34). Concerning this expedition he said:

A large number of Sioux were once moving camp, and five men left the party to steal horses. They were successful, and brought back 30 horses. The enemy were also moving camp. I made up my mind that I would go and see if I could get some horses, too. So I sent for a young man and talked with him about it. Then I said, "We will go;" and he replied, "I will go with you." One man asked to go with us, making three in the party. I said, "We will start without telling anyone and travel in the creek, so they will not know how we went." The one whom I invited gave up going at the last moment, but the man who had volunteered to go left camp with me while everyone was asleep.

On our expedition we sang this song, hoping that we would capture many horses:

*Analysis.* — This song contains only the tones of the <term>minor triad</term> and <term>fourth</term>. Unlike the preceding song, from which the <term>minor third</term> was entirely absent, that interval constitutes about one-third of the intervals in this song. The <term>fourth</term> is also prominent in the melody. Exactly two-thirds of the intervals move downward. Except for the accented B, the song would be classified as <term>harmonic</term> in structure. The form of the melody is simple; the song begins on the <term>octave</term> and twice descends to the <term>tonic</term> along the intervals of the <term>tonic chord</term>.

In conclusion, Old Buffalo said:

> We found the direction in which the Crows were traveling, went around, and headed them off. It was almost dark when we approached their village. They were camped in a circle. The afterglow was still in the sky, and this light was behind us as we went up a little creek from that direction toward the village. We could see the cooking fires. We were on horseback, and we lay flat on our horses, leaning close to the horses' heads. So we crept near to their horses.

<meta>This page continues Old Buffalo’s account of a war expedition against the Crow Indians, describing the immediate aftermath of their attempt to capture horses and the subsequent analysis of war songs.</meta>

When we stepped among the horses, one of them snorted at a stranger. Then the Crows came with their guns. They had seen us, though we did not know it. My eyes were only for the horses. They began firing, and before I had a chance to get away, my horse was shot. I snatched the reins and pulled, but the horse's jaw was broken. I went on. They shot again, and he fell. I jumped as he went down. The man who went with me ran away at the first attack and left me alone. I ran ahead, and as the Crows were loading their guns, I dodged from one shelter to another. They kept firing in the direction I had started to go.

The young man who ran away saw me. He was in a safe place, and he shouted, "Come this way." He was on horseback, and we sat double on his horse. We traveled some distance and came to the creek by which we had approached the Crow camp. We stayed at the creek that night. The Crows broke camp, and late the next day we went back to the deserted ground. There lay my horse, dead. We examined the horse and found that his shoulder was broken. My oldest sister had raised that horse.

We went back to the creek and stayed that night. The Sioux were moving to their last camp of the year, and there we joined them.

### PLOTS OF SONGS OF WAR

The songs of war, as already noted, are called "wolf songs." Many of them make reference to the wolf and many pertain to horses; therefore, we find among the plots of these songs (fig. 35) numerous examples of Class D (see p. 54). Song No. 120, however, is an example of Class A; No. 101 has the same general trend; and No. 136 is a good example of Class B. These types, as already stated, appear throughout the series. The <term>interval of a fourth</term> is prominent in songs concerning animals and implying motion, and this appears in the plots of the songs. Songs Nos. 111, 127, 145, and 174, as reference to their respective titles will show, are songs concerning horses, and the plots of the songs are seen to resemble one another. Songs 146 and 161 concern man and contain the idea of motion; their titles are, respectively, "He is returning," and "I wish to roam." These plots show the characteristics of Class D. No. 177 is called "A song of self-reliance," and we note in the plot of the song the emphasis and dwelling on the lowest tone, or <term>keynote</term>, which characterizes Class C and appears to be coincident with firmness of purpose and self-confidence. The <term>interval of a fourth</term> characterizes songs Nos. 99 and 100; the first of these is a song concerning the buffalo, and the second is the personal song of a man named Brave Buffalo, the words being "Brave Buffalo I am, I come." Such a song as the latter would undoubtedly be received in a dream of buffalo. The ascending interval at the opening of song No. 99 suggests Class E (see p. 519), and on reference to the words of the song, we find in them the idea of suffering on the part of the buffalo, who are being driven in such a way that the wind strikes their faces like a lance.

# ANALYSIS OF WAR SONGS

The songs of the military societies and the war songs are divided into two groups for analysis. The first group consists of songs where the majority are believed to be more than 50 years old, and the second group consists of songs thought to be of more recent origin.

->FIG. 35. Plots, Group 5.<-

The second group contains songs from the military societies that were more recently organized among the Teton—specifically the Fox, Badger, and Strong Heart societies, and the White Horse Riders. This group also includes war songs found in the description of the Sun Dance, and in the

# THE BUFFALO HUNT (WANA'SAPI <note>This word means "hunt"; the name of the animal being hunted is understood. (Compare the use of the word *itaŋ’čaŋ* in the footnote on page 70.)</note>)

The buffalo was the essential element in the life of the Plains Indians, as it supplied them with material for their tents, clothing, and moccasins; with food and containers for food and household articles; with tools for their crafts, and even with fuel for their fires. Every part of the animal was utilized. Among the less common articles made from parts of the buffalo were handles for small tools. These were fashioned from a certain heavy sinew in the neck. Sharp needles made of bone or metal, as well as knife blades, were inserted into pieces of "green" (raw) sinew. When dry, the sinew served as a firm and serviceable handle for the tool. It is also said that a heavy sinew from the buffalo’s hind leg was dried and cut into arrow points.

The tribal life of the Sioux passed away with the herds of buffalo. The last great buffalo hunt on the Standing Rock Reservation took place in 1882, under the supervision of Major James McLaughlin, who was the Indian agent on that reservation at the time. During this hunt 5,000 buffalo were killed by a hunting party consisting of about 600 mounted Sioux. <note>James McLaughlin, *My Friend the Indian*, pp. 97–116, Boston and New York, 1910.</note> Major McLaughlin became the agent at Standing Rock in 1881; that year is identified in the Sioux picture calendar as *Wable’za Tataŋ’ka-iyo’take wana’ nape’yuza wani’yetu*, "Winter in which Major McLaughlin shook hands with Sitting Bull." The following year is called *wable’za Lako’ta ob waŋa’sa ipi’ wani’yetu*, "Winter in which Major McLaughlin went on a buffalo hunt with the Sioux." The drawing that marks this year is shown in figure 36.

George Catlin, who took part in Indian buffalo hunts in the same region many years ago, provides a vivid account of buffalo hunting. <note>George Catlin, *The Manners, Customs, and Condition of the North American Indians*, vol. 1, pp. 251–261, London, 1841. See also a description of the hunting customs of the Omaha in *The Omaha Tribe*, by Fletcher and La Flesche, cited earlier, p. 275.</note>

In studying the customs of the buffalo hunt among the Teton Sioux, the author interviewed many old men, later reading the unfinished narrative back to them so they might discuss it and make corrections or additions. The completed material includes an account of making buffalo bows and arrows and the butchering of the buffalo by White Hawk; a narrative of the scouting party by Śiya’ka; and an account of the hunt consisting chiefly of information provided by Swift Dog and Gray Hawk.

<summary>This page describes the vital role of the buffalo in Plains Indian life, providing materials for survival, and details the final great hunt of 1882 at Standing Rock. It also lists the indigenous sources and historical references used to document these hunting traditions.</summary>

<keywords>Buffalo Hunt, Wana'sapi, Teton Sioux, Standing Rock Reservation, James McLaughlin, Sitting Bull, Material Culture, White Hawk, Śiya’ka, Swift Dog, Gray Hawk</keywords>

--- Page 583 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the buffalo hunt, transitioning from its historical significance to the specific social regulations, the role of medicine men, and the technical construction of hunting equipment.</meta>

DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC

The usual time for a buffalo hunt was early fall, when the buffalo migrated from the north, though some could be found during almost any season of the year. Medicine men played an important role in maintaining the camp's food supply. They occasionally warned of coming shortages and advised gathering a generous supply of food. This advice was followed, and a special hunt was organized. There were times when individual hunting was not permitted. During such times, if a man was found with a supply of fresh meat that he could not satisfactorily explain, it was the duty of the *aki'cita* <note>The tribal police or marshals.</note> to seize it. Furthermore, they might beat the man with clubs and tear down his tipi. (See p. 313.)

The construction of bows and arrows for the buffalo hunt was described by White Hawk (Ćetaŋ'ska), a Sioux from the Cheyenne River

<image-desc>A drawing in black silhouette style depicting a buffalo on the left and a hunter on horseback on the right, characteristic of Plains Indian pictorial art.</image-desc>

->FIG. 35. Drawing from picture calendar—the year of the last buffalo hunt.<-

Reservation (with Mr. Edward Swan interpreting). Although these were called "buffalo bows and arrows," it is likely that they were similar in design to those used in war. White Hawk said:

> The buffalo bows of two men were rarely exactly alike in either design or strength. However, one common characteristic was that the place for fitting the arrow was closer to the upper end than the lower, making the lower section longer and thicker than the upper. Some men used cherry or plum wood for their bows, while others preferred crab apple or some other hardwood. The back of the bow was covered with sinew that had been made flexible by rubbing and then dried. When this was ready, the back of the bow was notched in many places and covered with glue made from buffalo hide—specifically a strip taken from between the horns and behind the eyes. The sinew was then applied and became part of the bow. The bowstring was made of twisted and dried buffalo bull sinew.

White Hawk further stated that he knew of three kinds of arrowheads: (1) His great-grandfather used points made of cut flint; White Hawk had seen

He had seen these as a boy but had never used them. (2) His father used arrowheads made of bone, crafted from the outer thickness of ribs or marrow bones. (3) White Hawk himself used steel arrowheads. During his hunting days, it was customary to cut arrowheads from the thin frying pans sold by traders or used by soldiers. The feathers used on the arrows were not limited to any one species. Some hunters used feathers from the prairie hen, owl, or chicken hawk that were large enough to be split, while others used the smaller feathers of the eagle or buzzard. White Hawk said that after splitting a feather, he held one end in his mouth and "scratched it carefully with a knife to smooth it." Three feathers were attached to each arrow. Glue was applied under the feathers and under the arrowhead, and both were secured with wrappings of deer sinew.

It was said that a *good* bow would drive an arrow into a buffalo so that the arrowhead was embedded in the flesh; an *excellent* bow would drive it in almost to the feathers; while a *fine* bow would send that same arrow completely through the animal.

The proper length for a man's buffalo arrow was the distance on the outside of his arm from the elbow to the tip of his third finger, plus the length of his hand from the wrist to the large knuckle of the third finger. The intention was to make the arrow as light as possible; therefore, the preferred woods for the shaft were juneberry (*wi'pažukahu*) and wild currant (*wića'ganaśkahu*). These were so flexible that if a buffalo fell on an arrow, the shaft would bend without breaking. This allowed the arrow to be recovered and used again by its owner.

Certain lines were carved into the shaft of an arrow "to make it fly straight." A straight line about an inch long was cut into the shaft, extending downward from where the feather was attached. Then, the carving tool was held firmly in the hand while the shaft was moved sideways, so that the line became wavy. At a distance of about 3 inches from the arrowhead, the shaft was held still so that a straight line was formed again. White Hawk said that the correct way of cutting these lines was "the result of long experience," and that an arrow would not travel in a direct course without them.

After attaching the arrowhead and the feathers and carving the lines, the maker used a pair of small whetstones to polish the shaft. These were said to be made of a certain type of stone found in the Black Hills, which was relatively soft. A groove was cut into each whetstone, sized so that when the stones were fitted together, the opening formed by the two grooves matched the diameter of the arrow shaft. The shaft was then polished by moving the stones back and forth. To ensure the surface of the arrow shaft remained clean, the whetstones were brushed with buckskin after use and then carefully wrapped in the same material.

Each man had a special mark for his arrows. Bear Face (p. 78) said that he considered pelican feathers the best for arrows, and that he always used one pelican feather on his arrows, with the other feathers being taken from some other bird. Others are said to have painted their arrows red, or with a blue section in the middle, or to have made "dents" in the shaft, with each man using his own unique design.

As a final process, the shaft of the arrow was smeared with buffalo blood; White Hawk said this made the arrow pass more smoothly through the tissues of the animal.

Most quivers held 10 arrows. A man might make his own quiver, although he usually ordered arrows from an arrow maker, a hundred at a time. Red Fox (pp. 90, 375, *et seq.*) was known as a skillful arrow-maker in the old days.

A buffalo hunt frequently took place when the tribe was about to move to a new camping place. In describing such a hunt, Śiya'ka said:

> When the tribe was about to move to a new camp, the old men met to decide whether there was enough food to last for a considerable time. If it was decided that a hunt was advisable, these old men consulted the leaders in the various societies (such as the Strong Heart or White Horse societies), and together they decided on the young men who were to go and search for the buffalo. This task required young men who were known to be truthful and faithful to duty, as well as possessing the necessary physical ability and general equipment. Only men were selected who were known to be ready, as there was not enough time to prepare after they were notified. This was one of the greatest honors which could be conferred on a man, as it indicated that the tribe depended upon him for help with the food supply, without which it could not exist. It was necessary that these men know the topography of the country and understand the behaviors of the buffalo.
>
> These young men were notified, and as soon as they could make the arrangements which necessarily had to be left until the last moment, they went to the center of the tribal circle with their equipment of food and extra moccasins, each man carrying also a drinking cup and perhaps some cooking utensil. The man who was first selected was the leader of the searching party.¹ Their relatives were so pleased that the young men were thus honored that they gave away many presents when the party started out; these presents were valuable and included horses and blankets.
>
> The departure of the searching party was a great event.² They gathered in the middle of the camp circle, surrounded by rejoicing and gifts. A man recognized for high standing in the tribe was chosen to "start them off." A stick was placed upright in the ground, and he led them as they marched single file around this stick. The stick signified an enemy or a buffalo, and no one was allowed to strike it unless he had killed either an enemy or a buffalo. The man chosen to start off the party was usually a man who had done both. People on horseback were ready to escort the party from the camp. The direction in which the buffalo were probably located was pointed out, and the party started in that direction. They moved with a dancing step, and no drum or rattle was carried. The following song was sung at this time.

<note>¹ Śiya'ka was once appointed leader of a searching party, and six times was a member of such a party. Bows and arrows were used on those hunts.</note>
<note>² Compare this description of the departure to those who went to select the Sun-dance pole, p. 107.</note>

### ->No. 180. Song of the Buffalo Hunt (a) (Catalogue No. 475)<-

#### ->Sung by ŚIYA'KA<-

VOICE $♩$ = 92
DRUM $♩$ = 92
Drum-rhythm similar to No. 6

<image-desc>Musical notation for the song "Song of the Buffalo Hunt (a)". Two staves of music written in bass clef. The melody includes time signatures of 3/4, 2/4, 3/4, 2/4, 3/4, and 2/4. The notes consist of eighth and quarter notes with occasional accents and fermatas. The piece ends with a double bar and repeat dots.</image-desc>

*Analysis.*—The tones in this song are E-flat, G, B-flat, and C. By the test of the ear, E-flat seems the most satisfactory keynote; the song is therefore classified as major in tonality, and its tone material is considered to be the major triad and sixth. The tonic is found only in the upper octave and in connection with C, forming the interval of a minor third, which comprises 69 percent of the entire number of intervals. In this, as in many other Indian songs, the fact that a certain tone seems to be the keynote of the song does not imply that the corresponding "key" is fully established. Six performances were recorded; these are uniform throughout. The song as a whole has an interesting completeness of rhythm, though there is no repeated phrase which can be regarded as a rhythmic unit.

#### ->Śiya'ka continued:<-

After the escorting party had returned to the camp, the searchers were entirely under the control of their leader. Sometimes he assigned a territory to each of his men and scattered them over the prairie, directing them to meet at a certain time and place. When the men made their report to him, they were expected to be definite and certain in their statements. If they reported that they had seen buffalo, they had to be able to give an estimate of the number in the herd. It occasionally happened that a searching party was unsuccessful. In that event, they straggled back to the main camp, attracting as little attention as possible. The longest absence of a party remembered by Śiya'ka was 12 days.

As soon as the searching party had started, the tribe broke camp and began its journey to the place designated for the next camp, where the searchers were expected to make their report. Having reached this place and established their camp, they began an anxious watch for the return of the searchers. Men were stationed to watch for them, and if these men saw them coming, they returned to the camp, and the herald announced to the people that the searching party was in sight. The searching party gave certain signals to indicate the result of their search, running back and forth if the buffalo were close at hand, or waving a blanket at its full width and then laying it flat on the ground if they had seen a particularly large herd. Some went on horseback to meet them, and the entire tribe assembled in the middle of the circle to hear their report. The following song was sung as they returned.

# No. 181. Song of the Buffalo Hunt (b)
->(Catalogue No. 476)<-
->Sung by ŚIYA'KA<-

Voice ♩ = 80
Drum ♩ = 80
Drum-rhythm similar to No. 6

<image-desc>Musical notation for "Song of the Buffalo Hunt (b)". The score is written in treble clef with a key signature of three sharps (F#, C#, G#), indicating F# minor. The piece contains several meter changes, starting in 3/4 and moving to 2/4. The melody consists of descending rhythmic phrases utilizing eighth notes and triplets across two staves.</image-desc>

*Analysis.*—Five performances of this song were recorded. The timing was not strictly maintained, and the rhythm of the opening measures was difficult to identify; however, as in all such songs, when the correct note values are determined, it is found that all the performances are identical, and that the rhythm is in reality quite simple. The only ascending intervals in this song are the major second and fourth, and the only descending intervals are the major second and minor third. The song is based on the fourth five-tone scale, has a range of nine tones, and is melodic in structure.

The party entered the tribal circle with the leader in advance. <note>From this point the narrative is chiefly that of Swift Dog, interpreted by Mrs. McLaughlin.</note> The stick was again placed upright in the ground, and they circled around it, with many people striking it. In the middle of the council tent, a small space of bare ground had been prepared. This was hard and smooth, not pulverized as in the <term>Alo'waŋpi</term> ceremony, the Spirit-keeping lodge, and the Sun-dance ceremony. <note>See pp. 71, 82, 122.</note> A buffalo chip was placed on this bare ground, and beside it were placed a little sweet grass and a pipe, filled and ready to smoke. The scout who was the first to see the buffalo entered the lodge ahead of his companions. As they entered the lodge, many of the people stood with hands upraised, then, saying *Hi, hi!*, they stooped and placed the palms of their hands on the ground.

Beside the spot of bare ground stood a man whose reputation was beyond reproach and who had been selected to act as <term>itaŋ'ćan</term>, master of ceremonies. <note>See footnote, p. 70.</note> His entire body was painted red. Lifting the pipe from the ground, he took a little of the buffalo chip and sprinkled it on the tobacco in the pipe. He then took flint and steel, lit the chip on the ground, and laid the sweet grass upon it. After passing the pipe over the smoke of the sweet grass four times, he pretended to light it, holding the bowl first to one side and then to another side of the chip. This was done three times, and the fourth time he lit the pipe. The <term>itaŋ'ćaŋ</term> then swung the pipe in a circle over the chip, holding the bowl in the center, after which he offered it to the man who first saw the buffalo. He puffed it four times. The <term>itaŋ'ćaŋ</term> swung it again four times above the buffalo chip and offered it to the other scouts, who also puffed it four times. It was necessary that this be done four times; therefore, if there were only two scouts, the pipe was offered to each of them twice so that the proper number was observed. After the scouts had puffed the pipe, it was offered to all those sitting in the lodge, and they touched their lips to the pipe, even though it had gone out. When this was finished, the <term>itaŋ'ćaŋ</term> emptied the pipe, and the people in the front row of listeners sat with the palms of their hands on the ground as the scouts were

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the buffalo hunt preparations, specifically the formal reporting of the scouts' findings to the leader and the organization of the hunting party.</meta>

The <term>itan’ćan</term> asked for their report. He did not ask a direct question but said to the man who first saw the buffalo, “You are not a child. You must tell me truthfully what you have seen, and where you saw it.” The man might reply in this way: “I climbed a certain butte and looked down where I have seen buffalo before, and there I saw two herds, near the butte on which I was standing.” <note>It was the custom when speaking of buffalo to point with the thumb, not with the finger, and this custom was followed by Swift Dog when describing the event.</note>

“You say that you have seen the wallows and those who make the wallows. I am sure you have spoken truly, and you have made my heart glad,” said the <term>itan’ćan</term>, while the listeners shouted *Hi’* and touched the ground again with the palms of their hands.

Then the <term>itan’ćan</term> said, “If you saw anything beyond this which is worth reporting, tell it to me.” The scout might reply, “Beyond the two herds, I saw the plain black with buffalo.” And the people would shout *Hi’* once more.

Until that point, the people had remained very quiet, but when the report was completed, there was great excitement. The crier shouted, “Put saddles on your horses! Put saddles on your horses! We are going now to hunt the buffalo!” As soon as this announcement was made to the whole village, the horses were brought in, and both men and horses were painted. Whetstones were brought out and knives were sharpened. The scene was one of busy preparation for the great event.

Five or more men were selected from among the <term>aki’ćita</term> to keep order during the hunt. These men went to the council tent and received their final instructions from the chiefs, who told them to be sure to secure buffalo for the helpless, the elderly, and the disabled, as well as for women who had no one to provide for them. These <term>aki’ćita</term> were men of leadership ability, whose authority the people respected. They directed the people on their journey and required them to move quietly so that the buffalo would not become startled. When they were nearly in sight of the buffalo, other <term>aki’ćita</term> were selected. The method of approaching the herd was, of course, not always the same, but in an ordinary hunt, the party was divided into two sections, each led by about five <term>aki’ćita</term>. Under their direction, they surrounded the herd, and at their command, they charged into the chase. Those who were to chase the buffalo took the saddles off their horses. Every man had his arrows ready, each with a special mark so he could claim the animals he killed. It was like a horse race. As soon as a man shouted “Ready!” they were off, and you could see nothing but dust. The men with fast horses tried to get the fattest buffalo. Each man tried to get the best possible animals as trophies of the hunt.

The following is a song of the chase, sung by Gray Hawk (pl. 71), a successful buffalo hunter in the old days, who provided interesting details for the preceding narrative.

DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC 443

*Analysis.*—In many respects, this song is similar to Song No. 181. E-flat appears to be the most satisfactory keynote; analyzing it in the key of E-flat major, we find the melodic material consists of the tonic triad and the sixth, yet 73 percent of the intervals are minor thirds. The remaining intervals are two major seconds and one ascending fourth. The song is so short that the phonograph cylinder contains a large number of repetitions, in which there are no differences. The song was usually sung twice without a break in time, followed by shrill cries; after this, the song was resumed while the drum maintained a steady beat throughout the entire performance.

When the buffalo was killed, the meat was dressed and prepared for transport to the camp. White Hawk provided a description of how a buffalo is cut up, which was read to Heha'ka-wa'-kita (Looking Elk), who confirmed it was correct. These two men were said to be especially skilled in this phase of the buffalo hunt. The following description (interpreted by Edward Swan) details the butchering of a buffalo cow:

> If the hide was to be used for a tent, it was removed whole instead of being cut along the back. In this process, the animal was turned on its back, the head was turned to the left so it rested under the shoulder, and the horns were stuck in the ground so that the head formed a brace. In the old days, a clamshell was used as a skinning knife; Eagle Shield’s mother carried such a tool along with its case. <note>See Plate 67.</note> When steel knives became available, they were used instead of shells.
>
> When removing a hide intended for a tent, they began on the underside of a front leg, cut to the center of the breast and the lip, then up to a point between the horns, and then from one horn to the other. A cut was made down the belly and the inside of the hind legs; the tail was also split. When removing a hide to be used as a robe, they laid the animal on its belly with its legs extended forward and backward. In this case, the cut began on the upper lip and extended along the backbone to the tip of the tail. The hide from one side was folded back and spread on the ground, and the carcass was laid on that while the cuts were made along the belly as described above.
>
> When removing a hide, they did not cut all the meat from the inner surface but left a layer of meat on the hide of the back and a still thicker piece along the belly. This was later removed by the women and was said to be very good to eat. After removing the hide, it was the custom to take out the tongue, which was the part of the animal the Sioux considered the most delicious.
>
> Beyond this point, there were no established rules. White Hawk said, however, that the front quarters were usually removed first. He mentioned there was a "blanket of flesh" on the back and sides of the animal which was removed in one piece, but before taking this off, they "worked up under it" and detached the front quarters. The hind quarters were removed at the hip joints. The hump was underneath the outer "blanket of flesh." It was composed of fat and was cut off at the backbone. Below the outer "blanket of flesh" is the inner "blanket," which was removed in two parts. One side of it was turned down, exposing the ribs and the internal organs. The carcass was then cut along the belly, up the shoulder, and along the backbone. A fresh hoof was used as a hatchet, and in the old days, a knife made of a shoulder blade was used to cut the animal. <note>See Plate 67.</note> The ribs were removed in the form of a slab, and the kidneys, liver, and fat were also taken out, as were the brains. White Hawk said: "In the intestines there is a pocket-shaped piece about the size

...of a man's arm. This was turned inside out, fastened with a stick, and tied at one end. The brains were put into it, and the liver and hump were tied in a bundle with it. The stomach was turned inside out, and the heart, kidneys, and fat were put into it. The lower backbone was split and would later be chopped for boiling to extract the grease.

Each hunter usually provided two horses to bring home the meat of one buffalo. This meat was divided into eight portions, as follows: (1) The outer "blanket of flesh"; (2) the hump, brains, and liver; (3) the intestines and small split bones; (4) the inner "blanket of flesh"; (5) the slabs of ribs; (6) the front quarters; (7) the hind quarters; (8) the hip bones and backbone.

If the hide had been split to make a robe, it was customary to put half the hide on each horse. Then, the "outer blanket of flesh," which is a single piece, was laid on the horse, and the inner "blanket of flesh," which consists of two pieces, was laid on the other horse. The other bundles of meat were then piled on top but not tied, as the ends of the hide were folded over and held them in place. If the hide had been removed in one piece to make a tent, it was made into an additional bundle, and the hunter packed it separately.

A few women who were skilled riders usually went with a hunting party to help herd the pack horses until the men had the meat ready to load. After the hunting party returned to their camp, the women finished cutting up the meat; the long strips for drying were cut with the grain of the meat. These long strips were hung in the open air, and when thoroughly dried, they were pounded and mixed with wild cherries or with the animal's fat. Meat prepared in this way was kept for an indefinite length of time and was a staple food among the Sioux.

The following song is a medicine man's song to bring buffalo during a time of famine. Śiya'ka said that he had known of its successful use in this regard.

The medicine man painted a buffalo skull with red and blue stripes and laid it beside a filled pipe on a bed of fresh sage. <note>See page 185, footnote.</note> It was believed that "the skull turned into a real buffalo and called others." This song was sung in the dark. In the song, it is the buffalo who speaks. Śiya'ka said that in the old days, after the medicine man performed this ceremony and sang this song, the buffalo came near the camp, and thus the famine was relieved.

BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61

*Analysis.*—All the "verses" of this song were recorded, and the repetitions of the melody showed no differences except in note values affected by the words. It is not a rhythmic melody. In structure, the song is melodic. The tonality is minor, and all the tones of the octave are present except for the second. Two-thirds of the progressions are downward, and about 57 percent of the intervals are major seconds.

A white buffalo is said to have been particularly swift and wary; for this reason, as well as because of its rarity, it was very difficult to capture. It was a handsome animal; the rougher parts of its fur were soft and fine, and the smooth parts were shiny and glossy. The horns were black and the hooves were pinkish, and the end of its nose was also pink. The last white buffalo seen on the Standing Rock Reservation was killed near the Missouri River, in the vicinity of the present town of Pollock.

If a white buffalo were killed in a hunt, the fatal arrow was purified in the smoke of burning sweet grass. A knife was similarly purified before the animal was skinned, and the hide was removed in such a manner that no blood was shed on it. Only men who had dreamed of animals were allowed to eat any portion of the meat of a white buffalo.

Although a large prize was offered for the killing of this animal, the hide was not disposed of while the tribe was on the hunt, but was held until the people reached home so that all the requirements could be fulfilled. The skin was not treated like an ordinary buffalo hide. Only women noted for purity of life could touch or tan it, and after the tanning was finished, certain important ceremonies were required. It was the custom for a medicine man to purify the hide with sweet grass.

The tanned robe was always kept in a rawhide case. The owner of such a robe usually kept it to be buried with him. If, however, he was willing to dispose of it, he might call together men who had owned similar robes and make this known to them. Great honor was given to a man who was willing to dispose of a white buffalo robe. A small piece was worth a horse; even the smallest portion of the robe was a "sacred article" to the person who secured it, and it could be taken only by someone who had owned part or all of a similar robe.

Jaw said that he killed a white buffalo when his band of the tribe was in Canada. He was only 13 years of age at the time, and the buffalo he killed was the only white one in a herd of about a hundred. Not caring for the others, he killed only this one. It was a beautiful animal, with only its horns being black. Jaw killed it in the fall and kept the hide all winter, selling it in the spring to a man named Bone Club (Hohu'-ćan'lipi) for two horses and a large buffalo hide

tent, and many other articles. This exploit, as well as his killing of a bear and an elk with a bow and arrows, is shown in one of his drawings (see plate 60, *A*).

Jaw said that on three occasions he killed a bear with a gun, but that it was very hard to do so with a bow and arrows. The circumstances under which he was successful in this are as follows.

One summer he and another man had been hunting deer and were returning with their horses loaded with meat. Jaw had a gun, while his companion carried a bow and arrows. They saw a mother bear and two cubs coming toward them. Giving the gun to his companion, Jaw took his bow and arrows. The bear tried to fight him, and as it turned he hit the beast with an arrow. Three times the bear renewed the attack, but each time he wounded it with an arrow, finally killing it.

The elk hunt (shown in plate 60) took place in winter, when he was 22 years old. He had recently married a Yankton Sioux girl and was staying in her part of the country. There were two other families camping near them, making three tents in all. Early one morning Jaw's wife left the tent, but returned, saying: "Wake up! There are lots of elk. Come and see." Putting on moccasins and leggings, and taking his arrows and his best horse, he went after them. The snow was very deep. It was early in the morning when he shot the elk.

# COUNCIL AND CHIEF SONGS

## COUNCIL SONGS

The following are known as “council songs.” These were sung when the chiefs met in the council tent to decide matters of tribal importance. This tent was placed inside the camp circle and was decorated in various ways. Plate 72 shows the council tent at the gathering at Bull Head, South Dakota, July 4, 1912.

The first song of this group was sung by Many Wounds (Wopo’-tapi), who announced the song before singing. His announcement was recorded by phonograph and translated as follows: “Tribe, listen to me. I will sing a song of the dead chiefs. What are you saying? The chiefs have come to an end, and I sing their songs. I wish I could do as they have done, but I will try to sing their song.”

*Analysis.*—Three versions of this song were recorded, and in every instance the difference between the tones transcribed as C natural and C sharp was clearly marked. *Analysis.*—This song contains a wide variety of <term>intervals</term>, including seven types of upward and six types of downward progressions. Of these <term>intervals</term>, 75 percent are minor thirds and major seconds. The song has a major <term>tonality</term>, a <term>melodic</term> structure, and lacks the <term>seventh tone</term> of the complete <term>octave</term>. Three <term>rhythmic units</term> are found in the song, with the second and third sharing one common count division. The manner in which these units are used is particularly interesting.

### CHIEF SONGS

There appear to be two kinds of Chief songs: those that voice the thoughts of the chiefs, and those sung in honor of the chiefs. For instance, the second song in the Sun-dance group was said to be a Chief song. It contains the words, "Friends, take courage; we are coming right here; they see us." In explanation of this class of songs, a Sioux man said, "The chiefs do not sing these songs; the people sing them to mean 'the chief says such and such.'" The following belongs to the second class of Chief songs and is said to be an old and particularly good example. Two Bears was the head chief of the Lower Yanktonais band of Sioux, the most populous band on the Standing Rock Reservation, and was prominent in tribal councils. He died around the year 1886. An interesting record concerning this man is preserved in the report of the Indian agent for the year 1874:¹

> On July 1st, I was informed that a party of young men had left this agency to wage war on Indians up the river. I asked the principal chiefs to stop these proceedings. They promptly responded by sending their soldiers out, who overtook the war party and brought them back. The conduct of Chief Two Bears and Chief Antelope on this occasion deserves particular credit. The defeat of the party is mainly attributable to the energetic action of these two chiefs.

---

¹ Palmer, Edmond, in *Indian Affairs Report for 1874*, p. 248, Washington, 1874.

*Analysis.*—Like many other melodies based on the fourth five-toned scale, this song contains a large proportion of minor thirds; this interval forms more than 55 percent of the total number. *Analysis.*—This and the following song were recorded at Sisseton; the words are in the Santee dialect. The rhythmic form of this song is interesting. Three phrases make up nearly the entire melody: the first consists of three measures, the second also consists of three measures, and the third (following a connecting measure) consists of four measures, after which two minor measures close the song. Several performances were recorded, and in all of them, the drum is slightly slower than the voice. The song has a distinctly minor quality, although fewer than one-fourth of the intervals are minor thirds. All the tones of the octave except the sixth are included in the melody, which has a range of nine tones.
