# BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61

*Analysis.*—The triplet of eighth notes is repeated so constantly that it can hardly be called a rhythmic unit. It resembles a vibrato, yet it was sung evenly and distinctly in every performance of the song. With the exception of the octave, which occurs halfway through the song, there are no intervals other than minor thirds and major seconds. There are 24 progressions in the song, 17 of which are downward. The melody tones belong to the second five-tone scale, and the song's structure is melodic.

Probably no Sioux chief is more famous than Sitting Bull (Tataŋ'ka-iyo'take, literally translated as “Sitting Buffalo Bull”), plate 75, of whom the *Handbook of the Indians* (pt. 1, pp. 583–584) says:

> Sitting Bull . . . a noted Sioux warrior and tribal leader of the Hunkpapa Teton division, born on the Grand River, South Dakota, in 1834; his father was Sitting Bull, . . . a sub-chief. . . . He took an active part in the Plains wars of the sixties, and first became widely known to white people in 1866, when he led a memorable raid against Fort Buford. Sitting Bull was on the warpath with his band of followers from various tribes almost continuously from 1869 to 1876, either raiding the frontier posts or waging war on the Crows or the Shoshone, especially the former. . . . His refusal to move onto a reservation in 1876 led General Sheridan to begin the campaign against him and his followers which resulted in the surprise and annihilation of Custer’s troops on the Little Bighorn River, Montana, in June. During this battle, in which 2,500 to 3,000 Indian warriors were engaged, Sitting Bull was in the hills “making medicine,” and his accurate prediction of the battle enabled him “to come out of the affair with higher honor than he possessed when he went into it.” (McLaughlin.) Sitting Bull . . . escaped to Canada, where he remained until 1881, when he surrendered at Fort Buford under a promise of amnesty and was confined at Fort Randall until 1883. Although he had surrendered and moved to a reservation, Sitting Bull continued to be unreconciled. It was through his influence that the Sioux refused to sell their land in 1888; and it was at his camp . . . that Kicking Bear organized the first ghost dance on the reservation. The demand for his arrest was followed by an attempt by some of his people to rescue him, during which he was shot and killed by . . . the Indian police on December 15, 1890.

Part of the author’s work was done near the site of Sitting Bull’s camp, and most of her informants had known him in the days of his power. It was said that a striking feature of his everyday appearance was a bunch of shed buffalo hair painted red and fastened to the side of his head.<gloss>1</gloss> There are a large number of songs connected with his name; these are either songs which he sang or songs in which his name has been introduced. No attempt was made to collect many of these songs or to study the character of Sitting Bull. Two songs said to have been used by him in the practice of medicine appear as numbers 191 and 192. Sitting Bull is also mentioned on pages 218 and 220.

The following two songs of Sitting Bull’s are connected with the last years of his life.

---

1 Shed buffalo hair was, and still is, greatly valued by the Sioux. It is said to “signify the times when the buffalo were plentiful and also serve as a remembrance of the arrival of the White Buffalo Maiden.” In the old days, it was used as a head ornament, especially at a buffalo dance, and also as a charm by the Buffalo societies. (See page 64.)

->**No. 193. Song of Sitting Bull (a)** (Catalogue No. 612)<-

*Analysis.*—There is an unusually large variety of intervals in this song, two versions of which were recorded. It contains six kinds of upward and four kinds of downward progressions. The song is characterized by the descending fourth; about one-fourth of the intervals are fourths, a number exceeded only by the frequency of major second intervals. The tonal material consists of the minor triad and fourth. The tonic chord is prominent in the melody, but the accents are placed such that the song is classified as melodic with a harmonic framework.

[DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC

*Analysis.*—The upward and downward progressions are more equal in this song than in many of the others being analyzed; there are 18 upward intervals and 22 downward intervals. The fourth is prominent, making up 37 percent of the intervals, while the minor second makes up 31 percent. Like the fourth five-toned scale, this song lacks the fourth and seventh tones of the complete octave, but the fourth five-toned scale is major in tonality (the first third being a major third), while this song is minor. This tonal material is found in a few Chippewa songs and is discussed in the analysis of song number 26 in this work. Syncopations occur in this melody and are clearly heard in both performances. These are unusual in Sioux and Chippewa songs. (See Songs 165 and 237, and also Bulletin 53, page 130.)

### PLOTS OF CHIEF SONGS

While both Buffalo and Chief songs are included in the tabulated analysis, the plot of the hunt songs is grouped with the war songs; the plot of song number 177 appears in figure 35 on page 419.

<image-desc>Figure 37 shows two melodic plots on rectangular grids. Plot No. 189 on the left shows a line that begins near the top and follows a jagged, generally descending path toward the bottom right. Plot No. 193 on the right displays a much more volatile line with sharp, high peaks and deep valleys spanning the height of the grid.</image-desc>

->No. 189 — No. 193<-
->FIG. 37. Plots, Group 6.<-

An interesting peculiarity appears in the plots of the Chief songs (Figure 37). Of the 8 songs making up this group, 5 have a range of an octave, beginning on the upper tonic and ending on the lower tonic, with that note being repeatedly sounded in both octaves. It should be remembered that emphasis on the tonic is a characteristic of songs expressing self-reliance. The songs of the medicine men and also certain war songs show this emphasis on the lower tonic. Placing the emphasis on the upper as well as the lower tonic suggests a quality of character in the chiefs which was not found in the medicine men or the warriors. The two plots shown here are the songs of two men with radically different characters. The first (No. 189) is a song concerning Gabriel Renville, whose stable character earned him an enduring place in history. His song, in addition to the emphasis on the tonic, shows the steadily descending trend which may be called the simplest and most common type of Indian melody. No. 193, a song of Sitting Bull’s, shows a contrast as great as the difference between the two men. Not only are the intervals wider

and more irregular, but an ascent from the lowest to the highest tone appears midway through the song. Such an interval at the opening of songs has been found to be associated with disappointment or distress. In this regard, it is interesting to note that this song was associated with the final years of Sitting Bull's life and is reportedly sung by him during a gathering of the Sioux in 1889. This gathering was held for the purpose of considering the ceding of a large portion of their land and served as the introduction to the breaking up of the tribe. Sitting Bull, who was a man of exceptional insight, may have foreseen what would inevitably follow. Regarding this and other remarks about the structure of these songs, the author wishes to be understood as offering only tentative observations.

The songs in this analysis group share neither a common origin nor a common use; they are grouped together primarily for convenience. The buffalo hunt songs (Nos. 180, 181) were favorites for that activity, but the same songs could also be used by those who went out to scout for the enemy. These are followed by a song of the chase and a song to secure buffalo during a famine (Nos. 182, 183). Some of the council songs (Nos. 184–187) are undoubtedly very old, but it is impossible to determine their exact age. Some of the Chief songs (Nos. 5, 188–194) may also be old, as new names were often substituted for old names in songs of honor; however, one of the songs (No. 191) was said to have been composed only three years ago.

# SONGS CONNECTED WITH DANCES AND GAMES

## DANCES

In every Sioux village, there was a lodge of a suitable size for social gatherings or dances. An old type of Sioux dance lodge is shown in plate 76, *A*; the walls are made of logs and the roof is made of branches covered with earth, with a large smoke-hole left in the center. Plate 76, *B*, shows a lodge on the Standing Rock Reservation where the author witnessed a dance in 1912. The following summer, she learned that it had been torn down, as the government was more strictly enforcing restrictions on dancing among the Indians. In this lodge, as in the older type, the construction consisted of logs, branches, and earth, but the shape was rectangular, the logs were plastered with earth, and the roof was almost flat with projecting stovepipes, indicating that the lodge was heated by stoves instead of an open fire.
Regarding Indian dances, it was said that—

> In dancing, the Indians imitate the actions of animals. In the grass dance, the men imitate the motions of the eagle and other graceful birds. In the buffalo dance, they imitate the buffalo. The old-time dancing dress of the Indians imitated animals, but there was always a charm or a headdress that indicated the personality of the wearer. The Indians imitate the cries of birds or animals when they dance. Some headdresses imitate the comb of a bird, and a man wearing such a headdress would imitate the actions of that bird. The actions of a dancer always correspond to his costume. This is a matter of choice and usually is not connected with a dream.

### THE GRASS DANCE

The grass dance (<term>peží' waćí'pi</term>) currently exists among all the tribes of the northern plains, even reaching as far as the Kutenai. The name "Omaha" identifies it with the Omaha tribe, from which many other tribes received it, but in transmission, it has lost its original significance and has become simply a social dance. According to Miss Fletcher, the dance was originally connected with the <term>Hethu'shka society</term> of the Omaha, a society whose purpose "was to stimulate a heroic spirit among the people and to keep alive the memory of historic and valorous acts." <note>1</note>
Miss Fletcher describes one of its meetings, stating that <note>2</note>—

> No clothing except the breechcloth was worn by the members, and a long bunch of grass representing scalps the wearer had taken was fastened to the belt at the back. . . . When the dance became known to the Dakota tribes and the Winnebago, the significance of the bunch of long grass having been forgotten, they gave the

---

<note>1 Fletcher and La Flesche, The Omaha Tribe, cited above, p. 459.</note> 
<note>2 Ibid., p. 461.</note>

<summary>This page describes the construction of Sioux dance lodges and explains how Indian dances, such as the grass and buffalo dances, involve the imitation of animal movements and sounds. It specifically introduces the grass dance, noting its transition from an Omaha warrior society ritual to a widespread social dance among northern plains tribes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of songs connected with dances, specifically detailing the history and distribution of the grass dance—also known as the Omaha dance—across various Sioux groups and other tribes.</meta>

<page-num>469</page-num>
<header>DENSMORE] TETON SIOUX MUSIC</header>

name "grass dance" or the "Omaha dance," the latter name acknowledging the tribe from which the dance was obtained. Among the Omaha, the leader had to be of a high enough rank to be permitted to wear "the crow," a decoration of the highest order.

The grass dance was noted among the Yankton Sioux by De Smet, who described it in a letter to Father Terwecoren dated November 1867, as follows:¹

> The primary <note>society</note> among the Yanktons is called the Grass band or *Peji-makinnanka*. All the braves, or "men of heart" as the Indians express it, belong to this fraternity. . . . During the ceremonial dances, each member carries a long bunch of grass, which is their symbol for abundance and charity. . . . The badge or distinctive mark of the society is the braided bunch of grass attached to each member's waist, looking like a long tail.

In this description, we see the use of grass, though a different symbolism is assigned to it.

Mr. La Flesche, who saw the Omaha and Yankton Sioux perform the grass dance together on the Yankton Reservation in the 1870s, is quoted as follows:

> The rhythm of the *He-thu'-shka* songs sung by the Yanktons was the same as the Omaha songs, and the dance steps and movements that matched the rhythm were the same as those of the Omaha. In fact, the Yankton *He-thu'-shka* was, and still is, the same as the Omaha dance, except for certain preliminary ceremonies that the Omaha have also now discontinued. Until quite recently, only men danced the *He-thu'-shka*, as it was strictly a warrior's dance.

The grass dance among the Sioux is briefly mentioned by George Bushotter, a Teton Sioux, in his "Texts," written in 1887–88. He includes it among the "intrusive dances" that took place in the camp while a Sun Dance was in progress, and he mentions the wearing of grass at the dancers' belts.²

In 1903–1912, Wissler found a society called the Omaha among the Oglala Sioux,³ which he identifies with the grass dance.⁴ "Crow belts" were worn during this society's ceremonies, but there is no mention of grass being carried or hung from the belt. The grass dance among the Sisseton Sioux is described by Lowie, who says they also called it the Winnebago dance.⁵ This widely distributed dance is noted by Wissler as currently existing among the Blackfoot, Piegan, Crow, Gros Ventre, and Assiniboin Indians.⁶ A "feather-tail belt" seems to have been generally considered part of the dance regalia among these tribes.

Many similarities can be traced between the previously mentioned accounts of the grass dance and the descriptions of the dream dance as practiced by the Menomini and the Chippewa. These resemblances involve, among other things, the custom of "presenting the pipe to the sky," the position of the drum within the dancing circle, the wearing of "crow belts," and the practice of divorce in connection with the society's ceremony.¹

be removed, a heated iron being commonly used for the purpose. Ash and box elder were woods frequently selected. The open end of the instrument was usually carved to represent the head of a bird. Mr. Higheagle stated further that the instrument was called śi'yotaŋka (śi'yo, 'prairie chicken'; taŋ'ka, 'large') by the Teton Sioux. The instrument is said to have had two uses: It was used in dances, especially in the grass dance, and also by young men as a "courting call." Plain bone whistles and bead-decorated whistles were similarly used in dances; these also were known as śi'yotaŋka. Three or four dancers might carry these whistles, but the signal was usually given by the recognized leader of the dancers. If the singers "came near the end of the tune," and he wished the dancing to continue, he blew his whistle, at which point they continued their repetitions of the melody.

In construction, this instrument is a whistle, being an open pipe with the usual whistle or flageolet mouthpiece near one end. The pipe produces the series of harmonics obtained from a bugle or trumpet. The specimen illustrated <gloss>1</gloss> is old, having been in the possession of Mrs. James McLaughlin for about 30 years, and could not be played; however, a similar instrument in perfect condition was obtained among the Hidatsa at Fort Berthold, North Dakota, in 1915. The length of this instrument below the mouth is 22 5/8 inches. The instrument was played by its Hidatsa owner, and a phonograph record of the performance was made. It was also played by Mr. E. H. Hawley, curator of musical instruments at the United States National Museum. The following part of the long harmonic series could be produced on the Hidatsa whistle, with the tones named in ascending order: A flat (second space treble staff), D flat, F, A flat, C flat, D flat, E flat, F.

<gloss>1</gloss> This instrument has been described as follows by Mr. Hawley, mentioned above: "Length, 25 inches; diameter, 5/8 inch. A straight stick of wood, its lower end carved to represent a crane with an open beak, and its throat is the open end of the whistle. The bore appears to be from 3/8 to 1/4 inch in diameter. <meta>This page continues the description of the grass dance, specifically focusing on the songs, feasts, and ritual protocols associated with the ceremony among the Teton Sioux.</meta>

<page-num>472</page-num>
<header>BUREAU OF AMERICAN ETHNOLOGY [BULL. 61</header>

We have grass dance songs of our own, where both the melody and the words are Sioux. There is always a feast at a grass dance. The men in charge of the meeting decide who will provide the feast, and the Crier notifies them. The same people are not asked to provide for two successive feasts. Each "cook" brings what she likes—dried berries or grapes, wild turnips, and sometimes sweet corn, prepared by boiling it with ashes until the husk drops off, then washing it thoroughly and boiling it with a bone that has fat on it. Dog meat is not required, but if one of the appointed "cooks" wishes to provide a dog, it is greatly appreciated. The head and chest of the dog are cut into four pieces and placed in a large dish. Four young men are selected to eat them, and after the young men have finished, the bones are placed in a pile; the four young men then dance four times around it, one after another. The pile is not in the center of the circle formed by the young man as he dances; it is near one side, and as the young man passes near the pile of bones, he extends his hand over it.<sup>1</sup>

In a grass dance, the drum is outside the circle of dancers, near the side of the assembly where the men sit. A few women sing with the men at the drum.

One feature of this dance is that a lost article must be redeemed with a gift. For example, if a feather falls to the ground, the whole party dances around it, and one of the men goes forward and strikes it, afterwards giving a gift to an old man, who is not expected to give anything in return. More than one person may strike a feather, with each being required to give a gift to an old man. Sometimes four men do this, after which the feather is returned to its owner.

The men dance by themselves. The women also dance by themselves, but they occasionally summon a few men, whom they call by various terms of kinship, such as "brother" or "cousin." If a woman calls a married man into the dancing circle, his wife considers it an honor, which is even greater the longer he is required to dance. His wife always gives a gift to the woman who asked him to dance. Sometimes a woman stands and tells of the brave deed of a relative, and all the women respond with the high, quavering cry that is their customary applause.

At the end of the men's dances, the participants sit down, but the drumming continues for a moment or two, at which point one of the men rises and dances around the circle, singing a short phrase. This is called "dancing the tail" (see pl. 77, *B*), and words are often used only in this part of the song. The tail dancer is selected by the other dancers, and it is considered an honor to be so chosen. Only a man who has performed some brave deed may be chosen as a tail dancer. According to Mr. Higheagle, this feature of the grass dance originated in an honor dance, signifying that the dancer had successfully served as a rear guard on a war expedition, or had been left behind on the warpath and acted nobly. The same honor might be given to a man whose horse had been shot under him and who had

<image-desc>Musical notation for the "Song of the Grass Dance (b)". The score is written in bass clef across three staves. The piece features frequent changes in time signature between 2/4 and 3/4. The melody includes triplets, slurred notes, and several grace notes. There are no sharps or flats in the key signature, and the transcription represents only the vocal part.</image-desc>

*Analysis.*—The phonograph cylinder contains three complete renditions of this song, followed by four incomplete renditions in which the first and second measures, and also the sixth measure from the end, are occasionally omitted. The first tone in the transcription is not regarded as part of the melody but seems to be a mannerism of the singer. The writer recorded the songs of a Hidatsa member at Fort Berthold who sang the octave below the opening tone of a song in the same manner, but this is not a common custom among Indian singers. The progressions of this melody are such that they suggest either E or G as a possible keynote, placing the song in either the second or fourth five-toned scale. However, as the only accented tones are G and D, the song is analyzed as having G as its keynote and being in the fourth five-toned scale. This indicates its tonality as major, yet the major third is not present, and about one-third of the intervals are minor thirds. This is one of many instances in which the term “key” can hardly be applied to an Indian song with the full significance of the term as it is used by white musicians.

<image-desc>Musical notation for "Song of the Grass Dance (c)". The score is written in the treble clef with a key signature of one sharp. It is in 2/4 time. The melody is composed of two lines of staff, featuring eighth notes, sixteenth notes, and triplets. It primarily moves in descending patterns.</image-desc>

*Analysis.*—This is typical of the songs heard today on the reservation when the Indians gather for social occasions. Like other modern Sioux songs, it contains a wide variety of progressions, featuring five different ascending intervals and an equal number of different descending intervals. The minor second, an interval that occurs infrequently in older songs, is found here four times. The tonal material of this song is unusual. If we consider G to be the keynote of the entire song, the second, fifth, and seventh tones of the octave are missing. The drum was slightly slower than the voice in all of the performances.

*Analysis.*—Six performances of this song were recorded, some beginning with an unaccented tone an octave below the opening tone, as seen in No. 197. All but three of the progressions are minor thirds and major seconds; the remaining three progressions consist of two fourths and one ascending ninth. The melody contains the tones of the fourth five-toned scale, has a range of 13 tones, and is melodic in structure.

*Analysis.*—This is a simple melody, containing only the tones of the minor triad and the fourth. It contains only nine progressions, six of which are minor thirds. The melody has a range of 10 tones and is based on the tonic chord. The song was accurately repeated in many performances, with the drum and voice coinciding on every beat.

When the gathering ends, the men and women stand in their places and dance. The men move more than the women, but none of them move toward the center of the circle.

The author has made no attempt to record songs of every social dance. In addition to the grass dance, two other dances represent this phase of Sioux music: the shuffling-feet dance (<term>naślo'haŋ waći'pi</term>) and the night dance (<term>haŋhe'pi waći'pi</term>).

### SHUFFLING-FEET DANCE

The shuffling-feet dance is also called the Cheyenne, the glide, and the dragging-feet dance (Plate 78). Lowie¹ observed this dance among the Sisseton and Santee, and Wissler² noted it among the Oglala, who said they received it from a tribe living west of the Gros Ventre. Both men and women joined in the dance, and the style of the step is indicated by its name.

Two songs from this dance are provided here; a third song is No. 226.

# NIGHT DANCE

The night dance is mentioned by both Wissler and Lowie in connection with the shuffling-feet dance. It is also mentioned by Dorsey.<note>Dorsey, J. Owen, Study of Siouan Cults, cited above, p. 498.</note> Both young men and women took part in this dance, which Wissler<note>Cited above, p. 79.</note> describes as follows:

> The young men sat on one side of the tipi, and the young women on the other. As the songs for this dance were sung, a man would stand and dance with a gift which he then gave to one of the young women. In the same way, the young women danced with gifts for the young men.<note>Compare the giving of gifts in the woman's dance of the Chippewa, Bulletin 45, p. 192.</note> This was considered a type of courting ceremony. Then everyone danced in a circle, holding hands. At the end, a feast was held.

### BEGGING DANCE

The begging dance is sometimes mentioned as if it were one of the social dances of the tribe, but it should instead be regarded as a custom in which the dance step is merely incidental. The begging for food from tent to tent, which the author has witnessed at tribal gatherings, was sometimes accompanied by merriment. Such a begging dance was seen among the Chippewa at Red Lake, Minnesota (See Bulletin 45, page 171). Certain songs are known from use as begging-dance songs; most of these are very short. The songs originally used in begging for food were "praise songs," where the group stood in front of a tent and sang the praises of the occupant until he appeared with the desired donations. While this might be done for a social gathering, it was more often done for the council tent or for a specific society (See pages 103, 320, 327). When "praise songs" were used in this context, the tempo was gradually quickened; the begging party sang the song first at the usual speed, after which the tempo was increased with each repetition until the gifts were received.

The council of chiefs might request food contributions from three classes of men: those who had been successful leaders of war parties, those who had been victorious but not as leaders, and those who had been wounded in battle. The request was made using appropriately decorated sticks (plate 79), which were placed in the ground in front of the tents. It was considered that the chiefs met in council for the benefit of the tribe; therefore, it was an honor for certain members of the tribe to provide them with food while they were gathered. One of the military societies usually decorated the sticks and "sang around the camp" to collect the food. A man was sent ahead to find out who lived in the various tents and to place the appropriate sticks in the ground. When the group collecting the food reached a tent, they were ready to sing a song in honor of the occupant, who responded with a suitable contribution. In front of the tent of a man who had been a successful leader of war parties, they placed a stick covered in black paint with a black feather hanging from it. For a man who had been victorious but not as a leader, the stick was encircled with black bands (the number of which indicated the number of his victories), while for a man who had been wounded, a stick was decorated in red. The complexity of the stick varied according to the honor given to the man. The sticks with the feather and red tassels were used at a gathering of Sioux on the Standing Rock Reservation on July 4, 1911. The location of this gathering is shown in plate 80.

Separate from the songs used when a group of people went from tent to tent is the following song by four old women.

It is called simply <term>wići'lowan'pi</term>, or "begging song." Yellow Hair said that she had a relative who went to war, and that the man's wife, along with three other female relatives of the absent warrior, stood in the center of the village and sang this song until donations were brought to them. The words are not transcribed, but they are taunting in character; their general idea is, "If you have no buffalo chips in the tipi, go find some on the prairie for us." Buffalo chips, used as fuel, were mentioned as the smallest gift that could be given to the poor.

The minor third and major second are the only musical progressions.

The following song is said to have been composed around the year 1870 and is, therefore, relatively modern. It came into use when the Indians first obtained bread and coffee by trading with white men. If it were known that an Indian had bread and coffee in his tent, a party would go and sing this song, remaining in front of the tent and singing until he shared his luxuries with them.

### PLOTS OF GRASS-DANCE SONGS

The four song plots presented here (fig. 40) are of two grass-dance songs (Nos. 195, 196), one shuffling-feet dance (No. 202), and a begging song (No. 205). Songs Nos. 195 and 202 are of class A, which is a general type, and No. 196 is of class D, showing the characteristics of songs of motion or of animals.

# Games

## THE MOCCASIN GAME (HAN'PA APE'ÉCUŊPI)

Guessing the location of a hidden object was the central idea in one distinct class of Indian games, with the object varying in different games. The moccasin game is a familiar example of this class. Culin says: "The moccasin game was played by the Algonquian tribes, and is found among the Dakota and Navajo. Two, three, four, six, or eight moccasins are used, but four is the standard number. The objects hidden vary from one to four, and consist of either bullets, stones, or small sticks of wood." <note>¹ Culin, Stewart, *Games of the North American Indians*, Twenty-fourth Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, p. 339, Washington, 1907.</note> The game as played by the Santee Sioux in Minnesota is briefly described by Rev. E. D. Neill as follows: "A bullet or plum stone is placed by one party in one of four moccasins or mittens and sought for by the opposite side." <note>² *Dakota Land and Dakota Life* (1853), *Minnesota Historical Collections*, vol. 1, p. 280, St. Paul, 1872.</note> In the usual manner of playing the game, four bullets are hidden, one under each of four moccasins. One of these bullets is marked, and the score is determined by how quickly the marked bullet is found by the "guessing side," and also by the position of the moccasin under which it was hidden—whether it was at the end or in the middle of the row. The manner of playing the game among the Sioux is practically the same as among the Chippewa. Illustrated accounts of this game among the Chippewa have been given by Culin, <note>³ *Cited work*, pp. 340-344.</note> and also by the present writer. <note>⁴ Bulletin 53, pp. 210-213.</note> The Sioux songs of the moccasin game are especially rhythmic, but the drum is not steadily maintained in one rhythm, as it is among the Chippewa. Thus, we find several drum rhythms occurring in this group of songs. This is one of the instances which suggests a freer use of the drum among the Sioux than among the Chippewa.

<note>Cf. also *The Menomini Indians*, by Hoffman, W. J., *Fourteenth Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*, part 1, pp. 242-244, Washington, 1896; and Skinner, Alanson, *Social Life and Ceremonial Bundles of the Menomini Indians, cited work*, xiii, part 1, pp. 59-61, New York, 1913.</note>

## THE GAME OF HIDING A STICK

The game of hiding a stick is called by the same name as the moccasin-hiding game (*haŋ'pa ape'écuŋpi*). The tools used in the stick game are shown in figure 41. The rules of this game are provided based on the authority of Mr. Robert P. Higheagle, the writer's interpreter, who said:

> Ten people play on each side, and ten score sticks are used. One player from each side is chosen, and these two compete to see which side will hide the stick first. They sit on the ground opposite each other, and each has a small stick that he transfers rapidly from one hand to the other while his opponent watches and tries to determine which hand holds the stick. The player who conceals the stick most successfully

<image-desc>Three separate illustrations. The top two show short, cylindrical wooden sticks, intricately carved or painted with geometric patterns; the caption under them reads "(Actual size)". The third illustration below shows a bundle of plain, smooth sticks tied together with a thin cord or strip of leather; the caption under it reads "(Slightly reduced)". Below all three is the caption "FIG. 41. Implements used in the stick game."</image-desc>

->(Actual size)<-

->(Slightly reduced)<-

->FIG. 41. Implements used in the stick game.<-

> thereby wins two score sticks for his side, in addition to the privilege of his side being the first to hide the stick. The two lines of players sit on the ground, and the leader of each side selects two players. These players sit in front of the others, facing each other, and each holds a hiding stick. The side whose representative won the first contest is the side that first conceals the sticks, while the opposing players act as the guessers. If the location of one of the sticks is correctly guessed, the guessing side takes one score stick from the two acquired by their opponents in the first test. If the guessing side fails to locate the second hiding stick, the rules require that the score stick be returned to the hiding side. If the guessing side succeeds in locating the second hiding stick, they take the remaining score stick from the other side. The score sticks are taken from the opponent's pile as long as they have any, after which they are taken from the unallocated pile on the ground. The leader of either side may at any time withdraw a player who is not successful and substitute one from the remaining players. Each side's play continues until the opponents have guessed the location of both sticks, and the game continues until one side has won all the score sticks.
> 
> The following signals are used to indicate guesses: extending the index and middle fingers and pointing toward the right indicates a guess that both players have the

stick in their left hands. Similarly, pointing toward the left indicates a guess that both players have the stick in their right hands. Extending the right hand with the fingers spread means "the players have the sticks in the outside hands." The right arm descending with the hand cutting through the air like a knife means "the players have the sticks in the inside hands."

The author witnessed a game as described above at Bull Head, South Dakota, in 1912.

# MISCELLANEOUS SONGS

## CHILDREN’S SONGS

The little girls in the camp had their own plays, which could hardly be called games. In one of these childhood plays, the girls stood one behind another, each with her hands on the shoulders of the girl in front of her. Then they went around the village in a wavering line, singing the following song. The words of this song were not transcribed, but they mean "the deer follow each other."

Another play which provided much amusement was described by Yellow Hair, who said that the little girls sat in a circle. Each girl, putting one hand over the hand of the girl who sat next to her, lightly pinched the hand near the wrist. ## SONGS CONNECTED WITH LEGENDS

### LEGEND OF THE MAIDEN'S LEAP

The legend of the maiden who killed herself by leaping from a rock is said to be found among many tribes of Indians. The writer first recorded the story and a song at Sisseton, South Dakota, among the eastern Sioux. The song was said to have been sung by the maiden before she leaped from the rock, but the record, being unsatisfactory, was not transcribed. The incident was said to have taken place at Lake Pepin, which is formed by a widening of the Mississippi River on the eastern boundary of Minnesota. A promontory on the eastern shore of Lake Pepin is known as Maiden Rock, and tradition states that a Sioux maiden leaped from there and was killed on the rocks below.

A similar story was found by the writer at Standing Rock in North Dakota, among the Teton Sioux, who said they had been told that the rock was "somewhere in the west." Their version was as follows:

> A young woman had promised to marry a man, but he wished to "make a name for himself" before the marriage took place. He had been on the warpath, but he wished to go again so that he might distinguish himself by valor. When the war party returned, they said that he had been killed by the Crows. Sometime afterward, in the course of tribal wanderings, a camp was made at the place where, according to the report of the war party, the young man had been killed. Dressing herself in her best attire, the maiden went to the edge of a cliff, and after singing the following song and giving the shrill "woman's tremolo," jumped into the river below.

<summary>This page concludes the musical analysis of a Sioux lullaby and introduces the "Maiden's Leap" legend, a tragic story found in various forms among the Sioux and other tribes.</summary>

### LEGEND OF GHOST HILL

About 8 miles southeast of Fort Yates is a high butte known as Ghost Hill (Plate 81). The following legend (given by Śiya'ka) and song (recorded by Two Shields) are connected with this butte:

When Sitting Bull and his band were brought back from Canada, they camped one winter on the lowland beside the Missouri River, a few miles below Fort Yates. It was a large camp, including many Indians considered hostile, who were later located at Pine Ridge and at Cherry Creek on the Cheyenne River Reservation. Among these Indians was a particularly handsome young man who was very attractive to the young women. One day he disappeared. As no trace of him could be found, his parents consulted a man who possessed some sacred stones, giving him a horse and asking him to tell them about their son. This man said that during the following night, the voice of the missing man would be heard passing through the camp, and that everyone must follow the voice. On the designated night, the entire camp was on alert; just before dawn, they heard the voice of the young man approaching. Recognizing the voice, his parents and friends began to mourn, and the dogs barked as they would at the approach of a person. The voice passed through the camp, singing a love song, then turned and came back, retracing its way toward this hill. The people followed, but they could not go as fast as the voice, which gradually grew more distant until it was lost in the darkness.

<image-desc>A melodic plot diagram labeled "FIG. 42. Plot of song No. 218." The diagram consists of a line graph on a rectangular grid, showing the rise and fall of musical pitch over time. The graph contains several distinct descending phrases, typical of Plains Indian musical transcriptions of the era.</image-desc>

->FIG. 42. Plot of song No. 218.<-

This incident seemed to make the grief of the young man’s parents even more intense, and they went again to the owner of the stones, to whom they gave another horse, asking him to reveal who had killed their son. The man said he had been murdered by ten men who were jealous of him, and that one of these men would die in ten days, another in ten days after the first, and so on until all were dead. This happened just as he predicted. The parents of the missing man then went again to the owner of the sacred stones and begged to know where they could find the body of their son. The man said that their son had been chased a long distance by his enemies and finally had been killed far from home, and that his body had been devoured by wolves. He also told the parents to follow the voice (which was still heard at intervals singing the same song) and to keep following it until they reached the place where the voice disappeared, where they would see their son. The next time they heard the voice, they hurried toward the place where it originated and saw at some distance before them a figure wrapped in a gray Army blanket. They followed it but could never quite overtake it. Sometimes they would feel its presence behind them, and on looking back, they would see it, but it never quite reached them. It always followed the path toward Ghost Hill, and the parents believed it disappeared into the side of the hill. Consequently, they dug into the side of the hill and searched diligently, but the body of the young man was never found. A man named Walking Elk lived at the foot of Ghost Hill. He had a large family, and its members died one after another. He blamed their deaths on the ghost and shot at it with his rifle. The last appearance of the ghost was around the year 1889. It is said that a similar figure wrapped in a gray Army blanket was later seen at Pine Ridge and on the Rosebud Reservation.

<vocab>Ghost Hill, Sitting Bull, Fort Yates, Śiya'ka, Two Shields, Pine Ridge, Cherry Creek, Cheyenne River Reservation, Walking Elk, song No. 218, Rosebud Reservation</vocab>

### LEGEND OF GHOST HILL

About 8 miles southeast of Fort Yates is a high butte known as Ghost Hill (Plate 81). The following legend (given by Śiya'ka) and song (recorded by Two Shields) are connected with this butte:

When Sitting Bull and his band were brought back from Canada, they camped one winter on the lowlands beside the Missouri River, a few miles below Fort Yates. It was a large camp, including many Indians considered hostile, who were later located at Pine Ridge and at Cherry Creek on the Cheyenne River Reservation. Among these Indians was a particularly handsome young man who was very attractive to the young women. One day he disappeared. Since no trace of him could be found, his parents consulted a man who possessed some sacred stones, giving him a horse and asking him to tell them about their son. This man said that during the following night, the voice of the missing man would be heard passing through the camp, and that everyone must follow the voice. On the designated night, the entire camp was on alert; just before dawn, they heard the voice of the young man approaching. Recognizing the voice, his parents and friends began to mourn, and the dogs barked just as they would at the approach of a person. The voice passed through the camp, singing a love song, then turned and came back, retracing its path toward this hill. The people followed, but they could not move as fast as the voice, which gradually grew more distant until it was lost in the darkness.

The following group of 12 songs illustrates the Sioux custom of inserting a new name into a praise song that has been used for other people, and also of composing new words for songs. Three of

These songs belong to distinct classes of melodies: No. 225 is a song of the White Horse Riders, No. 226 is from the shuffling-feet dance, and No. 231 belongs to the Strong Heart society. Song No. 222 is said to have been composed recently. The others are praise songs that have been used by the tribe. In many instances, all the lyrics of the songs are new.

The person whose name appears in the songs is Two White Buffalo, whom Red Fox adopted in place of his deceased daughter and to whom he gave his daughter’s name. Red Fox stated that he had a right to give her this name because he had killed two white buffalo. Whenever these songs are sung, it is expected that Red Fox will make a gift—on behalf of Two White Buffalo—to the singers or to any project for which donations are being requested. Red Fox is a man who is highly respected within the tribe, and these songs have been widely performed.

*Analysis.*—This song was performed by four singers and was later recorded by Shoots First alone so that it could be more easily transcribed. The structure of the song is interesting. There are two rhythmic units that have the same division of the first beat; the first of these units appears nine times. There are also two similar phrases that begin on the unaccented beat instead of the accented one. The second unit occurs twice, with a slight difference in the second measure due to the structure of the words. The song has a range of nine tones and lacks the sixth and seventh tones of the complete octave. Of the melodic progressions, 60 percent are whole tones; the remaining intervals consist of 8 minor thirds, 7 fourths, and 1 ascending fifth.

*Analysis.*—This is a serenade song of the White Horse Riders, with the current words being substituted for words used previously. The man who recorded this song is a leader among the middle-aged singers of the tribe. The keynote appears to be G, and the tone material is therefore that of the fourth five-toned scale, but the second is sharped in every occurrence. The interval of an augmented second occurs three times and was sung with good intonation. This interval is also found in two other songs (see Nos. 63 and 106). The interval of a semitone appears seven times in this melody, and the minor third forms 47 percent of the total number of intervals. About two-thirds of the intervals are downward progressions.

*Analysis.*—This is a melody for the shuffling-feet dance. Two versions of the song were recorded: one sung by Haka'la as transcribed here, and another featuring the addition of women's voices an octave higher. The song contains only the tones E-flat, G, B-flat, and C. E-flat seems to be the most appropriate keynote, especially at the song's conclusion, though this tone is not prominent throughout the melody. Of the intervals, 68 percent are minor thirds, even though the song's tonality is major with E-flat as the keynote. The submediant chord (C—E-flat—G) forms the basis for a large part of the melody. The eighth-note triplets suggest song No. 192 (composed in honor of Red Fish) and, although they are repeated often, they have so little distinct character that they can hardly be considered a unique rhythmic unit of the song.

*Analysis.*—This is a praise-song melody. It is minor in tonality and lacks the seventh and second tones of the complete octave. Two accidentals occur—the sixth and third tones are raised by a semitone—both of which are clearly expressed in the two recorded renditions of the song. The intonation was good throughout the performances, and the semitone progression, which appears six times, was well-executed. The tonic chord is prominent in the formation of the melody, though the accented tones are such that the song is classified as melodic in structure.

## SIOUX SONGS RECORDED AT SISSETON, S. DAK.

All the songs in this group were recorded among the Santee Sioux at Sisseton, South Dakota, at the beginning of the author’s work among the Sioux. This location was chosen because Sioux from this area frequently visit the Chippewa, where the author’s previous work was conducted, and it was thought that this acquaintance would make the work easier. However, it was impossible to find a satisfactory interpreter at Sisseton, and most of the songs recorded there were translated from the phonograph records by Mr. Higheagle. Many of these songs were familiar to the Standing Rock Sioux and were identified by them when the recordings were played. In one instance, a Standing Rock singer provided words that were missing from the Sisseton version of a song. A few Sun Dance songs were recorded, but these were said to belong to the Santee ceremony and were therefore set aside. It is, however, interesting to observe Sioux material from more than one location, and the songs are therefore included in the series. Other Sisseton songs are Nos. 95, 96, 97, 189, and 190. The words of the songs recorded at Sisseton are in the Santee dialect. (See p. 2.)

On July 4, 1911, the author attended a gathering of Indians on the Sisseton Reservation. The number of dancers was small compared to those at Standing Rock, and the sharp contrast indicates how far the Sioux had progressed away from their old customs. A small group of dancers facing the setting sun is shown in plate 82. One of the mounted men was Good Thunder, the chief, who wore a gold-braided uniform and acted as “marshal of the day,” and the other was a mounted Indian policeman. The same plate also shows the prairie on this reservation, which is more rolling than the land at Standing Rock.

The three following songs are known at Standing Rock as songs of the <term>Ticketless society</term>. The term “society” is a misnomer here, as it was applied by the Sioux to those who were the first to be removed from the list of people receiving rations and, consequently, had no “ration tickets.” Such Indians were expected to be able to provide for themselves, and for that reason, they were expected to show unlimited generosity toward their friends. This name was used for only four or five years and

<summary>This page discusses the musical characteristics of modern Sioux songs and details the author's fieldwork among the Santee Sioux at Sisseton, South Dakota. It introduces the "Ticketless society," a group of Indians who no longer received government rations and were expected to show great generosity.</summary>

### No. 237. Song of the Ticketless Society (Catalogue No. 678)

->Sung by **Twin** (Čekpa')<-

Voice ♩ = 108
**Drum** not recorded

<image-desc>A musical score for the "Song of the Ticketless Society" consisting of four staves in bass clef. The melody includes various time signatures (2/4, 3/4, 2/4) and contains several notes marked with a plus sign (+) above them. It uses a mix of eighth, sixteenth, and quarter notes, ending with a double bar and repeat dots.</image-desc>

*Analysis*.—This song contains all the tones of the octave, which is an unusual feature in a song of minor tonality. It has a range of ten tones and is melodic in structure. Of the intervals, 63 percent are whole tones. The song is unique in that it contains only one note that is shorter than an eighth note in value.

Rev. John Eastman<note>Rev. Mr. Eastman's Sioux name is Mahpi'ya-wakan'-kidan' (Sacred Cloud Worshiper). See his biography in the *Handbook of American Indians*, part 1, pages 412–413.</note> of Sisseton, South Dakota, told the story of the following song, saying that the incident occurred when his father was 15 or 16 years old and was still remembered by many elders. The incident was as follows: A party of white men was driving cattle to one of the new settlements in the north. They lost their way and entered territory along the Red River where Sioux war parties were accustomed to traveling. They were seen by the Sioux, who, assuming they were Cree mixed-bloods, fired on them, killing one or more of the group. These Sioux were subject to the white man's law, and when they discovered they had killed a white man, they knew they were liable to be arrested for murder. Consequently, they "lost themselves" among various bands of Indians. The chiefs tried to locate them but could find only one man, whose name was Fierce Face (*Ite'-hiŋyan'za*). To demonstrate the good faith of the Sioux toward the white men, he traveled many miles without any kind of escort and voluntarily surrendered to the authorities. He went from camp to camp down the Minnesota River, with each camp encouraging him and praising him in the following song. His son, a boy of about 7 years, went with him to the edge of the

Indian territory. After following the Minnesota River to its confluence with the Mississippi, Fierce Face went down the Mississippi to Prairie du Chien, where he is said to have died in prison.

More than 70 years have passed since this took place, but through a song, the Indian who sacrificed himself for the honor of his tribe now receives the reward which an Indian most desires—that his name and deed shall be remembered.

oni' dota'p do . . . . . . . . . . . have borrowed you

*Analysis.*—This song is based on the second <term>five-toned scale</term> and contains a seventh raised by a <term>semitone</term>; this is an <term>accidental</term> which frequently appears in songs of <term>minor tonality</term>. The song begins with an <term>ascending octave</term> (see song No. 220) and begins and ends on the same tone (see song No. 82). Like many modern Sioux songs, it has a variety of <term>intervals</term>, with five kinds of ascending and five kinds of descending <term>progressions</term>. The last count of the <term>rhythmic unit</term> is not divided in the second instance as it is in the other occurrences; this measure was sung the same way in all four performances of the song. In one performance, the first note of the song was sung in the upper octave, avoiding the ascending octave.
See the plot of this melody on page 519.

->WORDS<-

| | |
|:---|:---|
| wića′hćana kiη | the old men |
| wana′ | now |

*Analysis.*—This song is characterized by a sixteenth note followed by a dotted eighth, but this combination is used in so many connections that the song can scarcely be said to have a <term>rhythmic unit</term>. The melody progresses chiefly by whole tones; about 77 percent of the <term>intervals</term> are <term>major seconds</term>. The song is melodic in structure and contains the tones of the second <term>five-toned scale</term>.

### PLOTS OF SONGS OF SADNESS

Only 13 of the 240 songs being studied show an ascending relationship between the first two accented tones. Upon examining these songs in relation to their titles, it was found that those beginning with a large ascending interval are songs associated with ideas—more or less evident—of sadness, disappointment, or suffering. This type of melodic plot, which appeared to be distinct from others and connected to the song's content, was therefore classified as Class E. The plots of songs No. 238 and 239 (fig. 43) are similar to each other; both are Sisseton songs, with the former linked to a tragic incident and the latter expressing discontent. Similar to these is the plot of song No. 99, which is about driving buffalo against a wind that cut their faces like a lance. (See p. 419.)

<image-desc>Four melodic plots, numbered 238, 239, 147, and 148, presented as line graphs on grid backgrounds. Each graph shows the melodic movement and intervals of a specific Teton Sioux song. They are arranged in two rows, with 238 and 239 on top, and 147 and 148 below.</image-desc>

->No. 238 &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; No. 239<-

->No. 147 &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; No. 148<-

->FIG. 43. Plots, Group 8.<-

Songs No. 147 and 148 are songs about slain warriors. The initial rise is not as large in these; the significant rise occurs later in the song. Song No. 149 begins with an ascending fifth and is similar in content to those previously mentioned. Song No. 191 is an exception, as it begins with an ascending sixth and shows no trace of the ideas mentioned. Other songs having an ascending relationship between the first and second accented tones are as follows: No. 207 (rise of a fifth), a moccasin-game song; No. 200 (rise of a third), a grass-dance song; No. 35 (rise of a whole tone), a Sun-dance song; No. 105, an Elk-society song; No. 206, a moccasin-game song; No. 212, a hiding-stick game song; and No. 219, the song of a ghost. This last one named is clearly a song of sadness; with one exception, the others have no words, and the origin of these songs is somewhat uncertain.

This final analysis group includes several small groups of songs. First are three incidental songs (Nos. 18, 24, 25) used during the Sun

Next are the songs of social dances—the grass, shuffling-feet, and night dances (Nos. 195–203); songs used in ordinary begging, which are distinct from requests for food accompanied by the singing of praise songs (Nos. 204, 205); and game songs (Nos. 206–213), together with songs used in children’s play (Nos. 215–217) and songs connected with legends (Nos. 218, 219). This group also includes songs in honor of the author that were sung to modern tunes; these are Nos. 220, 221, 222, 226, 227, 228, 229, and 230. There is a small group of modern love songs (Nos. 232–234). These are followed by a group of miscellaneous songs (Nos. 235–240) recorded at Sisseton, South Dakota, most of which were likely Santee rather than Teton Sioux in origin. Three songs recorded at Sisseton (Nos. 95–97) are analyzed with the Teton songs, as they are general in character and may have been used by both branches of the tribe.
